docs.title: About this book
docs.text: An English grammar and speaking book for Indian learners: the parts of speech, tenses and sentence building, pronunciation and everyday speaking, vocabulary, writing, and the mistakes learners really make. Every chapter ends with practice exercises with answers.

docs.title: Chapter 58: 50 most common mistakes
docs.text:
The 50 most common mistakes — in one place

This chapter is not for reading through; it is for looking things up. There are six groups — articles, tenses, prepositions, word choice, word order and plurals. Each mistake has three parts: wrong → right → why. When you are unsure while writing, come to this page, go to your group, and move on. Bookmark it on your phone.

In one line

Almost all of these 50 mistakes have the same cause — the Hindi pattern carried into English words. That is why the "why" part is the most important. Once you understand the cause, the whole group is fixed.

docs.title: 58.1 Where the most mistakes happen
docs.text:
The chart below shows which areas of Indian speakers' writing and speaking are corrected most often. If you are short of time, start with the top two groups — they will make the biggest difference.

Figure 58.1. Six groups, in order of how often mistakes occur. Articles and prepositions barely exist in Hindi — which is why they are the ones most often missed.

docs.title: 58.2 Group 1 — Articles (mistakes 1 to 7)
docs.text:
Hindi has nothing like a, an, the. So these words feel "useless" and get dropped. The firm rule: every singular countable noun needs something in front of it — a, an, the, my, this, one… anything, but never nothing.

1–7 · a / an / the

  • Wrong: 1. I am going to market.
  • Right: I'm going to the market.

  • Why: For a place both people know (the neighbourhood market), use "the". A singular countable noun cannot stand bare.

  • Wrong: 2. She is doctor.

  • Right: She's a doctor.

  • Why: When you state a job, a/an is always used: a teacher, an engineer, a driver.

  • Wrong: 3. He is a honest man.

  • Right: He's an honest man.

  • Why: a/an is decided by the sound, not the spelling. The H in "honest" is silent, so the sound starts with "o" — an. Likewise: an hour, but a university (the sound is "yoo").

  • Wrong: 4. I like the music.

  • Right: I like music.

  • Why: "The" is not used for general statements. "The music" means that particular music that is playing right now.

  • Wrong: 5. He went to the Mumbai.

  • Right: He went to Mumbai.

  • Why: No "the" before names of cities and countries. Exceptions: the US, the UK, the Netherlands, the Philippines.

  • Wrong: 6. I have an university degree.

  • Right: I have a university degree.

  • Why: "University" begins with the sound "yoo-" — that is a consonant sound, so "a".

  • Wrong: 7. Please pass me salt.

  • Right: Please pass me the salt.
  • Why: The salt on the table — a specific thing, so "the". Even uncountable nouns take "the" when the thing is specific.

docs.title: 58.3 Group 2 — Tenses (8 to 16)
docs.text:
The tense structures of Hindi and English are quite similar, but the present perfect (have/has + done) does not exist in Hindi. That is why it causes the most mistakes.

8–16 · tenses

  • Wrong: 8. I am working here since three years.
  • Right: I have been working here for three years.

  • Why: Two mistakes together: work that started earlier and is still going on = have been + -ing. And "for" goes with a duration, "since" with a point in time.

  • Wrong: 9. I didn't went to office.

  • Right: I didn't go to the office.

  • Why: "Did" already shows the past, so the verb stays in its base form. Did + go, never did + went.

  • Wrong: 10. He have finished the work.

  • Right: He has finished the work.

  • Why: "Has" with he, she, it. "Have" with I, we, you, they.

  • Wrong: 11. I am having a car.

  • Right: I have a car.

  • Why: "Have" meaning possession is not used in the continuous. But it works in the sense of eating or drinking: "I'm having lunch."

  • Wrong: 12. Yesterday I have gone to Delhi.

  • Right: Yesterday I went to Delhi.

  • Why: When a time in the past is stated (yesterday, last week, in 2019), use the simple past — never the present perfect.

  • Wrong: 13. I will tell you when he will come.

  • Right: I'll tell you when he comes.

  • Why: After "when", "if", "after", "before", the present tense is used even for the future. No two "will"s in one sentence.

  • Wrong: 14. She is knowing the answer.

  • Right: She knows the answer.

  • Why: Verbs of thinking and feeling do not go into the continuous: know, understand, believe, like, want, need, mean.

  • Wrong: 15. I have my breakfast at eight every day.

  • Right: I have breakfast at eight every day.

  • Why: No "my" with the meals of a daily habit: have breakfast, have lunch, have dinner.

  • Wrong: 16. By the time I reached, the train left.

  • Right: By the time I reached, the train had left.
  • Why: When two things happened in the past, the one that happened first takes "had". This is called the past perfect.

docs.title: 58.4 Group 3 — Prepositions (17 to 25)
docs.text:
One Hindi word becomes three English prepositions (me → in/on/at), and many English verbs take no preposition at all. Mistakes come from both causes.

17–25 · prepositions

  • Wrong: 17. Let's discuss about the plan.
  • Right: Let's discuss the plan.

  • Why: Discuss already contains the meaning of "about". Others in the same family: enter the room, reach Delhi, order two teas, request a copy, consider my application.

  • Wrong: 18. He is good in maths.

  • Right: He's good at maths.

  • Why: Skilled at something = good at. Good with = good at handling things (good with kids, good with numbers).

  • Wrong: 19. I am afraid from dogs.

  • Right: I'm afraid of dogs.

  • Why: Fear is always "of". Likewise: tired of, proud of, ashamed of, capable of.

  • Wrong: 20. She is married with an engineer.

  • Right: She's married to an engineer.

  • Why: Marriage is always "married to". "Married with" ends up meaning "married with children".

  • Wrong: 21. Please explain me the process.

  • Right: Please explain the process to me.

  • Why: After explain, describe, suggest and mention, the thing comes first, then "to" + the person.

  • Wrong: 22. I will reach at the station by six.

  • Right: I'll reach the station by six. / I'll arrive at the station by six.

  • Why: After reach, the place follows directly. Arrive takes a preposition: arrive at (a small place), arrive in (a city, a country).

  • Wrong: 23. He died from cancer.

  • Right: He died of cancer.

  • Why: Death from an illness = died of. From an accident or injury = died from injuries.

  • Wrong: 24. I have been waiting since two hours.

  • Right: I've been waiting for two hours.

  • Why: For = how long (duration). Since = from when (a point). "Since 4 o'clock" is right, "since two hours" is wrong.

  • Wrong: 25. He is angry on me.

  • Right: He's angry with me.
  • Why: Angry at a person = angry with. At a thing or situation = angry about the delay.

docs.title: 58.5 Group 4 — Word choice (26 to 35)
docs.text:
Here the mistake is not grammar but choosing the word. Often two words seem alike but do different jobs.

26–35 · choosing the word

  • Wrong: 26. I will give the exam next month.
  • Right: I'll take the exam next month.

  • Why: A student takes an exam; a teacher gives/sets one. The Hindi "dena" lands exactly backwards.

  • Wrong: 27. There is too much traffic — it's very bad.

  • Right: There's a lot of traffic.

  • Why: "Too much" means "more than is needed", not just "a lot". For "a lot", use "a lot of" or "a great deal of".

  • Wrong: 28. How much peoples came?

  • Right: How many people came?

  • Why: Two mistakes: if you can count it, use "many" (not much), and "people" is already plural.

  • Wrong: 29. I am boring in this class.

  • Right: I'm bored in this class.

  • Why: -ing = what the thing is like (the class is boring). -ed = how you feel (I am bored). Likewise: interesting/interested, confusing/confused, tiring/tired.

  • Wrong: 30. Myself Ravi.

  • Right: I'm Ravi.

  • Why: "Myself" is a reflexive pronoun (I hurt myself) — it cannot be a subject.

  • Wrong: 31. Please revert back at the earliest.

  • Right: Please get back to me by Thursday.

  • Why: Revert already contains "back", so "back" is redundant. And write a real date instead of "at the earliest".

  • Wrong: 32. He has less friends than me.

  • Right: He has fewer friends than me.

  • Why: If you can count it, use "fewer" (fewer friends, fewer errors). If you can't, use "less" (less water, less time).

  • Wrong: 33. Its raining outside.

  • Right: It's raining outside.

  • Why: It's = it is. Its = belonging to it (The dog wagged its tail). Here the apostrophe shows a shortcut, not possession.

  • Wrong: 34. I can able to finish it today.

  • Right: I can finish it today. / I'm able to finish it today.

  • Why: Both do the same job — choose one. "Can able to" joins the two, which is wrong.

  • Wrong: 35. Open the light.

  • Right: Turn on the light. / Switch on the light.
  • Why: The Hindi "kholna" does two jobs in English. A door is opened; a light, fan or TV is turned on/off.

docs.title: 58.6 Group 5 — Word order (36 to 42)
docs.text:
The Hindi order is Subject – Object – Verb (main khaana khaata hoon). The English order is Subject – Verb – Object (I eat food). The difference shows most in questions and adjectives.

36–42 · word order

  • Wrong: 36. What you are doing?
  • Right: What are you doing?

  • Why: In a question the helping verb comes before the subject: What are you… / Where did he… / Why has she…

  • Wrong: 37. Tell me where is the station.

  • Right: Tell me where the station is.

  • Why: When a question sits inside a larger sentence, the order becomes straight — the verb moves to the back.

  • Wrong: 38. I yesterday went to the bank.

  • Right: I went to the bank yesterday.

  • Why: The time word goes at the end (or the beginning) — not between the subject and the verb.

  • Wrong: 39. She speaks very well English.

  • Right: She speaks English very well.

  • Why: First the object (English), then the adverb (very well). Nothing comes between a verb and its object.

  • Wrong: 40. He gave to me the keys.

  • Right: He gave me the keys. / He gave the keys to me.

  • Why: Only two orders are correct: verb + person + thing, or verb + thing + to + person. The one in the middle is wrong.

  • Wrong: 41. A red big plastic box.

  • Right: A big red plastic box.

  • Why: The order of adjectives is fixed: opinion → size → age → colour → origin → material. "Big" (size) comes before "red" (colour).

  • Wrong: 42. Only I have one question.

  • Right: I have only one question.
  • Why: "Only" goes right before the word you want to stress. Change its place, and the meaning changes.

docs.title: 58.7 Group 6 — Plurals and countables (43 to 50)
docs.text:
Some things cannot be counted in English, while in Hindi the same things are counted without trouble. That is the root of these eight mistakes.

43–50 · plurals and counting

  • Wrong: 43. I need some informations.
  • Right: I need some information. / I need a few details.

  • Why: Information is uncountable — it never takes "s". To count it: two pieces of information.

  • Wrong: 44. He gave me good advices.

  • Right: He gave me good advice. / He gave me a piece of advice.

  • Why: Advice is uncountable. In the same list: furniture, luggage, equipment, machinery, traffic, homework, research, feedback, knowledge.

  • Wrong: 45. My hairs are wet.

  • Right: My hair is wet.

  • Why: All the hair on your head together is "hair" (uncountable). "Hairs" means single strands — the kind you find in food!

  • Wrong: 46. There are many equipments in the lab.

  • Right: There's a lot of equipment in the lab.

  • Why: Equipment is uncountable, so "many" has to change to "a lot of" and the verb becomes singular.

  • Wrong: 47. Peoples are waiting outside.

  • Right: People are waiting outside.

  • Why: "People" is already plural (the plural of person). "Peoples" means "several nations" — a completely different thing.

  • Wrong: 48. I bought two pant and three shirt.

  • Right: I bought two pairs of trousers and three shirts.

  • Why: Shirt is countable, so "shirts". Trousers/pants are always plural, and they are counted in "pairs" — like scissors and glasses.

  • Wrong: 49. Each of the students have a laptop.

  • Right: Each of the students has a laptop.

  • Why: Each, every, everyone, nobody — all are singular, even if a plural follows. Likewise: "Everyone is here."

  • Wrong: 50. The news are not good.

  • Right: The news is not good.
  • Why: "News" ends in "s" but is singular. Likewise: mathematics, physics, economics, politics — all take a singular verb.

docs.title: 58.8 Three rules that save 30 of the 50
docs.text:
Three things worth memorising

1. Every singular countable noun needs something in front of it — a, an, the, my, this. Never bare. 2. Show the tense only once in a sentence — did + go, will + come, has + finished. Don't put the past in two places. 3. In English the verb grabs its object directly — no time word, adverb or "to me" squeezes in between.

docs.title: 58.9 Fixed pairs — better learned by heart
docs.text:
Some adjectives and verbs have a fixed preposition. There is no point hunting for logic in these — they are pairs, so learn them as pairs. This table alone prevents half the mistakes of Groups 3 and 4.

Pair Example What people wrongly say good at good at cricket good in afraid of afraid of heights afraid from married to married to a teacher married with angry with (a person) angry with me angry on me angry about (a thing) angry about the delay angry for the delay die of (an illness) died of a heart attack died from a heart attack depend on it depends on you depends from you listen to listen to me listen me explain to explain it to me explain me agree with (a person) I agree with you I am agree with you interested in interested in design interested for design responsible for responsible for payroll responsible of payroll congratulate on congratulate her on the win congratulate her for the win apologise for apologise for the delay apologise of the delay no preposition discuss · enter · reach · order · request · consider · marry discuss about, enter into, reach at…

docs.title: 58.10 Six correct sentences — say them aloud
docs.text:
One corrected sentence from each group. Listening and speaking them settles the rules faster than memorising — because the ear learns to catch the mistake.

  • She's a doctor at the hospital near the market. Articles — "a" with a job, "the" with a familiar place.
  • I've been working here for three years. Tenses — the work started earlier and is still going on; "for" with a duration.
  • He's good at maths but he's afraid of exams. Prepositions — good at, afraid of. These pairs are fixed.
  • I'll take the exam next month, so please get back to me by Friday. Word choice — you "take" an exam, and "get back to me" replaces "revert back".
  • Could you tell me where the station is? Word order — the question sits inside a larger sentence, so the verb moves to the back.
  • The news is good, and each of the teams has its own budget. Plurals — "news" and "each" both take a singular verb.

How to use this page

Read it all the way through once — only once. After that, open it only when you need it. When you catch the same mistake three times, it fixes itself. Trying to memorise the whole list gets you nowhere.

docs.title: 58.11 Practice — 50 mistakes
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Which sentence is correct?

  • He is an honest man with a university degree.
  • He is a honest man with an university degree.
  • He is an honest man with an university degree.
  • He is a honest man with a university degree.

Hint: a/an is decided by the sound, not the spelling.

Answer

He is an honest man with a university degree.

The H in honest is silent and the sound begins with 'o' — an. University begins with the sound 'yoo', which is like a consonant — a.

Exercise 2

In Hindi: 'Main teen saal se yahan kaam kar raha hoon' (I started working here three years ago and still do). What is the correct English?

  • I have been working here for three years.
  • I am working here since three years.
  • I work here since three years.
  • I am working here for three years only.
Answer

I have been working here for three years.

Work that started earlier and is still going on = have been + -ing. And 'for' goes with a duration, 'since' with a point in time.

Exercise 3

Which sentence is wrong?

  • She is married with an engineer.
  • She is married to an engineer.
  • He is afraid of dogs.
  • He is angry with me.
Answer

She is married with an engineer.

Marriage is always 'married to'. 'Married with' ends up meaning married with children.

Exercise 4

Which verb goes with exam for a student?

  • take the exam
  • give the exam
  • do the exam paper only
  • put the exam
Answer

take the exam

A student takes an exam; a teacher gives or sets one. The Hindi 'dena' lands exactly backwards.

Exercise 5

Which is the correct order of adjectives?

  • a big red plastic box
  • a red big plastic box
  • a plastic big red box
  • a red plastic big box

Hint: Size first, colour later.

Answer

a big red plastic box

The order is fixed: opinion → size → age → colour → origin → material. So big (size) comes before red (colour).

Exercise 6

I have been waiting ___ two hours.

Hint: Is it a duration or a point?

Answer

for

For = how long. Since = from when. 'Since 4 o'clock' is right, 'since two hours' is wrong.

Exercise 7

He has ___ friends than me, but they are good ones.

Hint: Friends can be counted.

Answer

fewer

If you can count it, use fewer (fewer friends, fewer errors). If you can't, use less (less water, less time).

Exercise 8

Each of the students ___ a laptop.

Hint: Is each singular or plural?

Answer

has

Each, every, everyone, nobody — all are singular, even if a plural follows.

Exercise 9

Please ___ on the light, it's getting dark.

Hint: A light is not 'opened'.

Answer

turn / switch

The Hindi 'kholna' does two jobs. A door is opened; a light, fan or TV is turned on/off.

Exercise 10

Find the wrong word.

I didn't went to the office yesterday.

Answer

Wrong word: went.

Corrected: I didn't go to the office yesterday.

'Did' already shows the past, so the verb stays in its base form — did + go.

Exercise 11

One word has a needless 's' — tap it.

He gave me some very useful advices.

Answer

Wrong word: advices.

Corrected: He gave me some very useful advice.

Advice is uncountable. In the same list: information, furniture, luggage, equipment, feedback, homework.

Exercise 12

The order is wrong — tap the word in the wrong place.

Tell me where is the station please.

Answer

Wrong word: is.

Corrected: Tell me where the station is, please.

When a question sits inside a larger sentence, the order becomes straight — the verb moves to the back.

Exercise 13

One word is wrong — find it.

My hairs are wet because of the rain.

Answer

Wrong word: hairs.

Corrected: My hair is wet because of the rain.

All the hair on your head together is 'hair' (uncountable), so the verb becomes 'is' too.

Exercise 14

Match each wrong form to its correct form.

A B discuss about the plan good at maths explain me this afraid of dogs good in maths discuss the plan afraid from dogs explain this to me Answer

discuss about the plan — discuss the plan; explain me this — explain this to me; good in maths — good at maths; afraid from dogs — afraid of dogs

Some verbs take no preposition, and some adjectives have their own fixed pair.

Exercise 15

Match each word to its type.

A B information has 's' but is singular people always plural, counted in pairs news uncountable — no 's' trousers already plural Answer

information — uncountable — no 's'; people — already plural; news — has 's' but is singular; trousers — always plural, counted in pairs

Remember the counting rules and almost all the mistakes of Group 6 disappear by themselves.

Exercise 16

Put the words in the right order.

Words: very / She / English / speaks / well

Answer

She speaks English very well

First the object (English), then the adverb (very well). Nothing comes between the verb and its object.

Exercise 17

Build the question in the right order.

Words: What / this / are / evening / you / doing

Answer

What are you doing this evening

In a question the helping verb (are) comes before the subject (you).

Exercise 18

Say this line — it has fixes from three groups together.

Answer

Say: I have been working here for three years and I am good at my job

Tense (have been working), prepositions (for, good at), and word order — all three are correct in a single line.

docs.title: Chapter 21: Active & passive voice
docs.text:
Active and Passive — who comes first

In grammar, "voice" has nothing to do with sound. Voice means — whose story the sentence tells. In the active voice the doer comes first ("Ravi ne kaam kiya"), and in the passive voice the one who receives the action comes first ("kaam kiya gaya"). We do this in Hindi every day, so the idea is not new — you just need to learn the English formula, and to know when to use the passive and when not to use it at all.

In one line

Passive voice = correct form of "be" + V3 (past participle). That's the whole formula. When the tense changes, only the "be" changes — V3 never changes.

docs.title: 21.1 The swapping diagram
docs.text:
Turning active into passive involves just three things: the subject and object swap places, the verb becomes "be + V3", and the old subject moves behind "by". See the picture —

Figure 21.1. Blue = the doer (agent). Purple = the one who receives the action (object). In the passive the purple one comes first and the blue one moves behind by .

Five steps — active to passive

1. Bring the object to the front (and if it is a pronoun, change it to a subject form: me → I, him → he). 2. Choose the right "be" for the tense. 3. Change the main verb to V3. 4. Put the old subject at the end with "by". 5. If the doer is not important, drop the "by…" part.

docs.title: 21.2 The passive in every tense
docs.text:
Notice that in the right-hand column V3 (eaten) never changes. Only the form of "be" changes. The whole table rests on this one idea.

Tense Active Passive (be + V3) Present Simple She eats the mango. The mango is eaten by her. Present Continuous She is eating the mango. The mango is being eaten by her. Present Perfect She has eaten the mango. The mango has been eaten by her. Past Simple She ate the mango. The mango was eaten by her. Past Continuous She was eating the mango. The mango was being eaten by her. Past Perfect She had eaten the mango. The mango had been eaten by her. Future Simple She will eat the mango. The mango will be eaten by her. Future Perfect She will have eaten it. It will have been eaten by her. Modal She can eat it. It can be eaten by her. Infinitive She wants to eat it. It wants to be eaten.

Two kinds of tenses have no passive

The passive of the Future Continuous and the Perfect Continuous tenses (all three) is not used in practical English. A sentence like "The work will be being done" is possible in grammar, but nobody says it. In such cases, just keep the active.

docs.title: 21.3 The passive of questions and orders
docs.text: Type Active Passive Yes/no question Did he write the letter? Was the letter written by him? WH question Who wrote this? By whom was this written? Order (positive) Close the door. Let the door be closed. Order (negative) Don't touch the wires. Let the wires not be touched. Advice / rule You should submit the form. The form should be submitted.

docs.title: 21.4 Verbs with two objects — two passives are possible
docs.text:
give, send, teach, offer, tell, show, pay, lend — these verbs have two objects (to whom + what). So two kinds of passive can be made, and both are correct.

  • Active: The company gave Ravi a laptop.
  • Passive 1: Ravi was given a laptop. The person comes first — this is more natural in speech.
  • Passive 2: A laptop was given to Ravi. The thing comes first — the focus is on the laptop.

docs.title: 21.5 When to use the passive — four real situations
docs.text:
Reason Example Why the passive is better The doer is unknown My bike was stolen last night. You don't know who took it — so there is no need for "by…". The doer is not important The road is being repaired. It doesn't matter who is repairing it. The work is what counts. Processes / science Water is heated to 100 °C and then cooled. In science and recipes the steps matter, not the people. Being polite or neutral A mistake has been made in the bill. It doesn't blame anyone — very useful in offices and emails. Rules and notices Smoking is not allowed here. The rule applies to everyone — it is not about one particular person.

The magic of the passive in offices and emails

"You did not send the report." → sounds like an accusation. "The report has not been received yet." → the same point, without a quarrel. That is why the passive is an important part of professional English.

docs.title: 21.6 When not to use the passive
docs.text:
There is a big misunderstanding here. At school we think of the passive as "good English", and then we stuff it in everywhere. The truth is the opposite: over 85% of everyday sentences are active. The passive appears when there is a reason for it.

Where the passive sounds heavy and bad

  • Wrong: The decision to go to Shimla was taken by us.
  • Right: We decided to go to Shimla.

  • Why: The doer is clear and important — so put it first. The active is short, clear and strong.

  • Wrong: Tea is being drunk by me.

  • Right: I am drinking tea.

  • Why: In everyday talk, a passive like this sounds artificial. No native speaker would say it.

  • Wrong: The bus was arrived at six.

  • Right: The bus arrived at six.

  • Why: Intransitive verbs (verbs with no object — arrive, come, go, sleep, die, happen, laugh) have no passive.

  • Wrong: He was died in 2019.

  • Right: He died in 2019.
  • Why: "Die" is intransitive. But "born" is the opposite — it always appears in the passive: I was born in Patna.

The deciding question

Before you make a passive, ask yourself one question: "Whose story is it?" If it is the doer's — active. If it is the receiver's, or the doer is unknown or unimportant — passive. Never use the passive just "to sound formal".

docs.title: Leaving out "by" is perfectly fine
docs.text:
In about 80% of passive sentences the "by…" part is never written, because the doer is not important. Exams ask for "by"; real English doesn't.

  • English is spoken all over the world. No need to write "by people" — everyone understands.

docs.title: The "get" passive — very common in speech
docs.text: be passive get passive Feel My phone was repaired. My phone got repaired. more conversational He was selected. He got selected. it happened suddenly, a happy event The glass was broken. The glass got broken. it happened by accident

docs.title: 21.8 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
Top passive mistakes

  • Wrong: The letter is wrote by him.
  • Right: The letter is written by him.

  • Why: The passive always takes V3, not V2. write–wrote–written.

  • Wrong: The work is completed yesterday.

  • Right: The work was completed yesterday.

  • Why: The tense shows in "be". For the past you need "was/were".

  • Wrong: The matter is being discussed about.

  • Right: The matter is being discussed.

  • Why: "Discuss" doesn't take "about" — neither in the active nor in the passive.

  • Wrong: The thief was caught by the police yesterday by them.

  • Right: The thief was caught by the police yesterday.

  • Why: "By" only once. You have named the doer once; that is enough.

  • Wrong: This book is belonged to me.

  • Right: This book belongs to me.

  • Why: Some verbs have no passive — belong, resemble, lack, consist, have (to own), suit, fit.

  • Wrong: I born in Lucknow.

  • Right: I was born in Lucknow.
  • Why: "Born" always appears in the passive — was/were born. This one you just have to remember.

docs.title: 21.9 Practice — Active and Passive
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Make it passive: 'Shakespeare wrote this play.'

  • This play is written by Shakespeare.
  • This play was wrote by Shakespeare.
  • This play was written by Shakespeare.
  • This play has written by Shakespeare.

Hint: Which 'be' does the Past Simple passive use?

Answer

This play was written by Shakespeare.

The Past Simple passive = was/were + V3. So 'was written' — never 'was wrote', because the passive takes V3.

Exercise 2

Make it passive: 'They are repairing the road.'

  • The road is repaired.
  • The road is being repaired.
  • The road was being repaired.
  • The road has been repaired.

Hint: The continuous passive uses 'being'.

Answer

The road is being repaired.

The Present Continuous passive = am/is/are + being + V3. 'Being' is the sign of the continuous.

Exercise 3

Which of these sentences CANNOT be made passive?

  • She sang a song.
  • The baby slept quietly.
  • He painted the wall.
  • They built a bridge.

Hint: Which one has no object?

Answer

The baby slept quietly.

'Sleep' is an intransitive verb — it has no object. A verb with no object has no passive.

Exercise 4

When is the passive best?

  • When the doer is unknown
  • When you want a shorter sentence
  • When you want to sound formal
  • When the verb is difficult

Hint: Think about the doer.

Answer

When the doer is unknown

The real job of the passive is for when the doer is unknown, unimportant, or you don't want to name them. Using the passive just to 'sound formal' is a mistake.

Exercise 5

The thieves ___ arrested by the police last night.

Hint: A plural subject, and it happened in the past.

Answer

were

The subject 'thieves' is plural and it is past — so 'were arrested'. A singular subject would take 'was arrested'.

Exercise 6

Rice ___ grown in many parts of India.

Hint: A general fact — which tense?

Answer

is

A general fact uses the Present Simple, and 'rice' is an uncountable singular — so 'is grown'.

Exercise 7

I ___ born in Jaipur.

Hint: This always appears in the passive.

Answer

was

'Born' always takes was/were. 'I born' and 'I am born' are both wrong.

Exercise 8

There is one mistake in this sentence — tap the wrong word.

The homework was did by all the students.

Answer

Wrong word: did.

Corrected: The homework was done by all the students.

The passive takes V3. do–did–done, so 'was done'. Never 'was did'.

Exercise 9

Find the wrong word.

My grandfather was died two years ago.

Answer

Wrong word: was.

Corrected: My grandfather died two years ago.

'Die' is intransitive and has no passive. Just say 'died'.

Exercise 10

One word is wrong — catch it.

This land is belonged to my uncle.

Answer

Wrong word: belonged.

Corrected: This land belongs to my uncle.

'Belong' has no passive. Verbs like belong, resemble, consist, lack always stay in the active.

Exercise 11

Put the words in order to make a passive sentence.

Words: bridge / new / The / next / will / opened / month / be

Answer

The new bridge will be opened next month

The future passive = will + be + V3. 'Will be opened' — the form of 'be' never changes here; 'be' comes straight after 'will'.

Exercise 12

Match each active form with its correct passive.

A B She writes letters Letters have been written by her She wrote letters Letters are being written by her She has written letters Letters will be written by her She is writing letters Letters are written by her She will write letters Letters were written by her Answer

She writes letters — Letters are written by her; She wrote letters — Letters were written by her; She has written letters — Letters have been written by her; She is writing letters — Letters are being written by her; She will write letters — Letters will be written by her

See — the V3 'written' is the same every time. Only the form of 'be' changes: are / were / have been / are being / will be.

Exercise 13

Now say this line aloud — a polite passive that is useful in offices.

Answer

Say: The report has not been received yet

In the active this would be 'You did not send the report', which sounds like an accusation. The passive makes the point without a quarrel — which is why this form is so useful in emails.

What to do next

Try this: open one of your old emails or assignments and turn every passive sentence into an active one. Where the active reads more clearly, the passive was not needed. After doing this two or three times, the right use of the passive becomes clear by itself.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Adjectives
docs.text:
Adjective — what kind, how much, which one

An adjective is a word that tells you something about a noun — what kind, how much, which one, whose. Changing just the adjectives can change the whole sentence: a house and a beautiful old wooden house are worlds apart. The most valuable part of this chapter comes at the end — the order of adjectives, the rule that native speakers can't name but never break.

In one line

An adjective describes or limits a noun or pronoun. A word that tells you about a noun — what kind, how much, which one — is an adjective.

  • She has a sharp memory. "sharp" tells us what kind of memory it is.
  • Three boys were waiting outside. "three" tells us how many — numbers are adjectives too.
  • The tea is cold. An adjective can also come after the noun, through a linking verb.

docs.title: 9.1 Where an adjective sits — two places
docs.text:
Position Name Example Before the noun Attributive a heavy bag · an honest man After a linking verb Predicative The bag is heavy. · He seems honest.

Some adjectives only work in one place

asleep, alive, awake, afraid, alone, ill — these only come after a verb. ✓ The baby is asleep. ✗ an asleep baby (say "a sleeping baby" instead). On the other hand, main, mere, elder, former only come before a noun — the main road, but "The road is main" is wrong.

docs.title: 9.2 Types of adjective
docs.text: Type What it tells you Examples Quality what kind a clever boy, tall building, red cloth Quantity how much (not counted) some water, much noise, enough time Number how many (counted) five books, second chance, many people Demonstrative which one — pointing this pen, those chairs Possessive whose my bag, their house Interrogative asking a question Which shirt? Whose turn? Distributive one by one each student, every day, neither option Proper made from a proper noun Mughal architecture, Bengali sweets Emphasizing adds emphasis with my own eyes, the very thing Article specific or general a boy, an apple, the boy

docs.title: Emphasizing adjectives — "own" and "very"
docs.text:
These adjectives give no new information about the noun — they just put stress on it. Think of the Hindi "apni hi", "khud ki", "wahi" — the sense of "my very own" or "exactly that one".

  • I saw it with my own eyes. = I saw it myself, with my own eyes — nobody told me.
  • This is the very thing I was looking for. = This is exactly the thing I was looking for.
  • She runs her own business. = The business is hers — it belongs to nobody else.

Is 'very' an adjective or an adverb?

the very man — before a noun, after "the" → adjective (that exact man). very tall — before an adjective → adverb (extremely tall). "own" always comes after a possessive: my own, his own, their own — never "a own house".

docs.title: Quick guide — which type answers which question
docs.text:
Type Job / question Example Quality What kind? a kind man Quantity How much? some milk Number How many? / Which order? three pens, the first boy Demonstrative Which one? (pointing) that house Possessive Whose? our teacher Interrogative Used in questions Which bus? Distributive One at a time every child Proper From a proper noun Indian tea Emphasizing Gives emphasis my own eyes

many / much and few / little — these get mixed up

Countable Uncountable A lot many books much water Not much (negative feel) few friends little money Some (positive feel) a few friends a little money

"few friends" = hardly any friends (sad). "a few friends" = some friends (that's fine). One little "a" flips the whole feeling.

docs.title: 9.3 Degrees of comparison — three steps
docs.text:
When you compare two or more things, the adjective changes its form. There are three steps: positive → comparative → superlative.

How it is formed Positive Comparative Superlative Short words: + er / est tall taller tallest Ends in -e: + r / st large larger largest consonant + y: y → ier / iest happy happier happiest one vowel + one consonant: double the letter big bigger biggest Long words: more / most beautiful more beautiful most beautiful Completely different (irregular) good better best

docs.title: Irregular comparisons — ones to memorise
docs.text:
Positive Comparative Superlative Note good better best — bad worse worst — little less least for uncountable nouns many / much more most — far farther / further farthest / furthest farther = distance, further = more late later / latter latest / last latest = newest, last = final old older / elder oldest / eldest elder is only for family

What goes with the comparative and the superlative

Comparative goes with than — She is taller than her brother. Superlative goes with the — She is the tallest in the class. Use the comparative when comparing two things, the superlative for three or more.

Double comparative — the most common mistake

  • Wrong: He is more taller than me.
  • Right: He is taller than I am.

  • Why: The -er in "taller" already makes it a comparative — adding "more" in front says it twice. An adjective gets only one comparison marker: either -er or more. In Hindi we say "zyada lamba" (more tall), which is why "more" sneaks in.

  • Wrong: She is the most cleverest girl.

  • Right: She is the cleverest girl.
  • Why: The same mistake with the superlative — "most" is extra in front of "cleverest".

These adjectives can't be compared

perfect, unique, complete, dead, round, square, impossible, full, empty — these are absolute. "More perfect" or "very unique" is technically wrong, because nothing goes beyond perfect.

docs.title: 9.4 The order of adjectives — the most valuable part of this chapter
docs.text:
When two or three adjectives come before one noun, they follow a fixed order. We often break this order, and then the sentence sounds "odd" even though the grammar is correct. Native speakers don't remember the rule — they remember how it sounds. We'll start with the rule, and the ear will come later.

Figure 9.1. The adjective train: the engine (noun) is at the front, and the cars are coupled behind it in this order. # Category Question Examples 1 Opinion what do I think of it? lovely, ugly, boring, delicious 2 Size how big? big, small, tall, long 3 Age how old? old, new, young, ancient 4 Shape what shape? round, square, flat 5 Colour what colour? red, black, golden 6 Origin where is it from? Indian, Chinese, Punjabi 7 Material what is it made of? wooden, silk, steel, plastic 8 Purpose what is it for? writing (desk), sleeping (bag)

Mistakes caused by breaking the order

  • Wrong: a red big balloon
  • Right: a big red balloon

  • Why: Size (2) comes before colour (5). Remember the car numbers.

  • Wrong: a cotton white shirt

  • Right: a white cotton shirt

  • Why: Material (7) sits closest to the noun, and colour (5) comes before it.

  • Wrong: an old beautiful temple

  • Right: a beautiful old temple

  • Why: Opinion (1) sits farthest from the noun, and age (3) comes after it.

  • Wrong: a steel small Japanese watch

  • Right: a small Japanese steel watch
  • Why: All three were in the wrong order. The right order: size (2) → origin (6) → material (7). Close your eyes and ask yourself which car number each one is.

Don't use more than three

The rule covers eight categories, but in real English you will rarely see more than two or three adjectives together. Too many make a sentence heavy. If you need four, use a comma or "and", or split the sentence in two.

docs.title: 9.5 From adjective to adverb — when to add -ly
docs.text:
An adjective goes with a noun; an adverb goes with a verb. For most adjectives, adding -ly makes the adverb.

Adjective Adverb With a noun With a verb careful carefully a careful driver drives carefully quick quickly a quick answer answered quickly happy happily a happy child played happily good well good English speaks well fast fast a fast car runs fast hard hard hard work works hard

good and well

✓ Her English is good. (about a noun) ✓ She speaks English well. (about a verb) ✗ She speaks English good. "good" is the adjective, "well" is the adverb — always remember this pair.

docs.title: 9.6 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
Common Indian-English mistakes with adjectives

  • Wrong: My brother is more taller than me.
  • Right: My brother is taller than I am.

  • Why: One comparison per adjective — either -er or more. In Hindi we say "zyada lamba" (more tall), so both end up in the English sentence.

  • Wrong: She is senior than me.

  • Right: She is senior to me.

  • Why: A few adjectives — senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior, preferable — take to instead of "than", because they come from Latin.

  • Wrong: This is the most best option.

  • Right: This is the best option.

  • Why: "Best" is already a superlative — nothing goes beyond it. In the same way, "most worst" and "more better" are wrong.

  • Wrong: She speaks very good English… and she speaks English good.

  • Right: She speaks very good English… and she speaks English well.

  • Why: The first one is fine (good + the noun English). The second has a verb, so it needs an adverb — well.

  • Wrong: He bought a new nice phone.

  • Right: He bought a nice new phone.

  • Why: Opinion (nice) comes before age (new). The reversed version isn't ungrammatical, but it jars on a native speaker's ear straight away.

  • Wrong: I have less friends in this city.

  • Right: I have fewer friends in this city.

  • Why: Use "fewer" with nouns you can count and "less" with uncountable nouns — less water, fewer bottles.

  • Wrong: My all books are new.

  • Right: All my books are new.

  • Why: "All, both, half" come before the possessive — all my, both your, half his. The Hindi "mere saare" comes out in the wrong order if translated word for word.

  • Wrong: She is my elder than me.

  • Right: She is older than me. / She is my elder sister.
  • Why: "Elder" is used only before a noun, and only in the family — elder brother, elder sister. To compare, say "older than".

docs.title: 9.7 A short summary
docs.text:
Remember four things

1. An adjective describes a noun; an adverb describes a verb. 2. Only one comparison per adjective — either -er or more. 3. than goes with the comparative, the goes with the superlative. 4. With several adjectives, the order is: opinion farthest, material closest.

docs.title: 9.8 Practice — Adjectives
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Which order is correct?

  • a beautiful big old house
  • a big beautiful old house
  • an old big beautiful house
  • a big old beautiful house

Hint: Where does opinion go, and where does size go?

Answer

a beautiful big old house

The order is opinion (beautiful) → size (big) → age (old). Opinion sits farthest from the noun because it is the most personal judgement; the others are facts.

Exercise 2

She is ___ than her sister.

  • taller
  • more taller
  • tallest
  • more tall

Hint: How many comparisons can one adjective take?

Answer

taller

The -er in 'taller' already makes the comparison, so adding 'more' says it twice. Short adjectives take -er, not more.

Exercise 3

He is ___ to me in the office.

  • senior
  • more senior than
  • seniorer
  • most senior

Hint: Some adjectives don't take 'than'.

Answer

senior

Senior, junior, superior, inferior come from Latin and take 'to', not 'than'. So 'senior to me' is correct.

Exercise 4

I have ___ books than you.

  • fewer
  • less
  • lesser
  • little

Hint: Books can be counted.

Answer

fewer

Use 'fewer' with countable nouns and 'less' with uncountable ones — fewer books, less water. Books can be counted, so fewer.

Exercise 5

She sings very ___. (adverb form of 'good')

Hint: You are describing the verb, not a noun.

Answer

well

'sings' is a verb, and a word that describes a verb is an adverb. The adverb of 'good' is 'well' — so 'sings well'.

Exercise 6

This is the ___ day of my life. (superlative of 'happy')

Hint: The rule for words ending in consonant + y.

Answer

happiest

When -y follows a consonant, the y becomes -iest: happy → happiest. 'Most happy' isn't exactly wrong, but it sounds heavy.

Exercise 7

The order is wrong in this sentence — tap the word in the wrong place.

He wore a cotton white kurta to the wedding.

Answer

Wrong word: cotton.

Corrected: He wore a white cotton kurta to the wedding.

Material (cotton) sits closest to the noun, and colour (white) comes before it. The two were swapped.

Exercise 8

Find the wrong word.

This phone is more cheaper than that one.

Answer

Wrong word: more.

Corrected: This phone is cheaper than that one.

'cheaper' is already a comparative, so 'more' is extra. This habit comes from the Hindi 'zyada sasta'.

Exercise 9

One word is in the wrong place.

My all relatives came for the function.

Answer

Wrong word: all.

Corrected: All my relatives came for the function.

'all' comes before the possessive — all my, all your, all his. Translating the Hindi 'mere saare' word for word reverses the order.

Exercise 10

'I saw the accident with my own eyes.' — what type of adjective is 'own' here?

  • Emphasizing
  • Possessive
  • Quality
  • Distributive

Hint: It gives no new information, it only stresses.

Answer

Emphasizing

'own' and 'the very' put stress on the noun — they are Emphasizing adjectives. 'my' is possessive, but 'own' adds emphasis on top of it.

Exercise 11

This is the ___ book I wanted! (exactly that one)

Hint: The word that adds stress after 'the'.

Answer

very

'the very + noun' = exactly that thing. Here 'very' is an adjective, because it describes the noun (book).

Exercise 12

Match each type of adjective to its question.

A B Quality Whose? Quantity One at a time Possessive Which one? Distributive What kind? Demonstrative How much? Answer

Quality — What kind?; Quantity — How much?; Possessive — Whose?; Distributive — One at a time; Demonstrative — Which one?

Each type answers one question — what kind (quality), how much (quantity), whose (possessive), one by one (distributive), which one by pointing (demonstrative).

Exercise 13

Match each adjective to its order number.

A B lovely 3 — age huge 6 — origin ancient 7 — material Japanese 1 — opinion wooden 2 — size Answer

lovely — 1 — opinion; huge — 2 — size; ancient — 3 — age; Japanese — 6 — origin; wooden — 7 — material

The more personal the adjective is, the farther it sits from the noun; the more it is a real quality of the thing, the closer it sits. That is why opinion comes first and material comes last.

Exercise 14

Put the adjectives in the correct order.

Words: a / bought / round / table / wooden / She / small

Answer

She bought a small round wooden table

The order is size (small) → shape (round) → material (wooden) → noun (table). Material always stays right next to the noun.

Exercise 15

Say this line aloud — three adjectives together, without stopping.

Answer

Say: He has a beautiful old Indian painting

When you speak, you don't hear commas between the adjectives — it flows in one stream. In the right order your tongue glides; in the wrong order it stumbles.

What to do next

Today, pick five things in your home and describe each with two or three adjectives — "a small black plastic chair". The train order will stick. The next chapter is Adverb — the adjective's partner.

docs.title: Chapter 46: Advanced vocabulary
docs.text:
Advanced words — the ones educated people really use

Memorising advanced words does not help much — if you learn "Hegemony means dominance", you will never say it properly. A word sticks in your mind through its place: the kind of sentence it appears in, the kind of people who use it, and the words that travel with it. That is why, in this chapter, every word comes with its world — not just a definition.

In one line

A new word is not yours until you can say one real sentence with it without thinking. Remembering the meaning is half the job; remembering where the word lives is the whole job.

docs.title: nefarious — evil, with a planned, sneaky purpose
docs.text:
This word does not just mean "bad" — it carries hidden, planned wrongdoing. You see it in news, crime stories and films. The fun part: these days people also use it as a joke — "nothing nefarious, I promise". Words that go with it: nefarious scheme, nefarious purpose, nefarious activities.

  • The account was being used for something nefarious — fake invoices, mostly. = Someone was using the account for a dishonest purpose, mostly to make false invoices.

docs.title: myriad — too many to count
docs.text:
It means "a great many", but with the feeling of impossible to count. The biggest mistake is putting a singular noun after "a myriad of". Both forms are fine: myriad reasons (clean and short) or a myriad of reasons. But the noun after it is always plural.

  • There are myriad reasons why the launch slipped, but three matter most. = The launch was late for a huge number of reasons, but only three are really important.

docs.title: bucolic — like the countryside: peaceful and green
docs.text:
Bucolic is a picture of fields, meadows, cows and goats, and slow living — like a village in a painting. It always carries a feeling of love and calm, never poverty or backwardness. When to use it: it is a literary word — travel writing, books, reviews. In speech, peaceful countryside or rural sounds more natural. Words that go with it: bucolic setting, bucolic charm, bucolic landscape. Pronunciation: byoo-KOL-ik.

  • The homestay sits in a bucolic valley of tea gardens and slow rivers. = The homestay is in a calm, green country valley with tea gardens and quiet rivers.

docs.title: guile — cleverness, trickery
docs.text:
Guile is a noun — the cleverness used to fool other people. Note: the adjective guileful is not really used; people say cunning. But guileless (innocent, with no trickery) is a lovely word and is used as praise.

  • He won that negotiation with pure guile, not numbers. = He won the talks by being clever and tricky, not because of facts and figures.

docs.title: onerous — heavy, tiring (a task or a condition)
docs.text:
The work is not necessarily hard — it is like a burden. It is most often used with contract, rules, paperwork, duty. In an office email it complains politely: you are not saying "this is nonsense", only "this is a burden".

  • The reporting requirements are onerous for a team of three. = The reporting rules are too heavy a load for a team of only three people.

docs.title: enigmatic — puzzling, hard to understand
docs.text:
A person, a smile, an answer, or someone's behaviour — when it is not clear what is going on inside. It carries interest, not evil. If someone is simply quiet, they are reserved; an enigmatic person is someone you keep wondering about.

  • Her reply was enigmatic — a single line that could mean yes or no. = Her answer was a puzzle: one line that might mean yes or might mean no.

docs.title: lurid — shocking, sensational
docs.text:
Two meanings, both with a feeling of "too much": (1) a story or news report full of deliberately shocking, dirty or bloody detail; (2) colours that are harsh and glaring. The word always comes with a bit of disapproval. When to use it: news, reviews, criticism — the most common pair is lurid details. It is rare in conversation, but everyone understands it. Pronunciation: LOOR-id.

  • The tabloid printed every lurid detail of the case. = The newspaper published every shocking, gossipy detail of the case.

docs.title: hegemony — one power's total control
docs.text:
A word from politics, history and business analysis. It means: one country, company or group is so dominant that everyone else follows its lead. Do not use this word in everyday talk — it is very heavy. Pronounce it carefully: hi-JEM-uh-nee.

  • Two companies share almost complete hegemony over the search market. = Just two companies control almost the whole search market.

docs.title: felicity — deep happiness; or a perfect, beautiful way of putting something
docs.text:
Felicity is a noun with two meanings: (1) deep, peaceful happiness — in old, written language; (2) the exactly right and beautiful choice of words — felicity of expression. The opposite, infelicitous (awkward, out of place), is often used by editors and critics. When to use it: very literary — wedding cards, speeches, literary criticism. In daily life use happiness or joy. Pronunciation: fuh-LIS-ih-tee.

  • Her essays are admired for their felicity of expression. = People admire her essays because her word choices are so exact and beautiful.
  • We wish the couple a lifetime of felicity. = We hope the couple will be happy for their whole lives. (Formal and old-fashioned.)

docs.title: censure — official or formal criticism
docs.text:
This is not ordinary anger — it has an official feeling. A committee, board, parliament or institution censures someone. Be careful: it is a completely different word from censor (to cut out or remove a part); they only sound alike.

  • The board voted to censure him, though he kept his seat. = The board voted to formally criticise him, but he stayed in his position.

docs.title: jettison — throw off a load; give something up
docs.text:
The original picture: throwing cargo off a ship or plane to make it lighter. That gave us today's meaning — to drop a plan, feature or habit because you have to. It carries the feeling of giving something up to survive, so it is very common in business and project talk.

  • We had to jettison half the features to ship on time. = We had to drop half the features so we could release on time.

docs.title: disparate — completely different, not fitting together
docs.text:
Not just "different" — so different that putting them together is hard. That is why it usually appears as disparate sources, disparate systems, disparate groups. Pronunciation: DIS-puh-rut.

  • The report pulls together data from three disparate systems. = The report gathers data from three very different systems in one place.

docs.title: insidious — harming slowly, from the inside
docs.text:
The most important point: it has slow speed. Something you cannot see at first, and by the time you notice it, a lot of damage is done — that is insidious. It goes with disease, habits, rumours and ideas. An explosion is not insidious.

  • The most insidious part is how normal it starts to feel. = The most dangerous part is that, slowly, it all begins to seem normal.

docs.title: keen — very eager; or sharp (eyes, mind)
docs.text:
The most useful word on this list, and the easiest. Two meanings: (1) keen to / keen on = eager about something — great for interviews. (2) a keen eye, a keen sense = sharp eyesight, a sharp understanding. One more useful fact: in British English, "I'm not keen on it" is a very polite way of saying no.

  • I'm keen to take on more responsibility this year. = I really want to take on more responsibility this year.
  • She has a keen eye for detail — nothing gets past her. = She notices small details very well — she misses nothing.

docs.title: auspicious — lucky, a good sign
docs.text:
In India this word is used every day — weddings, housewarmings, new ventures. Native English speakers elsewhere use it less, but everyone understands it. Note: a thing is an auspicious occasion / auspicious day; a person is not. The opposite is inauspicious.

  • They picked an auspicious date for the opening. = They chose a lucky date for the opening.

docs.title: ubiquitous — found everywhere
docs.text:
A favourite word for talking about technology and trends: smartphones are ubiquitous. It carries a light feeling of "it is ordinary now". Pronunciation: yoo-BIK-wi-tus.

  • QR codes were rare five years ago; now they're ubiquitous. = You hardly saw QR codes five years ago; now you see them everywhere.

docs.title: ephemeral — lasting a very short time
docs.text:
It has both beauty and a little sadness. A status update, a story, fashion, weather, happiness — anything that came and went. The word is a bit literary, so it fits better in writing. Pronunciation: ih-FEM-er-ul.

  • Social media fame is ephemeral — gone in a week. = Fame on social media lasts a very short time — it disappears within a week.

docs.title: pragmatic — practical; whatever works is fine
docs.text:
The second most useful word on this list. It means: looking at results instead of theory. It is great for describing yourself in an interview — and it is a word of praise.

  • Let's be pragmatic — ship the simple version now, improve it later. = Let's be practical: release the simple version now and make it better later.

docs.title: 46.2 Where do these words live — a map
docs.text:
Link each word to its place. The map below shows two things together: how formal a word is (the further right, the more formal), and how often you will hear it (the higher up, the more common). Do not try the words in the bottom-right corner in speech — they are for reading.

Figure 46.1. Orange dots = words you can start speaking today. Blue dots = words to read and recognise first; speak them later.

docs.title: 46.3 At a glance — word, partner words, pronunciation
docs.text:
"Partner words" (collocations) are the most useful column: they show what comes before and after the word. Native speakers remember words in pairs and groups, not alone.

Word Meaning (plain English) Partner words Pronunciation nefarious wicked, with a planned purpose scheme, purpose, activities ni-FAIR-ee-us myriad too many to count myriad reasons / ways / forms MIH-ree-ud bucolic calm and green, like the countryside bucolic setting / charm / landscape byoo-KOL-ik guile cleverness, trickery (noun) with guile, without guile, guileless GY-ul onerous like a burden, heavy onerous terms / duty / requirements OH-nur-us enigmatic puzzling, mysterious enigmatic smile / figure / reply eh-nig-MA-tik lurid shocking, sensational; glaring (colour) lurid details / headlines / colours LOOR-id hegemony one power's total control hegemony over, cultural hegemony hi-JEM-uh-nee felicity deep happiness; exact, beautiful wording felicity of expression, infelicitous fuh-LIS-ih-tee censure formal, official criticism vote to censure, public censure SEN-shur jettison to give up because you must jettison a plan / feature / idea JET-ih-sun disparate very different, not matching disparate sources / systems / groups DIS-puh-rut insidious harming slowly and unnoticed insidious effect / spread / habit in-SID-ee-us keen eager; or sharp (eyesight) keen to, keen on, a keen eye keen auspicious lucky, a good sign auspicious day / occasion / start aw-SPISH-us ubiquitous found everywhere ubiquitous in, has become ubiquitous yoo-BIK-wi-tus ephemeral lasting a very short time ephemeral fame / beauty / trend ih-FEM-er-ul pragmatic practical a pragmatic approach, be pragmatic prag-MA-tik

docs.title: 46.4 Word traps — words that sound alike
docs.text:
Watch these pairs carefully

censure (to criticise) vs censor (to cut out a part) — completely different jobs. ephemeral (short-lived) vs ethereal (light, heavenly) — both poetic, but the meanings differ. disparate (very different) vs desperate (in great need) — the spelling is one letter apart, the meaning is miles apart. pragmatic (practical) vs dogmatic (stubborn about your own view) — one is praise, the other is a complaint.

docs.title: 46.5 Mistakes people make with these words
docs.text:
Watch out

  • Wrong: There are a myriad of reason for this.
  • Right: There are myriad reasons for this.

  • Why: After myriad, the noun is always plural. And "myriad reasons" is cleaner — "a myriad of" feels a little heavy.

  • Wrong: The bomb had an insidious effect on the building.

  • Right: The bomb had a devastating effect on the building.

  • Why: Insidious needs slow speed. For damage that happens in one blow, use devastating.

  • Wrong: He is a very auspicious person.

  • Right: It was an auspicious day to start.

  • Why: Auspicious is for days, chances and beginnings — not for people.

  • Wrong: The committee decided to censor the minister for his remarks.

  • Right: The committee decided to censure the minister for his remarks.

  • Why: Censure = to criticise formally. Censor = to cut out and remove a part. One letter, a completely different meaning.

  • Wrong: I am keen for learning new tools.

  • Right: I am keen to learn new tools.

  • Why: There are only two patterns: keen to + verb, or keen on + -ing. "Keen for" is not used.

  • Wrong: Our team has hegemony in this office.

  • Right: Our team has a lot of influence in this office.
  • Why: Hegemony is a word for the scale of countries, markets and cultures. It is far too big for an office.

docs.title: 46.6 One paragraph — five words, each in its place
docs.text:
Read it, then say it aloud

Cheap smartphones are now ubiquitous, and that has created myriad small businesses that did not exist ten years ago. Most are ephemeral — up one month, gone the next. The ones that last are run by pragmatic people who jettison whatever stops working. Notice: these are five heavy words, yet no sentence feels stiff, because each word sits in its right place.

docs.title: 46.7 Practice — Advanced vocabulary
docs.text:
Exercise 1

A habit that stays hidden for years and slowly does damage. Which word?

  • insidious
  • nefarious
  • ephemeral
  • onerous

Hint: The speed must be slow.

Answer

insidious

Insidious needs a slow, hidden pace. Nefarious means planned wickedness, and ephemeral means short-lived.

Exercise 2

Which word is best for describing yourself in an interview?

  • pragmatic
  • enigmatic
  • nefarious
  • onerous
Answer

pragmatic

Pragmatic is a word of praise — a person who looks at results. Enigmatic would suggest nobody can understand you, which is not good in an interview.

Exercise 3

Which sentence is correct?

  • There are myriad reasons for the delay.
  • There are a myriad of reason for the delay.
  • There is myriad reason for the delay.
  • There are myriads reason for the delay.
Answer

There are myriad reasons for the delay.

The noun after myriad is plural. 'Myriad reasons' is the cleanest form.

Exercise 4

To release the project on time, we had to drop half the features. Which verb?

  • jettison
  • censure
  • enhance
  • demonstrate
Answer

jettison

Jettison = to throw off a load in order to survive. The picture comes from throwing cargo off a ship.

Exercise 5

I'm ___ to take on more responsibility this year.

Hint: Eager — the interview word.

Answer

keen / eager

Keen to + verb. Remember: 'keen for learning' is wrong; 'keen to learn' or 'keen on learning' is right.

Exercise 6

The report pulls together data from three ___ systems that were never meant to talk to each other.

Hint: So different that they do not fit together.

Answer

disparate

Disparate = completely different in kind. It is stronger than just 'different' — it carries the feeling of 'hard to join'.

Exercise 7

One word has been chosen wrongly — tap it.

The board voted to censor the minister for his remarks.

Answer

Wrong word: censor.

Corrected: The board voted to censure the minister for his remarks.

Censure = formal criticism. Censor = to cut out and remove a part. They sound alike, but the meanings are different.

Exercise 8

This word does not describe a person — find it.

My uncle is a very auspicious man in our town.

Answer

Wrong word: auspicious.

Corrected: My uncle is a well-respected man in our town.

Auspicious is for days, chances and beginnings. For a person, use 'respected' or 'well-regarded'.

Exercise 9

Match each word to its real feeling.

A B hegemony a heavy, burdensome task guile over in a moment onerous one power controlling everything ephemeral getting things done by cleverness Answer

hegemony — one power controlling everything; guile — getting things done by cleverness; onerous — a heavy, burdensome task; ephemeral — over in a moment

All four are heavy words — recognise and read them first; speak them later.

Exercise 10

Match each word to its partner words.

A B keen has become ubiquitous nefarious an enigmatic smile ubiquitous a keen eye for detail enigmatic a nefarious scheme Answer

keen — a keen eye for detail; nefarious — a nefarious scheme; ubiquitous — has become ubiquitous; enigmatic — an enigmatic smile

Native speakers do not remember a word alone — they remember it in a pair. If you know the pair, the word falls into the right place by itself.

Exercise 11

Build the sentence — about technology.

Words: were / they / five / ago / QR / are / rare / but / years / now / codes / ubiquitous

Answer

QR codes were rare five years ago but now they are ubiquitous

Ubiquitous often comes with 'now' and a before-and-after comparison — that is its natural home.

Exercise 12

You want to describe a calm, green village in a travel blog. Which word?

  • bucolic
  • lurid
  • onerous
  • insidious

Hint: Fields, meadows, peace.

Answer

bucolic

Bucolic = calm and beautiful like the countryside. It is a literary word, so it fits a blog or a book. Lurid is the opposite — glaring and sensational.

Exercise 13

One word has been chosen wrongly — tap it.

The tabloid printed every bucolic detail of the murder.

Answer

Wrong word: bucolic.

Corrected: The tabloid printed every lurid detail of the murder.

Shocking, bloody detail = lurid details. Bucolic is for the peace of the countryside.

Exercise 14

Critics praised the poet for the ___ of her expression — every word felt exactly right.

Hint: The exact, beautiful choice of words — a noun.

Answer

felicity

'Felicity of expression' = the exactly right and beautiful choice of words. A very literary word — not for daily talk.

Exercise 15

Match the new words to their meanings.

A B bucolic deep happiness or exact wording lurid give up because you must felicity calm like the countryside jettison shocking, sensational Answer

bucolic — calm like the countryside; lurid — shocking, sensational; felicity — deep happiness or exact wording; jettison — give up because you must

Bucolic and felicity are literary; lurid is common in the news. Recognise all three when reading first, then try them in writing.

Exercise 16

When is a new word counted as really yours?

  • When you can say one real sentence with it without thinking
  • When you remember its spelling
  • When you remember the dictionary definition
  • When you remember its Hindi meaning
Answer

When you can say one real sentence with it without thinking

Remembering the definition is half the job. A word is yours when you remember its place and its partner words.

Exercise 17

Say this line. Put the stress in the middle of 'pragmatic' — prag-MA-tik.

Answer

Say: Let us be pragmatic and ship the simple version now

This is a real line from office meetings. Saying 'Let's be pragmatic' makes you sound sensible, not stubborn.

What to do next

Do not pick up all eighteen words at once. Look at the map, choose the five orange-dot words — keen, pragmatic, ubiquitous, auspicious, enigmatic — and use them this week. For the blue-dot words, it is enough to recognise them when you read; they will come to your tongue in their own time.

docs.title: Chapter 11: Adverbs
docs.text:
Adverb — how, when, where, how much

An adverb is a word that tells you more about a verb, an adjective or another adverb. An adjective works on a noun; an adverb works on everything else. Two things trip people up most — first, forgetting to add -ly ("she speaks good"), and second, putting the adverb in the wrong place ("I always am late"). Both get fixed in this chapter.

In one line

An adverb modifies a verb, an adjective, or another adverb. If a word describes anything other than a noun, that is an adverb's job.

  • He drove carefully. About the verb — how did he drive?
  • The exam was very easy. About the adjective — how easy was it?
  • She sings quite beautifully. About another adverb — how beautifully does she sing?
Figure 11.1. An adverb can work on three things — a verb, an adjective or another adverb. A noun is outside its reach.

docs.title: 11.1 Types of adverb
docs.text: Type Question Examples In a sentence Manner How? slowly, carefully, well, badly, loudly She writes neatly. Time When? now, then, today, yesterday, soon, already, yet He left yesterday. Place Where? here, there, outside, upstairs, everywhere, nearby Wait outside. Frequency How often? always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never I always walk to work. Degree How much? very, too, so, quite, almost, enough, hardly It is too hot. Affirmation / negation Yes or no? certainly, surely, definitely, not, never I certainly agree. Reason Why? therefore, hence, thus, consequently He was ill; therefore he stayed home. Interrogative asking a question when, where, why, how Why are you late? Relative joining two parts where, when, why This is the place where we met.

docs.title: Interrogative and relative adverbs — the same word, different jobs
docs.text:
where, when, why (and how in questions) can be used in two ways. At the start of a question, it is an interrogative adverb. Right after a noun (a place, a time, a reason), where it adds a whole extra clause about that noun, it is a relative adverb.

Word Interrogative (question) Relative (joining) where Where do you live? the place where we met when When does the film start? the day when I joined why Why is she crying? the reason why he left how How did you do it? (rarely used as a relative — say "the way" instead)
  • This is the café where we first met. "where" = in which — it adds a whole clause about the place (the café).
  • I still remember the day when I got my first job. "when" = on which — it comes after a time word (day).
  • Tell me the reason why you are upset. "why" = for which — it comes after "reason".

A short rule for relative adverbs

where = in which / at which (place) · when = on which / in which (time) · why = for which (reason). ✓ the house where I was born = the house in which I was born. A relative adverb is followed by a full clause (subject + verb), without the reversed question order: ✗ "the place where did we meet" → ✓ "the place where we met".

'the way how' — don't use both

  • Wrong: I like the way how she speaks.
  • Right: I like the way she speaks. / I like how she speaks.
  • Why: "the way" and "how" mean the same thing — use one of them, not both.

Think of frequency as a scale

always (100%) → usually → often → sometimes → occasionally → rarely / seldom → hardly ever → never (0%). In an interview, "I sometimes make mistakes" sounds more believable than "I never make mistakes".

docs.title: 11.2 Rules for forming adverbs
docs.text:
How the adjective ends What to do Example Normal + ly quick → quickly consonant + y y → ily happy → happily, easy → easily -le e → y simple → simply, gentle → gently -ic + ally basic → basically, tragic → tragically -ll + y full → fully, dull → dully -ue drop the e, + ly true → truly, due → duly

These adverbs don't take -ly — the form stays the same

Word As an adjective As an adverb fast a fast train drives fast hard hard work works hard late a late train came late early an early bus woke up early straight a straight line go straight high a high wall flew high

"fastly" and "hardly work" are both wrong — "hardly" means almost not at all: He hardly works = he almost never works!

Pairs where adding -ly changes the meaning

Without -ly With -ly hard = with great effort (He works hard.) hardly = almost not at all (He hardly works.) late = after the expected time (She came late.) lately = recently (I haven't seen her lately.) near = close by (He lives near.) nearly = almost (I nearly fell.) short = not long (Cut it short.) shortly = soon (He will arrive shortly.) high = at a great height (Birds fly high.) highly = very (She is highly qualified.)

docs.title: 11.3 Where to put an adverb — the most common mistakes happen here
docs.text:
The position of an adverb depends on its type. There are four fixed patterns, and once you know them your everyday speech improves by itself.

Figure 11.2. Four rules for adverb position — frequency, order, degree, and not splitting a verb from its object.

The fixed rule for frequency adverbs

Before the main verb — I always wake up early. After the verb "be" — She is always busy. After a helping verb — They have never been to Kerala. In one line: after "be", before everything else.

Mistakes with position

  • Wrong: I always am ready on time.
  • Right: I am always ready on time.

  • Why: A frequency adverb comes after the verb "be" (am) — this is the one exception.

  • Wrong: She speaks fluently English.

  • Right: She speaks English fluently.

  • Why: An adverb doesn't go between a verb and its object. Finish the action first (speaks English), then say how.

  • Wrong: He went yesterday to the market.

  • Right: He went to the market yesterday.
  • Why: Place first, time after — the order is manner → place → time.

An adverb at the start — for emphasis

An adverb can also go at the start of a sentence, where it affects the whole sentence: Suddenly, the lights went off. / Honestly, I didn't know. It's better to put a comma after it.

docs.title: 11.4 Comparative and superlative of adverbs
docs.text:
It works like adjectives, with one difference: adverbs ending in -ly always take more / most.

How it is formed Positive Comparative Superlative ending in -ly → more / most carefully more carefully most carefully ending in -ly → more / most quickly more quickly most quickly Short (no -ly) → er / est fast faster fastest Short (no -ly) → er / est hard harder hardest Short (no -ly) → er / est late later latest Irregular well better best Irregular badly worse worst Irregular little less least Irregular much more most Irregular far farther / further farthest / furthest
  • Ravi runs faster than his brother. "fast" is short, so it takes -er.
  • She explained it more clearly than the teacher. "clearly" ends in -ly, so it takes more.
  • Of all the students, he writes the most neatly. Superlative — comparing three or more.

docs.title: 11.5 Adverb or adjective — a one-second test
docs.text:
Ask: what is it describing?

Describing a noun → adjective. Describing a verb → adverb. a loud noise (noun) · shouted loudly (verb)

After a linking verb, use an adjective, not an adverb

✓ The food smells good. ✗ smells well ✓ She looks tired. ✗ looks tiredly These verbs describe the subject, not an action. One exception: He looks well = he looks healthy.

docs.title: 11.6 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
Common Indian-English mistakes with adverbs

  • Wrong: She speaks English very good.
  • Right: She speaks English very well.

  • Why: "speaks" is a verb, so you need an adverb — well. "good" goes only with a noun: her English is good. This good/well pair is the most common slip.

  • Wrong: He is more taller and runs more faster.

  • Right: He is taller and runs faster.

  • Why: The -er in "taller" and "faster" already makes the comparison. Adverbs ending in -ly take more (more slowly), but short adverbs take -er.

  • Wrong: I always am late for meetings.

  • Right: I am always late for meetings.

  • Why: A frequency adverb goes after the verb "be" — am always, is never, are usually. With all other verbs it goes before: always come, never eat.

  • Wrong: He drives his car fastly.

  • Right: He drives his car fast.

  • Why: "fastly" isn't an English word. "fast" is an adverb itself. Same list: hard, late, early, straight, high — none of these take -ly.

  • Wrong: She explained very nicely the problem.

  • Right: She explained the problem very nicely.

  • Why: Don't squeeze an adverb between the verb and its object. First "explained the problem", then say how.

  • Wrong: He hardly works, that's why he got promoted.

  • Right: He works hard, that's why he got promoted.

  • Why: "hardly" means almost not at all — the meaning flips! To talk about effort, say "works hard".

  • Wrong: I am very much tired today.

  • Right: I am very tired today.

  • Why: With an adjective, use only "very". "very much" goes with a verb: I like it very much.

  • Wrong: He don't come here never.

  • Right: He doesn't come here. / He never comes here.
  • Why: Two mistakes: "doesn't" is needed with "he", and one sentence can't have two negatives (doesn't + never). "never" is already negative, so the verb after it is a normal positive one.

docs.title: 11.7 A short summary
docs.text: Type of adverb Position Example Manner after the object, at the end of the sentence She read the letter slowly. Frequency before the main verb / after "be" He often calls. · He is often busy. Time at the end (or at the start for emphasis) We met yesterday. Place after manner, before time He sat quietly in the corner. Degree right before the word it describes It is too cold.

docs.title: 11.8 Practice — Adverbs
docs.text:
Exercise 1

She speaks English very ___.

  • well
  • good
  • better
  • goodly

Hint: What part of speech is 'speaks'?

Answer

well

'speaks' is a verb, and to describe a verb you need an adverb. The adverb of 'good' is 'well' — 'good' goes only with a noun: her English is good.

Exercise 2

Which sentence is correct?

  • She is always on time.
  • She always is on time.
  • Always she is on time.
  • She is on time always.

Hint: The rule for frequency adverbs and the verb 'be'.

Answer

She is always on time.

A frequency adverb goes after the verb 'be' — is always, am never, are usually. With all other verbs it goes before: always comes, never eats.

Exercise 3

He drives ___ than his father.

  • faster
  • more fast
  • more faster
  • fastly

Hint: Does 'fast' have an -ly?

Answer

faster

'fast' is a short adverb with no -ly, so it takes -er. Adverbs ending in -ly take 'more': more carefully, more slowly.

Exercise 4

'He hardly works.' — what does it mean?

  • He almost never works
  • He works very hard
  • He works sometimes
  • He works properly

Hint: hard and hardly are two different words.

Answer

He almost never works

'hardly' means almost not at all — it is not the adverb of 'hard'. To talk about effort, say 'works hard', without -ly.

Exercise 5

The child was crying ___. (adverb of 'loud')

Hint: What do you normally add to an adjective?

Answer

loudly

Adding -ly to a normal adjective makes the adverb — loud becomes loudly. Here 'crying' is a verb, so an adverb is needed.

Exercise 6

She solved the puzzle ___ than I did. (comparative of 'easily')

Hint: What goes with adverbs that end in -ly?

Answer

more easily

Adverbs ending in -ly take 'more', not -er. There is no such word as 'easilier'.

Exercise 7

One word in this sentence is in the wrong place — tap it.

She speaks fluently Hindi and Marathi.

Answer

Wrong word: fluently.

Corrected: She speaks Hindi and Marathi fluently.

An adverb doesn't go between a verb and its object. Finish the action first — speaks Hindi and Marathi — then say how.

Exercise 8

Find the wrong word.

He drives his new car very fastly.

Answer
