Wrong word: fastly.

Corrected: He drives his new car very fast.

'fastly' isn't an English word — 'fast' is an adverb itself. Same list: hard, late, early, straight.

Exercise 9

One word is in the wrong place.

I always am ready before eight.

Answer

Wrong word: always.

Corrected: I am always ready before eight.

A frequency adverb goes after the verb 'be' (am) — this is the one exception. With other verbs it goes before: I always wake up early.

Exercise 10

'This is the school where my father studied.' — what is 'where' here?

  • relative adverb
  • interrogative adverb
  • adverb of place
  • preposition

Hint: Is it asking a question, or joining a clause to a noun?

Answer

relative adverb

'where' comes after the noun 'school' and adds a whole clause about it — a relative adverb. In 'Where did he study?' it asks a question — that is interrogative.

Exercise 11

I will never forget the day ___ we won the cup.

Hint: Which relative adverb follows a time word (day)?

Answer

when

After a time noun (day, year, time) use 'when'. After a place use 'where', and after a reason use 'why'.

Exercise 12

One word is extra — tap it.

I love the way how my mother cooks.

Answer

Wrong word: how.

Corrected: I love the way my mother cooks.

'the way' and 'how' mean the same thing — they don't go together. Say 'the way my mother cooks' or 'how my mother cooks'.

Exercise 13

Match each adverb to its type.

A B slowly place — where yesterday frequency — how often outside degree — how much rarely manner — how almost time — when Answer

slowly — manner — how; yesterday — time — when; outside — place — where; rarely — frequency — how often; almost — degree — how much

An adverb's type is decided by the question it answers. And the type decides where it goes in the sentence.

Exercise 14

Put the words in the right order — remember manner, place, time.

Words: concert / the / at / last / beautifully / played / He / night

Answer

He played beautifully at the concert last night

When several adverbs come together, the order is manner (how) → place (where) → time (when). Breaking this order makes the sentence sound odd.

Exercise 15

Say this line aloud — say 'well' clearly, not 'good'.

Answer

Say: She speaks English very well

We are used to saying 'very good', so we skip 'well'. Practising 'well' out loud breaks the habit.

What to do next

From today, whenever you want to say "good", ask yourself — "am I describing an action?" If yes, say "well". The next chapter is Preposition, and after that comes Conjunction.

docs.title: Chapter 51: Applications & messages
docs.text:
Applications and messages — a ready model for every occasion

You need leave, the fridge has broken down, you need a certificate from college, you have to send a CV for a job, or you have to tell your boss the train is late — this is the writing you will use most in life. This chapter gives you a complete model for each occasion that you can use directly by changing the names and dates, and a template at the end that works everywhere.

In one line

Every application answers three questions in its first lines: what you want, why, and for which dates or details. What you want, why you want it, and when or for what — these three things should be clear right at the start.

docs.title: 51.1 Leave application — to your manager
docs.text:
These days a leave application at the office is just an email. The manager only has to say "yes" or "no" — so give them everything they need to decide, and nothing extra.

Figure 51.1. With all four, the manager can answer in one line. If even one is missing, the back-and-forth begins.

The four things in a leave email

Dates (day + date), reason (one line, no details), handover (who will look after the work), and one direct question — "Could you please confirm if these dates are approved?"

Model: Leave application to manager

Subject: Leave request: 18–20 November (sister's wedding)

Dear Ms Iyer,

I would like to request three days of annual leave, from Wednesday, 18 November to Friday, 20 November, for my sister's wedding in Jaipur.

I will finish the monthly GST reconciliation before I leave, and Rohan has agreed to handle any urgent vendor queries while I am away. I will be back at my desk on Monday, 23 November.

Could you please let me know if these dates are approved?

Thank you, Neha Kapoor Accounts Executive

  • I would like to request three days of annual leave… Much more polite than "I want leave", yet just as direct. How many days + which leave + from when to when.
  • …and Rohan has agreed to handle… The person covering is already named — this removes the manager's biggest worry.
  • I will be back at my desk on Monday, 23 November. The return date — this short line helps the manager with planning.

docs.title: 51.2 Leave application — to a school principal
docs.text:
Schools and colleges still use the old letter format — on paper or in an email. Teachers expect to see this format, so it makes sense to follow its rules here.

Figure 51.2. This structure is for school and college. Don't carry it into office email.

Two worlds, two formats

In a school/college application the old letter format is fine: To, date, Subject, "Respected Sir/Madam", "Thanking you". In office email, drop all of this — there "Dear Ms Iyer" and "Kind regards" are used.

Model: Leave application to school principal

To The Principal Green Valley Public School Nagpur

10 August

Subject: Application for leave, 6–8 August

Respected Madam,

I am Ananya Joshi, a student of Class 9 B. I was unable to attend school from 6 to 8 August because I had a high fever. The doctor advised me to rest at home, and I have attached a copy of the medical certificate.

I will complete the classwork I missed and submit my pending homework by Friday. Please grant me leave for these three days.

Thanking you, Yours sincerely, Ananya Joshi Class 9 B, Roll No. 14

  • I was unable to attend school from 6 to 8 August… The leave is already over, so the past tense. If you are asking in advance: "I will not be able to attend…"
  • I will complete the classwork I missed… It answers the teacher's worry in advance — this is the line that makes the application good.
  • Yours sincerely, — not "Yours obediently" "Obediently" is very old. Many schools still teach it, but "Yours sincerely" is right everywhere.

docs.title: 51.3 Complaint letter — proof, not anger
docs.text:
It is natural to feel angry when you complain. But the person at the company who reads your email will help you faster when they get facts, a reference number and a clear request — not CAPITAL LETTERS.

Figure 51.3. Four steps, in one order. Anger has no place in this order — and no need.

The complaint formula

What happened (with the date and order number) + what you want + by when. Anger, CAPITAL LETTERS and "!!!" do not get results; facts and proof do.

Model: Complaint email to customer care

Subject: Complaint: refrigerator not repaired after two visits (Order no. 58213)

Dear Customer Care Team,

I am writing to complain about the refrigerator I bought from your Andheri store on 2 September (Order no. 58213; invoice attached).

Since 20 September, the fridge has not been cooling. Your technician visited on 23 September and again on 30 September, but the problem is still not fixed. As a result, we have had to throw away food twice.

The product is under warranty. I would like you to either repair it fully or replace it by 15 October. Please confirm the next step by replying to this email.

Kind regards, Vikram Singh [Phone number]

  • The order number in the subject Customer care systems run on order numbers — if it is in the subject, the email reaches the right team faster.
  • Since 20 September… visited on 23 and 30 September… A short timeline of dates — nobody can argue with it.
  • I would like you to either repair it fully or replace it by 15 October. Two clear options and one deadline. Firm, but not rude.

docs.title: 51.4 Request letter — polite, but clear
docs.text:
In requests we often become so polite that the actual point gets lost — "I humbly request you to kindly please…". One please is enough; give clear details everywhere else.

The right amount of politeness

"Could you please…" or "I would be grateful if you could…" — that is all. Don't pile "humbly", "kindly" and "please" together. Politeness comes not from words but from giving clear and complete information.

Model: Request to college office

Subject: Request for a bonafide certificate — Rohit Kulkarni, TY BCom (Roll No. 2231)

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am a third-year BCom student (Division A, Roll No. 2231), and I need a bonafide certificate to apply for an education loan.

I would be grateful if you could issue the certificate by Wednesday, 21 October, as the bank's deadline is 23 October. I have attached a copy of my college ID card and my fee receipt.

Please let me know if you need any other document from me.

Yours faithfully, Rohit Kulkarni TY BCom, Division A

  • I would be grateful if you could issue the certificate by Wednesday. A polite request + a deadline + the reason for the deadline (the bank's date).
  • Dear Sir or Madam → Yours faithfully The name is not known, hence "faithfully". If the name were known (Dear Mrs Patil), it would be "Yours sincerely".
  • Please let me know if you need any other document. It makes the office's next step easy — it saves back-and-forth.

docs.title: 51.5 Job application — the cover note
docs.text:
Leaving the email body empty when you send a CV — or writing only "PFA my resume" — is the biggest mistake. A recruiter gives each application only a few seconds; a short, clear cover note sets you apart from the pile.

The three paragraphs of a cover note

(1) Which job, and where you saw it. (2) One or two real achievements, with numbers. (3) CV attached + your wish to talk. The whole note should be under 150 words.

Model: Job application cover note

Subject: Application for Junior Data Analyst (Ref. JDA-24) — Aditya Rao

Dear Ms Fernandes,

I am writing to apply for the Junior Data Analyst role advertised on your careers page.

I recently completed my BSc in Statistics and spent six months as an intern at a retail company, where I built weekly sales dashboards in Excel and Power BI. These dashboards cut the team's reporting time from two days to half a day.

My CV is attached. I would welcome the chance to discuss how I can support your analytics team.

Kind regards, Aditya Rao [Phone number] · [LinkedIn profile link]

  • The role, reference number and name in the subject HR fills several roles at once — the reference number sends your email to the right folder.
  • …cut the team's reporting time from two days to half a day. Everyone writes "I am hard-working and dedicated". An achievement with numbers is remembered.
  • I would welcome the chance to discuss… A confident ending — more modern than "kindly consider my candidature".

docs.title: 51.6 Professional messages on WhatsApp and text
docs.text:
Half of office work now happens on WhatsApp. The same rule applies here as in email: the whole point in one message. Sending only "Hi sir" and waiting for a reply wastes the other person's time and yours.

Figure 51.4. Left: four messages, two hours, and the point is still incomplete. Right: one message, the whole point.

Four rules for professional messages

One message, the whole point — who, what, by when. In the first message give your name and context (team, class). After 9 pm, only urgent matters. And ask before sending a voice note — not everyone can listen to one in a meeting.

Model: WhatsApp to your boss

Good morning, Mr Khanna. My train is running about 40 minutes late, so I will reach the office by 10:15. The slides for the 11 am meeting are already in your inbox. — Neha

Model: WhatsApp to a client

Hello Ms Banerjee, this is Arjun from Brightline Interiors. The cabinets for your kitchen have arrived. Would Tuesday at 11 am suit you for the installation? You can reply here or call me on this number.

Model: Message to a teacher

Good evening, Ma'am. This is Ananya Joshi from Class 9 B. I was absent today because of a fever. Could you please tell me which Maths topics were covered, so that I can catch up? Thank you.

  • This is Arjun from Brightline Interiors. The first message from a new number — name + company. Not "Myself Arjun".
  • Would Tuesday at 11 am suit you? Give the client one definite option — "tell me when you are free" slows down the reply.
  • Good evening, Ma'am. "Ma'am / Sir" is perfectly fine for a teacher — that is the norm in school culture.

docs.title: 51.7 Your own template — fill in the blanks
docs.text:
All the models above are built on one structure. Save it once in your phone's notes — then every new application is just a matter of filling in the blanks.

Template: application or formal email

Subject: [What you want]: [dates / reference number]

Dear [Mr/Ms + surname], — or if you don't know the name: Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to [request / inform you about / complain about / apply for] [the main point, in one line].

\[Reason or details — 2–3 lines. Dates, numbers, references.\] \[What arrangement you have made, or what you have attached.\]

Could you please [what to do] by [day, date]?

Kind regards, — or with Dear Sir or Madam: Yours faithfully, [Full name] [Job title / class / roll number] [Phone number]

Template: professional WhatsApp

[Good morning / Hello], [Mr/Ms + surname]. This is [your name] from [team / company / class]. [What happened or what you need — one line]. [By when / next step]. Thank you.

  • Before sending, 1: both day and date in the dates? "Wednesday, 18 November" — and check that it really is a Wednesday.
  • Before sending, 2: is the name spelled right? Getting someone's name wrong is the mistake that is noticed fastest.
  • Before sending, 3: is the attachment really attached? Writing "Please find attached" and forgetting the file — this happens every day in every office.
  • Before sending, 4: did you read it aloud once? The ear catches the mistakes the eye misses.

docs.title: 51.8 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
These sentences are so common in leave applications and office messages that they start to look right. Most of them are direct translations from Hindi.

Real mistakes in applications and messages

  • Wrong: I am suffering from fever since two days.
  • Right: I have had a fever for two days.

  • Why: With a duration (two days) use "for", not "since". And for something still going on, use the present perfect: have had.

  • Wrong: Please grant me leave as my health is not well.

  • Right: Please grant me leave as I am unwell.

  • Why: "Health is not well" says the same thing twice. Say it directly: I am unwell / I am not well.

  • Wrong: I want leave for tomorrow.

  • Right: I would like to take leave tomorrow, Friday 20 November.

  • Why: "I want" sounds like a demand. "I would like to" is polite — and writing the date prevents confusion.

  • Wrong: Respected sir, kindly do the needful.

  • Right: Good morning, Mr Khanna. Could you please approve my leave for Friday?

  • Why: On WhatsApp "Respected sir" feels heavy, and "do the needful" does not say what has to be done.

  • Wrong: I am having a doubt in chapter 5.

  • Right: I have a question about Chapter 5.
  • Why: Outside India, "doubt" means disbelief, not a question. And "have" (meaning to possess) is not used with -ing.

docs.title: 51.9 Practice — Applications
docs.text:
Exercise 1

A leave email to your manager — which is the best subject line?

  • Leave application
  • Leave request: 18–20 November (sister's wedding)
  • Sir please grant leave
  • Urgent leave needed!!!
Answer

Leave request: 18–20 November (sister's wedding)

Topic + exact dates + a short reason. The manager can decide in the inbox, even without opening the email.

Exercise 2

Which greeting is still in use in an application to a school principal?

  • Respected Madam
  • Hey Ma'am
  • Hi Principal
  • Dear Madam ji
Answer

Respected Madam

School and college applications use the old format — 'Respected Sir/Madam'. In an office email, write 'Dear Ms Iyer' instead.

Exercise 3

A WhatsApp message to your boss — your train is late. Which is the best message?

  • Hi sir
  • Sir late today
  • Good morning, Mr Khanna. My train is running 40 minutes late, so I will reach by 10:15. The slides for the 11 am meeting are already in your inbox.
  • Sorry sir traffic, coming
Answer

Good morning, Mr Khanna. My train is running 40 minutes late, so I will reach by 10:15. The slides for the 11 am meeting are already in your inbox.

The whole point in one message: what happened, when you will arrive, and how the work is covered. The boss has nothing to ask.

Exercise 4

What is the right length for a job cover note?

  • Under 150 words, three short paragraphs
  • Two full pages
  • Just one line: 'PFA my CV'
  • My whole life story from childhood until now
Answer

Under 150 words, three short paragraphs

A recruiter gives each application only a few seconds. Which job, one or two real achievements with numbers, and the CV attached — that is all.

Exercise 5

Find the mistake.

I am suffering from fever since two days.

Answer

Wrong word: since.

Corrected: I have had a fever for two days.

A duration (two days) takes 'for', not 'since' — 'since' is followed by a starting point (since Monday). And 'I have had a fever' is more natural.

Exercise 6

Which word makes this sentence sound odd?

I cannot come today because my health is not well.

Answer

Wrong word: health.

Corrected: I cannot come today because I am not well.

'Health is not well' says one thing twice. Say it directly: I am not well / I am unwell.

Exercise 7

Find the old phrase that says nothing clearly.

Kindly do the needful and approve my leave.

Answer

Wrong word: needful.

Corrected: Could you please approve my leave for 18–20 November?

'Do the needful' leaves it to the reader to work out what to do. Write directly what you want — and for which dates.

Exercise 8

I would be ___ if you could issue the certificate by Friday.

Answer

grateful / thankful

'I would be grateful if you could…' is the clearest and most professional way to make a polite request. There is no need for 'humbly request you to kindly please'.

Exercise 9

I am writing to ___ for the post of Junior Data Analyst.

Answer

apply

apply for a job / apply for a post. The first line of a cover note tells the reader which job you are writing about.

Exercise 10

Match each occasion to its correct first line.

A B Leave email to manager I am writing to apply for the post of Sales Associate. Complaint Could you please issue me a bonafide certificate? Cover note Good evening, Ma'am. This is Ananya from Class 9 B. Request to college office I would like to request leave from 18 to 20 November. Message to teacher I am writing to complain about a faulty refrigerator. Answer

Leave email to manager — I would like to request leave from 18 to 20 November.; Complaint — I am writing to complain about a faulty refrigerator.; Cover note — I am writing to apply for the post of Sales Associate.; Request to college office — Could you please issue me a bonafide certificate?; Message to teacher — Good evening, Ma'am. This is Ananya from Class 9 B.

Each first line states the purpose directly — the reader knows what it is about from the very start.

Exercise 11

Build the last line of a leave email in the right order.

Words: whether / approved? / dates / please / confirm / are / you / Could / these

Answer

Could you please confirm whether these dates are approved?

Could you please + verb (confirm) + whether-clause. End a leave email with a clear question like this.

Exercise 12

Say this line — as if you were telling your manager on the phone.

Answer

Say: I would like to request two days of leave next week.

'I would like to request' is much more polite than 'I want leave', and still direct. When speaking, join 'would like' together: wud-laik.

What to do next

Whenever you write an application or a professional message this week, open this chapter's template first. After three times with the template, the structure will come to you by itself the fourth time.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Articles
docs.text:
a, an, the — three small words, a big difference

Hindi has nothing called an article. "Main doctor hoon" — and that's it, the job is done. So when we speak English, the mind repeats the same habit: "I am doctor." In a grammar book this looks like a small mistake, but a listener notices it immediately. The good news: choosing an article is just the answer to three questions, and those three questions will be clear to you for good in this chapter.

In one line

An article is a small word before a noun that tells the listener whether you mean any one of something (a / an) or that particular one (the). An article says "any one" or "that special one".

  • I need a pen. = I need one pen — any pen will do, it doesn't matter which.
  • I need the pen. = I need that pen — the special one that we both know about.
  • I need pens. = I need pens (in general) — no article is used here.

docs.title: 6.1 The decision flowchart
docs.text:
Every time a noun comes up, ask these three questions — in order. The answer will come by itself. At the start it will feel slow; in two weeks it will start to happen automatically.

Figure 6.1. Ask the questions in order. The first question matters most — if the answer is yes , you don't need to ask the other two.

docs.title: 6.2 a or an — look at the sound , not the letter
docs.text:
The biggest mistake here is the thought that "an goes before a word that starts with a vowel". The rule is about the sound, not the letter. Say the word aloud — if the first sound from your mouth is a vowel, use an.

Word First sound Correct Why hour aa- an hour the "h" is silent — the sound starts with a vowel honest o- an honest man the "h" is silent university yu- a university "yu" is a consonant sound useful yu- a useful book the same "yu" sound one-rupee coin wa- a one-rupee coin "one" = "wan", a consonant sound MBA em- an MBA degree M is said "em" — a vowel sound LIC agent el- an LIC agent L = "el" European yu- a European country a "yu" sound

A sure test for abbreviations

With abbreviations (MBA, SP, FIR, NGO, RTI), say the name of each letter. The letters whose names start with a vowel sound — A, E, F, H, I, L, M, N, O, R, S, X — take an before them. The rest take a. an FIR · an NGO · an RTI · a BJP leader · a CA · a PhD

docs.title: 6.3 When "the" is used — seven sure occasions
docs.text:
Occasion Example Second mention (first time it is "a") I saw a dog. The dog was limping. Only one in the world the sun · the moon · the sky · the earth Superlatives and ordinals the best player · the first bus Rivers, seas, mountain ranges, deserts the Ganga · the Arabian Sea · the Himalayas · the Thar Musical instruments She plays the flute. Newspapers, names of books, buildings the Hindu · the Gita · the Taj Mahal Countries with a plural or "of" in the name the Netherlands · the United States · the Republic of India

The first occasion is the most important, so listen to it once:

  • Yesterday I met a teacher. The teacher told me about this book. First time, "a teacher" — the listener doesn't know which one. Second time, "the teacher" — now they know.

docs.title: 6.4 Zero article — where nothing is used
docs.text:
You need to remember this list, because this is where Indian English pushes in "the" where it isn't needed.

Category Correct Wrong General plural Dogs are loyal. The dogs are loyal. Uncountable (general) Milk is good for health. The milk is good for health. Names of people and places Ravi lives in Jaipur. The Ravi lives in the Jaipur. Languages She speaks Marathi. She speaks the Marathi. Sports He plays cricket. He plays the cricket. Meals We had lunch at two. We had the lunch at two. Transport — by + vehicle I came by bus. I came by the bus. Places, when you go for their purpose go to school · go to bed · go to court go to the school (for studying) Years, months, days in 2026 · on Monday · in June in the 2026

'go to school' vs 'go to the school' — both correct, different meaning

go to school = go to study (for its purpose) — My son goes to school. go to the school = go to that building — I went to the school to meet the principal. The same difference works with hospital, college, church, prison and court.

docs.title: 6.5 One noun, three forms — feel the difference
docs.text:
Sentence Meaning A tiger is dangerous. Any one tiger — taken as an example. The tiger is dangerous. That particular tiger we are talking about. Tigers are dangerous. Tigers (the whole species) are dangerous. This is the most natural.

A small test

When you are confused, ask yourself: "Which one?" If there is an answer ("the one I brought yesterday") → the. If the answer is "any one" → a / an. If the question makes no sense ("Which milk?" — milk in general) → nothing.

docs.title: 6.6 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
Top article mistakes

  • Wrong: I am engineer.
  • Right: I am an engineer.

  • Why: When you say what your job is, English needs an article — a doctor, an engineer, a teacher. In Hindi "main engineer hoon" is enough, but not in English.

  • Wrong: He is going to the office by the bus.

  • Right: He is going to the office by bus.

  • Why: "by + vehicle" takes no article — by bus, by train, by car, by auto, on foot.

  • Wrong: She plays the cricket very well.

  • Right: She plays cricket very well.

  • Why: Sports take no article. But musical instruments do: she plays the guitar.

  • Wrong: The honesty is the best policy.

  • Right: Honesty is the best policy.

  • Why: Uncountable nouns for feelings (honesty, love, patience, anger) come without an article when they are general. But "the best" needs "the" — it is a superlative.

  • Wrong: I have a good news for you.

  • Right: I have good news for you.

  • Why: "news" is uncountable — "a" doesn't go before it. To say one item of news: a piece of good news.

  • Wrong: She went to the home early.

  • Right: She went home early.

  • Why: "home" takes neither an article nor "to" — go home, reach home, stay home.

  • Wrong: My father is a best cook in our family.

  • Right: My father is the best cook in our family.

  • Why: Before a superlative (best, tallest, first) it is always "the" — because there can be only one.

  • Wrong: He gave me a advice.

  • Right: He gave me some advice.
  • Why: advice, information, furniture, luggage, equipment, work — these are all uncountable. Not "a" — "some" or "a piece of" will do.

Three things that are enough

1. When you say your job, use an article — I am a teacher. 2. First time "a / an", second time "the". 3. General plural and general uncountable → nothing.

docs.title: 6.7 Practice — Articles
docs.text:
Exercise 1

My brother is ___ MBA student.

  • a
  • an
  • the
  • no article

Hint: Say M aloud — what sound comes out?

Answer

an

The sound of M is 'em' — it starts with a vowel. So 'an MBA'. The letter M is a consonant, but the sound is a vowel, and the rule is about sound.

Exercise 2

She studies at ___ university in Pune.

  • a
  • an
  • the
  • no article

Hint: Say 'university' aloud — yu or u?

Answer

a

The first sound of 'university' is 'yu', which is a consonant sound. So 'a university' — 'an university' is wrong.

Exercise 3

___ Himalayas are in the north of India.

  • A
  • An
  • The
  • no article

Hint: It is the name of a mountain range.

Answer

The

Names of mountain ranges, rivers and seas take 'the' — the Himalayas, the Ganga, the Arabian Sea.

Exercise 4

___ milk is good for children. (in general)

  • A
  • The
  • An
  • no article

Hint: It is a general statement, not a particular milk.

Answer

no article

When an uncountable noun has a general meaning, no article is used. 'The milk' is only for a particular milk — like the milk kept in the fridge.

Exercise 5

I saw a snake in the garden. ___ snake was bright green.

Hint: It is being mentioned for the second time.

Answer

The

First time 'a snake', because the listener didn't know which one. Second time 'the snake' — now both know which snake we mean.

Exercise 6

One word in this sentence is wrong — tap it.

My uncle is a honest officer in the railways.

Answer

Wrong word: a.

Corrected: My uncle is an honest officer in the railways.

In 'honest' the h is silent — the sound starts with 'o', so 'an honest'. The rule is about sound, not the letter. In the same way: an hour, an heir.

Exercise 7

Rohit is ___ tallest boy in our class.

Hint: It is a superlative.

Answer

the

Before a superlative (tallest, best, first) it is always 'the', because there can be only one.

Exercise 8

There is one mistake in this sentence — tap the wrong word.

My brother comes home by the bus every evening.

Answer

Wrong word: the.

Corrected: My brother comes home by bus every evening.

'by + vehicle' takes no article — by bus, by train, by car. The 'the' has to go.

Exercise 9

Find the wrong word.

My sister plays the cricket after school.

Answer

Wrong word: the.

Corrected: My sister plays cricket after school.

Names of sports take no article. Musical instruments do — 'plays the guitar' is perfectly correct.

Exercise 10

One word is wrong — catch it.

She gave me a very useful information.

Answer

Wrong word: a.

Corrected: She gave me very useful information.

'Information' is uncountable, so 'a' doesn't go before it. To count it, say 'a piece of information'.

Exercise 11

Match each sentence to its correct article.

A B ___ sun rises in the east a I want ___ apple no article He is ___ good teacher the ___ children love sweets an Answer

___ sun rises in the east — the; I want ___ apple — an; He is ___ good teacher — a; ___ children love sweets — no article

Only one in the world → the. Vowel sound → an. Consonant sound → a. General plural → no article.

Exercise 12

Make the sentence in the right order.

Words: a / in / engineer / private / I / am / an / company

Answer

I am an engineer in a private company

When you say your job, an article is needed — 'an engineer'. And 'company' comes up for the first time, so 'a private company'.

Exercise 13

Now say this line aloud — say both articles clearly.

Answer

Say: I bought a book and the book was very good

First time 'a book', second time 'the book'. When speaking, pause lightly before 'the' — it tells the listener that you mean that same book.

What next?

Today take one news story from the newspaper and circle every a, an and the with a pencil. Then ask yourself — "why is it here?" This one exercise fixes articles for good, better than memorising any rule.

docs.title: Chapter 43: Basic → native English
docs.text:
From Basic to Native — the same message, a new style

Your English is not wrong. I am very tired is a perfectly correct sentence — grammar perfect, meaning clear. Still, a native speaker would probably not say it. They would say I'm running on fumes. In this chapter we learn exactly that difference: the short journey from correct English to natural English. And, most important of all — knowing where to say which phrase, because a natural phrase used in the wrong place sounds worse than a basic one.

In one line

Sounding native does not come from difficult words — it comes from putting the right phrase in the right setting. You do not need to memorise big words; learn a few phrases and use them correctly.

docs.title: 43.1 Four pairs you can use from today
docs.text: First understand these four properly. Make a picture in your mind for each one — that is the only way the real meaning of a phrase sinks in.

docs.title: I'm very tired → I'm running on fumes
docs.text:
"Fumes" are the vapour of petrol — the car has run out of petrol, only fumes are left, and it is still moving. That is the picture: the energy is gone but the work continues. So this phrase is not just for feeling sleepy; it is for when you are still sitting at your laptop after a three-day deadline.

  • Honestly, I'm running on fumes — can we finish this tomorrow morning? = To be honest, I have no energy left. Can we finish this tomorrow morning?

More options, from light to heavy: I'm beat (casual, with friends), I'm wiped out (a bit more tired), I'm exhausted (safe everywhere — office, interview, doctor).

docs.title: I don't understand → I'm not following
docs.text:
I don't understand can make the listener think "I can't get it, I am weak". I'm not following means "I have lost the thread of what you are saying" — nobody is blamed, neither you nor the speaker. For offices and meetings, this is the best one.

  • Sorry, I'm not following — could you walk me through that part again? = Sorry, I can't keep up — could you explain that part once more?
  • You've lost me. What happens after the payment fails? = I can't follow you any more. What happens after the payment fails?

docs.title: I need to leave → I should get going
docs.text:
I need to leave sounds like you are forced to, as if there is an emergency. I should get going is soft and polite, and leaving feels like your own choice. When leaving someone's house or ending a call — this is the line.

  • This was lovely, but I should get going — it's a long drive back. = I enjoyed this, but I ought to leave now — the drive back is long.
  • I'd better head out before the traffic starts. = I should leave before the traffic begins.

docs.title: I made a mistake → I dropped the ball
docs.text:
Pay attention here, because this pair is not equal. I dropped the ball is not for every mistake — it is for when the job was yours and you let it slip. Saying it about a typo would sound over-dramatic. Forgot to send a follow-up email to a client — now that is fine.

  • I dropped the ball on the vendor follow-up. I'm fixing it today. = I forgot to do the vendor follow-up that was my job. I will fix it today.
  • That one's on me — I misread the deadline. = That was my mistake — I read the deadline wrongly.

The native formula for admitting a mistake

Own it + a plan to fix it, not excuses. "I dropped the ball on this. Here's what I'm doing about it." In native English, after a mistake you do not say "sorry sorry"; you say what happens next. That sounds professional.

docs.title: 43.2 The everyday upgrade table
docs.text:
On the left is what we usually say; on the right is what sounds natural to the ear. The third column is the most important — when.

Plain Native When it is fine to say I am very busy I'm swamped Office, colleagues, WhatsApp. Fine with your boss too. Not in a first email to a client. I will think about it Let me sleep on it When the decision can wait until tomorrow. Works in meetings and with friends. Tell me about it later Fill me in later Casual and office. "Fill me in" = tell me what I missed. I agree completely Couldn't agree more Safe everywhere — meetings, interviews, friends. It is not a problem No worries Casual and normal office talk. In a formal email write "That's absolutely fine". I am confused I'm a bit lost here Meetings and class — it sounds honest, not weak. Please wait a little Bear with me When you are sharing your screen or looking for something. Very natural. I did it very fast, so it is rough It's a first pass Office. To set expectations when you send work. We have very little time We're cutting it close With the team. With a client it is better to say "the timeline is tight". I understood Got it / Makes sense Every day, everywhere. Much better than "Noted with thanks". Let us start Let's dive in The start of a presentation or a meeting. I will do it later I'll circle back on this Office only. Among friends it sounds corporate and makes people laugh.

docs.title: 43.3 Feeling upgrades — anger, fear, joy, tiredness
docs.text:
When talking about feelings, I'm very ___ is the most common habit. A native speaker replaces "very" with a picture phrase. Press 🔊 on every line and listen to the rhythm — these phrases are said in one breath.

Basic Native Meaning When to use it I'm very angry I'm seeing red right now So angry that everything looks red. Casual, with friends and family. It means very strong anger — said at the office, it will alarm people. There, say I'm really frustrated. I'm very scared I'm freaking out right now In a bad state from fear or panic. Casual only. It covers panic as well as fear. In formal settings say I'm really worried. I'm very confused I'm totally thrown off Something suddenly changed and I lost my balance. Casual and office both. Especially when a plan or an answer changes suddenly. I'm very nervous I'm a little worked up Restless and tense inside. Casual. Note — worked up can also include some anger or agitation. For nerves alone people also say I've got butterflies. I'm very surprised I'm completely caught off guard I was not ready at all; the news startled me. Safe everywhere — even in meetings. For good or bad surprises alike. I'm very happy I'm feeling great about it I feel very happy and confident about this. Safe everywhere. For happiness about a decision, result or plan — for mood alone say I'm in a great mood. I'm very tired I'm running on fumes No energy left, yet the work goes on. Casual and with the team. The full story is in Section 1 above — not in front of a doctor.

Three phrases that sound odd in the wrong place

seeing red = very strong anger, not for small irritation · freaking out = slang, not for an interview or in front of a client · worked up = nervousness or agitation — make it clear from the context. Feeling idioms are most natural with friends; at the office, choose the neutral version.

docs.title: 43.4 Work and daily talk — 12 more upgrades
docs.text:
These are lines that come up ten times a day — money, work, plans and saying no. Most of them are in the neutral zone, which means they work both at the office and with friends.

Basic Native Meaning When to use it I need to leave I need to get going I have to go now. Safe everywhere. I should get going (Section 1) is softer; need to has a little more hurry. I don't understand I'm not catching your drift I can't grasp what you are trying to say. Casual, a little old-fashioned. For a hinted or indirect point. In a meeting I'm not following is better. That's expensive That's gonna cost me big time This will hurt my pocket badly. Spoken only. Never write gonna. To a client: That's above our budget. I'm very busy I've got a lot on my plate My plate is already full of work. Safe everywhere — even with your boss. A little softer than I'm swamped. I don't want it I think I'll pass on that Thank you, but not this time. A polite no — food, an offer, an invitation. I don't want it sounds rude. That's very difficult That's a tough nut to crack A hard nut — difficult to break. Office and casual. For a problem, a question or a difficult person. The idiom is fixed — only crack works. I don't know yet I haven't figured it out yet I haven't worked it out or decided yet. Safe everywhere. It carries the feeling of "still trying". I made a mistake I dropped the ball on that That job was mine and I let it slip. Team and manager. Not for a small typo — see Section 1. Let's talk later Let's touch base later Let's have a short chat later. Office language. Among friends it sounds corporate — there say Let's catch up later. I'm ready to start I'm ready to get started I am ready to begin. Safe everywhere — meetings, class, interviews. That's very annoying That's getting on my nerves This thing is driving me crazy. Casual. Nerves is always plural. Saying it to someone's face sounds rude. I'll handle it I'll take care of it Don't worry, I'll manage it. Safe everywhere — with clients too. I'll handle it is also correct, just a little blunter.

Three that work everywhere

If you only want to take three from this table, take these: I've got a lot on my plate, I'll take care of it, I think I'll pass on that. All three are neutral — say them without worry to a friend, a manager or a client.

docs.title: 43.5 Register — a map of where a phrase belongs
docs.text:
English phrases sit on a line: very casual at one end, very formal at the other. The middle part is the most useful — phrases there work with friends and with your manager. If you are unsure, pick from the middle.

Figure 43.1. One message, three versions for three settings. If you are not sure where you are — use the middle column.

Over-correction — the real danger

The most common mistake is learning a new phrase and stuffing it in everywhere. If you tell a doctor "I'm running on fumes", they will not understand how sleepy you really are. Say it plainly there: "I've been sleeping badly for a week". A natural phrase in the wrong place is worse than a basic phrase. Look at the setting first, then choose the words.

docs.title: 43.6 Small habits that make an instant difference
docs.text:
Besides phrases, there are three habits that can make your English sound natural within a single week.

a) Speak in contractions

Natives do not say I am, do not, it is in full — they say I'm, don't, it's. The full form is only for emphasis: "I am listening!" English without contractions sounds bookish, not wrong — just a little stiff.

b) Add a softener

Native English avoids being too direct. Add a small word: a bit, kind of, maybe, I think, actually. "This is wrong" → "I think there's a small issue here." A softener makes you sound less aggressive — very useful at the office.

c) Make your answer longer than two words

The answer to "How was your weekend?" is not "Fine". "Pretty quiet, actually — I just caught up on sleep. You?" One small detail plus a question back. That is what keeps a conversation going.

docs.title: 43.7 Mistakes people make with native phrases
docs.text:
Right phrase, wrong use

  • Wrong: I am running in fumes.
  • Right: I'm running on fumes.

  • Why: Change a small word of an idiom and it breaks. Remember the phrase whole, exactly as it is — on fumes, because a car runs "on petrol".

  • Wrong: I dropped the ball — I made one spelling mistake.

  • Right: Sorry, typo. Fixed it.

  • Why: A big idiom for a small mistake sounds dramatic. Use "dropped the ball" only when a job you were responsible for slipped.

  • Wrong: I am not following your.

  • Right: I'm not following.

  • Why: This phrase is complete by itself — it needs no object. If you want to add one: I'm not following your point.

  • Wrong: I should get going now itself.

  • Right: I should get going right now.

  • Why: "Now itself" is a habit of Indian English — it is not understood abroad. The correct forms: right now or right away.

  • Wrong: Let me sleep over it.

  • Right: Let me sleep on it.
  • Why: "Sleep over" is when children stay the night at a friend's house. To put off a decision, say sleep on it.

docs.title: 43.8 A short script — what to say every day
docs.text:
Below is a standard office exchange in both versions. Read it aloud twice — first the left side, then the right. Your ear will notice the difference.

Textbook English What people actually say Good morning. How are you? Morning! How's it going? I have completed the report. I've wrapped up the report. I did not understand the second point. I'm not following the second point. Please give me some time. Bear with me for a minute. I will inform you afterwards. I'll let you know. I am very tired today. I'm running on fumes today. I have to go now. I should get going.

docs.title: 43.9 Practice — Basic to native
docs.text:
Exercise 1

In an office meeting you did not understand someone's point. Which line is the most natural?

  • Sorry, I'm not following.
  • I am not understanding.
  • I have a doubt in your talk.
  • Please repeat it again.

Hint: Nobody should be blamed.

Answer

Sorry, I'm not following.

'I'm not following' is neutral — you do not look weak and the speaker is not blamed. 'I am not understanding' is also grammatically wrong, and in 'repeat it again' the 'again' is unnecessary.

Exercise 2

You forgot to send an important client follow-up email. What do you tell your manager?

  • I dropped the ball on the client follow-up.
  • I am running on fumes.
  • Let me sleep on it.
  • I'm swamped so it is not my fault.
Answer

I dropped the ball on the client follow-up.

A job you were responsible for slipped = dropped the ball. The other phrases do not fit here, and the last line is making excuses — which never sounds good.

Exercise 3

You have to describe your tiredness to a doctor. What should you say?

  • I've been exhausted for two weeks and sleeping badly.
  • I'm running on fumes, doc.
  • I'm beat.
  • I'm totally wiped.

Hint: Clear information is needed here, not style.

Answer

I've been exhausted for two weeks and sleeping badly.

A doctor needs details, not an idiom. This is the danger of over-correction — a natural phrase in the wrong place does harm.

Exercise 4

This was fun, but I should get ___ — it's getting late.

Hint: A soft way to leave.

Answer

going

'I should get going' = I ought to leave now. It is more polite and more natural than 'I need to leave'.

Exercise 5

Give me a minute to find the file — please ___ with me.

Hint: Not the animal — it's a phrase: ___ with me.

Answer

bear

'Bear with me' = please be patient. Natives say this while sharing a screen or looking for something.

Exercise 6

The idiom is broken in this sentence — tap the wrong word.

After three night shifts I am running in fumes.

Answer

Wrong word: in.

Corrected: After three night shifts I'm running on fumes.

The small words of an idiom are fixed — 'on fumes', not 'in'. Change one word inside an idiom and the whole phrase sounds foreign.

Exercise 7

One word is an Indian English habit that is not understood abroad — find it.

I should get going now itself.

Answer

Wrong word: itself.

Corrected: I should get going right now.

'Now itself' works only in India. On an international call say 'right now' or 'right away'.

Exercise 8

Match each plain line with its natural version.

A B I am very busy Got it I will think about it Couldn't agree more I understood I'm swamped I agree completely Let me sleep on it Answer

I am very busy — I'm swamped; I will think about it — Let me sleep on it; I understood — Got it; I agree completely — Couldn't agree more

All four on the right belong to the neutral zone — they work at the office and with friends.

Exercise 9

Match each phrase with the right setting.

A B My bad in writing, a formal email I dropped the ball office language only I take full responsibility with a friend, fully casual I'll circle back on this with a team or a manager Answer

My bad — with a friend, fully casual; I dropped the ball — with a team or a manager; I take full responsibility — in writing, a formal email; I'll circle back on this — office language only

Remember the register map: one message, three versions, each with its own place.

Exercise 10

Put the words in the right order — a line for admitting a mistake to a manager.

Words: the / today / it / am / this / and / on / I / I / ball / fixing / dropped

Answer

I dropped the ball on this and I am fixing it today

The native formula: own the mistake first, then give the plan. Excuses do not come in between.

Exercise 11

Which habit makes your English sound natural straight away?

  • Speaking in contractions — I'm, don't, it's
  • Putting a big word in every sentence
  • Always saying the full form — I am, do not
  • Giving every answer in two words
Answer

Speaking in contractions — I'm, don't, it's

Contractions fix the rhythm. The full form sounds bookish, and two-word answers kill a conversation.

Exercise 12

Your manager gives you a new task, but your plate is already full. What is the most natural and polite line?

  • I've got a lot on my plate right now.
  • I am having many works today.
  • I'm seeing red right now.
  • That's gonna cost me big time.
Answer

I've got a lot on my plate right now.

'A lot on my plate' = already a lot of work. It is safe with a manager too. 'Seeing red' is anger, and 'cost me big time' is about money.

Exercise 13

You are writing a formal email to a client. Which line should you NOT write here?

  • That's gonna cost me big time.
  • I'll take care of it.
  • I'm ready to get started.
  • I haven't figured it out yet.

Hint: One line is for speaking only.

Answer

That's gonna cost me big time.

'Gonna' and 'big time' are spoken language only. To a client write 'That's above our budget'. The other three lines are safe everywhere.

Exercise 14

This bug has taken three days — it's a tough nut to ___.

Hint: Which verb goes with a nut?

Answer

crack

'A tough nut to crack' = a hard problem. The idiom is fixed — 'break' or 'open' ruins it.

Exercise 15

One word in the idiom is in the wrong form — find it.

The drilling next door is getting on my nerve.

Answer

Wrong word: nerve.

Corrected: The drilling next door is getting on my nerves.

In 'getting on my nerves', 'nerves' is always plural. 'Nerve' on its own changes the meaning (courage).

Exercise 16

Match each basic feeling with its native version.

A B I'm very angry I'm caught off guard I'm very scared I'm totally thrown off I'm very surprised I'm seeing red I'm very confused I'm freaking out Answer

I'm very angry — I'm seeing red; I'm very scared — I'm freaking out; I'm very surprised — I'm caught off guard; I'm very confused — I'm totally thrown off

All four phrases are picture phrases — a red colour, panic, no preparation, losing your balance. The first three are mostly casual.

Exercise 17

Now try saying this line. 'I'm' in a single sound, and stress 'foll' in 'not following'.

Answer

Say: Sorry I'm not following could you walk me through that again

When speaking, there is no pause inside 'I'm not following' — it flows together. That rhythm is what sounds native.

What to do next

Do not try to memorise the whole table. This week pick just three phrases — I'm not following, I should get going, bear with me — and say them every day. Three phrases that have settled in your mouth are worth more than thirty memorised ones.

docs.title: Chapter 25: Causative, inversion & emphasis
docs.text:
Powerful sentences

Once your grammar is correct, the next step is impact. "I got my car repaired", "I have never seen anything like it", "All I need is a holiday" — English has special ways of saying these things that give your words weight. This chapter has five tools: causative, inversion, cleft sentences, emphatic do and short replies (so do I, I hope not).

In one line

get it done = have someone else do it · Never have I… = reversed order for emphasis · What I need is… = a spotlight on one part · I do like it = I really do · So do I = me too. The meaning stays the same; you change the shape of the sentence to add emphasis.

docs.title: 25.1 Five tools — at a glance
docs.text:
Look at the whole map first. Each tool takes an ordinary sentence and makes it clearer, more formal or more emotional.

Tool Ordinary Powerful Causative A mechanic repaired my car. I got my car repaired. Inversion I have never seen this. Never have I seen this. Cleft I need a holiday. What I need is a holiday. Emphatic do I like it. I do like it. Ellipsis I like tea too. So do I.
  • Never have I seen such a crowd at Marine Drive. = I have never seen a crowd this big at Marine Drive.
  • What I need is a long holiday. = A long holiday is exactly what I need.

docs.title: 25.2 Causative — "karwana" in English
docs.text:
In Hindi, banana → banwana, kaatna → katwana, theek karna → theek karwana — a small "-wa-" shows that the work was done by someone else. In English you use have / get + thing + V3. This matters a lot, because without it an English speaker will think you did the work yourself.

Figure 25.1. In the causative, the person who does the work hides in the middle. The sentence only says: the work was done to the thing , and I arranged it.

The causative formula

have / get + object + V3 = have something done. get is more common in speech, have is a little more formal. The order is fixed: first the thing, then V3 — got my car repaired.

  • I got my car repaired last week. = Last week a mechanic repaired my car for me.
  • She had her hair cut short. = She went to a hairdresser, who cut her hair short.
  • We're having the house painted before Diwali. = Painters are painting our house before Diwali.
  • Where do you get your kurtas stitched? = Which tailor makes your kurtas?
  • You need to get your eyes tested. = You should go and have your eyes checked.
  • Don't worry, I'll get it done by Friday. = It will be finished by Friday (I'll arrange it or do it).

✗

I cut my hair yesterday. (the barber cut it)

✓

I got my hair cut yesterday.

✗

I got repaired my phone.

✓

I got my phone repaired.

object

docs.title: When something bad "happens" to you
docs.text:
The same pattern also works when something bad happens to you — here it does not mean you arranged it, only that it happened to you:

  • I had my phone stolen on the local train. = Someone stole my phone on the local train.

docs.title: 25.3 have someone do, get someone to do, make, let, help
docs.text:
Sometimes you want to name the person — "I had Ravi send the file", "he made me stop". Here every verb has its own pattern: some are followed directly by V1, some by to + V1. This is where most mistakes happen.

Verb Pattern Meaning / Example have have + person + V1 hand over a task: I'll have Ravi send it. get get + person + to V1 persuade: I got him to sign. make make + person + V1 force: She made me wait. let let + person + V1 allow: Let me go. help help + person + (to) V1 assist: Help me (to) carry this.
  • I'll have my assistant email you the details. = My assistant will email you the details (I'll ask him or her to).
  • I finally got the landlord to fix the geyser. = After a lot of effort, I persuaded the landlord to fix the geyser.
  • The teacher made us rewrite the essay. = The teacher forced us to write the essay again.
  • My parents didn't let me go on the trip. = My parents did not allow me to go on the trip.
  • Can you help me move this almirah? = Could you give me a hand to move this cupboard?

✗

He made me to wait for an hour.

✓

He made me wait for an hour.

I was made to wait.

✗

Please let me to explain.

✓

Please let me explain. / Please allow me to explain.

to

Three little words, three different strengths

make = force · let = allow · get … to = persuade. "My boss made me stay" (no choice) vs "My boss let me leave early" (a favour) vs "I got my boss to approve it" (my effort).

docs.title: 25.4 Inversion — the "Never have I…" emphasis
docs.text:
When a sentence starts with a negative or limiting word (never, rarely, not only, hardly, only then…), the subject and the helping verb swap places — exactly like a question. This is formal, written or speech-style English; it adds drama and weight to what you say.

Figure 25.2. Two steps: the negative word goes first, then helping verb + subject — just like Have I…? in a question.

The inversion rule

Negative/limiting word + helping verb + subject + the rest. If there is no helping verb, add do / does / did: Rarely do we eat out.

Opening Example Listen Never / Rarely / Seldom Rarely do we get such rain in April. Not only … but also Not only did she top the class, but she also won the debate. Hardly / Scarcely … when Hardly had I sat down when the phone rang. No sooner … than No sooner had we reached than it started pouring. Only then / Only after Only then did I realise my mistake. Under no circumstances Under no circumstances should you share your OTP. Little Little did he know what was coming.
  • Not only did she top the class, but she also won the debate. = She topped the class, and she won the debate too.
  • Hardly had I sat down when the phone rang. = The phone rang the moment I sat down.
  • Only after the results came out did he start studying. = He started studying only once the results were out.

✗

Never I have seen such a crowd.

✓

Never have I seen such a crowd.

I have never seen such a crowd.

✗

No sooner had we reached when it started raining.

✓

No sooner had we reached than it started raining.

No sooner … than

Hardly / Scarcely … when

✗

Not only she sings, but she also dances.

✓

Not only does she sing, but she also dances.

Rare in everyday talk

With friends, "Never have I eaten such good pani puri!" sounds a bit theatrical (fine as a joke). Inversion really belongs in essays, speeches, formal emails and IELTS writing. In conversation, "I've never eaten such good pani puri!" is enough.

docs.title: 25.5 "if" without if — Should you…, Had I…, Were I…
docs.text:
In formal English you can drop if and move the helping verb to the front. The meaning stays exactly the same as the conditional — just more sophisticated (the full story of conditionals is in the If sentences chapter).

With if Inversion If you need any help, … Should you need any help, … If I had known, … Had I known, … If I were you, … Were I in your place, … If it had not rained, … Had it not rained, …
  • Should you need any help, please call me. = If you ever need help, call me. (a favourite line in emails)
  • Had I known about the strike, I would have taken the metro. = I didn't know about the strike, so I didn't take the metro.
  • Were I in your place, I would accept the offer. = If I were you, I would accept the offer.
  • Had it not rained, we would have won. = It rained, so we didn't win.

✗

Hadn't I known, I would have gone.

✓

Had I not known, I would have gone.

docs.title: 25.6 Cleft sentences — a spotlight on one part
docs.text: "Cleft" means "split in two". You break one sentence into two parts to put the light on one particular thing — especially when you are correcting a misunderstanding. In Hindi, the word "hi" does this job: Ravi ne hi todi thi (it was Ravi who broke it).

docs.title: (a) It is / was … who / that …
docs.text:
• It was Ravi who broke the glass, not Amit. = Ravi broke the glass — not Amit.
  • It's the price that worries me, not the quality. = The price is my worry; the quality is not.
  • It was in Jaipur that they first met. = They first met in Jaipur, and nowhere else.

docs.title: (b) What … is / All … is / The reason … is
docs.text:
• What I need is a good night's sleep. = A good night's sleep is exactly what I need.
  • What she did was call the police immediately. = The thing she did was to call the police at once.
  • All I want is some peace and quiet. = I only want a little peace and quiet — nothing else.
  • The reason I called is to ask about Saturday. = I'm calling because I want to ask about Saturday.

Cleft = the 'hi' emphasis

It was X who/that… = it was X, and no one else. What I need is X = X is exactly what I need. All I want is X = only X, nothing else.

✗

All what I want is a holiday.

✓

All I want is a holiday. / What I want is a holiday.

✗

It was my sister which found the keys.

✓

It was my sister who (or that) found the keys.

Clauses

docs.title: 25.7 Emphatic do and fronting — "I really do!"
docs.text:
In a positive sentence, adding do / does / did + V1 (and stressing it) means "really", "truly", "I did do it!". It is useful when someone doubts you, or when you want to say something warmly.

  • I do like your new haircut — honestly! = I really like your new haircut!
  • I did call you — three times! = I definitely called you — three times!
  • She does know a lot about cars. = She really does know a great deal about cars.
  • Do sit down, Uncle — make yourself at home. = A warm, polite invitation: please sit down and relax.

✗

I did called you yesterday!

✓

I did call you yesterday!

The stress is in your voice

Emphatic do is more about speaking than writing — say "do / did" long and loud: "I DID call you." See the Rhythm and stress chapter for this.

docs.title: Fronting — the important thing first
docs.text:
Sometimes you move the object or another part to the start of the sentence to show contrast. The order (subject + verb) stays the same — this is not inversion.

  • Tea I can live without. Coffee, never. = I can manage without tea, but never without coffee.
  • Strange as it may seem, I enjoy Monday mornings. = It may sound odd, but I enjoy Monday mornings.

docs.title: 25.8 Short replies — so do I, neither do I, I hope not
docs.text:
Native speakers don't repeat the whole sentence. They reply with just the helping verb — this is called ellipsis (leaving words out). In Hindi we say "main bhi" or "main bhi nahi"; in English you have to match the helping verb of the previous sentence.

The other person said Same (positive) Same (negative) I love biryani. So do I. — I can't swim. — Neither can I. I'm tired. So am I. — I didn't go. — Neither / Nor did I. I've been there. So have I. —
  • "I love biryani." — "So do I!" = "I love biryani." — "I love it too!"
  • "I didn't sleep well." — "Neither did I." = "I didn't sleep well." — "I didn't either."
  • Informal: "Me too." / "Me neither." = The short forms are perfectly fine with friends.

✗

"I don't eat meat." — "Me also not." / "I also don't."

✓

"Neither do I." / "Me neither."

docs.title: so / not — instead of a whole sentence
docs.text:
After think, hope, guess, be afraid, so (for yes) and not (for no) take the place of the whole clause.

Question Reply Meaning Will it rain? I think so. I think yes Is the shop open? I don't think so. probably not Will we miss the flight? I hope not. I hope we won't Is it serious, doctor? I'm afraid so. sadly, yes Can you come? I'd love to. I'd really like to
  • "Will the match be cancelled?" — "I hope not." = "Will the match be cancelled?" — "I hope it won't be."
  • "Are you coming to the wedding?" — "I'd love to, but I can't." = "Are you coming to the wedding?" — "I'd like to come, but I can't."

✗

"Is he coming?" — "I think yes." / "I don't think."

✓

"I think so." / "I don't think so."

so

docs.title: 25.9 In real life — an interview answer
docs.text:
The interviewer asked: "Tell me about a challenge you faced." See how several tools work together in one answer to make it memorable.

Sentence Tool Listen Last year our biggest client threatened to leave. — What they wanted was a working app in two weeks. Cleft I got the whole team to work in two shifts. get + person + to Not only did we deliver on time, but we also cut costs. Inversion It was that project that taught me to plan backwards. Cleft

How much should you use?

One or two tools in an answer are enough. If every sentence is reversed or cleft, it will sound artificial. Like masala — a little, in the right place.

docs.title: 25.10 Practice — Powerful sentences
docs.text:
Exercise 1

My scooter broke down, so I ___ at the garage near my office.

  • got it repaired
  • got repaired it
  • repaired it
  • made it repair

Hint: The mechanic fixed it.

Answer

got it repaired

Causative: get + object + V3. The thing (it) goes in the middle, then V3.

Exercise 2

You should get your blood pressure ___ (check) regularly.

Hint: get + object + V3

Answer

checked

get + your blood pressure + checked = have it checked by someone.

Exercise 3

The teacher made us ___ the whole chapter again.

  • read
  • to read
  • reading
  • reads
Answer

read

make + person + V1, without 'to'. (In the passive: We were made to read…)

Exercise 4

Tap the extra word.

My father did not let me to go on the school trip.

Answer

Wrong word: to.

Corrected: My father did not let me go on the school trip.

let + person + V1. 'to' only with allow: allow me to go.

Exercise 5

Never ___ such a beautiful sunset.

  • have I seen
  • I have seen
  • I saw
  • seen I have
Answer

have I seen

Negative word first = helping verb + subject (question order).

Exercise 6

No sooner had we reached the platform ___ the train left.

Hint: 'sooner' is a comparative.

Answer

than

Fixed pair: No sooner … than.

Exercise 7

Hardly had I opened the laptop ___ the power went off.

  • when
  • than
  • then
  • that
Answer

when

Fixed pair: Hardly / Scarcely … when.

Exercise 8

Put the words in order.

Words: not / she / also / only / the / record / she / did / broke / but / win

Answer

not only did she win but she also broke the record

Not only + did + subject + V1, but + subject + also …

Exercise 9

___ I known about the metro strike, I would have left earlier.

Hint: third conditional without if

Answer

Had

Had I known = If I had known (formal inversion).

Exercise 10

___ I need right now is a cup of strong chai.

  • What
  • That
  • Which
  • All what
Answer

What

Cleft: What I need is … = a cup of strong chai is exactly what I need.

Exercise 11

Tap the wrong word.

It was my sister which found the lost keys.

Answer

Wrong word: which.

Corrected: It was my sister who found the lost keys.

For people use who / that, not 'which'.

Exercise 12

Match the reply to its meaning.

A B So do I. I hope that doesn't happen Neither do I. sadly, yes I hope not. me too (after a positive) I'm afraid so. me neither Answer

So do I. — me too (after a positive); Neither do I. — me neither; I hope not. — I hope that doesn't happen; I'm afraid so. — sadly, yes

In a short reply, a helping verb or so/not takes the place of the whole sentence.

Exercise 13

A: I can't drive. B: Neither ___ I.

Hint: The helping verb of the first sentence.

Answer

can

can't → Neither can I. You have to match the helping verb.

Exercise 14

"Will the flight be on time?" — "I think ___."

  • so
  • yes
  • it
  • that
Answer

so

After think / hope / guess, yes = so. 'I think yes' is wrong.

Exercise 15

Who fixed the AC?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

I didn't fix the AC myself. I had a technician come over on Sunday, and he got it working in ten minutes.

  • a technician
  • the speaker
  • the speaker's father
  • nobody
Answer

a technician

'I had a technician come over' = have + person + V1. The technician did the work.

Exercise 16

According to the speaker, what saved the project?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Not only did Ananya finish the report early, but she also found two mistakes in the budget. It was her careful checking that saved the project.

  • Ananya's careful checking
  • the early deadline
  • a bigger budget
  • the manager's help
Answer

Ananya's careful checking

The cleft 'It was her careful checking that…' puts the spotlight on exactly this.

Exercise 17

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

Had I known you were coming, I would have cooked something special.

Had I known = If I had known.

Exercise 18

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

What I need is a long holiday.

Cleft: What I need is …

Exercise 19

Say it with stress on 'do'.

Answer

Say: I do like your new haircut

Emphatic do = 'really'. Say 'do' long and loud.

What to do next

Put one Should you need… in your next formal email and one What I need is… in your next conversation. And whenever you visit a salon or a tailor, say in your head: I'm getting my hair cut. To work on speaking, see Rhythm and stress and Native speed English.

docs.title: Chapter 20: Clauses & complex sentences
docs.text:
Clauses — from short sentences to longer ones

If every sentence in your English is short — "I have a friend. He lives in Delhi. He is a doctor." — nothing is wrong, but it sounds childish. Learn to join clauses, and the same message fits into one clear, confident sentence. This chapter teaches that skill of joining.

In one line

A clause is a group of words with its own subject and verb. A sentence can have one clause or many. Remember the sentence structure chapter? A phrase has no subject-verb pair; a clause does.

  • I have a friend who lives in Delhi. Two clauses: "I have a friend" + "who lives in Delhi".
  • She was tired, so she went to bed early. Two clauses, joined by "so".

docs.title: 20.1 Independent and dependent clauses
docs.text:
Not all clauses are the same. Some can stand alone, and some cannot. It is important to know the difference, because treating an unfinished clause as a complete sentence is the biggest mistake in writing.

Figure 20.1. A dependent clause (dashed) needs the support of an independent clause (solid) to stand.

Independent vs dependent

An independent clause is a complete sentence on its own (I stayed at home.). A dependent clause begins with a word like because, when, if, although, who, which and stays unfinished on its own — join it to an independent clause.

Words that start a dependent clause Job Example because, since, as reason because he was ill when, while, after, before, until time when the bell rang if, unless condition if you call me although, though, even though contrast although it was late who, which, that, whose, where about a noun who lives next door

docs.title: 20.2 Four kinds of sentences
docs.text:
How many clauses there are, and how they are joined, gives four types of sentence. Good English uses a mix of all four; writing only one type makes a text dull.

Figure 20.2. Solid box = independent clause, dashed = dependent. The type is decided only by counting.

The four types

Simple = one independent clause. Compound = two independent clauses (joined by and, but, so). Complex = independent + dependent (joined by because, when, who). Compound-complex = two independent + at least one dependent.

docs.title: 20.3 Compound — joining two equal clauses
docs.text:
When two ideas are equally important, join them in a compound sentence. There are seven small words for this, with a trick to remember them — FANBOYS.

Word Job Example For reason (formal) He left early, for he was ill. And adding I cooked, and she cleaned. Nor not this, not that He didn't call, nor did he write. But contrast It was cheap, but it was good. Or choice Hurry up, or we'll miss the train. Yet even so She was tired, yet she kept working. So result It was raining, so we stayed in.

The compound rule

To join two independent clauses, use a comma + FANBOYS word (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so). A comma alone cannot join two complete sentences: I was tired, I slept. ✗ → I was tired, so I slept. ✓

When you can skip the comma

If both clauses are very short, the comma is not needed: I cooked and she cleaned. And if the second part has no subject of its own, it is not a clause — don't add a comma: She opened the door and smiled.

docs.title: 20.4 Complex — reason, time, condition and contrast
docs.text:
When one idea is the main one and the other gives its reason, time, condition or contrast, you get a complex sentence. These are the sentences that make your English sound thoughtful and mature.

  • I took an umbrella because it looked cloudy. Main idea: I took an umbrella. Reason: there were clouds.
  • When the guests arrived, we served lunch. The dependent clause comes first, so there is a comma after it.
  • Although the test was hard, she passed. = The test was hard, but she passed anyway. — no need for "but".

The complex rule

If the dependent clause comes first, put a comma after it (When it rained, we stayed in.); if it comes after, no comma. One linking word per pair: although or but — not both.

Hindi 'halaanki… lekin' does not work in English

  • Wrong: Although he is rich, but he is not happy.
  • Right: Although he is rich, he is not happy. / He is rich, but he is not happy.
  • Why: Hindi uses both "halaanki… lekin" (although… but); English uses only one. In the same way, "because… so" can't be used together either.

docs.title: 20.5 Relative clauses — who, which, that, whose, where
docs.text:
A relative clause gives more information about a noun, just like an adjective — only a whole clause instead of one word. It turns two short sentences into one: I met a man. He speaks six languages. → I met a man who speaks six languages.

Figure 20.3. A relative clause (dashed) sits right after its noun, and who/that takes the place of that noun.

The relative clause rule

who — people, which — things, that — both, whose — belonging to, where — place. The relative word takes the place of the noun, so don't repeat that noun or pronoun.

Word Used for Example who people the girl who won the prize which things, animals the bus which goes to Agra that people or things (no comma) the book that I lost whose possession — "of whom" the boy whose bike was stolen where place the village where I was born when time the day when we met

You can also leave out an object relative

When who/that is the object of the clause, you can drop it: the book (that) I lost, the man (who) I met. This is very common in speech. But not when it is the subject: the man who called — "who" is needed.

docs.title: 20.6 Defining vs Non-defining — the comma game
docs.text:
Two commas can change the meaning of a sentence. The question is: does the clause say which noun you mean, or does it just add extra information that could be removed without changing much?

Figure 20.4. The part between the commas is bonus information. The part without commas says which one is meant.

Defining vs non-defining

A defining clause says which noun is meant — no commas, and who/which/that all work. A non-defining clause only gives extra information — with commas, and it never uses "that".

  • The Taj Mahal, which is in Agra, attracts millions of visitors. There is only one Taj Mahal — "which is in Agra" is extra information, so commas.
  • Students who finish early can leave. Only the students who finish early — the clause is needed, so no commas.

docs.title: 20.7 Joining short sentences into better ones
docs.text:
Now let's bring it all together. When you write, first write short sentences, then see which ones you can join. Ask three questions: are these equal (FANBOYS)? Is one a reason or a time (because, when)? Is one about a noun (who, which)?

Before (short sentences) After (joined) I have a cousin. She lives in Canada. She is a nurse. I have a cousin who lives in Canada and works as a nurse. The train was late. We missed the meeting. The train was late, so we missed the meeting. It was raining. The match continued. Although it was raining, the match continued. This is the school. My father studied here. This is the school where my father studied. I met a writer. Her books are famous. I met a writer whose books are famous.

Don't cram everything into one sentence

Joining does not mean a whole paragraph should become one sentence. Two or three clauses in a sentence are enough. If it gets long, split it again — a clear message always beats a long one.

docs.title: 20.8 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
The most common Indian-English mistakes with clauses

  • Wrong: Although I studied hard, but I failed.
  • Right: Although I studied hard, I failed.

  • Why: A word-for-word translation of "halaanki… lekin". In English, use only one word for one pair — although or but.

  • Wrong: This is the man who I told you about him.

  • Right: This is the man (who) I told you about.

  • Why: "Who" has already taken the place of "the man". Adding "him" makes the same man appear twice. In the same way: the book which I bought it.

  • Wrong: I was very tired, I went to bed early.

  • Right: I was very tired, so I went to bed early.

  • Why: Two independent clauses can't be joined by a comma alone. Put a FANBOYS word between them, or use a full stop.

  • Wrong: My father, that is a teacher, loves reading.

  • Right: My father, who is a teacher, loves reading.

  • Why: A clause with commas (non-defining) never uses "that". Use "who" for people and "which" for things.

  • Wrong: Because the shop was closed.

  • Right: We came back because the shop was closed.
  • Why: A "because" clause is dependent — it can't be a sentence on its own. It's fine in spoken answers, but in writing join it to a main clause.

docs.title: 20.9 Practice — Clauses
docs.text:
Exercise 1

'I called her, but she didn't answer.' — what kind of sentence is this?

  • Compound
  • Simple
  • Complex
  • Compound-complex

Hint: How many independent clauses are there?

Answer

Compound

There are two independent clauses — 'I called her' and 'she didn't answer' — joined by 'but' (a FANBOYS word). There is no dependent clause, so it is compound.

Exercise 2

'When the power went off, we lit candles.' — what kind of sentence is this?

  • Complex
  • Compound
  • Simple
  • Compound-complex
Answer

Complex

'When the power went off' is a dependent clause and 'we lit candles' is independent. Independent + dependent = complex.

Exercise 3

This is the girl ___ father is a pilot.

  • whose
  • who
  • which
  • where

Hint: Think 'the girl's father' — it shows who he belongs to.

Answer

whose

We want to show possession — 'whose father'. That needs 'whose'. 'Who father' is wrong.

Exercise 4

Which sentence is correct?

  • Although it was late, we kept talking.
  • Although it was late, but we kept talking.
  • Although it was late, so we kept talking.
  • It was late, although but we kept talking.
Answer

Although it was late, we kept talking.

One word per pair. Once you use 'Although', you don't need 'but' — Hindi 'halaanki… lekin' (although… but) doesn't work in English.

Exercise 5

Mumbai, ___ is India's financial capital, is very crowded.

  • which
  • that
  • who
  • where

Hint: Between commas — non-defining.

Answer

which

A clause between commas never uses 'that', and Mumbai is a place/thing (the subject here), not a person — so 'which'. 'Where' would be used if the clause had its own subject: where my uncle lives.

Exercise 6

This is the village ___ my grandmother was born.

Hint: It is about a place.

Answer

where / in which

Use 'where' for a place — the village where she was born. 'In which' is also correct, but a little more formal.

Exercise 7

There is one extra word — tap it.

This is the laptop which I bought it last week.

Answer

Wrong word: it.

Corrected: This is the laptop which I bought last week.

'Which' has already taken the place of 'the laptop'. Adding 'it' makes the same thing appear twice.

Exercise 8

Find the wrong word.

Although the hotel was expensive, but the food was terrible.

Answer

Wrong word: but.

Corrected: Although the hotel was expensive, the food was terrible.

'Although' and 'but' don't go together. Remove one — here, 'but'.

Exercise 9

Match each relative word with its job.

A B who of whom / possession which place whose people where things Answer

who — people; which — things; whose — of whom / possession; where — place

Who is for people, which for things, whose for possession, where for place. 'That' works for both people and things in a defining clause.

Exercise 10

Join into one sentence: 'I have a friend. He speaks Japanese.'

Words: friend / Japanese / I / who / speaks / a / have

Answer

I have a friend who speaks Japanese

'Who' takes the place of 'He' and the clause sits right after 'a friend'. Two short sentences become one clear sentence.

Exercise 11

Make a complex sentence.

Words: inside / stayed / We / raining / because / was / heavily / it

Answer

We stayed inside because it was raining heavily

The main idea comes first (we stayed inside), the reason after (because…). The dependent clause comes second, so no comma is needed.

Exercise 12

Say this sentence aloud — pause lightly at the commas.

Answer

Say: My brother, who lives in Pune, is a doctor

When speaking, commas mean a short pause. That pause tells the listener that 'who lives in Pune' is only extra information.

What to do next
