Open one of your old emails or messages. Wherever three short sentences come in a row, join two of them with who, because or so. One paragraph a day — in a month your writing will be different.

docs.title: Chapter 37: Collocations
docs.text:
Which word goes with which — collocations

"I did a mistake" — there is no grammar error, and yet it sounds wrong. Why? Because in English some words travel as a pair, just like in Hindi you "make tea" and "cook food" — nobody says "cook tea". These fixed pairs are called collocations. They have no logic, only habit — and that habit is what turns your English from "correct" into "natural".

docs.title: 37.1 What is a collocation — fixed word pairs
docs.text:
If a collocation is wrong, people still understand you, but they can tell at once that you are translating. It is not enough for the dictionary meaning to be right — the partner word has to be right too.

Figure 37.1. Powerful and strong mean almost the same, but tea is only ever strong . That is a collocation.

Learn the pair, not the word

A collocation = two words that habitually go together: strong tea, heavy rain, make a mistake. They have no logic — so always write and say a new word together with its partner. Don't write "mistake"; write "make a mistake".

docs.title: 37.2 make or do?
docs.text:
In Hindi both are "karna", which makes this the biggest trap. A rough rule is very useful — and whatever does not fit the rule, you simply learn as a pair.

Figure 37.2. After make, something often comes out — a decision, money, a sound, a friend. After do, there is usually a job to be finished.
  • I made a few mistakes, but I did my best. A mistake is "created" (make); trying hard is an activity (do).
  • Could you do me a favour and make a quick call to the bank? Both in one sentence — favour = do, phone call = make.

make vs do

make = create or produce something new (a decision, a mistake, money, a noise, a call). do = work, duty or an activity (homework, the dishes, exercise, a favour, your best). "Do a mistake" is the most common Indian error — a mistake is always made.

docs.title: 37.3 have, take, give, get — four small verbs, hundreds of pairs
docs.text:
These four verbs are so small that they almost lose their own meaning — the meaning comes from the pair. So never learn them alone; always learn them with their partner.

Verb Fixed pairs Listen have a meal · a bath · a good time · a look · a party · a chat take a photo · a break · a seat · a bus · a chance · medicine give a speech · advice · an example · a hand · a call · a smile get ready · a job · home · lost · better · married

Exams and medicine — 'take'

A student takes an exam (British: sits it) — a teacher gives or sets it. Medicine is also taken, not "eaten": take your medicine. Everyone in India understands "I gave my exam", but abroad it sounds like the opposite — as if you were the one who set the exam.

docs.title: 37.4 Adjective pairs — heavy rain, strong tea, high fever
docs.text:
In Hindi we use one word, "tez", for rain, tea and fever alike. In English every noun has its own adjective. These are the pairs that get noticed most.

Figure 37.3. Expensive price is a very common mistake — a price is not expensive, it is high . The thing is expensive: an expensive phone .
  • There was heavy traffic because of the heavy rain. Both traffic and rain are "heavy" — meaning there is a lot of it.
  • She has a high fever, so she's in deep sleep now. A fever is "high", sleep is "deep".
  • I need a cup of strong tea and some fresh air. = I want a cup of strong tea and some clean, cool air.

Six faces of 'tez'

heavy rain / traffic · strong tea / coffee / wind · high fever / price / temperature · deep sleep. One Hindi "tez" changes in English depending on the noun. Avoid "big rain", "big fever" and "expensive price" — all three.

docs.title: 37.5 Verb + preposition — depend on, listen to
docs.text:
Some verbs bring a particular preposition with them — and the wrong preposition can even change the meaning. Remember them as one unit: depend-on, listen-to.

Pair Example Listen depend on It depends on the weather. listen to Listen to me carefully. wait for I'm waiting for the bus. agree with (a person) I agree with you. agree to (a proposal) They agreed to our plan. apologise for I apologise for the delay. look forward to + -ing I look forward to meeting you. believe in She believes in hard work.

Verbs that take nothing

Some verbs take no preposition: discuss the plan, enter the room, reach Delhi, marry someone, answer the question. "discuss about", "reach at", "answer to the question" — all three are wrong. And after "look forward to" comes -ing: "looking forward to meeting you", not "to meet you".

docs.title: 37.6 Verbs of speaking — say, tell, speak, talk
docs.text:
All four mean "to speak", but they have different partners. This is where mistakes like "say a lie" and "tell me sorry" are born. First understand the pattern of say and tell.

Figure 37.4. After tell, the person comes straight away (told me ). After say, if you need the person, add to (said hello to me ).
  • Always tell the truth, even when it's hard. The truth is "told" — and so is a lie: tell a lie.
  • He said sorry and told us what happened. say sorry · tell + us + the news.
  • Do you speak Tamil? Let's talk about it later. You "speak" a language; you "talk about" a topic.

say vs tell

tell + person (tell me, tell her) — and always tell the truth / a lie / a story / a joke. say + words (say hello, say sorry, say thank you) — if you need the person, use say … to me. You speak a language, and talk about a topic.

docs.title: 37.7 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
These pairs are so common in India that they start to feel right. But in a client call, an interview or IELTS, these small pairs make your English sound "translated".

Common collocation mistakes

  • Wrong: I did a big mistake.
  • Right: I made a big mistake.

  • Why: A mistake is always made. "Do" is for work.

  • Wrong: My son has big fever.

  • Right: My son has a high fever.

  • Why: A fever has a number, so it is high. And don't forget "a": a high fever.

  • Wrong: Don't say a lie.

  • Right: Don't tell a lie.

  • Why: Both lies and the truth are told: tell a lie, tell the truth.

  • Wrong: I gave my exam yesterday.

  • Right: I took my exam yesterday. / I sat my exam yesterday.

  • Why: A student takes an exam. Abroad, "give an exam" sounds like the teacher's job.

  • Wrong: Please close the light.

  • Right: Please switch off the light. / Please turn off the light.
  • Why: A translation of the Hindi "light band karo". Lights, fans and TVs are switched on / switched off; a door is closed.

Also watch out — and one piece of good news

eat medicine → take medicine · do a party → have / throw a party · strong rain → heavy rain. Good news: take a decision is perfectly correct (British and Indian English), and so is make a decision — you can say either.

docs.title: 37.8 How to learn collocations — build a word web
docs.text:
There is no formula for collocations, so your method is everything. Around every new important noun, write its partners — which verbs, which adjectives, which preposition. One web, one page.

Figure 37.5. We need to reach a final decision on the budget. — three parts of the web in a single sentence.

Three daily habits

1. While reading, underline the pair, not the word — "heavy traffic", "made a decision". 2. In your notebook, draw a small web for every noun, like the one above. 3. If in doubt, search the pair in quotes — "big fever" vs "high fever" — whichever gives more results is the natural one.

docs.title: 37.9 Practice — Collocations
docs.text:
Exercise 1

I need to ___ a phone call to the bank.

  • make
  • do
  • give
  • say
Answer

make

A phone call is 'made' — you create something new. 'Give me a call' is fine too, but the person calling 'makes a call'.

Exercise 2

We had very ___ rain last night.

  • heavy
  • strong
  • big
  • high
Answer

heavy

Rain is 'heavy'. 'Strong' is for wind (strong wind), and 'big rain' is never used.

Exercise 3

My son has a ___ fever. I'm taking him to the doctor.

  • high
  • big
  • heavy
  • strong
Answer

high

A fever has a number — so 'high fever', like high temperature or high price.

Exercise 4

Can you do me a ___? Please pick up my parcel.

Hint: Help for a friend — a fixed pair with 'do'.

Answer

favour / favor

'Do someone a favour' = help someone. A favour is 'done', not 'made'.

Exercise 5

It depends ___ the weather.

Hint: Which preposition goes with depend?

Answer

on

Always 'depend on' — 'depend upon' is also correct but sounds old-fashioned. 'depend of' is wrong.

Exercise 6

Tap the wrong verb in this sentence.

I did a big mistake in the exam.

Answer

Wrong word: did.

Corrected: I made a big mistake in the exam.

A mistake is always 'made' — make a mistake.

Exercise 7

One word is making a wrong pair — find it.

Never say a lie to your parents.

Answer

Wrong word: say.

Corrected: Never tell a lie to your parents.

Both lies and the truth are 'told' — tell a lie, tell the truth.

Exercise 8

Match each verb with its fixed partner.

A B make a photo do a speech take a mistake give your homework Answer

make — a mistake; do — your homework; take — a photo; give — a speech

make = produce something, do = work, take a photo, give a speech — learn them as pairs.

Exercise 9

Match each adjective with the right noun.

A B heavy temperature strong sleep high traffic deep coffee Answer

heavy — traffic; strong — coffee; high — temperature; deep — sleep

The Hindi 'tez / zyada' changes in English depending on the noun — heavy traffic, strong coffee, high temperature, deep sleep.

Exercise 10

Put the words in the right order — the last line of an email.

Words: forward / you / I / to / meeting / looking / am

Answer

I am looking forward to meeting you

After 'look forward to' comes -ing: meeting. 'to meet you' is wrong here.

Exercise 11

Say this sentence — two fixed pairs together.

Answer

Say: I made a mistake, but I told the truth

make a mistake + tell the truth. Join 'made a' when you speak — 'may-da'.

What to do next

This week, keep a "pair diary". Every day, write down three pairs from anything you read or hear in English. By the end of the month you will have ninety pairs — and half of them will be on your tongue.

docs.title: Chapter 42: Commonly confused words
docs.text:
Look-alike words — the ones that trick you every day

Some words are like twin brothers — they look alike, sound alike, but do completely different jobs. loose and lose, then and than, your and you're — these mistakes show up daily, even in the emails of well-educated people. Spell-check does not catch them, because both words are correct — just in the wrong place. This chapter has sixteen pairs, sensibly split into groups, and each group comes with a memory trick.

docs.title: 42.1 Three kinds of pairs — recognise them first
docs.text:
Every confusion has a different root, so the cure is different too. First recognise what kind of pair you are dealing with — half the work is done right there.

Figure 42.1. The first group catches you when you write , the second when you read , and the third when you speak — because in Hindi one word does both jobs.

How to read this chapter

One group at a time. Say the trick of each pair aloud, then make a sentence of your own. If you remember the trick, the pair will never confuse you again.

docs.title: 42.2 The apostrophe ones — its/it's, your/you're, their/there/they're
docs.text:
This is the most common written mistake — from WhatsApp to office email. When speaking it makes no difference, because the sound is the same. But in writing, one tiny apostrophe changes the whole meaning.

Figure 42.2. An apostrophe is a patch that sits where a letter is missing. If you see a patch, open it up and read the full words. Word Meaning Example it's / its it is / belonging to it It's raining. · The phone lost its charge. you're / your you are / belonging to you You're late. · Is this your seat? they're they are They're coming at six. their belonging to them Their car is new. there in that place / "there is" Put it over there. · There is a problem.

Open it up and read

Apostrophe = missing letter. Read "it's" as "it is", "you're" as "you are", "they're" as "they are" — if the sentence still makes sense, keep the apostrophe; if not, use the one without it (its / your / their). Is "Your welcome" the same as "You are welcome"? Yes! So it should be "You're welcome".

docs.title: 42.3 One sound, two spellings — stationary/stationery, principal/principle
docs.text:
These two pairs are pronounced exactly alike — only one letter differs. So the sound will not help you; a picture trick will.

Figure 42.3. One letter, one picture. A = a parked car, E = an envelope, PAL = a person, LE = a rule.
  • The bus was stationary, so I bought some stationery from the shop nearby. = The bus was not moving, so I bought pens and paper from the shop nearby.
  • Our principal never breaks her principles. = The head of our school never breaks her own rules.
  • The principal reason was cost. "principal" is also an adjective = main. It takes -al here too.

One letter, one picture

stationAry = At rest (not moving) · stationEry = Envelope (pen and paper). principAL = a person / main ("your PAL") · principLE = a rule (ruLE).

docs.title: 42.4 Noun or verb — affect/effect, advice/advise
docs.text:
In each of these pairs, one word is an action (a verb) and the other is a thing (a noun). Look at the sentence and ask whether it needs a verb or a noun — the answer comes by itself.

Figure 42.4. First the Action (affect), then the End result (effect) — in the alphabet too, A comes before E. Word What it is Example Listen affect verb — to influence Stress can affect your sleep. effect noun — a result The medicine had a quick effect. advice noun — a recommendation (the "s" sound) Can I give you some advice? advise verb — to give advice (the "z" sound) I advise you to wait.

A = Action, -ice = a thing

Affect = Action (verb), Effect = End result (noun). Advice is a thing like ice (noun, "s" sound); advise is an action (verb, "z" sound). Also, advice cannot be counted: "some advice", "a piece of advice" — never "an advice" or "advices".

docs.title: 42.5 One letter apart — lose/loose, quite/quiet, then/than, accept/except
docs.text:
In these pairs one letter moves around, and your eye skips over it while reading. Each pair has a small trick — attach the trick to the word, and the meaning comes by itself.

Figure 42.5. Then goes on the timeline, than goes on the weighing scale. Pair Meaning Trick lose / loose to misplace, to fail to win / not tight lose has lost an "o". loose has "oo" — baggy, with more room. quite / quiet fairly / silent quite = one syllable (kwait). qui-et = two syllables (kwai-yet) — speak softly in silence. then / than next / compared with thEn = timE, thAn = compArison. accept / except to agree to take / apart from accept = take it in. except = exit — keep it out.
  • These jeans are too loose. I must have lost weight! loose = "loos" (the "s" sound), lose = "looz" (the "z" sound). The speaking differs too.
  • The library is quite big, and it's always quiet. = Fairly big, and always silent.
  • I accept all the changes except the last one. = I agree to all the changes, apart from the last one.

Four tricks

lose has lost an "o" (to misplace) · loose = baggy · quiet = two syllables, silent · quite = fairly · thEn = timE · thAn = compArison · except = exit (out), accept = take in.

docs.title: 42.6 Direction pairs — borrow/lend, bring/take, say/tell
docs.text:
Hindi has separate words for "taking" and "giving", and for "bringing" and "carrying away" — yet in English these get mixed up, because we think with one word like "udhaar" or "le aao". The question here is: which way is the thing moving?

Figure 42.6. One book, two points of view: the giver lends , the receiver borrows . And wherever you are decides whether it is bring or take.
  • Could you lend me your pen? / Could I borrow your pen? Both are correct — but never "Can you borrow me…". The person who will give it = lend.
  • Please bring your ID card tomorrow, and take the old one home. Towards here (the office) = bring. Away to your home = take.
  • She told me the news and said it was a secret. tell + person (told me), say + the words (said it was…). "She said me" is wrong.

Which way is the thing moving?

lend = to give, borrow = to receive (lend to, borrow from). bring = towards the speaker, take = away from them. After tell comes a person (tell me), after say comes the words (say something).

docs.title: 42.7 Counting and placing — fewer/less, lie/lay
docs.text:
These two pairs look the most "advanced", but the rule is simple. For fewer/less the question is: can you count it? And for lie/lay: is something being put down, or are you lying down yourself?

Figure 42.7. Separate dots of people can be counted → fewer. Water just flows and cannot be counted → less. Verb Meaning Present Past Past participle lie to rest flat yourself lie · lying lay lain lay to put something down lay · laying laid laid lie to say something untrue lie · lying lied lied
  • I'm tired. I'm going to lie down for a bit. Lying down yourself = lie. No object follows it.
  • Please lay the files on my desk. Putting something down = lay + a thing (the files).
  • There were fewer cars today, so it took less time. You can count cars → fewer. You cannot count time → less.

Can you count it? Are you putting something down?

fewer + things you can count (fewer people), less + things you cannot count (less water). After lay there is always a thing (lay the table); after lie there is not (lie down). The biggest trap: the past of lie is "lay" — "Yesterday I lay in bed all day."

docs.title: 42.8 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
All of these mistakes are taken from real emails, WhatsApp messages and class notebooks. If even one of them is your habit, catch it today.

Common look-alike word mistakes

  • Wrong: Can you borrow me your charger?
  • Right: Can you lend me your charger? / Can I borrow your charger?

  • Why: The giver lends, the receiver borrows. Never "borrow me".

  • Wrong: I don't want to loose this chance.

  • Right: I don't want to lose this chance.

  • Why: To misplace or fail to keep = lose (one o). Loose = baggy — "loose shirt".

  • Wrong: The new rule will effect everyone.

  • Right: The new rule will affect everyone.

  • Why: A verb is needed after "will ___ everyone" → Affect = Action.

  • Wrong: My brother is taller then me.

  • Right: My brother is taller than me.

  • Why: After a comparison (taller) use than. "Then" is only for time.

  • Wrong: Your welcome!

  • Right: You're welcome!
  • Why: Open it up and read: "You are welcome" — it fits, so you're.

docs.title: 42.9 Practice — Look-alike words
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Match each word with its job.

A B affect verb — to give advice effect noun — a recommendation advise verb — to influence advice noun — a result Answer

affect — verb — to influence; effect — noun — a result; advise — verb — to give advice; advice — noun — a recommendation

A = Action (affect, verb), E = End result (effect, noun). Advice is a thing (noun), advise is an action (verb).

Exercise 2

One letter apart — match each word with the right meaning.

A B stationery head, main stationary a rule or belief principal pens, paper, files principle not moving Answer

stationery — pens, paper, files; stationary — not moving; principal — head, main; principle — a rule or belief

E = Envelope (stationery), A = At rest (stationary). The principal is your PAL; principLE = ruLE.

Exercise 3

Tap the wrong word in this sentence.

Can you borrow me your charger for an hour?

Answer

Wrong word: borrow.

Corrected: Can you lend me your charger for an hour?

The other person will give it, so they 'lend'. When you take it, say 'Can I borrow…?'

Exercise 4

Find the spelling trap.

I don't want to loose my job.

Answer

Wrong word: loose.

Corrected: I don't want to lose my job.

To misplace or fail to keep = lose (one o). Loose = baggy.

Exercise 5

The apostrophe is in the wrong place — tap that word.

The dog wagged it's tail happily.

Answer

Wrong word: it's.

Corrected: The dog wagged its tail happily.

Open it up and read: 'wagged it is tail'? Does not fit — so no apostrophe: its = belonging to it.

Exercise 6

I think ___ going to be late. The traffic is terrible.

  • they're
  • their
  • there
  • them
Answer

they're

Open it up and check: 'I think they are going to be late' — it fits, so they're.

Exercise 7

Everyone came to the party ___ Rahul. He was ill.

  • except
  • accept
  • expect
  • excuse
Answer

except

except = apart from (ex = exit, keep out). accept = to agree to take.

Exercise 8

Please ___ the baby gently on the bed.

  • lay
  • lie
  • lied
  • lain
Answer

lay

Putting a thing or a person down = lay + object (lay the baby). Lying down yourself = lie.

Exercise 9

There are ___ people here than yesterday.

Hint: People can be counted.

Answer

fewer

You can count them → fewer. 'less people' is a very common mistake; less is only for uncountable things (less water).

Exercise 10

Please be ___. The baby is sleeping.

Hint: Silent — the word with two syllables.

Answer

quiet

quiet (kwai-yet) = silent. quite (kwait) = fairly.

Exercise 11

Put the words in the right order.

Words: our / rain / heavy / will / affect / The / plans

Answer

The heavy rain will affect our plans

A verb is needed after 'will ___ our plans' — affect (A = Action).

Exercise 12

Say this polite request.

Answer

Say: Could I borrow your pen, please

You are the one taking → borrow. Stress the first part of 'borrow': BOR-row.

What to do next

Open your last ten emails or messages and look for just three things: your/you're, its/it's, then/than. Whenever you find a mistake, write it out once again using this chapter's trick.

docs.title: Chapter 23: Conditionals
docs.text:
If sentences — condition and result

A conditional sentence means: if this, then that. We say it in Hindi every day — "agar baarish hogi to match nahi hoga". English has four kinds of "if" sentences, and the only difference between them is one thing: how possible the idea is. A certain thing, a likely thing, an unlikely thing, and a thing that can never happen now. Four levels of possibility, four formulas. And one golden rule that gets broken more than any other: never "will" after "if".

In one line

A conditional sentence has two parts: the if-clause (the condition) and the main clause (the result). The order can be switched. If the "if" part comes first, a comma goes in the middle; if it comes second, no comma.

  • If it rains, we will stay home. "If" came first — so a comma.
  • We will stay home if it rains. "If" came second — no comma. The meaning is exactly the same.

docs.title: 23.1 Four branches — with their likelihood
docs.text:
The picture below shows each kind of "if" sentence with its likelihood. The fuller the bar, the more likely the idea.

Figure 23.1. Notice something neat: as the likelihood falls, the verb steps back one tense at a time. In English we say distant ideas in an older tense .

docs.title: 23.2 Zero conditional — what always happens
docs.text:
Here "if" means almost the same as "when". This is the form for rules, science, machines and habits. Both sides use the present simple.

  • If you heat water to 100 °C, it boils. It always happens — no doubt about it.
  • If the light turns red, the traffic stops. It is a rule. "When" would work here too.

docs.title: 23.3 First conditional — a real possibility
docs.text:
A real thing about the future. It may happen, or it may not. This is the form used most in speech — plans, promises, threats and warnings all use it.

Use Example Plan If the train is on time, we will reach by eight. Promise If you help me today, I will help you tomorrow. Warning If you touch that wire, you will get a shock. Condition / deal If you finish the work, you can go early.

The golden rule — no 'will' after 'if'

  • Wrong: If it will rain, we will cancel the match.
  • Right: If it rains, we will cancel the match.
  • Why: "Will" appears only once in a sentence, and it goes in the result part. The condition part stays in the present simple, even if the idea is about tomorrow.

The same rule holds with when, after, before, until, as soon as, unless.

Other words can replace will

In the result part of a first conditional you can also use can, may, should, must or a command: If you are tired, you should rest. If he calls, tell him I am busy.

docs.title: 23.4 Second conditional — imagination and advice
docs.text:
For things that are unlikely or imaginary in the present situation. See how the verb goes into the past, yet the idea is not about the past — it is about now. That is why it is also called the "unreal present".

  • If I won a lottery, I would buy a house for my parents. Winning a lottery is unlikely — so the past form, but the idea is about today.
  • If I were you, I would speak to the manager. The most polite and natural way to give advice.

'If I were' — not 'was' here

In the second conditional the form of "be" is were — with every subject. If I were rich… · If he were here… · If she were in charge… You will hear "If I was you" in casual talk, but the correct form, and the one that sounds better, is "If I were you" — and it is the standard sentence for giving advice all over the world.

docs.title: 23.5 Third conditional — what could not happen
docs.text:
Time that has passed and cannot be changed. It is used for regret, blame, or "if only it had been so". Each side steps one more tense back: had + V3 and would have + V3.

  • If I had left earlier, I would not have missed the train. I didn't leave early, and I missed the train. Nothing can be done now.
  • If she had told me, I could have helped her. Could / might can replace "would" — the shade of possibility changes.

docs.title: 23.6 Mixed conditional — two times in one sentence
docs.text:
Sometimes the condition is in the past and the result is today, or the other way round. Then the forms of both sides are mixed. It is advanced, but very useful — because real life works like this.

Type Formula Example Meaning Past condition → result today If + had + V3 , would + V1 If I had studied engineering, I would be an engineer today. I didn't study it, so I'm not an engineer today. Situation today → result in the past If + past simple , would have + V3 If I were braver, I would have told him the truth. I'm not a brave person, so I didn't tell the truth at that time.

docs.title: 23.7 Other forms of "if"
docs.text:
Word Meaning Example unless if not You will fail unless you work hard. as long as for as long as You can stay as long as you keep quiet. provided that only on the condition that I will sign it provided that you read it first. in case because it might happen Take an umbrella in case it rains. even if no matter whether Even if you apologise, he will not forgive you. otherwise or else Hurry up, otherwise we will be late.

No second 'not' with 'unless'

  • Wrong: Unless you do not hurry, you will miss the bus.
  • Right: Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.
  • Why: "Unless" already has a "not" hidden inside it (= if you do not hurry). Adding another "not" reverses the meaning.

docs.title: 23.8 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
Top conditional mistakes

  • Wrong: If I will go to Delhi, I will meet you.
  • Right: If I go to Delhi, I will meet you.

  • Why: No will in the condition part — use the present simple. Will appears only once in a sentence.

  • Wrong: If he would come, I would be happy.

  • Right: If he came, I would be happy.

  • Why: In the second conditional the "if" part takes the past simple, not would. Would belongs only in the result.

  • Wrong: If I was you, I would not accept that offer.

  • Right: If I were you, I would not accept that offer.

  • Why: Imaginary situations take "were", with every subject. This is the standard sentence for giving advice.

  • Wrong: If she would have told me, I would have helped.

  • Right: If she had told me, I would have helped.

  • Why: In the third conditional the condition is "had + V3". "Would have" belongs only in the result part.

  • Wrong: If you would study hard, you will pass.

  • Right: If you study hard, you will pass.

  • Why: Mixing two modals makes the sentence confusing. Stick to one plain formula.

  • Wrong: I will tell you if he will come.

  • Right: I will tell you if he comes.
  • Why: Even when "if" comes second, the rule is the same — present after if.

Four formulas, one line each

Zero: if + present, present First: if + present, will + V1 Second: if + past, would + V1 Third: if + had + V3, would have + V3 See — will/would never appear in the "if" part. This one point prevents 90% of mistakes.

docs.title: 23.9 Practice — Conditionals
docs.text:
Exercise 1

If it ___ tomorrow, we will cancel the picnic.

  • will rain
  • rains
  • would rain
  • rained

Hint: Which form comes after if?

Answer

rains

This is a first conditional — the if part takes the present simple (rains) and the result takes will. 'If it will rain' is the most common mistake.

Exercise 2

If I ___ a bird, I would fly to the mountains.

  • am
  • was
  • were
  • will be

Hint: It is imaginary — which form of be?

Answer

were

In the second conditional the form of 'be' is always 'were' — whether the subject is I, he or she. 'If I were a bird' is correct.

Exercise 3

If you had called me, I ___ at the station.

  • will come
  • would come
  • would have come
  • came

Hint: What is the result of a third conditional like?

Answer

would have come

Third conditional — about the past. The condition is 'had called', so the result is 'would have come'. It can't happen now; there is only regret.

Exercise 4

Which sentence is a zero conditional?

  • If I get time, I will call you.
  • If you mix blue and yellow, you get green.
  • If I were rich, I would travel.
  • If he had tried, he would have won.

Hint: Which one is always true?

Answer

If you mix blue and yellow, you get green.

A zero conditional has the present simple on both sides and is always true — the result of mixing colours never changes.

Exercise 5

If I ___ (have) more time, I would learn the guitar.

Hint: Second conditional — there is no time right now.

Answer

had

The second conditional takes the past simple after if. Writing 'had' doesn't mean the past — it means 'I don't have time now'.

Exercise 6

You will not pass ___ you work hard.

Hint: One word for 'if not'.

Answer

unless

'Unless' means 'if not'. The 'not' is already hidden inside it, so don't add another 'not'.

Exercise 7

If water ___ (freeze), it becomes ice.

Hint: Always true — zero conditional.

Answer

freezes

A zero conditional has the present simple on both sides. 'Water' is singular, so 'freezes' — it takes -s.

Exercise 8

There is one mistake in this sentence — tap the wrong word.

If I will get the job, I shall shift to Pune.

Answer

Wrong word: will.

Corrected: If I get the job, I shall shift to Pune.

Will/shall never appears in the if part. There the present simple stays — 'If I get'.

Exercise 9

Find the wrong word.

If I was the captain, I would change the batting order.

Answer

Wrong word: was.

Corrected: If I were the captain, I would change the batting order.

For an imaginary situation (I am not the captain) we use 'were', not 'was'.

Exercise 10

One word is wrong — catch it.

If she would have asked me, I might have helped her.

Answer

Wrong word: would.

Corrected: If she had asked me, I might have helped her.

In the third conditional the condition is 'had + V3'. 'If she would have' is wrong — it should be 'If she had'. Would/might have belong only in the result part.

Exercise 11

Put the words in order to make a second conditional.

Words: I / job / take / were / you / that / I / If / would

Answer

If I were you I would take that job

The standard form of advice — 'If I were you, I would…'. Remember: 'were' in the if part, 'would + V1' in the result.

Exercise 12

Match each conditional with its meaning.

A B If you heat ice, it melts not true now — imagination If I get leave, I will come impossible now If I had a car, I would drive always true If I had known, I would have come possible Answer

If you heat ice, it melts — always true; If I get leave, I will come — possible; If I had a car, I would drive — not true now — imagination; If I had known, I would have come — impossible now

Zero = a rule. First = a real possibility. Second = imagining today. Third = the past, which can no longer be changed.

Exercise 13

Now say this line aloud — the most useful sentence for giving advice.

Answer

Say: If I were you I would not worry about it

When speaking, say 'If I were you' in one breath — it sounds almost like a single phrase. This line is useful every day, at work and with friends.

What to do next

Do one thing today: write four sentences about yourself — one zero ("If I skip breakfast, I get a headache"), one first, one second and one third. Write about real things in your life. A sentence that is your own sticks in memory faster than any formula.

docs.title: Chapter 13: Conjunctions
docs.text:
Conjunction — the words that join

A conjunction is a word that joins two words, two phrases or two whole sentences. Without conjunctions, English turns into short, choppy lines — "I was tired. I went to work." Add a conjunction and the same idea flows — "I was tired, but I went to work." There are three families, and all three are in this chapter.

In one line

A conjunction joins words, phrases, or clauses together. A word that joins two parts is a conjunction. In Hindi, "aur, par, kyunki, agar, jab" do the same job.

  • Tea and biscuits. Two words are joined.
  • I called her, but she did not pick up. Two whole sentences are joined, on equal terms.
  • Because it was raining, we stayed home. One part depends on the other — this is a different family.

docs.title: 13.1 Three families — one map
docs.text: Figure 13.1. Three families: those that join on equal terms, those that make one part lean on the other, and those that come in pairs.

docs.title: 13.2 Coordinating conjunctions — FANBOYS
docs.text:
These seven words join two equal parts. Each part is complete on its own. To remember them, use FANBOYS — a word made from their first letters.

Word Meaning Example F — for because (formal) He stayed in, for it was raining. A — and adding She cooked and he cleaned. N — nor and not either He did not call, nor did he write. B — but contrast It is small but comfortable. O — or a choice Tea or coffee? Y — yet even so She was tired, yet she kept working. S — so as a result It was late, so we left.

When to use a comma

When you join two complete sentences, put a comma before the conjunction — I called her, but she was busy. When you join only two words or short parts, no comma — I called her but got no reply. Test: does a new subject come after the conjunction? If yes, use a comma.

After 'nor', the word order flips

✓ He did not call, nor did he write. ✗ He did not call, nor he wrote. After "nor" the order is like a question — the helping verb comes first, then the subject.

docs.title: 13.3 Subordinating conjunctions — the ones that make one part lean
docs.text:
These are the words that make one part depend on another. The part they introduce can't stand alone — it needs the other part to be complete.

  • Although he was ill, he came to class. "Although he was ill" on its own feels unfinished — you want to hear more. That is what dependence means.
What it shows Words Example Reason (because) because, since, as I left early because I was tired. Contrast (even so) although, though, even though, whereas, while Though she is young, she is wise. Condition (if) if, unless, provided that, in case Unless you study, you will fail. Time (when) when, while, before, after, until, as soon as, since Call me when you reach. Purpose (so that) so that, in order that, lest He ran fast so that he could catch the bus. Comparison than, as…as He is taller than his brother. Place where, wherever Sit where you like.

The position can change — just watch the comma

Because she was late, we started without her. (it comes first → use a comma) We started without her because she was late. (it comes second → no comma)

docs.title: 13.4 Correlative conjunctions — the ones that come in pairs
docs.text:
These come in pairs — one half at the front, the other in the middle. They have one fixed rule: the same kind of part on both sides. This is called "parallel structure".

Pair Meaning Example either … or this one or that one Either you come or I go. neither … nor not this and not that Neither Ram nor Shyam came. both … and the two together She is both clever and kind. not only … but also not just one — and more He not only sang but also danced. whether … or this possibility or that one I don't know whether he will come or not. no sooner … than the moment that No sooner did he arrive than it started raining. as … as equal to She is as tall as her mother.

Which subject does the verb agree with — the nearer one

With either…or and neither…nor, the verb agrees with the subject closest to the verb: ✓ Neither the boys nor the teacher was present. (teacher is nearer → was) ✓ Neither the teacher nor the boys were present. (boys are nearer → were)

Breaking parallel structure

  • Wrong: She not only plays the piano but also a good singer.
  • Right: She not only plays the piano but also sings beautifully.

  • Why: A verb came after "not only", so a verb must also come after "but also". A verb on one side and a noun on the other makes the sentence lopsided.

  • Wrong: He is interested in reading and to write.

  • Right: He is interested in reading and writing.
  • Why: Both sides of "and" need the same form — both gerunds, or both infinitives. Not a mix.

docs.title: 13.5 Conjunctive adverbs — they look like conjunctions but aren't
docs.text:
however, therefore, moreover, nevertheless, otherwise, hence, besides, meanwhile — these are adverbs, not conjunctions. So they can't join two sentences with just a comma. They need a semicolon or a full stop.

Comma splice — the most common mistake with 'however'

  • Wrong: I was tired, however I finished the work.
  • Right: I was tired; however, I finished the work.
  • Why: "however" isn't a conjunction, so it can't join two sentences by itself. There are two ways out: use a semicolon, or simply use "but". The second way is both easier and clearer.

docs.title: 13.6 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
Common Indian-English mistakes with conjunctions

  • Wrong: Although he was ill, but he came to work.
  • Right: Although he was ill, he came to work.

  • Why: One conjunction for one meaning. Hindi uses both in "halaanki… lekin", so both end up in the English sentence. In English, choose one: either "although" or "but". In the same way ✗ "Because he was late, so we left" is wrong too.

  • Wrong: As she was busy, so she didn't attend.

  • Right: As she was busy, she didn't attend.

  • Why: The same repetition — "as" has already given the reason, so "so" isn't needed. It comes straight from the Hindi "kyunki… isliye".

  • Wrong: Unless you don't study, you will fail.

  • Right: Unless you study, you will fail.

  • Why: "Unless" itself means "if not" — it already contains the negative. Adding another "don't" reverses the meaning.

  • Wrong: Neither he or his brother came.

  • Right: Neither he nor his brother came.

  • Why: Don't break the pair — "neither" goes with "nor", and "either" goes with "or". Swapping the partner is wrong.

  • Wrong: I don't know that she will come or not.

  • Right: I don't know whether she will come or not.

  • Why: "or not" goes with "whether", not "that". "if" also works, but "whether…or not" is clearer.

  • Wrong: She is more taller than her sister, but still she plays well.

  • Right: She is taller than her sister, but she plays well.

  • Why: Two mistakes: "more taller" is a double comparison, and "but still" repeats the idea — use "but" or "still", not both.

  • Wrong: She is my cousin brother and also my neighbour.

  • Right: He is my cousin and also my neighbour.

  • Why: "Cousin" is a complete word by itself — there is no need to add brother. The rest of the sentence was fine; "and also" works, although "and" alone would do the job.

  • Wrong: He don't have money and time.

  • Right: He doesn't have money or time.
  • Why: Two mistakes: "doesn't" is needed with "he", and in a negative sentence "or" replaces "and". In a negative, "and" joins the two things together, which changes the meaning.

docs.title: 13.7 A short summary
docs.text:
Family The two parts Words Comma Coordinating equal for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so yes, if joining two complete sentences Subordinating one leans on the other because, although, if, when, unless, since yes, if the dependent part comes first Correlative in pairs, parallel either…or, neither…nor, both…and, not only…but also usually not

Three fixed rules

1. One conjunction for one meaning — although or but, not both. 2. The same kind of part on both sides of a correlative pair. 3. however, therefore, moreover are not conjunctions — put a semicolon or a full stop before them.

docs.title: 13.8 Practice — Conjunctions
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Which sentence is correct?

  • Although he was tired, he kept working.
  • Although he was tired, but he kept working.
  • Although he was tired, so he kept working.
  • Although he was tired but so he kept working.

Hint: How many conjunctions for one meaning?

Answer

Although he was tired, he kept working.

'Although' has already shown the contrast, so adding 'but' repeats it. Hindi uses both in 'halaanki… lekin', which is why both slip into English.

Exercise 2

Neither Ravi ___ his friends were invited.

  • nor
  • or
  • and
  • but

Hint: Don't break the pair.

Answer

nor

'Neither' always has 'nor' as its partner, just as 'either' has 'or'. Swapping the partner makes the sentence wrong.

Exercise 3

___ you apologise, she will not talk to you.

  • Unless
  • If
  • Although
  • Because

Hint: The negative is already hidden inside this word.

Answer

Unless

'Unless' means 'if not' — the negative is already in it. That is why 'unless you don't apologise' would reverse the meaning.

Exercise 4

Which word is not in FANBOYS?

  • because
  • but
  • yet
  • nor

Hint: FANBOYS are the coordinating conjunctions.

Answer

because

'because' is subordinating — it makes one part lean on another. FANBOYS (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) join equal parts.

Exercise 5

I was very tired, ___ I finished the report. (a word showing contrast)

Hint: Two equal sentences, and the idea turns the other way.

Answer

but

Two complete sentences are joined on equal terms and the meaning turns the other way, so 'but'. 'however' gives the same meaning, but it would need a semicolon before it.

Exercise 6

She studied hard ___ she could clear the exam. (in order that)

Hint: You need to show a purpose.

Answer

so that

'so that' is used to show purpose. Plain 'so' would show a result, not a purpose — they are two different ideas.

Exercise 7

One word in this sentence is extra — tap it.

Because it was raining so we cancelled the match.

Answer

Wrong word: so.

Corrected: Because it was raining, we cancelled the match.

'Because' has already given the reason, so 'so' is extra. This comes straight from the Hindi 'kyunki… isliye'.

Exercise 8

Find the wrong word.

Unless you don't hurry you will miss the train.

Answer

Wrong word: don't.

Corrected: Unless you hurry, you will miss the train.

'Unless' already has a negative in it, so adding 'don't' makes two negatives and flips the meaning.

Exercise 9

One word is wrong.

I was tired, however I completed the task.

Answer

Wrong word: however.

Corrected: I was tired; however, I completed the task.

'however' is an adverb, not a conjunction — it can't join two sentences with just a comma. Use a semicolon, or simply use 'but'.

Exercise 10

Match each conjunction to its job.

A B because shows a condition although shows a purpose unless shows time so that shows a reason as soon as shows contrast Answer

because — shows a reason; although — shows contrast; unless — shows a condition; so that — shows a purpose; as soon as — shows time

You choose a subordinating conjunction by its meaning — reason, contrast, condition, purpose or time. Choosing the wrong one changes the whole meaning.

Exercise 11

Put the words in the right order — it uses a correlative pair.

Words: but / guitar / plays / only / sings / the / not / She / also

Answer

She not only sings but also plays the guitar

A verb came after 'not only', so a verb must also come after 'but also' — that is parallel structure. A verb on one side and a noun on the other makes the sentence lopsided.

Exercise 12

Say this line aloud — don't say 'but' after 'although'.

Answer

Say: Although it was raining we went out

When speaking, the Hindi habit makes 'but' slip out. Deliberately practising without 'but' breaks that habit.

What to do next

Take five of your own short sentences today and join them with conjunctions. Then read them back — notice how much better they sound. The last chapter of this section is Interjection.

docs.title: Chapter 28: Connected speech
docs.text:
Native speed English

You understand the English in books, but the English of Netflix, YouTube or a foreign colleague feels "too fast"? In fact they are not speaking fast — they join, squeeze and wear down their words. "Did you eat?" becomes "didja eat?". In this chapter we will learn the five rules behind this. The goal: to catch it when you listen, and to use it when you speak only as much as feels natural.

In one line

Native speech = weak forms + contractions + linking + elision + assimilation. The words are the same; only their edges get worn down. Don't think of it as "fast" — think of it as "joined up".

docs.title: 28.1 Why does it sound fast? — five rules
docs.text:
In Hindi we say almost every syllable in full. English is stress-timed: stressed words are long and clear, and the small words in between are quick and squashed (the basics are in the Rhythm and stress chapter). When small words are squashed, they stick to the words around them. These are the five ways:

Rule What happens Example Weak forms the vowel of a small word becomes "uh" for → fuh Contractions two words become one I would → I'd Linking the end of one word joins the next turn it off → tur-ni-toff Elision a sound disappears last night → las' night Assimilation two sounds blend into a new one did you → didja
  • What do you want to do? = What would you like to do? — it sounds like "Whaddaya wanna do?"
  • I don't know. = I have no idea. — often said as "I dunno."

docs.title: 28.2 Weak forms — small words, small sounds
docs.text:
Function words like to, for, of, and, can, was, them have two forms: strong (alone or stressed) and weak (in the middle of a sentence, with the schwa /ə/ "uh"). In a sentence, 90% of the time the weak form is used. If you say every "to" as "too", your English will sound heavy and stop-start.

Word Weak In a sentence Listen to /tə/ tuh I need to go. for /fə/ fuh It's for you. of /əv/ uhv, uh a lot of work and /ən/ un, n rice and dal can /kən/ kun I can help. was /wəz/ wuz It was late. them /ðəm/, /əm/ uhm Tell them. from /frəm/ fruhm She's from Kochi. her /ə/, /hə/ Ask her.

When is it strong?

The full (strong) form is used in three places: at the end of a sentence (Where are you from?), for stress/contrast, and when the word is said on its own. Everywhere else it is weak.

  • Who's it for? — It's fuh my mother. = The first "for" is strong, the second is weak: Who is it meant for? — It is meant for my mother.
  • What are you looking at? = What are you looking at? — "at" is said in full at the end.

docs.title: can or can't? — the biggest listening trap
docs.text:
In fast speech the "t" of can't is often not heard at all. So how do you tell the difference? Don't look for the "t" — listen to the vowel. can is weak and short (kun), and the stress falls on the next verb. can't is strong and long (British "kaant", American "kænt"), and it carries the stress itself.

Sentence What you hear Listen I can come. I kun COME. I can't come. I KAANT come. She can drive, but she can't park. kun DRIVE … KAANT park

docs.title: Contractions — the default English of speech
docs.text:
In speech, I am, do not, we will are almost always joined. Saying the full form is not wrong, but it sounds like emphasis: "I do not want it" = "I absolutely don't want it".

Full Contraction Listen I would / I had I'd we will we'll they are they're should have should've ("shuduv") it has / it is it's

✗

You should of told me.

✓

You should have told me. (said: should've)

have

docs.title: 28.3 Linking — words stick to each other
docs.text:
Native speakers talk without stopping between words. When one word ends in a consonant and the next begins with a vowel, the consonant becomes part of the next word. When two vowels meet, a light w or y slips in between. In the map below, each arc is one link.

Figure 28.1. Each arc is one link. A consonant jumps onto the next vowel; between two vowels a light w/y forms a bridge; and in British English a hidden r wakes up before the next vowel.
  • Turn it off. = Switch it off. — "tur-ni-toff"
  • Pick it up. = Lift it. — "pi-ki-tup"
  • Come on in. = Please enter. — "ku-mo-nin"
  • Check it out. = Have a look at this. — "che-ki-tout"
  • Go out and see. = Go outside and have a look. — "go-wou-tun see"
  • The idea is good. = It's a good idea. — "the-yidea-ris good" (British)

How to do it when speaking

Say a phrase as one long word: turnitoff, pickitup. Don't put a "glottal stop" (a little jerk) between words — let the air keep flowing. This makes your English smooth at once.

docs.title: 28.4 Elision — the sound that disappears
docs.text:
When a t or d is trapped between two consonants, it often vanishes in speech. To say the "t" in next day the tongue has to stop — so people simply say "nex day". Nothing changes in writing.

Written What you hear Listen next day nex' day last night las' night must be mus' be old man ol' man handbag hanbag I don't know I dunno first thing firs' thing
  • I went to bed late last night. = I went to bed late yesterday night. — "las' night"
  • She left the next day. = She left on the following day. — "nex' day"
  • I walked to the station. = I went to the station on foot. — the "t" of "-ed" and the "t" of "to" merge into one: "walk-tuh"

The past tense '-ed' seems to vanish

I walked to work and I walk to work sound almost the same in fast speech. So when listening, catch the tense from the context — words like yesterday, last week help. And in writing, never leave out "-ed". A vowel that disappears inside a single word (vegetable, comfortable) is covered in the Fix your pronunciation chapter.

docs.title: 28.5 Assimilation — didja, doncha, gotcha
docs.text:
Sometimes two sounds blend into a third sound. The most common case is when t, d, s, z is followed by the "y" of you / your / year. This is familiar to Hindi speakers — we also say "ye to" quickly as "yetto".

Figure 28.2. Four formulas, hundreds of phrases. This isn't laziness — the tongue simply takes the shortest route. Written What you hear Listen Did you eat? Didja eat? Don't you think so? Doncha think so? What are you doing? Wotcha doing? Would you like some tea? Wudja like some tea? I got you. Gotcha. Nice to meet you. Nice tuh meechoo. See you this year. See ya thi-shear.

A rule for your ears

t + you = ch, d + you = j, s + you = sh. Whenever you hear "-cha", "-ja" or "-shoo", think: a hidden you is behind it.

docs.title: 28.6 gonna, wanna, gotta — when to say them, when to write them
docs.text:
These are not "slang" but the real forms of speech — even news anchors say "gonna". But they have no place in writing (email, reports, exams). The simple rule: speak — fine; WhatsApp to a friend — fine; write at the office — never.

Spoken Full form Example Listen gonna going to (+ verb) I'm gonna call her. wanna want to / want a Do you wanna come? gotta have got to I gotta go. hafta have to We hafta wait. lemme let me Lemme see. gimme give me Gimme a minute. kinda kind of It's kinda cold. outta out of Get outta here!

✗

I'm gonna Delhi tomorrow.

✓

I'm going to Delhi tomorrow. / I'm gonna visit Delhi tomorrow.

going to + verb

✗

Dear Sir, I wanna apply for the post.

✓

Dear Sir, I would like to apply for the post.

Writing emails

Should you say them yourself?

Learn to hear them first. When speaking, "gonna" and "wanna" are natural in casual talk — but in an interview or presentation, going to and want to (with a weak "tuh") are the safest. Forcing "gotcha, wanna, lemme" into every line sounds like a film actor.

docs.title: 28.7 The melody of questions and lists
docs.text: The basic rules (statement ↘, yes/no question ↗, WH-question ↘) are in the Rhythm and stress chapter. Here are two cases where the melody changes the meaning itself.

docs.title: A choice or yes/no?
docs.text: How it is said Meaning Listen Tea ↗ or coffee ↘? Choose one of the two. Tea or coffee ↗? Would you like something to drink? (yes/no)

docs.title: Question tags — sure, or really asking?
docs.text:
• It's hot today, isn't it ↘ = A falling voice means "right?" — you only want agreement.
  • The meeting is at three, isn't it ↗ = A rising voice means you are really checking — you aren't sure.
  • I bought milk ↗, bread ↗, eggs ↗ and butter ↘. = In a list, the voice rises on each item and falls on the last = the list is finished.

Is the list finished or not?

When listening, if the voice stays up on the last item, the speaker still has more to add — don't cut in. When it falls, it is your turn.

docs.title: 28.8 A strategy for listening to fast English
docs.text:
Knowing the rules is half the work. The other half is training your ear. These five methods really work:

Method How 1. Catch the big words Not every word — only the stressed ones (nouns, verbs). "…MEET…STAtion…SIX" gives you the whole message. 2. Predict first Think from the situation about what is coming. In a shop, "wudja like a bag?" is almost certain. 3. Shadowing Play the audio and repeat half a second behind, with the same melody. 4. Dictation Listen to one line, write it, and compare. What you got wrong is your next rule. 5. Slow → fast 🐢 Understand it at slow speed, then at normal speed. Use English subtitles first, then switch them off.

Don't translate while listening

If you translate into Hindi in your head, you will miss the next sentence. Catch the stressed words and fill in the rest from context — native speakers do exactly the same.

✗

You missed one word → you stopped → you lost the whole message.

✓

You missed one word → keep listening → fill in from context → ask if you need to: "Sorry, did you say Tuesday?"

Phone and video calls

docs.title: 28.9 In real life — the office canteen
docs.text:
First play the 🔊 of each line without reading. Then look at the "what you hear" column — which rules were used?

Written What you hear Listen Hey, did you eat yet? Hey, didja eat yet? Not yet. I've got to finish this first. Not yet. I gotta finish this firs'. What are you working on? Wotcha workin' on? The report for Monday. It's kind of a mess. The report fuh Monday. It's kinda-uh mess. Do you want me to help? Dya wan' me tuh help? Let me look at it after lunch. Lemme look a-tit after lunch. Thanks! I'm going to get a sandwich and a cup of tea. Thanks! I'm gonna ge-ta sandwich un-a cuppa tea.

The daily 5-minute drill

Pick one line from the canteen conversation above. Listen three times, then shadow it, then write it without looking. Seven lines in a week — and your ear will start to hear "fast" English as "normal".

docs.title: 28.10 Practice — Native speed English
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Can the speaker stay for lunch?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

I can come to the meeting, but I can't stay for lunch.

  • No
  • Yes
  • Only on Friday
  • It isn't mentioned
Answer

No

can (kun) is short and squashed; can't is long and stressed. 'can't stay' = cannot stay.

Exercise 2

What is the speaker asking about?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

What are you going to do this weekend?

  • weekend plans
  • last weekend
  • work today
  • a holiday booking
Answer

weekend plans

'Wotcha gonna do' = What are you going to do — a future plan.

Exercise 3

What is the speaker offering?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Did you eat? I've got some leftover biryani if you want it.

  • leftover biryani
  • a cup of tea
  • a lift home
  • some money
Answer

leftover biryani

'Didja eat?' + 'I've got some leftover biryani' — the speaker is offering leftover biryani.

Exercise 4

What must they turn off?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

We need to leave at half past six. Don't forget your ticket, and turn off the lights.

  • the lights
  • the fan
  • the AC
  • the phone
Answer

the lights

'tur-noff the lights' — the consonant n joined the next vowel.

Exercise 5

What are they going to do?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Let me know if you want to come with us. We're going to grab a cup of coffee.

  • have coffee
  • have lunch
  • go shopping
  • go home
Answer

have coffee

'gonna grab a cuppa coffee' = going to grab a cup of coffee.

Exercise 6

When will the speaker call back?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

I've got to go now. I'll call you back in an hour.

  • in an hour
  • tonight
  • tomorrow
  • in ten minutes
Answer

in an hour

'i-na-nour' — three words joined by linking: in an hour.

Exercise 7

Write what you hear (in full, with correct spelling).

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

What do you want to do tonight?

'Whaddaya wanna do' — but in writing it is in full: What do you want to do.

Exercise 8

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

I don't know what he's going to say.

'I dunno what he's gonna say' — in writing it is don't know and going to.

Exercise 9

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

Could you turn it off, please?

'Cudja tur-ni-toff' — assimilation (could you) + linking (turn it off).

Exercise 10

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

We left the next day.

'nex' day' — the t seems to vanish, but it is written: next.

Exercise 11

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

Did you tell them about the party?

'Didja tell-uhm' — did you = didja, and them becomes a weak 'uhm'.

Exercise 12

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

She has got to finish it by Friday.

'She's gotta finish it' — in writing: has got to.

Exercise 13

Which sentence can naturally become 'gonna' in speech?

  • I'm going to call you later.
  • I'm going to Mumbai tomorrow.
  • She's going to the office.
  • We're going to the market.
Answer

I'm going to call you later.

gonna = going to + verb (future). Not with 'going to' that means travelling to a place.

Exercise 14

In fast speech, how do you tell 'can' from 'can't'?

  • the vowel of can't is long and stressed
  • listen only for the 't' sound
  • can is always said loudly
  • there is no difference
Answer

the vowel of can't is long and stressed

The 't' often disappears. can = kun (weak), can't = KAANT (strong, long).

Exercise 15

Which is right for a formal email?

  • I would like to apply for the post.
  • I wanna apply for the post.
  • I'm gonna apply for the post.
  • I gotta apply for the post.
Answer

I would like to apply for the post.

wanna/gonna/gotta are spoken forms, not for formal writing.

Exercise 16

Match the spoken form to the full form.

A B gonna have got to wanna let me gotta did you lemme going to didja want to Answer

gonna — going to; wanna — want to; gotta — have got to; lemme — let me; didja — did you

In listening you hear the short form; in writing, always the full form.

Exercise 17

Say it as one smooth phrase — don't pause between the words.

Answer

Say: Turn it off and pick it up

tur-ni-toff un pi-ki-tup — the consonant joins the next vowel, and 'and' becomes a weak 'un'.

What to do next

Choose a 2-minute YouTube clip you like and apply the 5-step strategy above. Then work on your speaking speed in the Fluency and filler words chapter, and give your ear a daily workout with the stories in the Listen and understand section.

docs.title: Chapter 52: CV, resume & LinkedIn
docs.text:
CV and LinkedIn — action verbs, bullet points, profile summary

A recruiter often spends only ten to fifteen seconds on a CV. In that time they are not looking for your "hard-working and sincere" personality — they are looking for what you did and what result it had. This chapter shows you how to structure a CV, how to write every bullet with one formula, what freshers should do, which old Indian CV habits to drop, and how to write your headline and About section on LinkedIn.

docs.title: 52.1 CV or resume — what is the difference?
docs.text:
In India the two words mean almost the same thing, and nobody will reject you for using the "wrong" word. Still, it is good to know the difference, especially if you are applying abroad.

Point Resume CV Length 1–2 pages UK/India: 2 pages · Academic: long Used mostly in US, Canada, private jobs in India UK, Europe, academic jobs What it contains Work chosen for this job Like a resume in the UK; the full record in academia Change it for each job? Yes Yes (less for an academic CV)

In one line

Fresher or under 10 years of experience: 1 page. More than that: 2 pages, no more. For every job, adjust your CV a little to use that job's words. Sending one CV everywhere = fitting nowhere.

  • Please find my CV attached. The simplest line for sending a CV by email. The full email is in Writing emails and the cover note is in Applications and messages.
  • I've tailored my resume to the job description. tailor = to sew to someone's measurements — here: to adjust it to fit the job.

docs.title: 52.2 Structure — from top to bottom
docs.text:
A recruiter's eye starts at the top left and moves down. So the most important things go at the top. People with experience put experience first; freshers put education and projects first.

Figure 52.1. A clean, one-page CV. The notes on the right tell you what goes in each part — and what does not. Section What to write What not to write Header Name, city, phone, email, LinkedIn Full address, a "Curriculum Vitae" heading Profile A 3–4 line introduction "Objective: To work in a reputed organisation…" Experience Role, company, years, 3–5 bullets A long list of every duty Skills Tools, languages, certifications "Hard-working, team player" Education Degree, college, year, CGPA The whole story from Class 5

docs.title: 52.3 Profile summary — a three-line introduction
docs.text:
The profile summary is the "trailer" of your CV. You write it without "I", in short sentences. The formula: who you are + how much experience + what you are especially good at + one big result + what you want next.

Summary formula

Role + years + specialty + one result + goal. "Data analyst with 3 years' experience in fintech. Built dashboards that cut reporting time by 50%. Looking to move into product analytics." Drop "I am" and "my" — on a CV they are understood without being written.

✗

Objective: To work in a challenging environment where I can utilise my skills for the growth of the organisation.

✓

Profile: Mechanical engineer with 2 years' experience in quality control at an auto-parts plant. Reduced defect rates by 18% through new inspection checklists. Seeking a process-improvement role.

who you are

what you have already done

  • Customer support lead with five years' experience in e-commerce. five years' experience — the apostrophe comes after the s (the experience of five years).
  • Final-year B.Com student with strong Excel and Tally skills. A fresher's profile — degree + skills.
  • Seeking an entry-level role in digital marketing. "Seeking" / "Looking to move into" — the closing goal line.

docs.title: 52.4 Action verbs — words that bring your work to life
docs.text:
"Responsible for" and "worked on" do not tell the recruiter what you yourself did. Start every bullet with a strong past-tense verb. For your current job the present tense is also fine — but keep to one tense within a single job.

Type of work Verbs Example Running a team led, managed, coordinated, mentored Led a team of six. Making something built, designed, developed, launched Launched a mobile app. Making things better improved, increased, streamlined Increased sales by 20%. Reducing reduced, cut, lowered, saved Cut costs by ₹4 lakh. Understanding analysed, identified, researched Identified a billing error. Communicating presented, negotiated, trained Trained 40 new staff. Solving problems resolved, fixed, solved Resolved 50+ tickets a day.
  • Led a team of six to deliver the project two weeks early. Delivered the project two weeks early with a team of six people.
  • Built an inventory tracker in Excel used by four branches. Made a stock tracker in Excel — four branches use it.
  • Reduced customer complaints by 30% in six months. Complaints went down by 30% in six months.
  • Negotiated a new contract with the courier partner, saving ₹2 lakh a year. A new contract with the courier company — the company saves ₹2 lakh a year.
  • Trained 25 interns on the new billing software. Taught 25 interns the new software.

No 'I' before the verb

Start the bullet straight with the verb: Led…, Built…, Reduced… — not "I led…", and definitely not "I was responsible for…". For stronger verbs, see the Verb upgrades chapter too.

✗

Responsible for handling social media.

✓

Grew Instagram followers from 2,000 to 15,000 in a year.

changed

docs.title: 52.5 The bullet formula — verb + task + result + number
docs.text:
Every good bullet is built from four pieces. Even if you have no number, always write the result — how many people, how much time, how much money, how many percent.

Figure 52.2. One line, four jobs: what you did (verb), on what (task), how (tool), and what result came out (with a number).
  • Automated monthly GST reports using Python scripts, cutting preparation time from three days to four hours. "cutting / saving / increasing…" — add the result with an -ing word.
  • Redesigned the onboarding emails, which increased trial sign-ups by 22%. You can also add the result with "which…".
  • Streamlined the loan approval process from ten steps to six, halving waiting time. streamline = to remove unnecessary steps and make something simpler; halve = to cut in half.
  • Resolved an average of 45 customer queries a day with a 95% satisfaction score. Even if nothing changed, say "how much" — how many per day, how satisfied.
  • Identified a pricing error that was costing the company ₹50,000 a month. Even a small discovery can be a big result — say it in money.

Where do you get the numbers?

Ask yourself: how many people? how much time? how much money? how many percent? If you have no exact number, give an honest estimate: about 30%, 50+ clients. An estimate is fine, a lie is not — you will be asked about it in the interview.

✗

Worked on sales.

✓

Closed 40 new B2B accounts in Gujarat, exceeding the annual target by 15%.

✗

Did coding of website and handled the testing part.

✓

Developed a college events website in React and tested it with 300 students before launch.

Developed

tested

✗

Increased sales. Am managing a team of 4. Prepared reports.

✓

Increased sales… · Managed a team of four… · Prepared reports…

docs.title: 52.6 Skills, education and a fresher's CV
Skills — show them, don't just say them
docs.text:
In the skills section, write things that can be tested: software, tools, programming languages, spoken languages, certificates. Show "hard-working, honest, team player" with proof in your bullets, not in the skills list.

  • Skills: Excel (pivot tables, VLOOKUP), SQL, Power BI, Tally ERP Use brackets to show what you can do inside a tool.
  • Languages: English (fluent), Hindi (native), Marathi (conversational) Give the level too — fluent / native / conversational / basic.

docs.title: Education — degree, college, year
docs.text:
• B.Tech in Computer Science, Shivaji Institute of Technology, Pune, 2025 · CGPA 8.4/10 Degree in a subject, college, year, score. Write the score "out of 10" — CGPA scales are different abroad.
  • Class XII (CBSE), 2021 · 91% Once you have some experience, you can drop Class X/XII.

docs.title: If you're a fresher — what goes in place of experience?
docs.text:
A fresher has no job, but does have work: internships, college projects, hackathons, freelance work, organising a college fest, NSS/NCC, giving tuitions. Write these with the same formula — verb + task + result + number. The order: Profile → Education → Projects / Internships → Skills → Achievements.

  • Organised a three-day tech fest with 1,200 participants and a ₹3 lakh budget. A college fest is real work too — budget, people, deadline.
  • Completed a two-month internship at a CA firm; reconciled accounts for 15 clients. reconcile = to check that two sets of accounts match.
  • Taught maths to 20 Class 8 students as a volunteer; average scores rose by 12 marks. Volunteer work + a result.

Before → after: a fresher's CV

Before

CURRICULUM VITAE · [photo] · Name: Rohit Kumar · Father's Name: Shri R. P. Kumar · DOB: 12/03/2003 · Marital Status: Unmarried · Objective: To work in a reputed company and grow with it. · Strengths: Hard-working, sincere, punctual. · Hobbies: Listening music, surfing net. · Declaration: I hereby declare that the above information is true to the best of my knowledge.

After

  • ROHIT KUMAR · Lucknow · 98xxx xxxxx · rohit.k@mail.com Only the name in the heading — not "Curriculum Vitae". The photo, father's name, DOB and marital status are gone.
  • Profile: BBA graduate with a summer internship in retail sales. Comfortable with Excel and customer calls. Seeking a sales-trainee role. A three-line profile instead of an objective.
  • Sales Intern, a fashion retail store, Lucknow (May–July 2024): Helped the store hit its monthly target by upselling accessories; added ₹60,000 in sales. Proof with a number, instead of writing "hard-working".

The declaration and hobbies were removed. The space that was freed went to projects and skills.

docs.title: 52.7 Common mistakes in Indian CVs
docs.text:
Many habits come from old government forms. In private companies and for jobs abroad they make a CV look dated — and some even raise the risk of discrimination. However, if the job ad itself asks for a photo or date of birth (some government, Gulf or airline jobs), then give them.

Remove all of these

  • Wrong: Photo, Father's Name, Date of Birth, Marital Status, Religion
  • Right: Name · City · Phone · Email · LinkedIn

  • Why: They have nothing to do with the work, and they increase unconscious bias. Save the space, show your work. (Give them only if the job ad asks.)

  • Wrong: I hereby declare that the above information is true to the best of my knowledge.

  • Right: (Nothing — delete the line.)

  • Why: This is the language of an affidavit. A private-sector CV does not need it; a government form that asks for it is a different matter.

  • Wrong: Heading: CURRICULUM VITAE / RESUME

  • Right: Heading: ANANYA IYER

  • Why: Everyone knows it is a CV. Make your name the biggest line.

  • Wrong: Hobbies: Listening music, surfing net, reading books.

  • Right: Interests: Long-distance running (2 half-marathons), Carnatic music.

  • Why: Grammar: listening to music. And "surfing net" says nothing. Write a hobby only when it says something about you — otherwise drop the section.

  • Wrong: I have done my B.Com from Delhi University.

  • Right: B.Com, University of Delhi, 2024
  • Why: A CV uses fragments, not full sentences. When speaking: I did / completed my B.Com at Delhi University.

Never lie, never copy-paste

Do not inflate your numbers. In an interview, any bullet can be questioned: "Walk me through how you cut the time by 50%." If you cannot explain a bullet for 2 minutes, do not keep it on your CV. To prepare, see Interview and office.

  • Walk me through your CV. The interviewer: explain your CV to me from the beginning.
  • Sure. I'll start with my current role and then go back. Your answer follows the CV's order too — newest first.

docs.title: 52.8 LinkedIn — headline and About
docs.text:
Your LinkedIn headline appears right under your name — it also shows up in search. Instead of the default "Student at XYZ College", say what you do and what you are good at.

Headline formula

Role | Specialty | Proof or value — "Data Analyst | SQL & Power BI | Turning sales data into weekly decisions". You get about 220 characters — keep it short and clear.

Weak headline Strong headline Looking for opportunities Final-year B.Tech (CSE) | Java & Spring Boot | 2 internships Working at ABC Pvt Ltd HR Executive | Campus hiring | Hired 120+ freshers in 2025 Hard-working professional Chartered Accountant | GST & audit | Helping SMEs stay compliant

docs.title: The About section — first person, like a conversation
docs.text:
Unlike a CV, the LinkedIn About section is written with "I" — as if you were introducing yourself to someone you have just met. Three short paragraphs: what you do, one or two results, and what kind of work or people you want to connect with.

  • I'm a data analyst who helps sales teams make faster decisions. The first line — what you do and who for.
  • At my current company, I built a weekly dashboard that replaced six manual reports. One result — the same bullet formula, but with "I".
  • I'm currently exploring roles in product analytics. Feel free to reach out. The last line — what you want. reach out = to contact someone.

✗

Myself Priya, a passionate and dynamic professional.

✓

I'm Priya, a UX designer who makes banking apps easier for first-time users.

Indian English habits

what you actually do

docs.title: 52.9 Practice — CV and LinkedIn
docs.text:
Exercise 1

How many pages should a fresher's CV be?

  • 1 page
  • 2 pages
  • 3 pages
  • The longer the better
Answer

1 page

Fresher or little experience: 1 page. 10+ years: up to 2 pages.

Exercise 2

Which bullet is the strongest?

  • Reduced invoice errors by 40% by adding Excel checks.
  • Responsible for invoices.
  • Worked on invoice-related tasks.
  • I was handling the invoice part.
Answer

Reduced invoice errors by 40% by adding Excel checks.

Verb + task + result + number — the others only state a duty.

Exercise 3

___ a team of six to deliver the project two weeks early. (past of lead)

Hint: Running a team — past tense.

Answer

Led / led

lead → led. CV bullets start straight with a past-tense verb.

Exercise 4

Find the mistake in the hobbies line.

Hobbies: listening music and travelling.

Answer

Wrong word: listening.

Corrected: Hobbies: listening to music and travelling.

listen needs 'to' after it: listening to music.

Exercise 5

Which of these should you keep in a private company's CV?

  • LinkedIn profile link
  • Father's name
  • Marital status
  • I hereby declare…
Answer

LinkedIn profile link

In the header, only name, city, phone, email, LinkedIn. The rest only if the job ad asks.

Exercise 6

Match the work to the right verb.

A B Ran a team Launched Reduced expenses Trained Built an app and released it Led Taught people Cut Answer

Ran a team — Led; Reduced expenses — Cut; Built an app and released it — Launched; Taught people — Trained

Every kind of work has a strong action verb.

Exercise 7

Find the weak part of this bullet.

Responsible for managing the company Instagram page.

Answer

Wrong word: Responsible.

Corrected: Grew the company Instagram page from 2,000 to 15,000 followers.

'Responsible for' is only a duty — you need an action verb and a result.

Exercise 8

What should NOT be in a profile summary?

  • To work in a challenging environment for the growth of the organisation
  • Years of experience
  • One big result
  • What you want next
Answer

To work in a challenging environment for the growth of the organisation

This is the old 'objective' — the same on every CV, it tells you nothing.

Exercise 9

Customer support lead with five ___ experience in e-commerce.

Hint: The experience of five years — where does the apostrophe go?

Answer

years' / years’

five years' experience — the apostrophe comes after the plural 'years'.

Exercise 10

Which is the best LinkedIn headline?

  • HR Executive | Campus hiring | Hired 120+ freshers in 2025
  • Looking for opportunities
  • Hard-working and sincere professional
  • Working at ABC Pvt Ltd
Answer

HR Executive | Campus hiring | Hired 120+ freshers in 2025

Role | Specialty | Proof — the headline formula.

Exercise 11

How do you write the LinkedIn About section?

  • First person — 'I'm…, I built…'
  • In fragments without verbs
  • Third person — 'He is…'
  • Just a list of skills
Answer

First person — 'I'm…, I built…'

A CV has no 'I'; the LinkedIn About uses 'I', like a conversation.

Exercise 12

From what you hear, which CV bullet is the best?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

In my last job I handled customer complaints. I set up a new ticket system, and our average response time came down from two days to six hours.

  • Set up a ticket system that cut response time from two days to six hours.
  • Responsible for customer complaints.
  • Handled complaints and tickets.
  • Worked in customer support for two days.
Answer

Set up a ticket system that cut response time from two days to six hours.

Verb (Set up) + task (ticket system) + result + number (2 days down to 6 hours).

Exercise 13

What did the response time become?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

In my last job I handled customer complaints. I set up a new ticket system, and our average response time came down from two days to six hours.

  • Six hours
  • Two days
  • Two hours
  • Six days
Answer

Six hours

'came down from two days to six hours' — it fell from 2 days to 6 hours.

Exercise 14

Listen to this bullet and write it down.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

Led a team of five to launch the app in three months.

Led (past of lead) + team + launch + number.

Exercise 15

Put the bullet in the right order.

Words: complaints / percent / in / 30 / customer / months / by / Reduced / six

Answer

Reduced customer complaints by 30 percent in six months

Verb + task + result (by 30 percent) + time.

Exercise 16

Find the tense mistake in one job's bullets.

Increased sales by 20%. Am managing a team of four.

Answer

Wrong word: Am.

Corrected: Increased sales by 20%. Managed a team of four.

A CV bullet has no helping verb like 'am', and one job uses one tense.

Exercise 17

Say one of your own bullets out loud, as in an interview.

Answer

Say: I reduced customer complaints by thirty per cent
