When speaking, add 'I' — you don't write it on a CV, but it is needed in conversation.

What to do next

Today, rewrite three bullets from your CV with the formula. Then see Applications and messages for the cover note you send with your CV, and Interview and office for interview preparation.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Determiners & quantifiers
docs.text:
Determiners — the small choice before a noun

Before we say a noun, we often put a small word in front that tells us which one, how many, or whose. In Hindi, "ye, wo, kuch, bahut, har, mera" do the job. In English the same "bahut" sometimes becomes many and sometimes much, and "kuch" sometimes becomes some and sometimes a few. This choice is made with one question — and that question is the key to this chapter.

In one line

A determiner comes before a noun and tells us which one, how many / how much, or whose. Articles (a, an, the) are determiners too — they have a separate chapter of their own.

  • These mangoes are sweet. = Which ones? The ones here. (which)
  • We don't have much time. = How much? Not a lot. (how much)
  • Is this your bag? = Whose? Yours. (whose)

docs.title: 7.1 The first question, always — can you count it?
docs.text:
Almost every determiner mistake comes from one place: we didn't stop to think whether the noun can be counted or not. Ask this question first, and half of the determiners will start to feel right by themselves.

Figure 7.1. First ask can you count it? , then one or many? — the determiner finds itself.

The very first question

Before choosing a determiner, ask: can the noun be counted or not? If countable, one or many — a, many, a few, these. If uncountable — much, a little, this. A few work with both: some, any, all, enough.

These words are not counted in English

work, advice, information, furniture, luggage, equipment, news, homework, traffic — they have no plural and don't take a / many. To count them, add a piece: a piece of advice, two pieces of furniture, an item of news. In Hindi we can say "do salaah", which is why mistakes happen here the most.

docs.title: 7.2 this, that, these, those — near or far
docs.text:
These four words work like a finger — they point at something. There are only two questions: is the thing near or far, and is it one or many.

Figure 7.2. The top row is for one thing, the bottom row for many. Near on the left, far on the right.

Near-far, one-many

this (near, one) · these (near, many) · that (far, one) · those (far, many). The determiner and the noun must agree in number: this book, these books.

'These type of' — the most common slip

  • Wrong: These type of questions are easy.
  • Right: This type of question is easy. / These types of questions are easy.
  • Why: "these" is plural, so the noun after it must be plural too — types. Or keep both singular.

docs.title: 7.3 some and any — sentences with "yes" and sentences with "no"
docs.text:
Both mean roughly "a certain amount", and both work with countable plurals and uncountables. The difference is in the mood of the sentence: a plain statement, a denial, or a question.

Sentence Word Example Plain (positive) statement some I bought some apples. Negative any I didn't buy any apples. General question any Do you have any questions? Offer or request some Would you like some tea? "Whichever" (in a positive) any Take any seat you like.

some vs any

some — in positive sentences, offers and requests. any — in negatives and general questions, or when it means "whichever". When offering tea we say "some" — because you hope the answer is "yes".

  • There isn't any milk in the fridge. = There is no milk at all in the fridge.
  • Can I have some water, please? It is a request, so we use "some" even though it is a question.

docs.title: 7.4 much, many, a lot of — how much and how many
docs.text:
The one Hindi "bahut" takes two roads in English. Here the countable question works directly — many for nouns you can count, much for a mass.

Word Goes with Used mostly Example many countable plural everywhere How many students came? much uncountable negatives, questions I don't have much money. a lot of / lots of both positives, conversation She has a lot of friends / patience. fewer countable comparisons fewer cars less uncountable comparisons less traffic

much vs many

many + countable plural (many books), much + uncountable (much water). In positive statements "a lot of" sounds more natural — it works with both.

'How much' or 'How many'?

How much is this shirt? — the price (money is uncountable). How many shirts did you buy? — the number.

docs.title: 7.5 a few / few, a little / little — the magic of "a"
docs.text:
Here one small "a" changes the whole mood. With "a" the statement is positive — there is a little, and it is enough. Without "a" the statement is negative — there is very little, and the lack is felt.

Figure 7.3. With a the glass looks half full. Without a the glass looks empty.

'a' is positive, without 'a' is negative

a few (countable) / a little (uncountable) = there is some, and it is enough. few / little = there is very little, and it is a problem. I have a little money → we can have tea. I have little money → that's difficult.

  • She has a few good friends in Chennai. She has some good friends — she is not alone.
  • Few people came to the meeting. Hardly anyone came — fewer than expected.

docs.title: 7.6 each, every, both, either, neither, all
docs.text:
These words talk about a group — the whole group, one of two, or everyone one by one. Their biggest feature: after them the noun is definitely singular or plural.

Figure 7.4. Except for both , all of these take a singular noun. all is for three or more — all students, all water.

Group determiners

each, every, either, neither + singular noun + singular verb (Every student has a book). both = two, plural. all = three or more, or a whole mass (all the milk).

Word When Example each two or more, focus on one by one Each player gets a shirt. every three or more, the whole group I walk every day. both the two of them Both my parents work. either one of the two You can sit on either side. neither not one of the two Neither answer is correct. all three or more, or uncountable All the shops were closed.

If you add 'of', add 'the / my / these' too

each student ✓ each of the students ✓ each of students ✗ both my hands ✓ both of my hands ✓ neither of them** ✓

docs.title: 7.7 enough, and my / your / their
docs.text:
Two small determiners that you use every day. enough says "as much as is needed", and the possessive determiners say "whose".

enough — before a noun, after an adjective

enough* money · enough chairs — before a noun. old enough · fast *enough — after an adjective or adverb. ✗ He is enough old. ✓ He is old enough to vote.

Pronoun Possessive determiner Example I my my phone you your your idea he / she his / her his car, her office it its The dog wagged its tail. we / they our / their our house, their children

Two things that catch people out

1. Only one determiner with one noun: the my book ✗ → my book ✓. 2. its = belonging to it (possessive), it's = it is. The company changed its name. "his / her" depends on the gender of the owner, not of the thing: Priya's brother = her brother.

docs.title: 7.8 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
The most common Indian-English mistakes with determiners

  • Wrong: I have many works today.
  • Right: I have a lot of work today.

  • Why: "work" (tasks to do) is uncountable — it has no plural and doesn't take "many". "works" means pieces of art or writing: the works of Premchand.

  • Wrong: Each students must bring an ID card.

  • Right: Each student must bring an ID card.

  • Why: After each and every the noun is always singular. If you want a plural, say "each of the students" or "all students".

  • Wrong: Can you give me some informations?

  • Right: Can you give me some information?

  • Why: information, advice, furniture, luggage — all uncountable. They never take -s.

  • Wrong: There are less buses on Sunday.

  • Right: There are fewer buses on Sunday.

  • Why: You can count buses, so "fewer". "less" is for uncountables: less traffic, less noise.

  • Wrong: I don't have some money.

  • Right: I don't have any money.
  • Why: In a negative sentence use "any". "some" is for positive statements and offers.

docs.title: 7.9 Practice — Determiners
docs.text:
Exercise 1

How ___ sugar do you take in your tea?

  • much
  • many
  • few
  • a few

Hint: Can you count sugar?

Answer

much

Sugar is uncountable — we don't say 'two sugars' this way. With an uncountable we use 'much', and 'How much' asks for the quantity.

Exercise 2

Don't worry, we still have ___ time before the train leaves.

  • a little
  • little
  • a few
  • few

Hint: The meaning is positive — there is a little time, and it is enough.

Answer

a little

Time is uncountable, so it is the 'little' pair. And 'don't worry' shows the meaning is positive — so with 'a': a little.

Exercise 3

Look at ___ birds on that far tree!

  • those
  • these
  • this
  • that

Hint: They are far away, and there are many.

Answer

those

'that far tree' — the things are far away, and 'birds' is plural. Far + many = those.

Exercise 4

I asked two shopkeepers, but ___ of them had the charger.

  • neither
  • either
  • both
  • none

Hint: Not one of the two.

Answer

neither

There were two people and neither had a charger — 'not one of the two' = neither. 'none' is used more for three or more.

Exercise 5

Is there ___ milk left in the fridge?

Hint: It is a general question.

Answer

any

In general questions and negatives we use 'any'. 'some' would come when we are offering or requesting something.

Exercise 6

Every child ___ a gift at the party. (get — present simple)

Hint: After 'every', singular.

Answer

gets

'every child' is singular, so the verb is singular too — gets. In Hindi 'har bachche ko' may sound plural, but in English 'every' takes one at a time.

Exercise 7

Tap the wrong word in this sentence.

Sir, I have many works to finish today.

Answer

Wrong word: works.

Corrected: Sir, I have a lot of work to finish today.

'work' (tasks) is uncountable — it has no 'works', and 'many' doesn't go with it. Say 'a lot of work' or 'much work'.

Exercise 8

Find the wrong word.

Each students has a locker.

Answer

Wrong word: students.

Corrected: Each student has a locker.

After 'each' the noun is always singular — student. The verb 'has' is already singular, and that is correct.

Exercise 9

There is one mistake — find it.

She gave me some useful advices about the interview.

Answer

Wrong word: advices.

Corrected: She gave me some useful advice about the interview.

'advice' is uncountable and has no plural. To count one, say 'a piece of advice'.

Exercise 10

Match each determiner to the right noun.

A B many minutes much patience a few chairs a little furniture Answer

many — chairs; much — furniture; a few — minutes; a little — patience

You can count chairs and minutes — many, a few. You can't count furniture and patience — much, a little.

Exercise 11

Make the sentence in the right order.

Words: to / not / is / old / enough / He / drive

Answer

He is not old enough to drive

'enough' comes after the adjective — old enough. 'enough old' is wrong.

Exercise 12

Say this line — don't add -s at the end of 'information'.

Answer

Say: Could you give me some information about the course

You have to break the 'informations' habit by saying it aloud. It is a request, so 'some' — and 'information' with no -s.

What next?

Make a small list of your own: work, advice, information, luggage, furniture, news. Every time you say one of these words, stop and think — "can I count it?" In a week this question will become a habit.

docs.title: Chapter 54: Easy stories
docs.text:
Short stories — listen, understand, write

You have studied the grammar and learnt the words — but when someone speaks English, it all sounds fast. There is only one cure: listen a little every day. This chapter has six short stories — Priya's first day, a phone lost on a train, the Sunday market, a surprise party, a rainy day and the new neighbours. Listen to each story first, then open the transcript. At the end, in the quiz, you will answer by listening and write by listening (dictation).

docs.title: 54.1 How to listen — before, during, after
docs.text:
A good listener does not just press 🔊 and start. They listen in three steps: before listening they make a guess, while listening they catch only what matters, and after listening they check against the transcript.

Figure 54.1. Before → While → After. The most important rule: do not look at the transcript for the first two listens. You are training your brain to get meaning from the sound.

Listen twice, then read

The first time, listen for the gist (roughly what happened); the second time, for the detail (names, times, places). Use the transcript only in the third step. You don't need to understand every word — you need to understand the story.

Keep five questions in mind for every story. This "story map" fits every story — and most quiz questions come from it.

Figure 54.2. Story map: Who, Where, When, What happened, How did they feel. If you can fill in even three of them after the first listen, you are on the right track.

docs.title: 54.2 Story 1 — Priya's first day
docs.text:
Priya lives in Pune, and it is the first day of her new job. The story is in the past simple (woke, wore, took, was). Listen: how was Priya feeling in the morning, and who sat with her at lunch?

Word Meaning nervous worried or a little afraid manager boss, the person in charge introduced made people meet each other colleagues people who work with you wore had clothes on (past of wear)

🎧 Listen to the whole story

  • Story 1 — Priya's first day First time: what happened? Second time: catch the names and times.
Transcript

Priya is twenty-three years old, and she lives in Pune. Last Monday was her first day at a new job. She woke up at six o'clock and wore her new blue kurta. She took a bus to the office. She was a little nervous. Her manager, Mr Desai, was very kind. He showed her the office and introduced her to the team. At lunch, two colleagues, Neha and Farhan, sat with her. In the evening, Priya called her mother. She said that she loved her new job.

  • She was a little nervous. She was slightly worried. "a little" = a small amount — not very.
  • He showed her the office and introduced her to the team. He took her around the office and helped her meet the team. In "showed her", "her" is said very softly — "sho-der".
  • She said that she loved her new job. She told her mother she really liked her new job. By evening, her nervousness had turned into happiness.

The -ed sound is short

The -ed of the past simple is said in three ways: called (d), walked (t), wanted (id). The sound is soft — listen carefully. This is the sound that gets dropped most often in dictation.

docs.title: 54.3 Story 2 — The lost phone
docs.text:
Arjun takes the Mumbai local train to the office. One day, in the crowd, his phone goes missing. Listen: where was the phone found, and how did Arjun feel when he could not find it?

Word Meaning crowded full of people got off left a train or bus exit the way out explained told someone clearly what happened thanked said "thank you"

🎧 Listen to the whole story

  • Story 2 — The lost phone Notice: the story starts in the present (takes — a daily habit), then moves into the past.
Transcript

Arjun takes the local train to work every day. On Friday, the train was very crowded. He got off at Dadar station and walked to the exit. Then he put his hand in his pocket. His phone was not there! He felt terrible. He ran back, but the train was gone. A railway policeman asked him what was wrong, and Arjun explained. The policeman called the next station. An hour later, a kind woman brought the phone to the station office. She found it under a seat. Arjun thanked her again and again.

  • Arjun takes the local train to work every day. Arjun goes to work by local train daily. "every day" = a daily habit → present simple.
  • His phone was not there! He felt terrible. The phone was missing! He felt very bad. "terrible" = very bad — here, fear and worry.
  • She found it under a seat. The phone was lying below a seat. "found it" runs together and sounds like "faun-dit".

A listening mistake — words that run together

  • Wrong: He gotto fat Dadar station.
  • Right: He got off at Dadar station.
  • Why: In speech, "got off at" becomes one long sound — "go-to-fat". When you hear a strange word, ask yourself: which two or three short words have joined together?

docs.title: 54.4 Story 3 — Sunday at the market
docs.text:
Every Sunday, Meena goes to the vegetable market with her grandfather. The story has both the present simple (habit) and the past simple (what happened today). Listen: why do they go early, and what did Meena buy today?

Word Meaning fresh new, not old or stale stalls small open shops, carts expensive costs a lot of money instead in place of that heavy weighs a lot

🎧 Listen to the whole story

  • Story 3 — Sunday at the market Watch the numbers: what time did they leave, and how much were the mangoes?
Transcript

Every Sunday, Meena and her grandfather go to the vegetable market near their house. They leave early, at seven, because the vegetables are fresh in the morning. Grandfather always buys tomatoes, onions and green chillies. Meena likes the fruit stalls. Today she wanted mangoes, but they were very expensive. They cost two hundred rupees a kilo! So she bought bananas instead. Grandfather talked to all the shopkeepers, because he knows everyone. They walked home slowly with two heavy bags.

  • They leave early, because the vegetables are fresh in the morning. They set out early since vegetables are fresh in the morning. After "because" you always get the reason — the answer to a "why?" question is right here.
  • So she bought bananas instead. So she bought bananas in place of mangoes. When you hear "instead", know that the plan changed.
  • Grandfather talked to all the shopkeepers, because he knows everyone. Grandfather chatted with every shopkeeper, since he knows them all. "knows" is present — it is always true.

because = the door to the reason

When the question is "Why…?", wait for because or so in the story. After because comes the reason; after so comes the result. These two little words give you half the answer to "why" on their own.

docs.title: 54.5 Story 4 — The birthday surprise
docs.text:
It is Rahul's birthday, but it seems everyone has forgotten. The story has a twist — pay attention to "but" and "when". Listen: why was Rahul sad in the afternoon, and where was the party?

Word Meaning busy having a lot to do terrace the flat roof of a house shouted said something very loudly planned decided in advance how to do something surprise something happy you did not expect

🎧 Listen to the whole story

  • Story 4 — The birthday surprise After "but" comes the worry; after "When he opened the door" comes the twist.
Transcript

Saturday was Rahul's birthday, but his wife, Anjali, said she was busy all day. Rahul was a bit sad. In the evening, she asked him to come up to the terrace for some fresh air. When he opened the door, the lights came on. All his friends were there! They shouted happy birthday and laughed. There was a big chocolate cake on the table. Anjali planned the party for two weeks, and Rahul knew nothing about it. He said it was the best birthday of his life.

  • His wife said she was busy all day. Rahul was a bit sad. His wife said she would be busy all day, and Rahul felt a little low. The reason and the feeling come one after the other — that is the answer to "why was he sad?"
  • When he opened the door, the lights came on. The moment he opened the door, the lights switched on. "came on" = began to work (for lights, TV).
  • It was the best birthday of his life. No other birthday in his life had been better. The whole journey of the story: from sadness to joy.

docs.title: 54.6 Story 5 — A rainy day
docs.text:
Heavy rain in Kolkata — schools closed, and a fun day for a little girl. This story is full of time words: on Tuesday morning, in the afternoon, in the evening. Listen: why was Tara at home, and what did the children make?

Word Meaning heavily very strongly, in large amounts closed shut, not open paper boats toy boats folded from paper sailed made a boat move on water the power went off the electricity stopped

🎧 Listen to the whole story

  • Story 5 — A rainy day The time words make a map: morning → afternoon → evening.
Transcript

On Tuesday morning, it rained very heavily in Kolkata. The streets were full of water, and the schools closed. Ten-year-old Tara was happy. She stayed at home with her little brother, Babu. They made paper boats and sailed them in the water near the gate. Their mother made hot pakoras and tea. In the afternoon, the power went off, so Tara read a story book by the window. In the evening, the rain stopped and the sky turned orange.

  • The streets were full of water, and the schools closed. There was water everywhere on the roads, so the schools shut. The reason Tara stayed at home is in this very line.
  • Tara read a story book by the window. Tara read a storybook next to the window. Here "read" is past, and it is said "red" — not "reed".

read — spelt the same, said differently

  • Wrong: Tara reads a story book. (misheard in dictation)
  • Right: Tara read a story book.
  • Why: Past "read" sounds like "red". The story is in the past (rained, stayed, made), so it cannot be "reads" here. The tense of the rest of the story is a clue too.

docs.title: 54.7 Story 6 — The new neighbour
docs.text:
In this story "I" is speaking — the storyteller is a character in the story. Listen: who is the new neighbour, what does he do, and what did he bring?

Word Meaning neighbour a person who lives next door or nearby moved into came to live in a new home doorbell the bell at the door nurse a person who cares for sick people invited asked someone to come

🎧 Listen to the whole story

  • Story 6 — The new neighbour First the past (moved, saw, rang), then the present (is, works, teaches) — today's facts.
Transcript

Last week, a new family moved into the flat next to ours. On the first day, I saw a lot of boxes on the stairs. The next morning, the doorbell rang. It was a young man with a plate of sweets. His name is Joseph, and he is from Kochi. He works at a hospital as a nurse, and his wife teaches music. My mother invited them for dinner on Sunday. Now our children play together every evening.

  • It was a young man with a plate of sweets. A young man stood at the door holding a plate of sweets. "a plate of" runs together and sounds like "uh-PLAY-tuv".
  • He works at a hospital as a nurse. His job at the hospital is nurse. "as a" = in the role of. This is the most common way to say what job someone does.
  • Now our children play together every evening. Now our children play together every evening. The end of the story — the families became friends.

Listen for the small words too — a, the, of

In fast English, a, the, of, to, and are said very softly ("uh", "thuh", "uv"). In dictation, if a sentence feels incomplete, add these. a plate of sweets → "uh PLAY-tuv sweets".

docs.title: 54.8 Getting ready for dictation — five listening mistakes
docs.text:
The quiz has four dictations: you will listen and type the whole sentence. Every word is checked separately. These are the mistakes that Hindi speakers make most often — know them in advance.

Common mistakes in dictation

  • Wrong: He walk to the exit.
  • Right: He walked to the exit.

  • Why: The final "t" of "walked" blends into the next word "to". Is the story in the past? Then add -ed to the verb.

  • Wrong: They cost two hundred rupee.

  • Right: They cost two hundred rupees.

  • Why: More than one = plural -s. When you hear "two hundred", the noun after it will be plural, even if the -s is not clearly heard.

  • Wrong: Mangoes cost fifteen rupees a kilo.

  • Right: Mangoes cost fifty rupees a kilo.

  • Why: In fif-TEEN the stress is on the last part and the "n" is long; in FIF-ty the stress is at the start and the final "ty" is short. The same difference applies in 13/30, 14/40, 16/60.

  • Wrong: She took bus to office.

  • Right: She took a bus to the office.

  • Why: Hindi has no articles, so the ear "skips" them. In English a noun is often preceded by a / the — after dictation, check in front of every noun.

  • Wrong: The sky turn orange in the evening.

  • Right: The sky turned orange in the evening.
  • Why: In "turned orange" the -ed and the "o" run together: "tern-DOR-inj". When two vowels or two consonants meet, the end of one word becomes the start of the next.
  • Fifteen. Fifty. Fifteen rupees. Fifty rupees. Hear the difference: fif-TEEN vs FIF-ty.
  • Thirteen. Thirty. Fourteen. Forty. The same pattern — in -teen the stress is at the back, in -ty at the front.
  • He walked to the exit. He called his mother. "walkt" and "cawld" — two sounds of -ed.

The three-step method for dictation

1. Listen to the whole thing; write nothing. 2. Listen again and write. 3. Check with grammar: tense, -s, a/the. Ear + grammar = a correct dictation.

docs.title: 54.9 Practice — Short stories
docs.text:
Exercise 1

What matters most the first time you listen to a story?

  • The gist — roughly what happened
  • The meaning of every word
  • Reading the transcript at the same time
  • Memorising the spelling

Hint: Remember Before → While → After.

Answer

The gist — roughly what happened

Gist the first time, detail the second time. The transcript only at the end.

Exercise 2

How did Priya feel in the morning?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Last Monday was Priya's first day at a new job. She woke up at six o'clock and wore her new blue kurta. She took a bus to the office. She was a little nervous.

  • a little nervous
  • very angry
  • bored
  • sick
Answer

a little nervous

'She was a little nervous' — nervous = worried or slightly afraid.

Exercise 3

Who sat with Priya at lunch?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Her manager, Mr Desai, was very kind. He showed her the office and introduced her to the team. At lunch, two colleagues, Neha and Farhan, sat with her.

  • Neha and Farhan
  • Mr Desai
  • her mother
  • nobody
Answer

Neha and Farhan

Mr Desai showed her the office, but at lunch 'two colleagues, Neha and Farhan, sat with her'.

Exercise 4

Where did the woman find Arjun's phone?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

The policeman called the next station. An hour later, a kind woman brought the phone to the station office. She found it under a seat.

  • under a seat
  • in his pocket
  • at the exit
  • on the platform
Answer

under a seat

'She found it under a seat' — under = below.

Exercise 5

How did Arjun feel when his phone was not in his pocket?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

He got off at Dadar station and walked to the exit. Then he put his hand in his pocket. His phone was not there! He felt terrible.

  • terrible
  • happy
  • sleepy
  • calm
Answer

terrible

'He felt terrible' — he felt very bad. Nobody stays calm when a phone goes missing.

Exercise 6

Why do Meena and her grandfather go to the market early?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Every Sunday, Meena and her grandfather go to the vegetable market near their house. They leave early, at seven, because the vegetables are fresh in the morning.

  • because the vegetables are fresh
  • because the market closes at eight
  • because it is hot later
  • because Meena has school
Answer

because the vegetables are fresh

'because the vegetables are fresh in the morning' — the reason comes after because.

Exercise 7

What did Meena buy?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Meena likes the fruit stalls. Today she wanted mangoes, but they were very expensive. They cost two hundred rupees a kilo! So she bought bananas instead.

  • bananas
  • mangoes
  • tomatoes
  • green chillies
Answer

bananas

She wanted mangoes, but they were expensive — 'so she bought bananas instead'.

Exercise 8

Why was Rahul a bit sad?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Saturday was Rahul's birthday, but his wife, Anjali, said she was busy all day. Rahul was a bit sad.

  • His wife said she was busy.
  • He was ill.
  • He lost his job.
  • It was raining.
Answer

His wife said she was busy.

On his birthday his wife said she was busy all day — that is why he was sad.

Exercise 9

Where was the party?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

In the evening, she asked him to come up to the terrace for some fresh air. When he opened the door, the lights came on. All his friends were there!

  • on the terrace
  • in a restaurant
  • at his office
  • in the garden
Answer

on the terrace

'come up to the terrace' — the terrace is the flat roof. His friends were there when he opened the door.

Exercise 10

Why did Tara stay at home?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

On Tuesday morning, it rained very heavily in Kolkata. The streets were full of water, and the schools closed. Ten-year-old Tara was happy. She stayed at home with her little brother.

  • The schools closed.
  • She was ill.
  • It was a holiday.
  • Her mother was away.
Answer

The schools closed.

The rain filled the streets with water — 'the schools closed'.

Exercise 11

What did Tara and Babu make?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

She stayed at home with her little brother, Babu. They made paper boats and sailed them in the water near the gate. Their mother made hot pakoras and tea.

  • paper boats
  • pakoras
  • tea
  • a kite
Answer

paper boats

The children made paper boats; their mother made the pakoras and tea.

Exercise 12

What is Joseph's job?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

His name is Joseph, and he is from Kochi. He works at a hospital as a nurse, and his wife teaches music.

  • a nurse
  • a music teacher
  • a doctor
  • a shopkeeper
Answer

a nurse

'He works at a hospital as a nurse.' It is his wife who teaches music.

Exercise 13

What did the new neighbour bring?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

The next morning, the doorbell rang. It was a young man with a plate of sweets.

  • a plate of sweets
  • a lot of boxes
  • flowers
  • a cake
Answer

a plate of sweets

'a young man with a plate of sweets' — the boxes were on the stairs on the first day.

Exercise 14

How much do the mangoes cost?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Those mangoes are very good. They cost fifty rupees a kilo.

  • fifty rupees
  • fifteen rupees
  • five rupees
  • five hundred rupees
Answer

fifty rupees

FIF-ty — the stress is at the start. In fif-TEEN it would be at the end.

Exercise 15

Match each story word to its meaning.

A B nervous costs a lot of money crowded lives next door expensive worried or a little afraid neighbour full of people Answer

nervous — worried or a little afraid; crowded — full of people; expensive — costs a lot of money; neighbour — lives next door

These four words were the keys to the stories — Priya nervous, the train crowded, the mangoes expensive, Joseph the neighbour.

Exercise 16

Listen and write.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

She took a bus to the office.

Notice 'a bus' and 'the office' — both articles.

Exercise 17

Listen and write.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

His phone was not there.

'was not' — past simple; 'was' for one thing.

Exercise 18

Listen and write.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

They walked home slowly with two heavy bags.

Don't forget the -ed of 'walked' (a t sound) and the -s of 'bags'.

Exercise 19

Listen and write.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

The streets were full of water, and the schools closed.

'were' (plural streets), 'full of', and the -ed of 'closed'.

Exercise 20

Say this line as Rahul — as if it were your own birthday.

Answer

Say: It was the best birthday of my life

Say both b's clearly in 'best birthday'; 'of my' runs together as 'uv-my'.

Next step

Listen to one story three times every day — first with no text, then with the text, then speaking along with it (shadowing). When all this feels easy, move on to Everyday stories: an office meeting, a customer-care call and a friend's voice note.

docs.title: Chapter 53: Essays & reports
docs.text:
Essays and reports — intro, body, conclusion, IELTS style too

At school we memorised essays — starting with "Since ancient times, man has…", three pages long. The essay in the real world is the opposite: short, clear, and with one opinion. This chapter gives you the whole structure — the thesis, the PEEL paragraph, three kinds of essay, linking words for essays, a formal voice, a straightforward introduction to IELTS Writing Task 2, an annotated model essay, and the format of an office report.

docs.title: 53.1 The map of an essay — intro, body, conclusion
docs.text:
Every essay has three parts. The intro starts with the big topic and moves towards your opinion (the thesis). Two or three body paragraphs give evidence for that opinion. The conclusion restates the opinion and thinks a little bigger.

Figure 53.1. The intro goes from wide to narrow (topic → thesis); the conclusion goes from narrow to wide (opinion → big picture). In the middle, each body paragraph is one PEEL.

The four-paragraph essay

Intro (2–3 lines) → Body 1 → Body 2 → Conclusion (2–3 lines). This is enough for an essay of 250–300 words. Every body paragraph = one main idea. For the basics of a paragraph (topic sentence, one idea), see From sentence to paragraph.

docs.title: 53.2 The thesis statement — one line for the whole essay
docs.text:
The thesis is the last line of the intro. It tells the reader what you think and what you will prove. A weak thesis just repeats the topic; a strong thesis takes a clear position — and often gives the reason too.

Weak Strong This essay will discuss online classes. Online classes are a useful addition to school, but they cannot replace a real teacher. Pollution is a big problem. The most effective way to cut urban pollution is to make public transport faster, not just cheaper. There are many advantages and disadvantages. Although working from home saves time, its effect on teamwork outweighs that benefit.
  • While technology has made learning easier, it cannot replace a good teacher. Use "While…" to accept the other side, then give your own opinion — balance in one line.
  • I firmly believe that cities should invest more in cycling lanes than in flyovers. In an opinion essay, "I believe" is perfectly fine.

✗

Since ancient times, education has been a burning question in today's modern world.

✓

In many Indian cities, students now spend more time on coaching than in school.

real and current

docs.title: 53.3 PEEL — the formula for a body paragraph
docs.text:
Every body paragraph moves in four steps. Once you remember this formula, the "what do I write?" problem is gone.

Step Job Words to begin with Point The one main idea of the paragraph Firstly, … · One major advantage is … Explain Why? How? This is because … · This means that … Evidence Example, data, experience For instance, … · A recent survey found … Link Tie it back to the thesis Therefore, … · This shows that …

One PEEL paragraph — spot the pieces

  • [P] One major benefit of online classes is flexibility. Point — one idea, stated clearly.
  • [E] Students can watch lessons at any time, which helps those who work part-time or live far from a college. Explain — how this is a benefit.
  • [E] For instance, a student in a small town can now attend lectures from a university in Delhi without moving there. Evidence — one solid example.
  • [L] This shows that online learning can widen access to higher education. Link — connect it back to the thesis.

PEEL in one line

What (Point) → why (Explain) → proof (Evidence) → so what (Link). A paragraph without evidence is just an opinion. No data in the exam? One realistic example is enough — "For instance, in my city…".

docs.title: 53.4 Three kinds of essay — spot the question type
docs.text:
Before you write, identify the type of question. If you answer the wrong type, you lose marks even with good English. The type is hidden in the last line of the question.

Type What the question looks like Structure Opinion To what extent do you agree or disagree? Opinion in the intro → 2 reasons → opinion again Discussion Discuss both views and give your opinion. View A → View B → your opinion (in the intro and conclusion) Problem–solution What are the causes? What can be done? Causes / problem → solution Advantages–disadvantages Do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages? Advantages → disadvantages → which is heavier
  • Some people think that all university education should be free. To what extent do you agree? Opinion — a clear yes, no or partly, and why.
  • Some believe children should start school at four, while others think seven is better. Discuss both views. Discussion — both sides, then your opinion.
  • Many young people in cities feel lonely. Why is this, and what can be done about it? Problem–solution — both the causes and the solutions.

Answer every part of the question

In "Discuss both views and give your opinion", you must give your opinion. In "Why is this, and what can be done?", you must answer both questions. Miss one part = a direct loss in Task Response.

docs.title: 53.5 Linking words — by function
docs.text:
In From sentence to paragraph we saw however, therefore, for example. An essay needs a few more — especially for accepting a point and then pushing back (concession) and for reporting other people's opinions. Each word has its own grammar, and that is the most important thing.

Function Words Grammar Accept, then push back although, while, whereas + a full clause Accept, then push back despite, in spite of + noun / -ing Other people's opinions It could be argued that…, Critics claim that… + clause Result consequently, as a result, thus start of the sentence + comma Emphasis in particular, indeed, above all anywhere in the sentence Ending In conclusion, On balance, Overall first line of the conclusion
  • Although metro fares are high, the service saves commuters a great deal of time. although + clause (subject + verb).
  • Despite the high fares, many people prefer the metro. despite + noun. (Not "despite of"!)
  • It could be argued that exams measure memory rather than understanding. Presents the other opinion politely — useful in a discussion essay.
  • Fuel prices rose sharply. Consequently, more people switched to electric scooters. consequently = as a result of this (a little more formal than therefore).
  • On balance, the benefits of the scheme outweigh its costs. On balance = after weighing everything up — a good way to begin a conclusion.

✗

Although the metro is expensive, but it is fast.

✓

Although the metro is expensive, it is fast. / The metro is expensive, but it is fast.

although

but

✗

Despite of the rain, the match continued.

✓

Despite the rain… / In spite of the rain…

despite

in spite of

docs.title: 53.6 Formal register — the voice of an essay
docs.text:
In an essay you are not talking to a friend. No contractions (don't → do not), no slang, and slightly more formal words in place of short spoken ones. But remember: formal does not mean heavy, it means clear.

Spoken In an essay a lot of / lots of many, a large number of, a great deal of kids children, young people get better improve go up / go down rise / fall, increase / decrease things factors, issues, aspects really bad serious, harmful I think I believe, In my view (in an opinion essay)
  • A large number of young people now rely on social media for news. The formal version of "Lots of kids get news from Insta".
  • Air quality tends to improve when private vehicles are restricted. "tends to" — not every time, but often. Hedging sounds good in an essay.
  • This issue is becoming increasingly serious in smaller cities as well. "increasingly serious" instead of "really bad".
  • Several factors contribute to this problem, the most important being cost. "several factors" instead of "many things".

Hedge — don't put 'always' on everything

tend to, can, may, often, in many cases — these words make your point honest and stronger. Better than "Social media always destroys students": "Social media can distract many students."

✗

In my opinion, I think that it doesn't work.

✓

In my view, this approach does not work.

docs.title: 53.7 IELTS Writing Task 2 — at a glance
docs.text:
IELTS Writing has two tasks. Task 2 is an essay — almost the same in Academic and General Training. It carries more weight than Task 1, so spend more time on it. (For full details of the exam format, see IELTS, TOEFL and your level.)

Figure 53.2. Skipping the plan is the biggest mistake. Five minutes of planning saves ten minutes while you write.

docs.title: How the band is awarded — four criteria in plain language
docs.text:
Criterion In plain language Task Response Did you answer every part of the question? Is your opinion clear? Did you explain your ideas and give examples? Coherence & Cohesion Is the order of paragraphs sensible? One paragraph = one idea? Are the linking words correct and used only as much as needed? Lexical Resource Do you use a range of words and correct word pairs (collocations)? Is the spelling right? Grammatical Range & Accuracy A mix of short and long sentences? Few mistakes?

The fixed rules of IELTS Task 2

40 minutes, at least 250 words, all four criteria carry equal weight. Fewer than 250 = a penalty. Memorised lines and copying words from the question = a loss. Exam rules can change — always check the current details on the official IELTS website.

docs.title: 53.8 A model essay — understand it piece by piece
docs.text:
Below is an opinion essay (about 270 words). Under each paragraph there is a note on what it is doing. First listen with 🔊, then read.

Question

  • Some people believe that public transport in cities should be free for everyone. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Type: opinion ("To what extent…"). You must give a clear opinion.

Introduction

  • In many Indian cities, roads are choked with private vehicles, while buses and metro trains often run below capacity. Some argue that the best solution is to make public transport free for all. While this idea has clear benefits, I believe that free travel should be offered only to those who need it most, rather than to everyone. Line 1: background (something real and current). Line 2: the question in your own words (paraphrase). Line 3: the thesis — "While… I believe…" — a balanced but clear opinion.

Body 1 — accept the other side

  • Admittedly, free public transport could significantly reduce traffic and pollution. If travel cost nothing, many commuters would leave their cars and motorbikes at home, which would mean cleaner air and shorter journeys. It would also help families on low incomes, who often spend a significant part of their earnings on daily travel. For example, Luxembourg made all public transport free in 2020, partly to tackle congestion. This suggests that, in principle, removing fares is a serious option for crowded cities. P: Admittedly… reduce traffic (the concession). E: If travel cost nothing… (second conditional). E: the Luxembourg example. L: This suggests that…

Body 2 — the reason for your own opinion

  • However, offering free travel to everyone would be extremely expensive. Ticket sales pay for a large share of maintenance and new routes, so governments would have to raise taxes or cut services. In a country with limited public funds, this money might be better spent on schools or hospitals. As a result, buses might become older and more crowded, which would discourage the very people the policy aims to attract. It would therefore be more sensible to target support at students, senior citizens and low-income workers. P: However… expensive. E: where the ticket money goes. E: the result — older, more crowded buses. L: It would therefore… — back to the thesis.

Conclusion

  • In conclusion, although free public transport for all is an attractive idea, its cost would be difficult to sustain. On balance, I believe that free or discounted passes for those in need, combined with more frequent and reliable services, would achieve the same goals far more effectively. The opinion again, in new words. No new reasons — just a summary and a way forward.

What to borrow from the model

Borrow the structure, not the lines: background → paraphrase → thesis, accept → push back, and the "On balance" ending. Examiners recognise memorised lines — and give no marks for them. Words copied from the question are also not counted in the word count.

docs.title: 53.9 Reports — headings, findings, recommendations
docs.text:
An essay gives an opinion; a report gives information and suggestions. You have to write reports at the office, in college projects and in some exams (such as Cambridge B2 First). A report is recognised by its headings, short paragraphs, and clear recommendations at the end.

Heading What goes in it Ready-made openings Title What the report is about Report on the staff canteen Introduction Purpose and method The purpose of this report is to… Findings What was found (data) It was found that… · The majority of… Conclusion A one-line summary Overall, … Recommendations What should be done It is recommended that… · The company should…

Mini report — staff canteen

  • Introduction. The purpose of this report is to assess staff satisfaction with the office canteen. It is based on an online survey of 120 employees conducted in March. The purpose + where the data came from.
  • Findings. The majority of respondents, 68 per cent, said the food was good value. However, nearly half complained about long queues between one and two pm. Only a few mentioned hygiene. Words for numbers: the majority of, nearly half, only a few. No opinions — only facts.
  • Recommendations. It is recommended that lunch be served in two shifts and that a pre-order option be added to the office app. "It is recommended that + subject + base verb (be served)" — formal. A simpler version: "The company should serve lunch in two shifts."

docs.title: Ready-made report lines
docs.text:
• This report is based on interviews with twenty shop owners. Where the data came from — in the Introduction.
  • A significant number of respondents said they would pay more for faster delivery. respondents = the people who answered the survey.
  • Only a small minority were unhappy with the timings. the majority ↔ a small minority — numbers put into words.
  • The management should consider extending the opening hours. The simple form of a recommendation — should + consider + -ing.

How to recognise a report

Headings + facts + suggestions. No opinions in Findings; in Recommendations use "should" or "It is recommended that…". Essay = "I believe…"; report = "It was found that…".

✗

I think the canteen is very bad and people are very angry.

✓

Nearly half of the respondents complained about long queues at lunchtime.

docs.title: 53.10 Practice — Essays and reports
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Where does the thesis statement go in an essay?

  • The last line of the intro
  • The last line of the conclusion
  • The first line of Body 1
  • In the title
Answer

The last line of the intro

The intro starts with background and ends with the thesis.

Exercise 2

Match each letter of PEEL to its job.

A B Point an example or data Explain tying it back to the thesis Evidence the main idea of the paragraph Link why and how Answer

Point — the main idea of the paragraph; Explain — why and how; Evidence — an example or data; Link — tying it back to the thesis

What → why → proof → so what.

Exercise 3

'Discuss both views and give your opinion.' — which type is this?

  • Discussion
  • Opinion
  • Problem–solution
  • Report
Answer

Discussion

Both views + your own opinion = a discussion essay.

Exercise 4

One word must be removed — which one?

Although the metro is expensive, but it is very fast.

Answer

Wrong word: but.

Corrected: Although the metro is expensive, it is very fast.

although and but cannot be used together — choose one.

Exercise 5

___ the heavy rain, the match continued. (not although)

Hint: A concession word that comes before a noun — without 'of'.

Answer

Despite / despite / In spite of / in spite of

despite / in spite of + noun. 'Despite of' is wrong.

Exercise 6

Find the wrong word.

Despite of the cost, many families buy smartphones.

Answer

Wrong word: of.

Corrected: Despite the cost, many families buy smartphones.

'of' does not come after despite.

Exercise 7

What is the best essay version of 'lots of kids'?

  • a large number of children
  • plenty kids
  • a lot of kiddos
  • many many kids
Answer

a large number of children

Formal register: kids → children, lots of → a large number of.

Exercise 8

What is the minimum number of words in IELTS Writing Task 2?

  • 250
  • 150
  • 200
  • 350
Answer

250

Task 2: at least 250 words, about 40 minutes. (Task 1: 150 words.)

Exercise 9

What does IELTS 'Coherence and Cohesion' check?

  • Paragraph order and linking
  • Spelling and vocabulary
  • Whether you answered the question
  • Accent
Answer

Paragraph order and linking

Coherence = order and clarity; cohesion = linking words and connection.

Exercise 10

The purpose of this ___ is to assess staff satisfaction with the canteen.

Hint: The document with headings, findings and recommendations.

Answer

report

'The purpose of this report is to…' — the standard opening of a report.

Exercise 11

What do you write in the Findings section of a report?

  • What the survey found
  • Your own feelings
  • What should be done
  • The question again
Answer

What the survey found

Findings = facts. What should be done = Recommendations.

Exercise 12

Which part of an essay is this?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

In conclusion, although free public transport is an attractive idea, its cost would be difficult to sustain. On balance, targeted support would work better.

  • Conclusion
  • Introduction
  • Body paragraph
  • Title
Answer

Conclusion

'In conclusion… On balance…' — the opinion again, no new point.

Exercise 13

According to this report, how many people think the food is good value?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

The majority of respondents, sixty-eight per cent, said the food was good value. However, nearly half complained about long queues at lunchtime.

  • 68 per cent
  • Nearly half
  • A few
  • All of them
Answer

68 per cent

'The majority of respondents, sixty-eight per cent' — 68%.

Exercise 14

What was people's biggest complaint?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

The majority of respondents, sixty-eight per cent, said the food was good value. However, nearly half complained about long queues at lunchtime.

  • Long queues at lunchtime
  • The price
  • Hygiene
  • The taste
Answer

Long queues at lunchtime

'nearly half complained about long queues at lunchtime.'

Exercise 15

Listen and write.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

Although technology has made learning easier, it cannot replace a good teacher.

Although + clause, then a comma, then the main clause — the classic thesis form.

Exercise 16

Put the report line in the right order.

Words: be / It / shifts / served / is / two / recommended / in / that / lunch

Answer

It is recommended that lunch be served in two shifts

It is recommended that + subject + base verb (be served).

Exercise 17

What is unnecessary in this line from an essay?

In my opinion, I think online exams are unfair.

Answer

Wrong word: think.

Corrected: In my opinion, online exams are unfair.

'In my opinion' and 'I think' mean the same — choose one.

Exercise 18

Say a thesis out loud with conviction.

Answer

Say: I firmly believe that cities need better public transport

In an opinion essay, 'I firmly believe that…' states a clear opinion.

What to do next

This week, write one essay in 40 minutes — any of the four questions above. Then compare it with the model: is the thesis clear? Does every body paragraph have PEEL? For essay vocabulary see Work and the world, and to understand your level see IELTS, TOEFL and your level.

docs.title: Chapter 30: Everyday conversations
docs.text:
Everyday conversations — ready answers

There is no grammar in this chapter. It has ready-made lines — sentences you can memorise and use from tomorrow: at the shop, in an auto, at the doctor's, on the phone, in a restaurant, and when asking for directions. Here is the real secret: fluent people do not build every sentence from scratch — they have ready-made pieces that come out at once. Every line has a 🔊. Listen, speak, memorise.

How to study

Do not do the whole chapter in one sitting. One day = one situation. Today do only "the shop" — say its five lines 10 times. Tomorrow "the auto". In six days you will have six situations ready, and you will never forget them.

docs.title: 30.1 At the shop — buying
docs.text:
Figure 30.1. On the left are your lines; on the right are the shopkeeper's lines that you need to recognise . Listening is half of a conversation — that is why both sides are given. You want to English line Listen Ask if they have it Excuse me, do you have this in blue? Ask the price How much is this? Say you are only browsing I'm just looking, thanks. Ask for a smaller or bigger size Do you have a smaller size? Ask to try it on Can I try this on? Ask for a lower price Can you do it for a little less? Say it is too expensive That's a bit more than I wanted to spend. Decide to buy it I'll take it. Ask if they accept cards Do you take cards? Ask for the bill Could I have the receipt, please? Ask about exchanging Can I exchange it if the size is wrong?

A full mini-dialogue — the shop

Speak both sides. First your line, then the shopkeeper's line too — this gets your ear ready.

  • You: Excuse me, do you have this shirt in medium? = Is this shirt available in medium?
  • Shopkeeper: Let me check. Yes, here you go. "Here you go" = here, take it. A very common line.
  • You: Thanks. How much is it? = What is the price?
  • Shopkeeper: It's nine hundred and fifty. 950. Note: "nine hundred AND fifty" — there is an "and" in the middle.
  • You: Could you do nine hundred? I'll take two. = Will you take 900 if I buy two? The politest way to bargain.
  • Shopkeeper: All right, nine hundred each. Cash or card? "each" = for one piece. Notice it is not just "nine hundred".
  • You: Card, please. And could I have the receipt? receipt = "ri-SEET", the P is silent.

docs.title: 30.2 Auto and cab
docs.text:
You want to English line Listen Ask if they will go to the station Will you go to the railway station? Ask the fare How much will it be? Ask for the meter Could you go by the meter, please? Say the fare is too high That's too much. Two hundred is fine. Ask how long it takes How long will it take? Ask the driver to go faster Could you go a bit faster? I'm running late. Ask the driver to go slower Could you slow down a little, please? Ask the driver to stop You can stop here, thanks. Tell the driver where to turn Take a left at the next signal. Say you have no small change Sorry, I don't have change. Ask if you can pay online Can I pay online? Ask for the AC Could you turn on the AC, please?

A full mini-dialogue — the cab

  • You: Hi, are you going towards the airport? = Are you heading in the direction of the airport?
  • Driver: Yes, hop in. It'll take about forty minutes. "Hop in" = get in. "About forty" = around forty.
  • You: Perfect. My flight is at six, so I have time. = The flight is at six, so there is enough time.
  • Driver: There's some traffic near the bridge, is that okay? = The road is busy near the bridge. Is that fine?
  • You: That's fine. Take whichever route is faster. = Use the quicker road, whichever it is.
  • You (on arrival): You can drop me at gate three. Thanks a lot. = Please leave me at gate three. "Drop me" = let me get out.

docs.title: 30.3 At the doctor's
docs.text:
A pattern that always works

"I have [problem] + for [how long]." I have a bad headache. It's been two days. What it is, and since when — these are the only two things a doctor needs.

Problem English line Listen Fever I have a fever. It started last night. Headache I've had a headache since yesterday. Cough and cold I have a cough and a blocked nose. Stomach pain I have a stomach ache, mostly after eating. Feeling dizzy I feel dizzy when I stand up. Feeling weak I've been feeling weak and tired all week. Pain in one place It hurts here, right below the knee. Cannot sleep I'm not sleeping well these days. Allergic to a medicine I'm allergic to penicillin. Already taking a medicine I'm already taking a tablet for blood pressure. What the doctor will ask In simple words Listen How long have you had this? Since when do you have it? Does it hurt when I press here? Do you feel pain when I push on this spot? Are you on any medication? Are you taking any medicine now? Take this twice a day after meals. Two times a day, after you eat. Come back if it doesn't improve in three days. If you are not better in three days, visit again.

Always ask these two questions

How many times a day should I take this? Before food or after food?

docs.title: 30.4 Phone call
docs.text:
The phone feels the hardest — you cannot see the face, and the sound cuts in and out. That is why memorising lines helps the most here.

Purpose English line Listen Answering a call Hello, this is Ravi speaking. Asking who is calling May I know who's calling? Asking for someone Could I speak to Mr Sharma, please? Asking someone to wait Hold on a second, please. Saying the person is not there He's not at his desk right now. Offering to take a message Can I take a message? The sound is cutting out Sorry, you're breaking up. Could you say that again? The network is bad The line is bad. Let me call you back. Wrong number I think you have the wrong number. Talking later Can I call you back in ten minutes? Ending the call Thanks for your time. Have a good day.

Three common phone mistakes

  • Wrong: "Hello, myself Ravi."
  • Right: Hello, this is Ravi.

  • Why: "Myself Ravi" is not a sentence in English. On the phone, always use "This is…".

  • Wrong: "Who is this?" (blunt, a little rude)

  • Right: May I know who's calling?

  • Why: "Who is this?" sounds harsh. "May I know…" says the same thing, but politely.

  • Wrong: "I didn't get you." (it sounds like you did not recognise the person)

  • Right: Sorry, I didn't catch that.
  • Why: "Didn't catch that" has a clear meaning: I could not hear or understand what you said.

docs.title: 30.5 In a restaurant
docs.text:
You want to English line Listen Ask for a table for two A table for two, please. Ask for the menu Could we see the menu, please? Ask what is good here What would you recommend? Ask how spicy it is Is this very spicy? Ask for less spice Could you make it less spicy, please? Place your order I'll have the paneer tikka, please. Ask if it is vegetarian Is this vegetarian? Ask for water Could we get some water, please? The food has not come Excuse me, our order hasn't come yet. They brought the wrong dish Sorry, I think this isn't what I ordered. Ask for a takeaway box Could you pack the rest, please? Ask for the bill Could we have the bill, please?

A full mini-dialogue — the restaurant

  • Waiter: Good evening. How many of you? = How many people are in your group?
  • You: Three, please. Somewhere away from the AC, if possible. "If possible" = only if it can be done. These two words make any request softer.
  • Waiter: Sure. Are you ready to order? = Do you want to tell me what you would like to eat now?
  • You: Give us a couple of minutes. What would you recommend? "A couple of minutes" = two or three minutes.
  • Waiter: The butter chicken is very popular here. = Many people order it here.
  • You: We'll have that, two rotis and a plain rice. And could you make it less spicy? The pattern for ordering: "We'll have…" + a list. Completely natural.
  • You (later): That was lovely, thanks. Could we have the bill? = The food was very good. "Lovely" is a very natural word for food.

docs.title: 30.6 Asking for and giving directions
docs.text: You want to English line Listen Start by asking for help Excuse me, could you help me with directions? Ask where the metro is How do I get to the metro station? Ask how far it is Is it far from here? Ask if you can walk Can I walk there, or should I take an auto? Say you are lost I think I'm lost. I'm looking for Lake Road. Ask them to repeat Sorry, could you say that once more, slowly? The answer you will get In simple words Listen Go straight for about five minutes. Keep walking forward for five minutes. Take the second left. Turn into the second street on the left. It's right opposite the bank. It is directly across from the bank. It's next to the chemist. It is right beside the medical store. You'll see it on your right. It will be on your right-hand side. You've come too far — turn around. You went past it — go back.

docs.title: 30.7 Small phrases that work everywhere
docs.text:
Line When to say it Listen Excuse me… Before you speak to a stranger — always. Sorry to bother you. When you interrupt someone. No worries. "It's nothing" — when someone says sorry. That's all right. "It's fine, forget it." Thanks a lot — that helps. Thanking someone for their help. Appreciate it. A short, natural thank-you. Take care. Saying goodbye — to a friend or someone you know.

Four lines we say, but that sound odd in English

  • Wrong: What is your good name?
  • Right: May I know your name?

  • Why: "Good name" is a word-for-word copy of the Hindi "shubh naam". English does not say this.

  • Wrong: Please do the needful.

  • Right: Could you take care of this, please?

  • Why: "Do the needful" does not tell the other person what to do. Say it clearly.

  • Wrong: I am having two brothers.

  • Right: I have two brothers.

  • Why: "Have" does not take -ing when it means "to own or possess".

  • Wrong: Where you are going?

  • Right: Where are you going?
  • Why: In a question the helping verb comes before the subject: Where are you…

docs.title: 30.8 Practice — Everyday conversations
docs.text:
Exercise 1

What is the most natural way to ask the price in a shop?

  • How much is this?
  • What is the cost of this?
  • How much price?
  • This is how much rupees?
Answer

How much is this?

Short, direct, works everywhere. 'What is the cost' sounds bookish.

Exercise 2

How do you give your name when you pick up the phone?

  • Hello, this is Ravi speaking.
  • Hello, myself Ravi.
  • Hello, I am Ravi speaking here.
  • Hello, Ravi this side.

Hint: Not with 'Myself'.

Answer

Hello, this is Ravi speaking.

On the phone, always give your name with 'This is…'. 'Myself Ravi' is not a sentence in English.

Exercise 3

What is the pattern for telling a doctor your problem?

  • What it is + since when
  • Only the name of a medicine
  • How much it hurts, from 1 to 10
  • Say your age first
Answer

What it is + since when

'I have a fever. It started last night.' At the start, the doctor needs only these two things.

Exercise 4

The sound on the phone keeps cutting out. What do you say?

  • Sorry, you're breaking up. Could you say that again?
  • I didn't get you.
  • Your voice is not coming.
  • Speak loudly please.
Answer

Sorry, you're breaking up. Could you say that again?

'Breaking up' is the right phrase for a bad phone connection. 'I didn't get you' sounds like you did not recognise the person.

Exercise 5

What is the natural pattern for ordering in a restaurant?

  • I'll have the… / We'll have the…
  • Give me one…
  • I want to eat…
  • Bring me…
Answer

I'll have the… / We'll have the…

'I'll have the paneer tikka, please.' The most common and the most polite way.

Exercise 6

What is the right English for asking an auto driver to go by the meter?

  • Could you go by the meter, please?
  • Please put meter on.
  • Meter only please.
  • Go in meter.
Answer

Could you go by the meter, please?

'by the meter' is the right phrase. 'Could you…, please' makes it a request, not an order.

Exercise 7

At the shop: Do you have this ___ a smaller size?

Hint: Which preposition goes with size or colour?

Answer

in

Use 'in' with size and colour: in blue, in medium, in a smaller size.

Exercise 8

Restaurant: Could we have the ___, please? (what you ask for when you want to pay)

Answer

bill / cheque / check

'Bill' in India and the UK, 'check' in the US. Both are fine.

Exercise 9

Directions: Take the second ___. (the second street on the left)

Answer

left

'Take the second left' = the second turn on the left. 'Take a left at the signal' is also common.

Exercise 10

There is a mistake in this sentence — tap the word.

I am having two brothers and one sister.

Answer

Wrong word: having.

Corrected: I have two brothers and one sister.

When 'have' means 'to own or possess', it does not take -ing.

Exercise 11

Find the wrong word.

What is your good name, sir?

Answer

Wrong word: good.

Corrected: May I know your name, sir?

'Good name' is a word-for-word copy of the Hindi 'shubh naam'. English does not say this.

Exercise 12

Match each situation to its ready-made line.

A B Shop — just browsing It started last night. Cab — stop here Can I call you back in ten minutes? Doctor — since when I'm just looking, thanks. Phone — I will talk later You can stop here, thanks. Answer

Shop — just browsing — I'm just looking, thanks.; Cab — stop here — You can stop here, thanks.; Doctor — since when — It started last night.; Phone — I will talk later — Can I call you back in ten minutes?

One ready-made line for each situation. You do not have to think and build it.

Exercise 13

Build the shop line.

Words: please / Could / have / I / receipt / the

Answer

Could I have the receipt please

'Could I have…' is the politest pattern for asking. receipt = ri-SEET, the P is silent.

Exercise 14

At the shop. Say the first line.

Answer

Say: Excuse me, do you have this in blue

Start with 'Excuse me'. 'in blue' — always 'in' with a colour.

Exercise 15

Bargain politely.

Answer

Say: Could you do it for a little less

Better than saying 'Reduce the price' directly. 'Could you' makes the same thing softer.

Exercise 16

Your first words as you get into a cab.

Answer

Say: Are you going towards the airport

'towards' makes it easy. The voice rises slightly at the end — it is a question.

Exercise 17

When you get out of the cab.

Answer

Say: You can drop me at gate three. Thanks a lot

'drop me at' = leave me here. End with a thank-you — short and natural.

Exercise 18

Tell the doctor your problem — what and since when.

Answer

Say: I have a bad headache. It's been two days

Problem + time. These are the two things a doctor needs at the start.

Exercise 19

An important question about the medicine.

Answer

Say: How many times a day should I take this

How many times a day. Ask 'Before food or after food?' as well.

Exercise 20

Pick up the phone — give your name.

Answer

Say: Hello, this is Ravi speaking

'This is' + name. Never 'Myself'.

Exercise 21

You did not understand on the phone. Ask politely.

Answer

Say: Sorry, you're breaking up. Could you say that again

Use 'breaking up' for a network problem. Then ask them to repeat.

Exercise 22

As soon as you sit down in the restaurant.

Answer

Say: A table for two please

That is enough. You do not need a long sentence.

Exercise 23

Ask for the food to be less spicy.

Answer

Say: Could you make it less spicy please

'less spicy' = not so hot. 'Could you' makes every request polite.

Exercise 24

Ask for directions.

Answer

Say: Excuse me, how do I get to the metro station

'How do I get to…' is the most useful pattern for asking directions — for any place.

Exercise 25

You are lost. Ask for help.

Answer

Say: I think I'm lost. I'm looking for Lake Road

Say your situation first, then the name of the place. People help at once.

What next?

Today's task: choose one situation — one that will really come up tomorrow — and say its five lines 10 times. Then use the same lines in the real place tomorrow. The first time your heart will beat fast; the second time it will be easier; the third time it will be a habit. Next chapter: Interview and office — your introduction, questions and answers, and the language of meetings.

docs.title: Chapter 55: Everyday stories
docs.text:
Everyday stories — English at the office, at home and on the road

English in real life is not as tidy as in short stories. In a meeting people sum things up quickly, the customer care agent reads from a script, and a friend swallows half the words in a voice note. This chapter has five longer pieces (100–200 words). Here you don't just catch "what happened" — you also catch why it happened and how the speaker feels. And new words? You will learn to work out their meaning from context.

docs.title: 55.1 Listening between the lines — what is inference?
docs.text:
People often don't say "I am angry" or "I am worried" directly. They show it through their words, their tone of voice and their situation. Joining these three clues to work out the meaning = inference. Intermediate-level listening questions ("How does she feel?", "Why does he say…?") are all about this.

Figure 55.1. Inference = three clues added together. One clue can mislead you; if all three point the same way, the answer is certain.

Feeling = words + tone + situation

The answer to "How does she feel?" comes not from one word but from three clues: what was said, how it was said, and in what situation. First understand the situation, then the words, then the tone.

  • Rohit, I know that's frustrating, but it's the safer choice. The speaker knows Rohit will be annoyed, and she is trying to calm him down: this is the safer decision.
  • Honestly, I don't blame her. To be honest, I think she is not at fault. It means "what she does is fair" — the mistake was mine.
  • And please don't be late this time, okay? Don't be late this time. "this time" gives away a hidden fact — she was late last time.

docs.title: 55.2 A team meeting summary
docs.text:
Kavita leads a software team. At the end of the meeting she quickly repeats everything. In a summary like this, signpost words make the map: First, Second, Third, And finally. Listen: why did the launch date change, and what time is the stand-up now?

Phrase Meaning (in this context) sum up to give the main points briefly launch date the date a product goes live stand-up a short daily meeting of 10–15 minutes take over to start doing someone else's work have a think think about it (British, friendly)

🎧 Listen to the whole summary (2 parts)

  • Part 1 — good news and a new date Catch two numbers: the old date and the new date.
  • Part 2 — the stand-up and Sana's work When you hear "instead of", know that something is changing.
Transcript

Kavita: Okay, everyone, let me quickly sum up today's meeting. First, the good news: the new billing app is almost ready, and the client loved the demo on Tuesday. Second, we've moved the launch date from the tenth of March to the seventeenth, because the testing team needs one more week. Rohit, I know that's frustrating after all those late nights, but honestly, it's the safer choice.

Third, from next Monday, our daily stand-up will start at nine forty-five instead of ten, so please don't be late. And finally, Sana is moving to the design team next month, so someone will need to take over her weekly reports. Have a think and let me know by Friday. Any questions? No? Great. Thanks, everyone, and well done on the demo.

  • We've moved the launch date from the tenth of March to the seventeenth. The launch has moved from 10 March to 17 March. "from … to …" = old → new. The reason comes right after "because".
  • After all those late nights. After working late on so many nights. Inference: Rohit worked very hard — so he may be upset.

Signposts = the map of a summary

The moment you hear First… Second… Third… And finally…, write 1, 2, 3, 4 in your notes. Next to each number put one or two words — not a full sentence. "And finally" = the last point is coming; pay attention again.

docs.title: 55.3 A customer care call — the internet is down
docs.text:
Mrs Lata Iyer works from home, and her internet has been down since last night. She phones the BlueRiver Broadband customer care line. Here one voice reads both parts — work out who is speaking from the names ("Hi, Deepak", "Thank you, Mrs Iyer") and from the questions and answers. Listen: why is this so urgent for her, and what will she get if it is not fixed by two o'clock?

Phrase Meaning (in this context) down (of a machine or network) not working at all fault a technical problem arrange to organise, to set up complaint number the reference number for your complaint patience the ability to wait calmly (PAY-shuns)

🎧 Listen to the whole call (2 parts)

  • Part 1 — what is the problem ID letters and digits are said one by one — B R seven two zero five.
  • Part 2 — when will it be fixed Listen carefully to the condition and the promise after "If it isn't…".
Transcript

Deepak: Good morning, thank you for calling BlueRiver Broadband. My name is Deepak. How may I help you today?

Mrs Iyer: Hi, Deepak. My internet has been down since last night, and I work from home, so this is really urgent.

Deepak: I'm very sorry to hear that, ma'am. May I have your customer ID, please?

Mrs Iyer: Yes, it's BR7205.

Deepak: Thank you, Mrs Iyer. I can see there's a fault in your area, and our engineers are already working on it.

Mrs Iyer: How long will it take?

Deepak: It should be fixed by 2 p.m. today. If it isn't, I'll arrange a technician visit, and you'll get a 50% discount on this month's bill.

Mrs Iyer: Okay, but please make sure it's done. I have an important client call at three.

Deepak: Absolutely, ma'am. Your complaint number is SR4481. Is there anything else I can help you with?

Mrs Iyer: No, that's all. Thank you.

Deepak: Thank you for your patience. Have a good day.

  • I work from home, so this is really urgent. I work from home, which is why this matters so much. The reason comes before "so", the result after.
  • Okay, but please make sure it's done. Fine, but be certain it gets done. "Okay, but…" = she accepts it, but she doesn't fully trust it. Inference: she is worried and a little impatient.
  • It should be fixed by two p.m. today. It ought to be fixed by 2 p.m. today. "should" = we expect so, not a guarantee. "by 2" = at any time up to 2 o'clock.

Customer care English — easy to misunderstand

  • Wrong: "It should be fixed by two" = it will definitely be fixed at two.
  • Right: "It should be fixed by two" = we hope so, before two o'clock.
  • Why: "should" is a guess, not a promise. That is why Deepak immediately gives a plan B: "If it isn't, …".

docs.title: 55.4 A journey gone wrong — three past tenses
docs.text:
A brother tells the story of travelling with his sister to a wedding in Jaipur. The story uses three kinds of past — the past simple (one event after another), the past continuous (something that was going on) and the past perfect (something even earlier). If you understand the tenses, you understand the order of time. (The full rules are in All 12 tenses.)

Figure 55.2. The moment you hear had + V3 , think: this happened even earlier . were + -ing = the background, and in the middle one past simple event — the shock of the story. Phrase Meaning (in this context) security queue the line for the security check (queue = "kyoo") realised suddenly understood or noticed furious extremely angry got through passed through (the check) I don't blame her I think she is not at fault

🎧 Listen to the whole story (2 parts)

  • Part 1 — a shock at the airport His sister said nothing — that silence is a clue too.
  • Part 2 — another problem "But the adventure wasn't over" = there is more trouble to come.
Transcript

Last December, my sister and I were travelling to Jaipur for our cousin's wedding. We had booked an early flight from Bengaluru, so we left home at four in the morning. While we were standing in the security queue, I suddenly realised that I had left my ID card at home. I couldn't believe it. My sister was furious, and for a minute she didn't say a word.

Luckily, a staff member told me that I could show a digital copy of my ID on my phone. I downloaded it in five minutes, and we got through just in time. But the adventure wasn't over. When we landed in Jaipur, we discovered that our suitcase had gone to Delhi! We spent the first evening of the wedding in our travel clothes. Now, whenever we travel, my sister checks my bag twice. Honestly, I don't blame her.

  • While we were standing in the security queue, I suddenly realised that I had left my ID card at home. We were in the line, and suddenly it hit me that I had left my ID at home. One sentence, three tenses — the background, the event, and what came before.
  • Luckily, a staff member told me that I could show a digital copy. By good luck, a staff member said a digital copy would do. "Luckily" = the story turned in a good direction.
  • Now, whenever we travel, my sister checks my bag twice. These days, every time we travel, my sister checks my bag two times. Present simple = a new habit, the lesson of the story.

Turning-point words in a story

suddenly (a sudden shock) · luckily (good news) · but (the opposite) · when we landed (a new scene). The moment these words appear, the story changes direction. When you hear a turning-point word, listen even more closely to the next sentence.

docs.title: 55.5 A podcast — talking about working from home
docs.text:
In a podcast called "Chai and Careers", two hosts — Nikhil and Aisha — talk about the pros and cons of working from home. In a podcast people give opinions, so words like mostly, but, to be honest, for me matter most. Listen: what does Nikhil like, what does he dislike, and what is his solution?

Phrase Meaning (in this context) remotely away from the office, from home or elsewhere commute to travel to work and back every day overhear to hear something by accident hidden cost a disadvantage you don't notice at first best of both worlds the advantages of two different things together

🎧 Listen to the podcast (2 parts)

  • Part 1 — Nikhil's experience "Mostly, yes" — yes, but not completely. Now wait for the "but".
  • Part 2 — a listener's story and a solution "For me, it's…" = his own opinion is coming now.
Transcript

Nikhil: Welcome back to Chai and Careers. I'm Nikhil.

Aisha: And I'm Aisha. Today we're talking about working from home. Nikhil, you've been working remotely for three years now. Do you still enjoy it?

Nikhil: Mostly, yes. I save almost two hours a day because I don't have to commute. I cook a proper lunch, and I see much more of my kids. But to be honest, I sometimes feel a bit lonely. There's no chat by the coffee machine, you know?
