Aisha: That's interesting, because a lot of our listeners say the same thing. One listener, Pooja from Indore, wrote in to say that she works better at home, but she misses learning from senior colleagues.

Nikhil: Yes, I think that's the hidden cost. You don't overhear how experienced people solve problems.

Aisha: So what's the answer?

Nikhil: For me, it's a hybrid model. Two days in the office for teamwork, and three days at home for focused work.

Aisha: That sounds like the best of both worlds.

  • I see much more of my kids. I spend a lot more time with my children. "see more of someone" = to meet or be with them more often.
  • But to be honest, I sometimes feel a bit lonely. But, truthfully, I sometimes feel lonely. After "to be honest" you often get the thing that is a little hard to say.
  • You don't overhear how experienced people solve problems. You can't pick up how skilled people solve difficult problems. Here "you" = anyone, people in general — not just Aisha.

docs.title: 55.6 A friend's WhatsApp voice note
docs.text:
Tanvi sends her friend Riya a voice note. This is informal English — fast, half-sentences, "kind of", "six-ish", "anyway". In real life this is what you will hear most. Listen: why isn't Karan coming, what is the new plan, and what does Riya need to bring?

🎧 Listen to the voice note

  • Voice note — Tanvi → Riya Catch three useful facts: who isn't coming, where to meet, what to bring.
Transcript

Hey Riya! Sorry, sorry, I know I didn't reply yesterday. It was a crazy day at work. Listen, about Saturday. The plan's changed a bit. Karan can't make it, because his flight got cancelled, so it's just the four of us now. Instead of the movie, how about that new café in Bandra, the one with all the board games? I'm kind of bored of movies anyway. Oh, and can you bring your speaker? Mine's broken. Let's meet at six-ish outside the station. And please don't be late this time, okay? I'm joking. Well, mostly! Anyway, text me when you get this. Bye!

Voice note (informal) Formal version Meaning Karan can't make it. Karan is unable to attend. Karan won't be able to come I'm kind of bored of movies. I'm rather tired of films. I'm a bit fed up with them at six-ish at around six o'clock at about six Mine's broken. Mine is not working. mine doesn't work Anyway, text me. Please reply when you can. so, send me a message
  • Karan can't make it, because his flight got cancelled. Karan can't come; his flight was cancelled. In "can't" the "t" almost disappears — "kaan(t) make it". The context (because… cancelled) confirms that it means "no".
  • I'm joking. Well, mostly! I'm kidding. Well, mostly! Inference: she really does want Riya to come on time.
  • Let's meet at six-ish outside the station. Let's meet outside the station at about six. "-ish" = approximately (six-ish, tallish, greenish).

can vs can't — catch it from context

In fast speech can becomes a weak "kn" and can't a longer "kaant" — but the "t" is often not heard. Look at the next words: because… cancelled = can't. Sound + context = the right meaning.

docs.title: 55.7 Meaning from context — and listening traps
docs.text:
In longer English, a new word will turn up every time. Don't stop. Ask three questions: 1) is this good news or bad? 2) what do the words around it tell me? 3) what does the next part of the story say? Often that is enough. (For a full list of phrasal verbs, see the Phrasal verbs chapter.)

Phrases that are misunderstood when taken word for word

  • Wrong: "My internet is down" = the internet is low / slow.
  • Right: "down" = completely off, not working.

  • Why: For a machine, website, server or network, "down" = not working. The opposite: "It's up again" = it is working again.

  • Wrong: "I don't blame her" = I hold her responsible.

  • Right: "I don't blame her" = I don't think she is at fault; she is right.

  • Why: "don't" sounds short and is easily missed. One "not" reverses the whole meaning — always listen out for negatives.

  • Wrong: "Karan can't make it" = Karan can't build anything.

  • Right: "can't make it" = he won't be able to come (to a party or meeting).

  • Why: "make it" = to manage to get there. "Can you make it on Friday?" = are you able to come on Friday?

  • Wrong: "Take over her reports" = carry away the reports.

  • Right: "take over" = you will now look after her work.
  • Why: Sana is moving to the design team — the context itself says that someone else has to do her work.

A new word? Don't stop

Keep listening to the next sentence — it often explains the word before it. First decide whether it is good or bad, then work out the meaning from context. furious → "didn't say a word" → very angry.

docs.title: 55.8 Practice — Everyday stories
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Why has the launch date been moved?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Second, we've moved the launch date from the tenth of March to the seventeenth, because the testing team needs one more week.

  • The testing team needs more time.
  • The client didn't like the demo.
  • Rohit is on leave.
  • The app is already finished.
Answer

The testing team needs more time.

'because the testing team needs one more week' — the reason comes after 'because'.

Exercise 2

How does Kavita think Rohit feels about the new date?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Rohit, I know that's frustrating after all those late nights, but honestly, it's the safer choice.

  • frustrated
  • relieved
  • excited
  • bored
Answer

frustrated

'I know that's frustrating after all those late nights' — Rohit worked late, and now the date has moved. Kavita understands that he will be annoyed.

Exercise 3

What time will the daily stand-up start from next Monday?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Third, from next Monday, our daily stand-up will start at nine forty-five instead of ten, so please don't be late.

  • 9:45
  • 10:00
  • 10:15
  • 9:15
Answer

9:45

'nine forty-five instead of ten' — the new time comes first, the old time after 'instead of'.

Exercise 4

Why is the problem really urgent for Mrs Iyer?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Hi, Deepak. My internet has been down since last night, and I work from home, so this is really urgent.

  • She works from home.
  • Her children have online exams.
  • She is moving house.
  • She has already paid twice.
Answer

She works from home.

'I work from home, so this is really urgent' — the reason comes before 'so'.

Exercise 5

What will happen if the internet is not fixed by 2 p.m.?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

It should be fixed by two p.m. today. If it isn't, I'll arrange a technician visit, and you'll get a fifty percent discount on this month's bill.

  • a technician visit and a 50% discount
  • a free new router
  • a full refund for the year
  • a call from the manager
Answer

a technician visit and a 50% discount

After 'If it isn't' come two promises: a technician visit + a 50% discount.

Exercise 6

How does Mrs Iyer probably feel at the end of the call?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Okay, but please make sure it's done. I have an important client call at three.

  • still worried and a little impatient
  • completely relaxed
  • angry with Deepak personally
  • very happy
Answer

still worried and a little impatient

'Okay, but…' + 'please make sure' + a client call at three = she agrees, but she is still anxious.

Exercise 7

What had the speaker forgotten?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

While we were standing in the security queue, I suddenly realised that I had left my ID card at home. I couldn't believe it.

  • his ID card
  • his phone
  • the flight tickets
  • his suitcase
Answer

his ID card

'I had left my ID card at home' — past perfect: he had left it behind even before setting out.

Exercise 8

How did his sister react?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

I couldn't believe it. My sister was furious, and for a minute she didn't say a word.

  • She was very angry and silent.
  • She laughed at him.
  • She cried loudly.
  • She went home alone.
Answer

She was very angry and silent.

furious = extremely angry; 'didn't say a word' = completely silent.

Exercise 9

What does the speaker mean by 'I don't blame her'?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Now, whenever we travel, my sister checks my bag twice. Honestly, I don't blame her.

  • She is right to check his bag.
  • He is angry with his sister.
  • She made the mistake.
  • He doesn't want her help.
Answer

She is right to check his bag.

'I don't blame her' = I think she is not at fault — the mistake was mine, and her checking is fair.

Exercise 10

How much time does Nikhil save every day?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Mostly, yes. I save almost two hours a day because I don't have to commute. I cook a proper lunch, and I see much more of my kids.

  • almost two hours
  • about thirty minutes
  • three hours
  • one day a week
Answer

almost two hours

'almost two hours a day' — he does not have to commute.

Exercise 11

What is Nikhil's solution?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

So what's the answer? For me, it's a hybrid model. Two days in the office for teamwork, and three days at home for focused work.

  • two days in the office, three at home
  • five days at home
  • five days in the office
  • working only at weekends
Answer

two days in the office, three at home

'For me, it's a hybrid model' — 2 days in the office (teamwork), 3 days at home (focused work).

Exercise 12

Why can't Karan come on Saturday?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Listen, about Saturday. The plan's changed a bit. Karan can't make it, because his flight got cancelled, so it's just the four of us now.

  • His flight got cancelled.
  • He is ill.
  • He has to work.
  • He doesn't like movies.
Answer

His flight got cancelled.

'can't make it, because his flight got cancelled' — make it = to be able to come.

Exercise 13

What does Tanvi ask Riya to bring?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Oh, and can you bring your speaker? Mine's broken. Let's meet at six-ish outside the station.

  • her speaker
  • board games
  • movie tickets
  • snacks
Answer

her speaker

'can you bring your speaker? Mine's broken.' The board games are already at the cafe.

Exercise 14

What can we guess about Riya?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Let's meet at six-ish outside the station. And please don't be late this time, okay? I'm joking. Well, mostly!

  • She was late last time.
  • She lives far from the station.
  • She doesn't like cafes.
  • She is Tanvi's sister.
Answer

She was late last time.

'this time' + 'Well, mostly!' — she was late last time, and Tanvi is half serious.

Exercise 15

Match each phrase to its meaning in context.

A B sum up to be unable to come take over the advantages of both things can't make it to give the main points briefly the best of both worlds to start doing someone else's work Answer

sum up — to give the main points briefly; take over — to start doing someone else's work; can't make it — to be unable to come; the best of both worlds — the advantages of both things

Understand these phrases by their whole meaning, not word for word — context is the key.

Exercise 16

Which line is informal (like a friend's voice note)?

  • I'm kind of bored of movies, so six-ish?
  • Thank you for your patience.
  • May I have your customer ID, please?
  • Let me quickly sum up today's meeting.

Hint: Look for -ish and kind of.

Answer

I'm kind of bored of movies, so six-ish?

'kind of' and 'six-ish' are signs of informal chat. The other three are office or customer care English.

Exercise 17

Listen and write.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

The testing team needs one more week.

'team' is singular → 'needs' (with -s).

Exercise 18

Listen and write.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

My internet has been down since last night.

'has been … since' = present perfect, from last night until now.

Exercise 19

Listen and write.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

While we were standing in the queue, I realised that I had left my ID card at home.

Three tenses together: were standing (going on), realised (the event), had left (earlier still).

Exercise 20

Say this to your team, like Kavita — friendly, but clear.

Answer

Say: Have a think and let me know by Friday

'let me know' runs together like 'lemme know'; 'by Friday' = on or before Friday.

Next step

Shadow each piece once — speak along with the audio, half a second behind. When you can say Kavita's summary and Tanvi's voice note without stopping, move on to Real-world English: station announcements, news and interviews.

docs.title: Chapter 59: Exams & your level
docs.text:
IELTS, TOEFL and your level — from A1 to C2

"How good is my English?" — the answer is not "good" or "okay", it is a level. All over the world English is measured on a six-step ladder: A1 to C2. In this chapter you will see what you can do at each level (with a list to check yourself), a straightforward introduction to the big exams — IELTS, TOEFL, PTE, Cambridge — how many hours it takes, and which chapters of this book to read for each level.

docs.title: 59.1 CEFR — six steps
docs.text:
CEFR (Common European Framework of Reference) is an international scale. It has three big parts: A = beginner (basic user), B = on your own (independent user), C = expert (proficient user). Each part has two levels. Most jobs and universities ask for B2 or C1.

Figure 59.1. Hours = the rough total study time from the beginning up to that level (a common estimate of guided learning hours). The IELTS band is only a rough comparison — each exam has its own official table.

Levels in one line

A = survive · B = manage on your own · C = say what you want, the way you want. Each next level takes more time than the one before. The journey from B1 to B2 often feels as long as A1 to B1 — don't panic, it is normal.

  • My English is at B2 level, but my speaking is closer to B1. The right way to state your level — "at B2 level".
  • I'd like to reach C1 by the end of next year. A goal — reach + level + by + a time.
  • Which level do I need for this job? How good does my English need to be for this job?

docs.title: 59.2 A1 and A2 — the beginning
docs.text: Each level is described with "can-do" statements — that is, what you can do. Read the list below and tick honestly. If most of your answers are "yes", you are at that level.

docs.title: A1 — Beginner
docs.text:
• ☐ I can say my name, age, city and job.
  • ☐ I can ask and understand simple questions: What's your name? Where do you live?
  • ☐ I can understand numbers, prices and times when someone speaks slowly.

  • ☐ I can fill in a short form (name, address, phone).

  • Hi, I'm Pooja. I'm from Indore. I'm a nurse. A1 — short, fixed sentences.

  • How much is this? Can you say that again, please? A1 — asking a price, asking someone to repeat.

docs.title: A2 — Elementary
docs.text:
• ☐ I can say a few lines about my family, my work and my daily routine.
  • ☐ I can manage ordinary tasks at a shop, bank or station.
  • ☐ I can write a short message or note: I'm late. See you at 6.

  • ☐ I can talk simply about yesterday or last week: Last Sunday I went to…

  • I work in a hospital. I usually start at eight and finish at four. A2 — a routine, "usually", two linked sentences.

  • Last weekend I visited my aunt in Bhopal. We went to the lake. A2 — a short story in the simple past.

docs.title: 59.3 B1 and B2 — on your own
B1 — Intermediate
docs.text:
• ☐ I can handle most situations that come up when I travel.
  • ☐ I can talk in connected sentences about my experiences, dreams and plans.
  • ☐ I can give a short reason for my opinion: I prefer trains because…
  • ☐ I can write a simple email or short paragraph on familiar topics.

  • ☐ I understand the main points of clear, normal-speed English.

  • I prefer working in a team because I learn a lot from other people. B1 — an opinion + a reason with "because".

  • When I was in college, I wanted to be a pilot, but I changed my mind. B1 — experiences and plans, in connected speech.

docs.title: B2 — Upper-intermediate
docs.text:
• ☐ I can talk with native speakers fairly smoothly, without strain on either side.
  • ☐ I can explain my view on an issue, with its advantages and disadvantages.
  • ☐ I can follow the main point of news, long articles and technical texts in my field.
  • ☐ I can write clear, detailed text — such as an essay or a report.

  • ☐ I often notice my own mistakes and correct them myself.

  • Working from home saves time, but it can make teamwork harder, especially for new joiners. B2 — an advantage + a disadvantage + fine detail with "especially".

  • The article argues that cities should ban cars, although it doesn't really explain how. B2 — the main point of a long text + your own criticism.

The real difference between B1 and B2

B1 = you get by. B2 = you are comfortable — you follow fast speech, and you back up an opinion with reasons and examples. Most Indian graduates are somewhere between B1 and B2. A large part of this book is for that jump.

docs.title: C1 — Advanced
docs.text:
• ☐ I can speak fluently, without searching for words.
  • ☐ I understand long, difficult texts — and also what is not said directly (implied meaning).
  • ☐ I use English flexibly in meetings, presentations and studies.

  • ☐ I can write well-structured, connected text on a difficult subject.

  • I take your point, but I'm not convinced the savings would outweigh the risks. C1 — polite disagreement, and a precise word like "outweigh".

  • What she didn't say was more telling than what she did. C1 — understanding what is left unsaid (implied meaning).

docs.title: C2 — Proficient
docs.text:
• ☐ I understand almost everything I hear or read, with ease.
  • ☐ I can summarise information from different sources and explain it in connected speech.

  • ☐ I can express fine shades of meaning accurately — including humour, irony and hints.

  • It's not that the plan is wrong, exactly; it's more that it's been oversold. C2 — a fine distinction: not wrong, just described as better than it is.

  • Taken together, the three reports suggest a slowdown rather than a crisis. C2 — a summary of several sources, with a precise conclusion.

Each skill can be at a different level

Many people are B2 in reading and B1 in speaking. This is completely normal. That is why exams give a separate score for each skill — and why you should work most on your weakest skill.

docs.title: 59.5 The big exams — at a glance
docs.text:
Below is a rough introduction to each exam. Format, fees, scores and rules change from time to time — always check the current details on the official website before you book an exam, and also check the requirement of the place you are applying to (university, visa, company).

Exam Format (roughly) Score IELTS Academic Listening, Reading, Writing, Speaking · about 2 hours 45 minutes · speaking is face to face with an examiner Band 0–9 (half bands too) IELTS General Training The same four parts; Reading and Writing use everyday and work texts Band 0–9 TOEFL iBT Reading, Listening, Speaking, Writing · on a computer · speaking is recorded on a mic A new 1–6 scale from 2026 (the old 0–120 runs alongside for a while) PTE Academic Speaking & Writing, Reading, Listening · on a computer, about 2 hours · scored by computer 10–90 Cambridge B2 First / C1 Advanced Reading & Use of English, Writing, Listening, Speaking (often in pairs) Cambridge English Scale + grade

docs.title: IELTS — Academic or General Training?
docs.text:
Academic = studying at a university or professional registration (for example doctors, nurses). General Training = work, migration, or school-level study. Listening and Speaking are the same in both; Reading and Writing are different. In Writing Task 1 you describe a graph or chart in Academic, and write a letter in General.

  • I'm taking IELTS Academic next month. I need a band seven overall. You "take" an exam; "band seven overall" — 7 as the total score.
  • The speaking test is a face-to-face conversation with an examiner. IELTS speaking — a face-to-face talk with an examiner (about 11–14 minutes).
  • Most universities accept scores that are less than two years old. IELTS, TOEFL and PTE scores are usually valid for 2 years. A Cambridge certificate does not expire — but an institution may ask for a recent result.

An exam is not pass or fail

IELTS, TOEFL and PTE have no pass or fail — only a score. The question is how high a score your destination asks for. So instead of "I want to clear IELTS", say: "I need a band 7 in IELTS."

docs.title: 59.6 Which exam should you choose?
docs.text:
The first question in choosing an exam is not English, it is your destination: where do you want to go and why? That institution will tell you which exams it accepts.

Figure 59.2. Even within one country, different universities or visas accept different exams. Before you apply, read the English language requirements on their website.

The rule for choosing an exam

Destination → its list → your comfort. If you are comfortable typing on a computer and speaking into a mic, go for TOEFL/PTE; if you would rather talk to a person, choose IELTS speaking. Don't prepare for two exams at once — pick one and take its sample tests.

  • Which English tests does your university accept? The first line to ask a university.
  • What's the minimum score for each skill? Many places set a separate minimum for each skill.
  • I'm aiming for at least a seven in writing. aim for = to have something as your target.
  • I've booked the computer-delivered test for the fifteenth of March. computer-delivered = a test taken on a computer.

docs.title: 59.7 How long will it take? — a study plan
docs.text:
Moving up one level usually takes 150 to 250 hours, and more at the higher levels. One hour a day = about 30 hours a month. So B1 to B2 takes about 6 to 8 months, if you study every day.

Day What to do Time Every day One section of this book, everything said aloud 15–20 min Every day Listen to English — a podcast, the news, YouTube (English subtitles) 20 min Every day 5 new chunks in your phone notes 5 min 3 days a week Writing — an email, a paragraph or an essay 20–40 min 2 days a week Speak with someone, or record yourself and listen back 15 min Once a month One mock test, or redo a chapter quiz 1 hour
  • I study for an hour every day, and I take a mock test once a month. Saying your routine in English is practice too.
  • My weakest skill is speaking, so I record myself twice a week. Most time goes to the weakest skill.
  • I've improved a lot, but I still make mistakes with articles. Describing your progress honestly.

Count hours, not days

"IELTS in three months" means nothing unless you know how many hours a day. Keep a small diary: date + minutes + what you did. 5 hours a week x 30 weeks = 150 hours = about one level.

docs.title: 59.8 Your level, and the chapters of this book
docs.text:
Pick your level from the lists above, then focus on the chapters for that level below. Go back over the chapters of the lower levels once — they are the foundation.

Level · focus Read these chapters A1 · Sounds, words, simple sentences How to Use This Book · English Sounds · The 8 Parts of Speech · Sentence Structure · Noun · Articles — a, an, the · Pronoun · Verb A2 · Managing daily life All 12 Tenses · Adjective · Adverb · Preposition · Conjunction · Interjection · Determiners (some, any, much, many) · Asking questions · Subject-verb agreement · Everyday conversations · Number, date, time, paise · Everyday topics B1 · Speaking and writing in connected sentences Modal Verbs · Gerunds & Infinitives · If sentences · Fix your pronunciation · Small talk and giving opinions · Phone and video calls · Punctuation · Spelling rules · From sentence to paragraph · Writing emails · Applications and messages · Phrasal verbs · Which word goes with which · Short Stories · Indian English habits B2 · Fast English, opinions, work writing Clauses · Active and Passive voice · Reporting what someone said · used to, wish, had better · Rhythm and stress · Native speed English · Interview and office · Giving a presentation · One word, ten words · Work and the world · Look-alike words · CV and LinkedIn · Everyday Stories · The 50 most common mistakes C1 · Precise words, flexible style Powerful sentences · Fluency and filler words · Essays and Reports · Idioms · From Basic to Native · Verb upgrades · Choosing the right adjective · Real-World English C2 · Fine shades and style Advanced words · Final Test — and then real books, podcasts, debates

Use the book like a ladder

Take the quizzes of the chapters at your level. Above 80% = the next level. Below = the same chapter once more, this time saying everything aloud. The mixed test for the whole book is in the Final Test.

docs.title: 59.9 Exam English — mistakes we make when talking about it
docs.text:
Even when talking about the exam, some common Indian English habits creep in. Say the clean version in an interview or to a visa officer.

✗

I have given IELTS last month.

✓

I took IELTS last month. / I sat the IELTS test last month. (UK)

give

take

sit

✗

I got 7 bands in IELTS.

✓

I got a band 7 / an overall band score of 7.

I got 6.5 in writing.

✗

I want to clear IELTS.

✓

I need a band 7 in IELTS for my university.

✗

A memorised answer in speaking: "Well, that's a very interesting question. Since my childhood…"

✓

A direct, personal answer: "I'd say my favourite place is the old market near my house, mainly because…"

structure

  • I'd say my favourite place is the old market near my house, mainly because of the food. "I'd say…" + "mainly because…" — a natural start in the speaking test.
  • Sorry, could you repeat the question, please? If you don't understand the question, it is perfectly fine to ask.
  • That's not something I've thought about much, but I suppose… Buying thinking time on a hard question — better than staying silent.

docs.title: 59.10 Practice — Exams and levels
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Which is the highest level in CEFR?

  • C2
  • C1
  • B2
  • A1
Answer

C2

A1 → A2 → B1 → B2 → C1 → C2. C2 = proficient.

Exercise 2

'I can handle most situations when I travel, and I can describe my experiences in connected speech.' — which level is this?

  • B1
  • A1
  • C1
  • C2
Answer

B1

B1 = the start of the independent user — travel, experiences, short reasons.

Exercise 3

Match each level to its big group.

A B A1, A2 Independent user B1, B2 Proficient user C1, C2 Basic user Answer

A1, A2 — Basic user; B1, B2 — Independent user; C1, C2 — Proficient user

A = beginner, B = on your own, C = expert.

Exercise 4

What is different between IELTS Academic and General Training?

  • Reading and Writing
  • Listening and Speaking
  • Only Speaking
  • Nothing
Answer

Reading and Writing

Listening and Speaking are the same in both; Reading and Writing differ.

Exercise 5

What scale is the IELTS score on?

  • Band 0–9
  • 10–90
  • 0–100 percent
  • A to F grade
Answer

Band 0–9

IELTS: band 0–9, with half bands (6.5). PTE: 10–90.

Exercise 6

Tap the wrong word.

I have given IELTS last month.

Answer

Wrong word: given.

Corrected: I took IELTS last month.

You 'take' an exam (UK: sit). Last month = simple past.

Exercise 7

Find the mistake about the score.

I got 7 bands in IELTS.

Answer

Wrong word: bands.

Corrected: I got a band 7 in IELTS.

A band is a score — 'a band 7' or 'an overall band score of 7'.

Exercise 8

I'm ___ IELTS Academic next month. (to do an exam)

Hint: Not give.

Answer

taking / sitting

take an exam (in the UK, sit an exam too).

Exercise 9

Which exam is scored by computer and gives a result on a 10–90 scale?

  • PTE Academic
  • IELTS
  • Cambridge B2 First
  • None of them
Answer

PTE Academic

PTE Academic is computer-based with automated scoring, and a score of 10–90.

Exercise 10

What is the very first step in choosing an exam?

  • Check the official list of your destination (university / visa)
  • The cheapest exam
  • Whatever a friend took
  • The one that seems easiest
Answer

Check the official list of your destination (university / visa)

First the destination's list, then the exam — it tells you which score is accepted.

Exercise 11

Who do you do the IELTS speaking test with?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

The IELTS test has four parts: listening, reading, writing and speaking. The speaking test is a face-to-face conversation with an examiner, and it lasts between eleven and fourteen minutes.

  • With an examiner
  • With a computer
  • With another candidate
  • On the phone
Answer

With an examiner

'a face-to-face conversation with an examiner'.

Exercise 12

How long does the speaking test last?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

The IELTS test has four parts: listening, reading, writing and speaking. The speaking test is a face-to-face conversation with an examiner, and it lasts between eleven and fourteen minutes.

  • 11 to 14 minutes
  • 40 minutes
  • 2 hours
  • 5 minutes
Answer

11 to 14 minutes

'it lasts between eleven and fourteen minutes'.

Exercise 13

Which level does Arjun seem to be at?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Hi, I'm Arjun. I can talk about my work and my family, and I can handle most situations when I travel. But in meetings, when people speak fast, I often get lost.

  • B1
  • A1
  • C1
  • C2
Answer

B1

He manages travel and everyday talk (B1), but gets lost in fast speech — not B2 yet.

Exercise 14

Where does Arjun have the most trouble?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Hi, I'm Arjun. I can talk about my work and my family, and I can handle most situations when I travel. But in meetings, when people speak fast, I often get lost.

  • In meetings when people speak fast
  • When he travels
  • Talking about his family
  • Writing emails
Answer

In meetings when people speak fast

'in meetings, when people speak fast, I often get lost' — see the 'Native speed English' chapter for this.

Exercise 15

Listen and write.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

I need an overall band score of seven to study in Canada.

an overall band score of seven — the right way to say a score.

Exercise 16

With one hour of study a day, about how long does it take to get from B1 to B2?

  • 6 to 8 months
  • 2 weeks
  • 1 month
  • 5 years
Answer

6 to 8 months

One level ≈ 150–250 hours; 1 hour a day ≈ 30 hours a month.

Exercise 17

Put the words in the right order.

Words: every / weakest / is / I / skill / speaking / so / practise / My / day

Answer

My weakest skill is speaking so I practise every day

Your weakest skill + what you do about it — a natural line about your preparation.

Exercise 18

Now say it aloud.

Answer

Say: I need a band seven in IELTS

Not 'clear IELTS' — state the score.

What to do next

Today, count the ticks on your self-check list and write down your level. Then pick two chapters for that level and finish them this week. At the end of the month take the Final Test — and see how far up you have climbed.

docs.title: Chapter 60: Final test
docs.text:
Final test — the whole book at once

Nothing new is taught here. This test is only to show which parts of the book have really sunk in and which should be opened again. The questions are mixed on purpose — one about tenses, the next a phrasal verb, then an article. Real life works the same way: nobody warns you that a grammar chapter is coming up.

How to take it

Do it in one sitting, and think for yourself before looking at the answer. Making a mistake is not bad — why you made it is explained in the "Why" part. If your score is above 80%, the book is yours. If it is below 50, that is fine — start again, but this time stop only at the chapters where you made mistakes.

docs.title: 60.1 What is in the test
docs.text:
The bar below shows how the 30 questions are spread across the five parts of the book. If your mistakes pile up in one colour, go straight back to that part — there is no need to repeat the whole book.

Figure 60.1. The map of the test. More important than the score is which colour your mistakes pile up in.

Six kinds of questions

Choose (MCQ) · fill in the blank (fill) · spot the mistake (spot) · put in order (reorder) · match pairs (match) · say it aloud (speak). The "say it aloud" questions need a microphone. If you don't have one, listen and repeat, then move on — it doesn't affect your score.

docs.title: 60.2 Before you start — a three-minute warm-up
docs.text:
These three mistakes have come up most often in the whole book. Look at them once, say the corrected sentences aloud once, and then start the test.

Three things, one last time

  • Wrong: I am working here since three years.
  • Right: I've been working here for three years.

  • Why: Use for with a length of time, and since with a starting point. And work that is still going on = have been + -ing.

  • Wrong: She is doctor and she is good in surgery.

  • Right: She's a doctor and she's good at surgery.

  • Why: Always use a/an with a profession, and being skilled = good at.

  • Wrong: Tell me where is the lift.

  • Right: Could you tell me where the lift is?
  • Why: When a question sits inside a longer sentence, the order becomes normal again — the verb goes to the end.

docs.title: 60.3 Final test — the whole book
docs.text:
Exercise 1

In this sentence, which part of speech is 'quickly'? — She finished the report quickly.

  • Adverb
  • Adjective
  • Verb
  • Preposition

Hint: It tells how the work was done.

Answer

Adverb

An adverb tells us about a verb — how, when, where. Here 'quickly' tells how 'finished' happened.

Exercise 2

Ravi and I finished the work ___ .

Hint: We did it on our own — the reflexive form.

Answer

ourselves

The reflexive pronoun matches the subject: I → myself, we → ourselves. Note: there is no such word as 'ourself'.

Exercise 3

Which sentence is correct?

  • I have been waiting for twenty minutes.
  • I am waiting since twenty minutes.
  • I wait since twenty minutes.
  • I have waited since twenty minutes.
Answer

I have been waiting for twenty minutes.

An action that started earlier and is still going on = have been + -ing. And use 'for' with a length of time, 'since' with a starting point.

Exercise 4

Find the wrong word.

She didn't came to the meeting yesterday.

Answer

Wrong word: came.

Corrected: She didn't come to the meeting yesterday.

'Did' already shows the past, so the verb stays in its first form — didn't come.

Exercise 5

By the time we reached the platform, the train ___ .

  • had left
  • has left
  • left
  • was leaving

Hint: Two actions in the past — which happened first?

Answer

had left

When two things happened in the past, the earlier one takes 'had'. This is called the past perfect.

Exercise 6

She ___ the answer, so just ask her.

Hint: Verbs of thinking don't go into the continuous.

Answer

knows

Know, understand, believe, like, want — these don't go into the continuous. 'She is knowing' is wrong.

Exercise 7

Which sentence is correct?

  • It took an hour to find a university nearby.
  • It took a hour to find an university nearby.
  • It took an hour to find an university nearby.
  • It took a hour to find a university nearby.

Hint: a/an depends on the sound.

Answer

It took an hour to find a university nearby.

The H in hour is silent, so the sound starts with a vowel — an. University starts with a 'yoo' sound, which is like a consonant — a.

Exercise 8

One word is unnecessary — tap it.

I really enjoy the music in my free time.

Answer

Wrong word: the.

Corrected: I really enjoy music in my free time.

In a general statement, 'the' is not used. 'The music' would mean one particular music that is playing now.

Exercise 9

My sister is very good ___ mathematics.

Hint: Being skilled.

Answer

at

Skilled in a subject = good at. Good with = good at handling things or people.

Exercise 10

One word should be removed — find it.

Let us discuss about the new policy on Monday.

Answer

Wrong word: about.

Corrected: Let's discuss the new policy on Monday.

The word 'about' is already inside discuss. Same family: enter the room, reach Delhi, order two teas.

Exercise 11

The meeting is ___ 4 pm ___ Monday ___ July.

  • at / on / in
  • in / at / on
  • on / in / at
  • at / in / on
Answer

at / on / in

Exact time = at, day/date = on, month/year = in. Small to big — that is the order.

Exercise 12

Each of the three teams ___ its own budget.

Hint: Is each singular or plural?

Answer

has

Each, every, everyone, nobody are all singular, even when a plural noun follows.

Exercise 13

Make the question in the right order.

Words: jacket / Where / you / did / that / buy

Answer

Where did you buy that jacket

In a question the helping verb (did) comes before the subject (you), and then the verb is in its first form.

Exercise 14

The order is wrong — tap the word in the wrong place.

Could you tell me where is the lift?

Answer

Wrong word: is.

Corrected: Could you tell me where the lift is?

When a question sits inside a longer sentence, the order becomes normal again — the verb moves to the end.

Exercise 15

Which is the active form of 'The report was approved by the committee'?

  • The committee approved the report.
  • The report approved the committee.
  • The committee was approving by the report.
  • The report has approved the committee.
Answer

The committee approved the report.

When changing passive to active, the 'by' part becomes the subject, and the old subject becomes the object.

Exercise 16

Rekha said that she ___ busy that evening.

Hint: In reported speech the tense goes one step back.

Answer

was

When reporting what someone said, the tense goes one step back: 'I am busy' → she said she was busy.

Exercise 17

Which sentence is correct for punctuation?

  • It's raining, so take its cover along.
  • Its raining, so take it's cover along.
  • Its raining, so take its cover along.
  • It's raining, so take it's cover along.
Answer

It's raining, so take its cover along.

It's = it is. Its = belonging to it. Here the apostrophe shows a shortened form, not possession.

Exercise 18

Where is the stress in 'village'?

  • On the first part — VIL-lage
  • On the second part — vil-LAGE
  • Equally on both
  • Nowhere, all the sounds are equal

Hint: It has two parts — VIL-lage.

Answer

On the first part — VIL-lage

In most two-part English nouns the stress falls on the first part. This rhythm is what creates fluency.

Exercise 19

When speaking, you need time to think. What is best?

  • That's a good question — let me think for a second.
  • Basically, basically, what happens is…
  • Actually, actually, let me tell you…
  • Stay silent for twenty seconds
Answer

That's a good question — let me think for a second.

Repeating filler words (basically, actually) lowers confidence. Buying time with one short, complete sentence sounds natural.

Exercise 20

You didn't understand what someone said in a meeting. What is the most natural line?

  • Sorry, I'm not following.
  • I am not understanding.
  • I have a doubt in your talk.
  • Please repeat it again.
Answer

Sorry, I'm not following.

'I'm not following' is neutral — you don't look weak, and you don't blame the speaker. In 'repeat it again', 'again' is unnecessary.

Exercise 21

This was lovely, but I should get ___ — it's getting late.

Hint: A soft way to leave.

Answer

going

'I should get going' = I should leave now. More polite and more natural than 'I need to leave'.

Exercise 22

'The new form removed almost all the errors' — which verb fits?

  • eliminated
  • enhanced
  • authorized
  • demonstrated
Answer

eliminated

Eliminate = to remove completely. Enhance means to make something good better, and authorize means to give official permission.

Exercise 23

One word is unnecessary — tap it.

After two night shifts I was very exhausted.

Answer

Wrong word: very.

Corrected: After two night shifts I was exhausted.

Exhausted is already a very strong word. For more force, say 'utterly exhausted', not 'very'.

Exercise 24

Which advanced word sounds best when you describe yourself in an interview?

  • pragmatic
  • enigmatic
  • nefarious
  • onerous
Answer

pragmatic

Pragmatic = practical, focused on results — a word of praise. Enigmatic would mean nobody can figure you out.

Exercise 25

The music is too loud. Which sentence is correct?

  • Please turn it down.
  • Please turn down it.
  • Please turn down.
  • Please it turn down.

Hint: Where does the pronoun go?

Answer

Please turn it down.

Turn down is separable, and the pronoun (it) must go in the middle. 'Turn down it' is never correct.

Exercise 26

The order is wrong — tap the wrong word.

She will look the baby after this evening.

Answer

Wrong word: after.

Corrected: She will look after the baby this evening.

Look after is inseparable — the object comes after the particle, never in the middle.

Exercise 27

Match each idiom to its meaning.

A B on the same page stop work for today the ball is in their court unlikely, but worth trying call it a day sharing the same understanding a long shot now it is their decision Answer

on the same page — sharing the same understanding; the ball is in their court — now it is their decision; call it a day — stop work for today; a long shot — unlikely, but worth trying

You hear all four in offices every day. Recognising them matters; using them is optional.

Exercise 28

Match each Indian English habit to its international form.

A B Myself Ravi move the call up I have a doubt graduated in 2019 prepone the call I'm Ravi passed out in 2019 I have a question Answer

Myself Ravi — I'm Ravi; I have a doubt — I have a question; prepone the call — move the call up; passed out in 2019 — graduated in 2019

All four are perfectly clear in India — you just need a different gear for an international call.

Exercise 29

Build one clear email line — without 'kindly' or 'needful'.

Words: can / we / so / release / invoice / Could / by / the / Friday / approve / you / payment

Answer

Could you approve the invoice by Friday so we can release payment

The formula: what to do + for whom + by when. All three in one line, and the message is perfectly clear.

Exercise 30

Say this line aloud. Run 'I have been' together smoothly, and put light stress on 'at'.

Answer

Say: I have been working here for three years and I am good at my job

Three things are right in one line — tense, preposition and word order. In an interview this could be your first answer.

What your score means

Above 80% — the book is yours. Now, instead of more practice, you need real conversation. Talk to someone in English for ten minutes every day. 50 to 80 — your foundation is strong, with a few loose spots. Look at the chart, spot the colour of your mistakes, and go back to only those two or three chapters. Below 50 — that's fine, and it is not a bad score at all. It only means the book needs one more read. The second time, things settle in much faster, because your mind recognises them.

docs.title: 60.4 Where did you go wrong? Go straight back there
docs.text:
Note your score, but more important is what kind of question you got wrong. The table below shows where to go back.

The mistake was of this kind Reopen this chapter a / an / the missing or wrong Articles — a, an, the since / for, had / have, didn't + verb All 12 Tenses in / on / at, good in, afraid from Preposition · The 50 most common mistakes Question order, "where is the lift" Asking questions has / have, each, news Subject-verb agreement Passive to active, reported speech Active and Passive voice · Reporting what someone said it's / its, comma, capital Punctuation Where the stress falls, filler words Rhythm and stress · Fluency and filler words A natural phrase felt wrong or odd From Basic to Native A big verb or adjective in the wrong place Verb upgrades · Choosing the right adjective turn down it, look the baby after Phrasal verbs Idiom meaning or use was wrong Idioms Myself, revert back, prepone, doubt Indian English habits can / must / should, have to Modal Verbs enjoy to read, want going Gerunds & Infinitives who / which / that, joining long sentences Clauses used to / be used to, I wish, had better used to, wish, had better get it done, Never have I…, What I need is… Powerful sentences Couldn't follow fast English (gonna, wanna) Native speed English 15 or 50, dates, saying rupee amounts Number, date, time, paise Starting a conversation, giving opinions, talking on calls Small talk and giving opinions · Phone and video calls The start or end of a presentation Giving a presentation happy / unhappy / happiness — wrong form One word, ten words do a mistake, strong rain-type pairs Which word goes with which Missing a word for doctor, bank, travel or office Everyday topics · Work and the world affect / effect, lose / loose, borrow / lend Look-alike words Spelling mistakes Spelling rules The shape of a paragraph, email or application From sentence to paragraph · Writing emails · Applications and messages CV bullets, essays or reports CV and LinkedIn · Essays and Reports Understanding by listening, or dictation Short Stories · Everyday Stories · Real-World English Want to know your level and next step IELTS, TOEFL and your level

One last thing

English is not an exam — it is a habit. The real aim of this book was not for you to memorise every rule. The aim was that when you speak English, you are no longer afraid of "I'll make a mistake". Once that fear goes, everything else will come on its own — a little at a time, every day. Those who speak, learn. Those who fear mistakes stay silent. Be one of those who speak.

docs.title: Chapter 29: Fluency
docs.text:
Fluency — learn to pause, drop "basically"

Fluency does not mean speaking fast. Fluency means to keep speaking without panic — even when you pause. The best speakers in the world speak slowly and pause a lot. The difference is that when they pause, they do not fill the gap with "um, uh, basically, matlab" — they stay silent, or they say a ready-made phrase that gives them time to think. That skill is what this chapter teaches.

What fluency really means

Fluency = to keep going, even after a mistake, even after getting stuck. A fluent person is someone who gets stuck in the middle of a sentence and still finishes the thought. Speed, perfect grammar and a big vocabulary all come later.

docs.title: 29.1 The filler habit — the plain truth
docs.text:
We all use fillers. A few are normal — native speakers use them too. The problem starts when they come after every three words, because then the listener hears your habit, not your message. Look at your own list honestly:

Filler The real problem What to do basically It almost always means nothing. In "Basically I went to the market", "basically" does no job. Remove it completely. The sentence gets better. actually Its real meaning is "in fact / the truth is". We add it to every sentence, so it loses its meaning. Use it only when you are correcting a misunderstanding. like "It was like, you know, like very big." — three times in one sentence. It makes you sound younger and less prepared. Pause. Silence is better than "like". matlab The most common Hinglish filler. A Hindi filler in the middle of English conversation is noticed at once. Replace it: "I mean…" or "What I'm trying to say is…" na / haan / theek hai na It gets stuck on the end of a sentence: "It is good, na?" Replace it: "…, isn't it?" / "…, right?" only (in the wrong place) "I am from Delhi only." — "only" has no meaning here in English. Remove it: "I'm from Delhi." you know It is used when you assume the listener knows, but they do not. Say the whole thing. Or "Let me explain…" umm / uhh This is the most natural one — but a long "ummmm" shows nervousness. Stay silent there. Two seconds of silence sounds confident.

First wrong, then right

  • Wrong: Basically, umm, I am, like, working in sales only, matlab since two years.
  • Right: I work in sales. I've been there for two years.

  • Why: Break it into short sentences. Three short sentences are much better than one long, stuck sentence.

  • Wrong: Actually the thing is that actually I actually forgot.

  • Right: To be honest, I forgot.

  • Why: Only one "signpost" word per sentence. If it comes again and again, it loses its effect.

  • Wrong: It is very good, na?

  • Right: It's really good, isn't it?
  • Why: Use a question tag in place of "na". It does the same job, but in English.

docs.title: 29.2 The skill of silence — pause, do not fill
docs.text:
When your brain is looking for the next word, your mouth starts to fill that gap. The real cure is this: let the gap stay empty. Two seconds of silence make you look like a thinker; two seconds of "ummmm" make you look nervous.

Figure 29.1. Both took almost the same time. The only difference is that in the second one the gap was filled by silence and a ready-made phrase , not by um .

docs.title: 29.3 Phrases that buy thinking time
docs.text:
This is the most valuable part of the chapter. Memorise these phrases — so well that they come out without thinking. They give you 2-4 seconds, and the listener feels you are speaking thoughtfully.

Purpose Phrase Listen You need time after a question That's a good question. Let me think about that for a second. Hmm, I haven't thought about it that way. Well, it depends. Before you begin your answer The way I see it… To be honest with you… In my experience… Explaining it again What I mean is… Let me put it another way. In other words… You got stuck in the middle Sorry, what's the word… give me a second. How do I say this… I'm blanking on the word — it's the thing you use for… You did not understand Sorry, could you repeat that? I didn't catch the last part.

Start with three phrases

Do not try to memorise the whole list. Choose just three today — my suggestion: "That's a good question." · "What I mean is…" · "Sorry, could you repeat that?" Say them 20 times today. Tomorrow they will come out on their own.

docs.title: 29.4 Speed control — speaking slowly is a strength
docs.text:
When we are nervous we speak fast, and in fast speech the sounds run together, and then people cannot understand, and then we get more nervous. This cycle has to be broken.

Situation Speed Why Interview, presentation Slow — slower than everyday speech Slow speech sounds confident, and gives you time to think. On the phone Slow + clear On the phone half the sounds get cut. Say numbers and names letter by letter. Giving your name / email Very slow, in pieces "R-A-M-E-S-H. Ramesh." Repeating is polite, not weak. With a friend Whatever comes easily Practise here — mistakes cost little.
  • Let me slow down — my name is Ramesh. R for Rakesh, A, M, E, S, H. The clearest way to give your name on the phone. Link each letter to a word.
  • Sorry, I'm speaking too fast. Let me start again. Correcting yourself is very professional. There is nothing to be embarrassed about.

docs.title: 29.5 Stuck in the middle of a sentence — now what?
docs.text:
This is the biggest fear: you cannot find a word halfway through a sentence, and your mind goes blank. There are three reliable cures. All three are learnable skills, not luck.

Cure 1 — Say it another way (paraphrase)

Cannot find the word? Describe what the thing does. This is the most powerful skill — it is how people talk about the whole world with 500 words.

Word you forgot Say it like this Listen stapler The thing you use to join papers together. landlord The person who owns the house I live in. deadline The last date to finish the work. puncture There's a hole in my tyre — the air went out.

Cure 2 — Start again from the beginning

Is the sentence tangled? Do not try to rescue it. With a short apology, start again with a new, short line. "Sorry, let me start that again." Native speakers do this every day. It is not a mistake, it is a method.

Cure 3 — Ask for help

Asking for the English name of something is not weakness — it is the right behaviour for a learner. "What do you call the thing that…?" "Is that the right word?"

docs.title: 29.6 After a mistake — do not stop, fix it and move on
docs.text:
English has a short, natural way to correct yourself: say the wrong word, then say "sorry" or "I mean", put in the right word, and keep going. You do not need to stop or apologise at length.

  • I went there yesterday — sorry, last week. You spotted the mistake, fixed it in one word, and moved on.
  • She don't— she doesn't work here any more. The grammar mistake was fixed in the middle. This is the most natural way.
  • We have three— I mean four meetings today. "I mean" is the most common and correct tool for corrections.

What not to do

When you make a mistake, do not start the "Sorry, sorry, my English is very poor, sorry" routine. One short apology is enough, and even better is to put in the right word and move on without stopping. If you keep apologising, the listener stops paying attention to your message.

docs.title: 29.7 A pattern for longer answers
docs.text:
A simple trick to sound fluent: do not give one-word answers. In every answer add one piece of information + one reason. This keeps the talk going and also gives you time to think.

Question Weak answer Fluent answer Listen Do you like cricket? Yes. Yes, I do. I watch most matches, especially the one-day games. Where are you from? Delhi. I'm from Delhi, but I've been living in Pune for three years now. How was your weekend? Good. It was good, thanks. I mostly stayed home and caught up on sleep. Can you finish it today? No. Not today, I'm afraid. I could have it ready by tomorrow afternoon.

Remember the pattern

Answer + one detail + one reason or what comes next. Three parts, that is all. You do not need more, and with less the talk stops.

docs.title: 29.8 Daily fluency drill — 5 minutes
docs.text:
A one-minute monologue

Set a timer on your phone for 60 seconds. Choose an ordinary topic — your day, your room, your work — and speak for 60 seconds without stopping. Only one rule: silent pauses are fine, but do not switch to Hindi. If you cannot find a word, say it another way (Cure 1). One minute every day. In two weeks you will hear the difference yourself.

  • Today I woke up at seven, had tea, and then I checked my phone for a while. Start a monologue like this — short sentences, joined with "and then".
  • It's hard to explain, but let me try. Say this line when you get stuck — then make an attempt. It is a completely native line.

docs.title: 29.9 Practice — Fluency
docs.text:
Exercise 1

What is the right meaning of fluency?

  • To keep speaking without panic, even when you pause
  • To speak very fast
  • To speak without a single mistake
  • To have a big vocabulary

Hint: It has nothing to do with speed.

Answer

To keep speaking without panic, even when you pause

Good speakers speak slowly and pause a lot. The only difference is that they do not fill the gaps with fillers.

Exercise 2

What is the biggest problem with 'basically'?

  • In most sentences it means nothing at all
  • It is a wrong word
  • It is hard to pronounce
  • It is only used in writing
Answer

In most sentences it means nothing at all

Remove it from 'Basically I went to the market' and the sentence gets better. The word is not wrong, the habit is.

Exercise 3

You are thinking of the next word. What is best to do?

  • Stay silent, or say a ready-made phrase
  • Stretch a long 'ummmmm'
  • Start speaking faster
  • Say it in Hindi
Answer

Stay silent, or say a ready-made phrase

Two seconds of silence looks like thinking; two seconds of 'ummmm' looks nervous. Both take the same time.

Exercise 4

You cannot remember the English name of a thing. What is the best way?

  • Describe what the thing does — 'the thing you use to…'
  • Drop the subject
  • Use the Hindi word
  • Stay silent until you remember

Hint: Cure 1.

Answer

Describe what the thing does — 'the thing you use to…'

Saying it another way is the most powerful skill. It is how people say everything with few words.

Exercise 5

How fast should you speak in an interview?

  • Slower than everyday speech
  • As fast as possible
  • Very fast, to save time
  • Fast at first, slow later
Answer

Slower than everyday speech

Slow speech sounds confident and gives you time to think of the next sentence. In fast speech the sounds run together.

Exercise 6

You made a grammar mistake in the middle of a sentence. What is the right way?

  • Say 'I mean' or 'sorry', put in the right word and move on
  • Say the whole sentence again, saying nothing
  • Keep apologising
  • Leave the mistake and do nothing
Answer

Say 'I mean' or 'sorry', put in the right word and move on

Native speakers do exactly this: 'She don't— she doesn't work here.' Stopping for a long apology breaks the flow.

Exercise 7

Say 'matlab' in English: What I ___ is…

Hint: The word for explaining again.

Answer

mean

'What I mean is…' — the direct English form of 'matlab', and it gives you thinking time too.

Exercise 8

Fix 'It is good, na?': It's good, ___ it?

Hint: A question tag.

Answer

isn't / isnt / is not

Hindi 'na' becomes a question tag in English: isn't it? / right? / don't you think?

Exercise 9

One word in this sentence is extra — tap it.

I am from Mumbai only.

Answer

Wrong word: only.

Corrected: I'm from Mumbai.

'only' gets added from the Hindi habit of 'hi / sirf'. In English it has no meaning here.

Exercise 10

Find the filler word that should be cut.

Basically I finished the report yesterday.

Answer

Wrong word: Basically.

Corrected: I finished the report yesterday.

Remove it and the sentence is cleaner. Here is the test: if removing it does not change the meaning, it is filler.

Exercise 11

Match each filler to its right English replacement.

A B matlab two seconds of silence na? nothing — cut it ummmm What I mean is… basically isn't it? Answer

matlab — What I mean is…; na? — isn't it?; ummmm — two seconds of silence; basically — nothing — cut it

Every Hinglish filler has a clear English form. Learn it once and it starts coming out by itself.

Exercise 12

Build a phrase that buys thinking time.

Words: for / that / about / a / Let / me / think / second

Answer

Let me think about that for a second

It gives you 3-4 seconds, and the listener feels you are thinking carefully.

Exercise 13

Buy time after a question. Speak calmly.

Answer

Say: That's a good question. Let me think about that for a second

Two phrases together — you have 5 seconds. In an interview this is gold.

Exercise 14

Explain it again — do not say 'matlab'.

Answer

Say: What I mean is we should wait one more week

A full sentence after 'What I mean is'. A useful phrase in place of filler.

Exercise 15

You cannot find the word — say it another way.

Answer

Say: It's the thing you use to join papers together

If you forget 'stapler', describe what it does. The talk never stops — that is fluency.

Exercise 16

You got tangled. Make a fresh start.

Answer

Say: Sorry, let me start that again

A short apology, then a new short line. Native speakers do this every day.

Exercise 17

Give a fluent answer in place of one word — 'Where are you from?'

Answer

Say: I'm from Delhi but I've been living in Pune for three years now

Answer + detail + what comes next. Three parts — this is what keeps the talk going.

Exercise 18

You did not understand. Ask politely.

Answer

Say: Sorry, could you repeat that

Voice rises slightly at the end. You will use this line every day — so it should come out without thinking.

Exercise 19

You are stuck but not giving up. Say this line.

Answer

Say: It's hard to explain but let me try

A completely native line. By saying it you also get time to think.

What next?

Today's task: choose three thinking phrases and say them 20 times. And do a one-minute monologue — today, right now. Next chapter: Everyday conversations — the shop, the auto, the doctor, the phone. You will get ready-made lines that you can use from tomorrow.

docs.title: Chapter 19: Gerunds & infinitives
docs.text:
Gerund or Infinitive — doing or to do?

When one verb is followed by another verb, the second verb takes either -ing (enjoy reading) or to + V1 (want to read). In Hindi both cases use the same form — "padhna pasand hai", "padhna chahta hoon" — so we usually guess. In this chapter we will not guess; we will learn a sure method.

In one line

A gerund is a verb + -ing used as a noun (Swimming is fun). An infinitive is to + base verb (I want to swim). In both, the verb becomes the "name of an activity" — like "tairna" in Hindi.

  • I enjoy cooking. = I like making food. — enjoy + -ing
  • I want to cook tonight. = I would like to make food this evening. — want + to

docs.title: 19.1 The first verb decides
docs.text:
The most important point: you don't choose the form of the second verb — the first verb chooses it. Every verb has its own preference. So the easiest way to remember them is to sort the verbs into three boxes.

Figure 19.1. Look at the first verb, then remember its box. Verbs in the middle box can take both — but the meaning is different.

The first verb decides

The first verb decides the form of the second verb (-ing or to + V1). A rough guide: -ing looks at an actual action, one that is happening or already happened; to looks at an action that is still ahead.

As the subject, -ing is more natural

Walking is good for health. — the most common and natural. To walk is good for health. — correct, but it sounds bookish.

docs.title: 19.2 Verb + -ing: enjoy, avoid, finish, suggest
docs.text:
These verbs usually talk about an actual or ongoing activity — one you like, one you avoid, one you finished. Adding "to" after them is the most common mistake.

Verb Meaning Example enjoy to get pleasure from We enjoyed watching the match. avoid to stay away from Avoid eating junk food. finish to complete Have you finished writing? suggest to give an idea She suggested taking a taxi. mind to be bothered by Do you mind waiting? keep to continue doing He kept calling me. practise to train by repeating Practise speaking every day. give up to stop for good My uncle gave up smoking.

Verbs that take -ing

enjoy, avoid, finish, suggest, mind, keep, practise, consider, give up — always followed by verb-ing, never "to". ✓ I enjoy reading. ✗ I enjoy to read.

How to add a person after suggest

  • Wrong: He suggested me to go by train.
  • Right: He suggested going by train. / He suggested that I go by train.
  • Why: "Suggest" has no "person + to" pattern. Either use -ing, or use "that + person + V1".

docs.title: 19.3 Verb + to: want, decide, hope, plan
docs.text:
These verbs mostly talk about thoughts about the future — wishes, decisions, hopes, plans. The action has not happened yet; it is going to happen. That is why we use "to" — like an arrow pointing at the action.

Verb Meaning Example want to wish for I want to learn French. decide to make up your mind They decided to move to Pune. hope to expect something good We hope to see you soon. plan to make a plan She plans to start a business. agree / refuse to say yes / to say no He refused to sign. promise to give your word I promise to call you. manage to succeed in doing something hard We managed to finish on time.

Verbs that take to

want, decide, hope, plan, agree, refuse, promise, manage, need, expect — followed by to + V1. If a person comes in between: want / ask / tell / advise someone to do.

  • My mother wants me to become a doctor. = My mother hopes I will become a doctor. — not "that I become"; use "me to become" directly.
  • The teacher told us to sit down. tell, ask, advise, allow, remind — all take "person + to".

docs.title: 19.4 Both are possible — but the meaning changes
docs.text:
Some verbs take both forms, and this is the most interesting part. Here, choosing the wrong form does not make a mistake; it gives a completely different meaning — so study these carefully.

Figure 19.2. The -ing arrow points back, the to arrow points ahead. This one picture explains stop, remember and forget.

stop, remember, forget, try

-ing = an earlier or actual action: remember meeting (we have already met). to = a later action: remember to meet (we still have to meet). try doing = do it and see what happens; try to do = make an effort.

Verb + -ing + to V1 stop to quit an activity — stop talking to pause in order to do something else — stop to talk remember to remember something that happened — remember meeting her to remember a job still to be done — remember to call forget to forget a past moment — I'll never forget seeing the Taj to forget to do something — I forgot to lock it try to test a method — try restarting the phone to make an effort at something hard — try to lift the box

Some verbs show very little difference

like, love, hate, start, begin, continue — both forms work and the meaning stays almost the same: It started raining = It started to rain.

docs.title: 19.5 After a preposition, always -ing
docs.text:
This is the easiest and surest rule in this chapter. After a preposition comes a noun — and when you want a verb there, you have to make it noun-like, that is, -ing.

  • I am interested in learning Japanese. = I find learning Japanese interesting.
  • She is good at solving puzzles. = She solves puzzles well.
  • Thank you for coming. = Thanks, because you came.
  • Wash your hands before eating. = First wash your hands, then eat. — after before, after, without, instead of, by — always -ing.

Preposition + -ing

in, at, of, for, about, before, after, without, by, instead of — if a verb follows them, it is always -ing: interested in learning, tired of waiting, without asking. Never "to + V1".

docs.title: 19.6 The "to" trap — look forward to meeting
docs.text:
Not every "to" belongs to an infinitive. Sometimes "to" is really a preposition — and remember the rule from the last section? After a preposition, -ing. You just have to recognise which "to" is which.

Figure 19.3. If a noun like the party can sit after to , then it is a preposition — and the verb takes -ing.

The preposition 'to'

look forward to, be used to, get used to, object to, be committed to, when it comes to — in these, "to" is a preposition, so the verb takes -ing: I look forward to meeting you.

  • I am used to working late. = Working late is normal for me. (test: used to late nights ✓)
  • When it comes to cooking, my father is the best. = On the subject of cooking, my father is better than anyone.

docs.title: 19.7 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
The most common Indian-English mistakes with -ing and to

  • Wrong: I look forward to meet you.
  • Right: I look forward to meeting you.

  • Why: This mistake appears at the end of almost every formal email. Here "to" is a preposition (look forward to the meeting ✓), so the verb takes -ing.

  • Wrong: I am interested to learn coding.

  • Right: I am interested in learning coding.

  • Why: "Interested" goes with the preposition "in", and after a preposition comes -ing. To express interest, always say "interested in + -ing".

  • Wrong: He suggested me to go home.

  • Right: He suggested that I go home. / He suggested going home.

  • Why: "Suggest" does not take "person + to". That pattern belongs to "advise": He advised me to go home.

  • Wrong: I enjoy to travel.

  • Right: I enjoy travelling.

  • Why: "Enjoy" is a verb from the -ing box. The Hindi "ghoomna pasand hai" pulls in a "to" — but never after "enjoy".

  • Wrong: Thank you for give me this chance.

  • Right: Thank you for giving me this chance.
  • Why: "For" is a preposition — the verb after it is always in the -ing form.

docs.title: 19.8 Practice — Gerunds & infinitives
docs.text:
Exercise 1

We have decided ___ a new car.

  • to buy
  • buying
  • buy
  • to buying

Hint: Which box does 'decide' belong to?

Answer

to buy

'Decide' is about a decision for the future — a verb from the 'to' box. So decide + to + V1.

Exercise 2

Please avoid ___ your phone while driving.

  • using
  • to use
  • use
  • used
Answer

using

'Avoid' always takes -ing — avoid using, avoid eating. 'Avoid to use' is a very common mistake.

Exercise 3

I clearly remember ___ the gas. I'm sure it's off.

  • switching off
  • to switch off
  • switch off
  • to switching off

Hint: The action already happened, and you remember it.

Answer

switching off

Turning off the gas happened earlier — and you remember it now. Remembering a past action = remember + -ing.

Exercise 4

The driver stopped ___ some tea, then continued the journey.

  • to have
  • having
  • have
  • had

Hint: Why did he stop?

Answer

to have

The driver stopped in order to drink tea — he paused one activity to do another. stop + to = pause so that you can do something. 'Stopped having tea' would mean he gave up drinking tea.

Exercise 5

I look forward to ___ from you soon. (hear)

Hint: This 'to' is a preposition.

Answer

hearing

In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition (look forward to your reply ✓), and after a preposition we use -ing. So 'hearing'.

Exercise 6

She is very good at ___ people laugh. (make)

Hint: What comes after 'at'?

Answer

making

'At' is a preposition. After a preposition the verb is always in the -ing form — good at making.

Exercise 7

Tap the wrong word.

My manager suggested me to take a short break.

Answer

Wrong word: me.

Corrected: My manager suggested that I take a short break.

The 'me to' pattern does not work after 'suggest'. Say 'suggested that I take' or 'suggested taking'.

Exercise 8

One word is in the wrong form — find it.

I am interested in join the music class.

Answer

Wrong word: join.

Corrected: I am interested in joining the music class.

'In' is a preposition, so the verb after it takes -ing — joining.

Exercise 9

Match each verb with its correct pattern.

A B enjoy + verb-ing (preposition) want + to V1 (after a person) interested in + verb-ing advise someone + to V1 Answer

enjoy — + verb-ing; want — + to V1; interested in — + verb-ing (preposition); advise someone — + to V1 (after a person)

Enjoy belongs to the -ing box, want to the 'to' box. 'In' is a preposition, so -ing. After advise comes a person, and then to + V1.

Exercise 10

Put the words in the correct order.

Words: the / midnight / She / report / at / writing / finished

Answer

She finished writing the report at midnight

'Finish' is followed by -ing — finished writing. Then the object (the report) and the time (at midnight).

Exercise 11

Build this sentence — the 'person + to' pattern.

Words: study / want / parents / me / to / My / abroad

Answer

My parents want me to study abroad

After 'want' comes the person (me) and then to + V1 (to study). We don't say 'want that I study' the way Hindi does.

Exercise 12

Say this last line of an email aloud — mind the word 'meeting'.

Answer

Say: I look forward to meeting you

This line is written wrongly so often that saying it correctly aloud is the best cure. 'To' is a preposition here, so 'meeting'.

What to do next

Draw three boxes on paper — "-ing", "to", "both". Every time you meet a new verb, put it in one of the boxes. In a month you will have your own sorter, and no more guessing.

docs.title: Chapter 24: Habits, wishes & advice
docs.text:
used to, wish, had better

"I used to play cricket every day", "I'm used to it", "I wish I had studied", "You'd better leave soon, or…" — in Hindi we say these four things ten times a day. English has short, fixed structures for them: used to, be used to, I wish, had better, would rather. Understand them clearly once, and your English will sound much more natural straight away.

In one line

used to + V1 = it happened in the past, but not now. be used to + -ing = you are accustomed to it. wish + past = if only. had better + V1 = or there will be trouble. Each structure needs a fixed verb form — that is the real game in this chapter.

docs.title: 24.1 The map first — which "habit" when?
docs.text:
In Hindi, "aadat" (habit) is one word, but English has three different structures — and all three mean something completely different. This is where mistakes happen. Before you speak, ask yourself one question: Is this about the past, about a habit today, or about a new habit forming?

Figure 24.1. Three paths, three structures. In the first one, used to is followed by V1 ; in the other two, to is followed by -ing or a noun .

A map straight from Hindi

"pehle karta tha" → used to do · "aadat hai" → be used to doing · "aadat pad jaayegi" → get used to doing.

docs.title: 24.2 used to + V1 — it happened before, but not now
docs.text:
used to describes a habit or situation in the past that has now ended. It is always followed by the first form of the verb (V1). It works for both actions (doing things) and states (being, living, having).

  • I used to live in Patna. = I lived in Patna before, but I don't live there now.
  • We used to walk to school every day. = We walked to school every day in the past.
  • Priya used to have very long hair. = Priya's hair was very long before (it isn't now).
  • There used to be a cinema hall here. = There was a cinema hall here once, but it's gone.

docs.title: Negatives and questions — the "d" disappears
docs.text:
When did / didn't appears, it already shows the past — so the "d" on used drops off: didn't use to, Did you use to…? It works just like didn't go, not didn't went.

Form Formula Example Positive used to + V1 I used to smoke. Negative didn't use to + V1 I didn't use to like coffee. Negative (stronger) never used to + V1 He never used to call. Question Did … use to + V1? Did you use to play cricket?
  • I didn't use to like coffee, but now I love it. = I disliked coffee in the past; today I love it.
  • Did you use to play cricket in college? = Was cricket something you played regularly in college?

Pronunciation: 'yoos-tuh'

Don't say used to as "yooz-d too". Say /ˈjuːstə/ — "yoos-tuh", with an "s" sound, and use to sounds exactly the same.

docs.title: used to has no present form
docs.text:
This is the most common Indian mistake. For a habit today, don't use use to — use the present simple, often with usually (see All 12 tenses).

✗

I use to drink tea every morning.

✓

I usually drink tea every morning.

✗

I used to go to Goa three times.

✓

I went to Goa three times.

docs.title: 24.3 would — the story of old memories
docs.text:
When English speakers tell stories about the past (summers at grandma's house, school days), they set the scene once with used to, and then carry the story on with would + V1. It sounds a little bookish and nostalgic.

  • Every summer, we used to go to Nani's village. = We went to our grandmother's village every summer.
  • We'd climb the mango trees all afternoon. = We climbed the mango trees again and again all afternoon.
  • In the evening, Nani would tell us ghost stories. = Every evening our grandmother told us ghost stories.

would = repeated actions only

would is for old actions (playing, going, listening), and never for states (be, have, live, like, know). For states, use only used to.

✗

We would have a dog called Moti.

✓

We used to have a dog called Moti.

Verb used to? would? play, go, visit (action) ✓ ✓ live, be, have (state) ✓ ✗ like, love, know, believe ✓ ✗ First line of a story ✓ (better) Give the time first

docs.title: 24.4 be used to / get used to + -ing — the no. 1 confusion for Hindi speakers
docs.text:
Here used works like an adjective (= accustomed) and to is a preposition, not the infinitive "to". After a preposition comes a noun, a pronoun or -ing — never V1. This is the same rule you saw in the to do or doing? chapter with look forward to meeting.

  • I am used to waking up early. = Waking up early feels normal to me.
  • She isn't used to spicy food. = Spicy food is new to her, and she finds it hard.
  • Are you used to the Delhi winters yet? = Have the Delhi winters started to feel normal to you?
  • I'm getting used to my new job. = My new job is slowly starting to feel normal.
  • Don't worry, you'll get used to it. = It will feel normal after some time, so don't worry.
  • It took me months to get used to driving in Bengaluru traffic. = Driving in Bengaluru traffic felt hard for months, and then it felt normal.

be used to vs get used to

be used to = you are accustomed (a state). get used to = you are becoming / will become accustomed (a change). Both are followed by -ing or a noun, and "be/get" can change with every tense: was used to, will get used to, have got used to.

The most common mistake

  • Wrong: I am used to wake up early.
  • Right: I am used to waking up early.
  • Why: Here "to" is a preposition, so it is followed by -ing. If you mean "I woke up early in the past", drop "am": I used to wake up early.

✗

I used to living alone, so I don't mind it.

✓

I'm used to living alone, so I don't mind it.

Structure Meaning Example used to + V1 did it in the past (not now) I used to work nights. be used to + -ing am accustomed to it I'm used to working nights. get used to + -ing am becoming accustomed to it I'm getting used to working nights.

A formal word

In writing, be accustomed to + -ing also works: The staff are accustomed to working under pressure.

docs.title: 24.5 I wish / If only — three kinds of "if only"
docs.text:
To say "kaash" (if only), English uses I wish or the more emotional If only. The trick is that after wish the verb goes one step back — because what we want is not true. This is the same backshift you saw in the second and third conditionals of the If sentences chapter.

Figure 24.2. The further back the regret, the further back the tense. A wish about now → past simple; a regret about the past → past perfect; annoyance with others → would.

docs.title: (a) A wish about now — wish + past simple
docs.text:
• I wish I had a car. = I don't have a car now, and I'd like one.
  • I wish I knew the answer. = I don't know the answer, and I'd like to.
  • I wish I could swim. = I can't swim, and I'd like to be able to.
  • If only we lived closer to the office! = We live far from the office, and we wish we didn't.
  • I wish I were taller. = I'm not very tall, and I'd like to be taller.

were or was?

I wish I were is formal and safe for exams; in everyday speech I wish I **was is also perfectly fine. In exams and formal writing, use were.

docs.title: (b) A regret about the past — wish + had + V3
docs.text:
• I wish I had studied harder for the exam. = I didn't study hard enough, and I regret it.
  • I wish I hadn't said that to her. = I said it, and now I'm sorry I did.
  • If only we'd left ten minutes earlier! = We left too late and missed the train.

docs.title: (c) A complaint about others — wish + would
docs.text:
Use wish + someone + would when someone else (or even the weather!) keeps doing something and you want it to change. There is a little annoyance in it.

  • I wish you would stop interrupting me. = Please stop interrupting me — it annoys me.
  • I wish it would stop raining. = I'm tired of this rain and want it to stop.

✗

I wish I would speak French.

✓

I wish I could speak French.

docs.title: wish or hope?
docs.text:
