For things that might happen, use hope (+ a normal tense). For things that are not true, use wish (+ past). And wish + person + noun is only for good wishes in a fixed phrase: I wish you a happy birthday.

✗

I wish you will pass the exam.

✓

I hope you pass the exam.

I wish you all the best for the exam.

  • I hope you get the job. = I'm hoping you get the job — it could really happen.
  • I wish you all the best. = A kind, fixed phrase: good luck to you.

docs.title: 24.6 had better — advice with a warning inside
docs.text:
had better + V1 (in speech, 'd better) means "do it, or there will be trouble". The word "had" is in the name, but it is about now or the future, not the past. And it is never followed by "to".

  • You'd better leave now, or you'll miss the train. = Leave now — otherwise you'll miss the train.
  • We'd better not tell Mummy about this. = It's wiser not to tell Mummy — she may get upset.
  • I'd better charge my phone before the meeting. = I should charge my phone before the meeting, or I'll have a problem.

had better

'd better + V1 / 'd better not + V1 — "do it, or else…". No "to", no past meaning, and stronger than should.

✗

You had better to submit it today.

✓

You'd better submit it today.

had better not go

Don't say 'had better' to your boss

"Sir, you had better check the file." sounds like a threat. To senior people, say "You might want to check the file" or "It might be a good idea to…". For ordinary advice, should is enough (see can, could, should, must).

docs.title: 24.7 would rather — "I'd prefer to…"
docs.text: would rather ('d rather) shows a preference or choice — "I'd choose to do this". It has two patterns, and the second one surprises even advanced learners.

docs.title: (a) Your own preference — would rather + V1 (than + V1)
docs.text:
• I'd rather walk than take an auto. = I prefer walking to taking an auto.
  • Would you rather have tea or coffee? = Which would you prefer, tea or coffee?
  • I'd rather not talk about it. = A polite way to say you don't want to talk about it.

docs.title: (b) Wanting someone else to act — would rather + someone + past
docs.text:
When you want someone else to do something, use a new subject and a verb in the past — just like wish, even though you are talking about now.

  • I'd rather you didn't smoke in the car. = Please don't smoke in the car — I'd prefer that.
  • I'd rather you came on Monday. = I'd like you to come on Monday.

✗

I would rather to stay at home.

✓

I'd rather stay at home. / I'd prefer to stay at home.

I prefer tea to coffee.

Pattern Example would rather + V1 I'd rather stay. would rather + V1 + than + V1 I'd rather walk than wait. would rather + person + V2 I'd rather you stayed. would prefer + to + V1 I'd prefer to stay. prefer + noun/-ing + to I prefer tea to coffee.

docs.title: 24.8 It's time — "it's already time"
docs.text:
To simply say that the time has come, use It's time to + V1 or It's time for + noun. But if you mean "this should have happened already", use It's (high / about) time + subject + past simple.

  • It's time to go. = The time to leave has come.
  • It's time for lunch. = It's lunchtime now.
  • It's time we left — it's nearly midnight. = We should go now — it's nearly midnight.
  • It's high time you got a proper job. = You should have found a proper job already (a little critical).
  • It's about time the government fixed this road. = The government should have fixed this road long ago.

✗

It's high time you get married.

✓

It's high time you got married.

One pattern, four places

I wish you came · If only you **came · I'd rather you came · It's time you **came — when something is not real, even a meaning of "now" is built with the past simple.

docs.title: 24.9 In real life — a phone call
docs.text:
Meera has joined a new job and moved to Pune. Her father calls. Listen to the whole conversation, then spot the structure in every line.

Who What they say Listen Papa So, are you used to the new place yet? Meera Slowly. I'm still getting used to cooking for myself. Papa At home you never used to enter the kitchen! Meera I know. I wish I'd learnt a few recipes from Mummy. Papa Well, you'd better not live on Maggi! Meera Honestly, I'd rather order food than cook after work. Papa Then it's high time you found a good tiffin service. Wrong Right Why I am used to wake early. I'm used to waking early. to = preposition → -ing I use to go to the gym. I usually go to the gym. used to has no present Did you used to…? Did you use to…? no "d" after did I wish you will come. I hope you can come. possible = hope You had better to go. You'd better go. had better + V1 I'd rather you don't. I'd rather you didn't. new subject → past

docs.title: 24.10 Practice — used to, wish, had better
docs.text:
Exercise 1

I moved to Shimla last year. I'm still not used to ___ in the cold.

  • drive
  • driving
  • drove
  • driven

Hint: What comes after 'be used to'?

Answer

driving

In 'be used to', 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by -ing: used to driving.

Exercise 2

When I was a child, I ___ to hate vegetables. Now I love them.

Hint: It happened before, but not now.

Answer

used

An old habit that has ended = used to + V1.

Exercise 3

Did you ___ to play cricket in school?

Hint: Does the 'd' stay after 'did'?

Answer

use

did / didn't already show the past, so it is 'use to' — 'Did you used to' is wrong.

Exercise 4

We ___ a dog called Moti when we lived in Lucknow.

  • would have
  • used to have
  • are used to having
  • got used to have
Answer

used to have

'have' (to own) is a state. With states we use only 'used to', not 'would'.

Exercise 5

Tap the wrong word.

After ten years in the army, he is used to wake up at five.

Answer

Wrong word: wake.

Corrected: After ten years in the army, he is used to waking up at five.

'is used to' = is accustomed, and after the preposition 'to' comes -ing: waking.

Exercise 6

I wish I ___ more free time. (I don't have it now)

  • have
  • had
  • will have
  • am having
Answer

had

A wish about now that isn't true: wish + past simple.

Exercise 7

I wish I ___ (not / eat) that street food last night. My stomach hurts!

Hint: A regret about the past.

Answer

hadn't eaten / had not eaten

A regret about the past = wish + had (not) + V3.

Exercise 8

My neighbour plays loud music every night. I wish he ___ it.

  • stops
  • would stop
  • will stop
  • had stop
Answer

would stop

Annoyance at someone else's behaviour = wish + someone + would + V1.

Exercise 9

Your friend has an interview tomorrow. You say: 'I ___ you get the job!'

  • wish
  • hope
  • would rather
  • had better
Answer

hope

Getting the job is possible — hope + a normal tense. 'wish' is for unreal things.

Exercise 10

Tap the extra word.

You had better to leave now or you will miss the bus.

Answer

Wrong word: to.

Corrected: You had better leave now or you will miss the bus.

had better is followed directly by V1, not 'to'.

Exercise 11

I'd rather you ___ (not / smoke) inside the house.

Hint: would rather + another subject → past

Answer

didn't smoke / did not smoke

would rather + someone + past simple, even when the meaning is about now.

Exercise 12

Put the words in order.

Words: time / it's / we / money / high / saving / started

Answer

it's high time we started saving money

It's high time + subject + past simple = this should have happened already.

Exercise 13

Match each structure to its meaning.

A B used to + V1 becoming accustomed to it be used to + -ing do it, or there's trouble get used to + -ing did it before, not now had better + V1 am accustomed to it Answer

used to + V1 — did it before, not now; be used to + -ing — am accustomed to it; get used to + -ing — becoming accustomed to it; had better + V1 — do it, or there's trouble

Three 'used to' structures — three different meanings. And had better has a warning hidden inside.

Exercise 14

What does the speaker do now?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

When I was in college, I used to take the bus everywhere. Now I drive to work, but I'm still not used to the traffic.

  • drives to work
  • takes the bus
  • walks to work
  • works from home
Answer

drives to work

'used to take the bus' = in the past. 'Now I drive to work' = now.

Exercise 15

How does the speaker feel about the traffic?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

When I was in college, I used to take the bus everywhere. Now I drive to work, but I'm still not used to the traffic.

  • it still feels difficult
  • they enjoy it
  • they never notice it
  • it was worse in college
Answer

it still feels difficult

'still not used to' = it hasn't become normal yet — so it feels difficult.

Exercise 16

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

I wish I had listened to my mother.

A regret about the past: wish + had + V3 (listened).

Exercise 17

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

You had better take an umbrella. It is going to rain.

had better + V1 (take) — with the feeling of 'or you'll get wet'.

Exercise 18

Say it aloud — the 's' sound in 'used'.

Answer

Say: I'm getting used to my new job

get used to + noun = becoming accustomed. 'used to' = 'yoos-tuh'.

What to do next

Tonight, write five sentences: two with used to (childhood habits), one with I'm used to, one with I wish I had… and one with I'd rather…. Then say them aloud. The next chapter, Powerful sentences, will add emphasis and weight to your sentences.

docs.title: Chapter 1: How to use this book
docs.text:
If you feel a little nervous even opening this page — "I don't know anything", "I get stuck when I speak" — you are in exactly the right place. This book is not here to teach you about English. It is here to make you speak English. And there is only one way to learn to speak: by speaking. Starting today, alone in your room, out loud.

The one rule of the whole book

Whenever you see an English line in this book, don't just read it with your eyes. Say it with your mouth. English that you only read silently never reaches your tongue. Silent reading gives you understanding. Speaking gives you fluency. They are two different things.

docs.title: 1.1 15 minutes every day — that's all
docs.text:
Studying for two hours once a week does very little. 15 minutes every day does everything. Your brain learns a language by repetition, not by long sessions. Split your 15 minutes like this:

Figure 1.1. Notice: the biggest block is orange — speaking . Reading is only a quarter of your time.

Where to find 15 minutes

Before your bath. On the bus or metro. In bed before sleep. Pick one fixed place and one fixed time — then you won't need to remember at all, because the habit will pull you in.

docs.title: 1.2 Say everything out loud — that is the whole game
docs.text:
People study grammar for years and still get stuck when they speak. Why? Because the grammar went into the brain, but not into the muscles of the tongue. To make English sounds, your lips, tongue and jaw must learn new positions — and muscles learn only by repetition, not by understanding.

  • I am learning English, and I am getting better every day. Your first line to say today. Press 🔊, listen, then say it three times yourself.
  • I make mistakes, but I keep speaking. = I do make mistakes, but I never stop speaking. Make this sentence your personal rule.
  • Could you say that again, please? Use this when you didn't understand — don't be shy. Native speakers say this every day too.

Speaking alone in your room is not 'crazy' — it is a method

Many people stop themselves: "How can I talk to myself? I'll feel silly." The truth is that every fluent speaker has spoken alone first, a thousand times. Close the door, put a mirror in front of you, and speak. Nobody can hear you, so mistakes cost nothing. It is the safest practice you will ever get.

docs.title: 1.3 The 🔊 button and the 🎤 mic — how they work
docs.text:
Feature What it does What you should do 🔊 Say button Reads that line aloud in your device's voice. Listen first. Then pause and say the same line yourself. Then listen again and compare. Slow voice Some difficult lines are read slowly, so that every sound is clear. Say it slowly the first time. Speed will come later — the goal is not fast, the goal is clear. 6 types of quiz Multiple choice, fill in the blank, spot the mistake, match the sentence, match the pairs, and say it aloud. Do all of them. Don't skip. The explanation you get after a wrong answer is the most valuable part. 🎤 Speak (mic) In a "say it aloud" question, the mic listens to your voice and checks it. The first time, your browser will ask for permission — press "Allow". Sit in a quiet room and speak about 20 cm from your phone.

What if the mic doesn't work?

No problem — not every browser has speech recognition. In that case the page will simply ask you to listen and repeat. The mic is only a helper, not a requirement. Your own ear is the best judge: listen with 🔊, record yourself in a recorder app, play both, and hear the difference. This is what professionals do.

docs.title: 1.4 Where to start — choose your path
docs.text:
There are three kinds of learners. Find your line:

A. 'I know nothing, I'm starting from zero'

Go in order. Read the next chapter — English Sounds — first, because it is the foundation. Then Grammar basics, then Learn to Speak. One part a day. In three months you won't recognise yourself.

B. 'I know the grammar, but I get stuck when I speak'

This is the most common situation — and grammar is not the cure. Go straight to the "Learn to Speak" section: Pronunciation → Rhythm → Fluency → Everyday conversation. Open the grammar chapters only when one particular thing confuses you.

C. 'I have an interview / I'm joining an office'

First the Interview and office chapter, then Fluency, then Indian English habits (the mistakes that interviewers notice immediately). Leave the rest of the book for later, at your own pace.

If you get lost anywhere

The sidebar has the list of all chapters — open any one you like. The book remembers your progress by itself: every quiz you finish gets a tick on the contents page. No login, nothing to fill in.

docs.title: 1.5 When you feel like giving up
docs.text:
Let me tell you something straight, because no book does: after two or three weeks you will feel that nothing is improving. This is completely normal. Learning a language is not a smooth slope — it is a staircase. Many days feel the same, and then suddenly one day you say a whole sentence without thinking.

  • It is normal to feel stuck. I will speak anyway. = Feeling stuck is normal. I will speak anyway. On a day when you don't feel like it, say this line and do just 5 minutes.
  • Sorry, my English is improving. Please bear with me. Say this in real life when you get stuck — it means "please be patient with me". People almost always help.

Three habits that do the most damage

  • Wrong: "I'll make my grammar perfect first, then I'll speak."
  • Right: Start speaking today, mistakes and all — your grammar will improve along the way.

  • Why: People who wait to be perfect before they speak never start at all.

  • Wrong: Thinking in Hindi and translating in your head before you speak.

  • Right: Memorise short, ready-made sentences and say them directly.

  • Why: Translating takes 3-4 seconds — and confidence breaks in that gap. That is why this book gives you ready-made lines.

  • Wrong: Only reading with your eyes and never making a sound.

  • Right: Say every line aloud at least once.
  • Why: This is the difference between this book and all the others. If you read silently, your results will be silent too.

docs.title: 1.6 A small first step — right now
docs.text: The quiz below is a small beginning. Some questions ask you to answer by speaking. Close the door of your room, and start. Five minutes, that's all.

docs.title: 1.7 Practice — Start
docs.text:
Exercise 1

What is the biggest rule of this book?

  • Say every English line out loud
  • Finish a whole chapter every day
  • Memorise all the grammar first
  • Only read carefully

Hint: Which was the biggest block out of the four?

Answer

Say every English line out loud

Reading gives you understanding, speaking gives you fluency. The muscles of the tongue learn only by repetition.

Exercise 2

How much time is best to give each day?

  • 15 minutes, every day
  • 2 hours, one day a week
  • 45 minutes, two days a week
  • Whenever I feel like it, as much as I feel like
Answer

15 minutes, every day

The brain learns a language by repetition, not by long sessions. A little every day beats a lot once in a while.

Exercise 3

Which activity takes the most time in the 15 minutes?

  • Speaking aloud (6 minutes)
  • Reading (4 minutes)
  • Quiz (3 minutes)
  • Review (2 minutes)
Answer

Speaking aloud (6 minutes)

In the diagram the orange block was the biggest — speaking. Reading was only 4 minutes.

Exercise 4

What should you do when you give a wrong answer in a quiz?

  • Read the explanation carefully — that is where the learning is
  • Quit the quiz
  • Memorise the whole chapter again
  • Skip the next quizzes

Hint: What is the biggest benefit of a mistake?

Answer

Read the explanation carefully — that is where the learning is

A right answer only confirms what you know. The 'why' after a wrong answer is the real learning.

Exercise 5

If your grammar is fine but you get stuck when speaking, where should you start?

  • Straight from the Learn to Speak section
  • From the 8 parts of speech
  • From idioms
  • From the final test
Answer

Straight from the Learn to Speak section

Getting stuck is not a lack of grammar, it is a lack of practice. Start with pronunciation, rhythm and fluency.

Exercise 6

It is ___ to feel stuck.

Hint: Feeling stuck is a 'common thing' — what word in English?

Answer

normal

'It is normal to…' is a very useful pattern: It is normal to feel nervous. It is normal to make mistakes.

Exercise 7

I make mistakes, ___ I keep speaking.

Hint: The word that joins two opposite ideas.

Answer

but

'but' joins two opposite ideas. Make this whole sentence your personal rule.

Exercise 8

There is one mistake in this sentence — tap the word.

I am learning English since two months.

Answer

Wrong word: since.

Corrected: I have been learning English for two months.

To say how long, use 'for'. 'since' is used when there is a starting point — since June.

Exercise 9

Your first line in this book. Say it aloud — slowly and clearly.

Answer

Say: I am learning English

Start with a short line. Say the 'ning' in 'learning' fully, not 'learnin'.

Exercise 10

Now say your rule.

Answer

Say: I make mistakes but I keep speaking

When you say it, 'mistakes' and 'speaking' get a little extra stress — those words carry the meaning.

Exercise 11

Use this when you don't understand. Say it politely.

Answer

Say: Could you say that again please

Starting with 'Could you' is the most polite way. Your voice rises slightly at the end — it is a question.

Exercise 12

Today's promise. Say it aloud to finish.

Answer

Say: I will practise for fifteen minutes every day

In 'fifteen' the stress is on the second part — fif-TEEN. In 'fifty' it is on the first — FIF-ty. That is the difference.

What next?

If you are starting from zero, don't skip the next chapter — English Sounds. It is the foundation, and without it everything else will keep sounding a little bit wrong. And remember: door closed, voice loud. 🔊

docs.title: Chapter 41: Idioms
docs.text:
Idioms — the ones a dictionary will not explain

An idiom is a phrase whose words mean one thing, while the whole phrase means something completely different. It's not rocket science has no rocket and no science in it — it means "this is not a hard task". The real benefit of learning idioms is in understanding, not in speaking. Until you can recognise ten idioms properly, half of every meeting goes over your head. And for speaking? Five or six are enough — but used in the right place.

In one line

Learn twenty to recognise, five to speak. Someone who uses too many idioms does not sound like a native — they sound like they memorised a list.

docs.title: 41.1 The first rule of idioms — they never change
docs.text:
An idiom is a frozen mould. Change a single word inside it and it breaks — the listener will think you made a mistake, not that you found a new way to say it.

Broken idioms

  • Wrong: It's not rocket technology.
  • Right: It's not rocket science.

  • Why: The words of an idiom are fixed — synonyms do not work.

  • Wrong: Let's play it from ear.

  • Right: Let's play it by ear.

  • Why: Even the small words are fixed. Change one preposition and the idiom is gone.

  • Wrong: He is on the same boat.

  • Right: He is in the same boat.
  • Why: People sit "inside" a boat, not "on top of" it — so it is in the same boat.

docs.title: 41.2 Three signals — which idiom, where
docs.text:
This is the most important part. Sort idioms into three boxes: safe everywhere, fine at the office but not in writing, and never in formal settings. In interviews, client calls and written emails, the third box is completely closed.

Figure 41.1. Three boxes, three signals. If you cannot remember which is which, the green box is always safe.

docs.title: 41.3 Idioms for work and decisions
docs.text:
Idiom Meaning Signal on the same page to understand things the same way Green — fine in email too in the long run over a long period of time Green play it by ear to decide as things develop Yellow back to the drawing board to start thinking again from the beginning Yellow the ball is in their court it is now their decision Yellow on the back burner set aside for now Yellow cut corners to take shortcuts and lower the quality Yellow call it a day to stop work for today Yellow bite the bullet to do a difficult thing bravely Red — too casual
  • Before we start, let's make sure we're all on the same page. = Before we begin, let's be sure we all understand the same thing.
  • We don't have the numbers yet, so let's play it by ear. = The figures are not here yet, so we will decide as we go.
  • I've sent the proposal — the ball is in their court now. = I have sent the proposal — now it is up to them.
  • It's seven already — shall we call it a day? = It is already seven o'clock — shall we stop for today?

docs.title: 41.4 Idioms for people and relationships
docs.text:
Idiom Meaning Signal see eye to eye to agree Green in the same boat to be in the same situation Yellow a safe pair of hands a person you can trust Green — good for praise rub someone the wrong way to irritate someone without meaning to Yellow pull someone's leg to tease someone as a joke Red — only among friends let someone off the hook to free someone from a duty or blame Yellow get cold feet to become nervous at the last moment Yellow
  • We don't always see eye to eye, but we work well together. = We do not always agree, but we work well together.
  • Put her on the project — she's a safe pair of hands. = Put her on the project — you can rely on her.
  • Everyone's waiting on the same approval — we're all in the same boat. = Everyone is waiting for the same approval — we are all in the same situation.

docs.title: 41.5 Money, time and difficulty
docs.text:
Idiom Meaning Signal in the pipeline being prepared, coming soon Green a long shot unlikely to succeed, but worth trying Yellow down to the wire lasting until the very last moment Yellow cost an arm and a leg very expensive Red — casual tighten one's belt to spend less money Yellow a drop in the ocean so small that it makes no difference Green round the clock all day and all night Green a piece of cake very easy Red — sounds childish
  • Two more features are in the pipeline for next quarter. = Two more features are being prepared for next quarter.
  • It's a long shot, but it costs us nothing to ask. = It probably will not work, but asking costs nothing.
  • The approval came through right down to the wire. = The approval arrived at the very last moment.

docs.title: 41.6 Idioms you should not use in formal settings
docs.text:
There are three different reasons — and each has a different cure.

a) Too casual — they sound childish

a piece of cake, hit the sack, spill the beans, under the weather, pull someone's leg, cost an arm and a leg. In an interview, "The test was a piece of cake" sounds both arrogant and childish. Say this instead: "The test was straightforward." In formal settings, drop the idiom and use the plain word — your point becomes clearer.

b) Too worn out — clichés

think outside the box, give 110 percent, at the end of the day (again and again), touch base, hit the ground running, low-hanging fruit. They are not wrong — they have just been used so often that the listener stops paying attention. In an interview, "I always give 110 percent" has zero effect. Give a real example instead.

c) Not understood outside India

Some phrases are completely normal in India, but on an international call they bring blank faces: "Do the needful" → "Please go ahead and process it." "Same to same" → "Exactly the same." "What is your good name?" → "May I have your name?" "Hats off to him" → fine, but "Full credit to him" is more common. Be careful with cricket idioms too — "He was on a sticky wicket" or "clean bowled" will not be understood by anyone in America. There is nothing wrong with these phrases — they are part of Indian English. The only question is whether the other person will understand.

docs.title: 41.7 How to manage without idioms
docs.text:
The most useful skill is this: say the plain meaning instead of the idiom. That way you will never get caught out.

Casual idiom Formal version It was a piece of cake. It was straightforward. Let's play it by ear. Let's decide once we have more information. We're back to the drawing board. We're revisiting the approach. It cost an arm and a leg. It was extremely expensive. I'm under the weather. I'm not keeping well today. Let's call it a day. Let's stop here and continue tomorrow. The ball is in their court. We're waiting for their decision. It's on the back burner. It's been deprioritised for now.

A trick that always works

If you are unsure about using an idiom, say a clear line first, then add the idiom: "We're waiting on their decision — the ball's in their court." The meaning is already clear, so even if the idiom is not understood, the conversation does not stop.

docs.title: 41.8 Mistakes people make with idioms
docs.text:
Pay attention

  • Wrong: We are on the same page with this.
  • Right: We're on the same page about this.

  • Why: After this idiom comes "about": on the same page about the plan.

  • Wrong: Please do the needful and revert back.

  • Right: Please go ahead and let me know once it's done.

  • Why: This is completely normal in India, but both phrases sound foreign abroad — and in "revert back", the "back" is unnecessary.

  • Wrong: In the interview I said the test was a piece of cake.

  • Right: I said the test was straightforward.

  • Why: In an interview, a casual idiom sounds arrogant. The plain word sounds more confident.

  • Wrong: I will touch base you tomorrow.

  • Right: I'll touch base with you tomorrow.

  • Why: "With" is needed. Besides, this idiom is worn out — plain "I'll check in with you" is better.

  • Wrong: Every point he made was same to same.

  • Right: Every point he made was exactly the same.

  • Why: "Same to same" is not understood abroad. It works in India, not on an international call.

  • Wrong: She spilled the beans in the client presentation.

  • Right: She shared the details early in the client presentation.
  • Why: The idiom is fine, but the place is wrong. In front of a client, an idiom weakens the meaning.

docs.title: 41.9 Practice — Idioms
docs.text:
Exercise 1

What is better to say about a test in an interview?

  • The test was straightforward.
  • The test was a piece of cake.
  • The test was child's play.
  • The test was nothing for me.

Hint: A casual idiom sounds arrogant.

Answer

The test was straightforward.

In formal settings, drop the idiom and use the plain word. 'A piece of cake' sounds both childish and arrogant.

Exercise 2

What does 'The ball is in their court' mean?

  • It is now their decision
  • They are playing a game
  • It is their fault
  • We have won
Answer

It is now their decision

The next move belongs to the other side. It is a polite way to say you are waiting at the office.

Exercise 3

Which idiom is completely safe in emails and client calls too?

  • in the long run
  • hit the sack
  • spill the beans
  • pull my leg
Answer

in the long run

'In the long run' is from the green box — it works in formal writing too. The other three are very casual.

Exercise 4

What should you say on an international call instead of 'Please do the needful'?

  • Please go ahead and process it.
  • Please do the necessary.
  • Kindly do the needful immediately.
  • Please needful it.
Answer

Please go ahead and process it.

'Do the needful' is clearly understood in India but sounds foreign abroad. Say plainly what needs to be done.

Exercise 5

Let's make sure we're all on the same ___ before we start.

Hint: Understanding things the same way.

Answer

page

'On the same page' = understanding things the same way. After it comes 'about': on the same page about the plan.

Exercise 6

We don't have the numbers yet, so let's play it by ___.

Hint: A part of the body.

Answer

ear

'Play it by ear' = decide as things develop. Note: 'by ear', not 'from ear'.

Exercise 7

The idiom is broken — tap the wrong word.

We are all on the same boat this month.

Answer

Wrong word: on.

Corrected: We are all in the same boat this month.

People sit inside a boat — 'in the same boat'. The small words of an idiom are fixed.

Exercise 8

One word is unnecessary — find it.

Please do the needful and revert back to me.

Answer

Wrong word: back.

Corrected: Please go ahead and let me know once it's done.

'Revert' already means 'come back', so 'back' is unnecessary. And it is better to write the whole sentence plainly.

Exercise 9

Match each idiom with its meaning.

A B call it a day to become nervous at the last moment cut corners a person you can trust get cold feet to stop work for today a safe pair of hands to take shortcuts and lower the quality Answer

call it a day — to stop work for today; cut corners — to take shortcuts and lower the quality; get cold feet — to become nervous at the last moment; a safe pair of hands — a person you can trust

You will hear all four at the office every day — recognising them is necessary, speaking them is optional.

Exercise 10

Match each casual idiom with its formal version.

A B It was a piece of cake I'm not keeping well It cost an arm and a leg It's been deprioritised I'm under the weather It was straightforward It's on the back burner It was extremely expensive Answer

It was a piece of cake — It was straightforward; It cost an arm and a leg — It was extremely expensive; I'm under the weather — I'm not keeping well; It's on the back burner — It's been deprioritised

This is the most useful skill: say the plain meaning instead of the idiom. That way you will never get caught out.

Exercise 11

How many idioms are enough for speaking?

  • Five or six, but in the right place
  • The more the better
  • At least fifty
  • None — idioms are wrong
Answer

Five or six, but in the right place

Learn twenty to recognise, five to speak. Someone who uses too many idioms sounds like they memorised a list, not like a native.

Exercise 12

Put the words in the right order — a line for the office.

Words: are / the / ball / court / in / decision / We / waiting / is / their / for / so / their

Answer

We are waiting for their decision so the ball is in their court

This is the trick: plain meaning first, then the idiom. Even if the idiom is not understood, the point is complete.

Exercise 13

Say this line. In 'same page' both words get equal stress.

Answer

Say: Before we start let us make sure we are on the same page

This is the most common line for starting a meeting. You can write it in an email too — it is a green-box idiom.

What to do next

Draw three columns on a sheet of paper — green, yellow, red. Whenever you hear a new idiom, put it into one of the columns straight away. In two months you will have your own list, and it will be more useful than any list from a book — because it comes from your own surroundings.

docs.title: Chapter 57: Indian English habits
docs.text:
Let's make one thing clear first: nothing in this chapter is "uneducated". Indian English is a real, fully developed English — it has its own rhythm, its own words, and hundreds of millions of speakers. Prepone is a clever word: the opposite of postpone, perfectly logical. Out of station comes straight from the days of the British Raj. These are habits — not flaws, and certainly not stupidity.

So why this chapter? Because in one particular room — an international call, an interview abroad, an email to a client overseas — the person on the other side may not understand these phrases. There it is not a question of right and wrong; it is only a question of not being understood. And when you are not understood, you also seem less capable — which is completely unfair. So the goal is not to change your English. The goal is to learn a second gear that you can shift into when you need it.

The real question of this chapter

Not "is this wrong or right?" but "which room am I in?" In a Delhi office, "out of station" is perfectly fine. With a client in London, "out of town" is better. Both are right — the places are different.

docs.title: 57.1 Where the real problem lies — a map
docs.text:
The middle column below is the most important. It shows what goes through the other person's mind when you say the phrase. They are not angry — they are confused, and they stop to think. That one moment of stopping weakens the effect of what you say.

Figure 57.1. Remember the middle column. The listener is not angry — they stop to think, and that one moment of stopping weakens the effect of what you say.

docs.title: 57.2 Introducing yourself — "Myself Ravi"
docs.text:
This is a direct copy of Hindi: "Main Ravi" — a complete sentence with no verb. In English myself is a reflexive pronoun (I hurt myself); it cannot be the subject. That is why the listener stops when they hear "Myself Ravi".

Three ways to introduce yourself

  • Wrong: Myself Ravi, I am from Pune.
  • Right: I'm Ravi, and I'm from Pune.

  • Why: Casual and normal — on the phone, in a meeting, when meeting new people. This is the most common form.

  • Wrong: I am Ravi this side.

  • Right: Hi, this is Ravi.

  • Why: On the phone and on video calls, "this is" is the natural form. "This side" is used only in India.

  • Wrong: What is your good name?

  • Right: May I have your name?
  • Why: "Good name" is a direct translation of the Hindi "shubh naam" — it is charming, but not understood outside India.
  • Hi, I'm Ravi — I handle the vendor side of things. = Hello, I'm Ravi, and I look after the vendor work.

docs.title: "Please revert back"
docs.text:
There are two things here. First: the real meaning of revert is to return to an earlier state — "The file reverted to its old version." Using it to mean "reply" works only in Indian English. Second: revert already contains "back", so adding back again is redundant. The same happens with return back and reply back.

Clear ways to ask for a reply

  • Wrong: Kindly revert back at the earliest.
  • Right: Please get back to me by Thursday.

  • Why: Two fixes: "revert back" → "get back to me", and "at the earliest" → a real date. Giving a date is what makes things actually happen.

  • Wrong: Please reply back soon.

  • Right: Please reply when you can.
  • Why: Reply, return, revert — all three already contain "back". Never add "back" to them.

docs.title: "Kindly do the needful"
docs.text:
This phrase comes from old official English, and everyone in India understands it: "please do whatever needs to be done". But for a reader outside India it leaves the biggest question unanswered — what is the needful? The whole point of an email is that the other person knows what they have to do. "Do the needful" hides exactly that information.

Learn to write a clear request

  • Wrong: Kindly do the needful and revert back.
  • Right: Could you approve the invoice and forward it to accounts? Let me know once it's done.

  • Why: The other person needs two things: what to do, and by when. Write both — the email becomes half as long and ten times more useful.

  • Wrong: Kindly share the file.

  • Right: Could you share the file?
  • Why: "Kindly" is not wrong, but abroad it sounds old-fashioned or a bit stiff. "Could you" is the safest.

The one-line email formula

Task + who + by when. "Could you approve the PO by Friday so we can release payment?" Three things in one line. There is no need for "kindly", "needful" or "at the earliest".

docs.title: 57.4 "Prepone" — a good word that never left India
docs.text:
Honestly: prepone is a very sensible word. Pre is the opposite of post, so why shouldn't prepone be the opposite of postpone? The logic is perfect, and some dictionaries now list it with an "Indian English" label. But an American or British colleague has probably never heard the word in their life.

What you mean In India For outside India Do it earlier prepone the meeting move the meeting up / bring it forward Do it later postpone the meeting push the meeting back / postpone it Cancel it completely cancel call it off / cancel
  • Could we move Thursday's call up to Tuesday? = Can we have the Thursday call earlier, on Tuesday?

Note — 'postpone' is perfectly fine

Only the partner word "prepone" is missing abroad. Postpone is used all over the world, so you do not need to give it up.

docs.title: 57.5 Words for study, family and travel
docs.text:
'Passed out from college'

  • Wrong: I passed out from college in 2019.
  • Right: I graduated in 2019.

  • Why: Outside India, pass out means "to faint"! People are startled to hear this line. The right form: graduated from Pune University in 2019, or finished college in 2019.

  • Wrong: I am doing my graduation.

  • Right: I'm doing my bachelor's degree. / I'm an undergraduate.

  • Why: Abroad, "graduation" means the ceremony when you receive your degree (convocation), not the studying.

  • Wrong: I gave my twelfth standard exam.

  • Right: I took my final school exams. / I finished high school.
  • Why: Two things: you don't "give" an exam, you take it (the teacher gives it). And "grade" or "class" is better understood than "standard".

'Cousin brother' and family words

  • Wrong: He is my cousin brother.
  • Right: He's my cousin.

  • Why: In English "cousin" does not distinguish boy from girl, so adding brother/sister sounds odd. If you must explain the difference: "my cousin — my uncle's son".

  • Wrong: My real brother lives in Indore.

  • Right: My brother lives in Indore.

  • Why: "Real brother" suggests the other brothers are fake. In English "brother" already means a brother by birth.

  • Wrong: She is my co-brother's wife.

  • Right: She's my wife's sister. / My sister-in-law.
  • Why: Hindi has many very precise family terms; English does not. So explain the relationship directly — "my wife's brother", "my mother's cousin".

'Out of station'

  • Wrong: I will be out of station next week.
  • Right: I'll be out of town next week. / I'm travelling next week.
  • Why: This phrase comes from the "posting station" of the British Raj — it is clear in India, not abroad. For email the clearest is: "I'm away from the office until the 14th."

docs.title: 57.6 "I have a doubt" — a small word, a big difference
docs.text:
Saying "Sir, I have a doubt" in class is perfectly normal in India. But in English doubt = suspicion, not believing. "I doubt it" means "I don't think so". So in an international class or meeting, when a teacher hears this line, they feel you are doubting what they said.

What you mean Right form You want to ask a question I have a question. You didn't understand one part I'm not clear on the second step. You are a little confused Could you clarify that bit? You really do have a suspicion I doubt that will work. (here doubt is correct)
  • I have a question about the second step — should it run before or after the backup? = I want to ask about step two: does it run before the backup or after it?

docs.title: 57.7 Four small habits
docs.text:
'Same to same'

  • Wrong: Both reports are same to same.
  • Right: Both reports are exactly the same. / They're identical.
  • Why: "Same to same" is very expressive, but it is an India-only form. One word does the job: identical.

'Discuss about'

  • Wrong: Let's discuss about the budget.
  • Right: Let's discuss the budget. / Let's talk about the budget.
  • Why: Discuss already contains the meaning of "about". Other words in the same family: enter the room (not "enter into"), reach Delhi (not "reach at"), marry her (not "marry with"), consider it (not "consider about").

'Order for'

  • Wrong: I ordered for two coffees.
  • Right: I ordered two coffees.

  • Why: After order, the thing comes directly. "For" comes in only when it is for a person: "I ordered a coffee for you."

  • Wrong: Let me request for a copy.

  • Right: Let me request a copy. / Let me ask for a copy.
  • Why: Request does not take "for" either. But "ask" does need "for". These are the pairs you have to remember.

Three more you see every day

  • Wrong: I will do it now itself.
  • Right: I'll do it right now.

  • Why: Using "itself" for emphasis comes from the Hindi "hi" (abhi hi). In English use "right": right now, right there, right away.

  • Wrong: What all did he say?

  • Right: What exactly did he say? / What did he say?

  • Why: "What all", "where all", "who all" come from the Hindi "kya kya". They are charming, but not used abroad.

  • Wrong: He is my batchmate only.

  • Right: We were in the same class. / He's a classmate of mine.
  • Why: "Batchmate" and "only" at the end of a sentence are both Indian English. Outside India, this use of "only" is not understood at all.

docs.title: 57.8 At a glance — the full list
docs.text: Common in India International form Why Myself Ravi I'm Ravi "Myself" cannot be a subject Please revert back Please get back to me Revert = return to an earlier state; "back" is redundant Kindly do the needful Could you approve and forward it? The reader doesn't know exactly what to do Prepone Move it up / bring it forward The word doesn't exist abroad Passed out from college Graduated in 2019 "Pass out" = to faint Cousin brother Cousin Cousin doesn't show gender Out of station Out of town / away "Station" isn't clear I have a doubt I have a question Doubt = suspicion, not a question Same to same Exactly the same / identical An India-only form Discuss about Discuss Discuss already includes "about" Order for two teas Order two teas No preposition after order Now itself Right now The English way to stress is "right" What all did she say? What exactly did she say? A direct translation of "kya kya" I am having a car I have a car "Have" for possession isn't used in the continuous She is in my good books only She's in my good books A final "only" isn't understood abroad

docs.title: 57.9 Finally — English with two gears
docs.text:
Every speaker in the world has two gears: the home form and the outside form. A Scotsman does not speak in a New York meeting the way he speaks in his village. A Texan softens his accent in London. There is no shame in this — it is a skill.

Remember this

You do not need to give up your Indian English. It is yours, and it is perfectly fine. Just keep a second gear ready — for an international call, an interview abroad, a client overseas. Once you learn to shift gears, you can talk anywhere. Two gears = two strengths. Giving up one gear to take the other is a loss.

docs.title: 57.10 Practice — Indian English habits
docs.text:
Exercise 1

How should you introduce yourself in an interview abroad?

  • Hi, I'm Ravi.
  • Myself Ravi.
  • I am Ravi this side.
  • Myself is Ravi.

Hint: Myself cannot be a subject.

Answer

Hi, I'm Ravi.

'Myself' is a reflexive pronoun, not a subject. 'This side' is used only in India — abroad, on the phone, people say 'this is Ravi'.

Exercise 2

What does a person abroad understand when they hear 'I passed out from college in 2019'?

  • You fainted in college
  • You got your degree
  • You left college
  • You failed the exam
Answer

You fainted in college

'Pass out' means to faint. To say you got a degree, use 'graduated'.

Exercise 3

Which of these statements is true?

  • Indian English is a real variety; the problem arises only when the listener doesn't understand it
  • Indian English is wrong English
  • Indian English is spoken only in villages
  • Indian English should be given up completely
Answer

Indian English is a real variety; the problem arises only when the listener doesn't understand it

The question is not 'wrong or right' but 'which room am I in?'. Keep two gears — giving up one to take the other is a loss.

Exercise 4

What is the biggest problem with 'Kindly do the needful and revert back'?

  • The reader doesn't know what they are supposed to do
  • The sentence is too short
  • 'Kindly' is very rude
  • It has no verb

Hint: What is the purpose of an email?

Answer

The reader doesn't know what they are supposed to do

An email's job is to say clearly what needs doing. 'Do the needful' hides exactly that information. The formula: task + who + by when.

Exercise 5

I'll be out of ___ next week, so let's meet after the 14th.

Hint: Not station.

Answer

town

'Out of station' is clear in India but confuses people abroad. Say 'out of town' or 'away from the office'.

Exercise 6

I have a ___ about the second step — does it run before the backup?

Hint: Doubt means suspicion.

Answer

question / query

Doubt = suspicion. To ask something, use 'question'. If you don't understand, say 'I'm not clear on…'.

Exercise 7

Could we move the Thursday call ___ to Tuesday?

Hint: Which particle replaces prepone?

Answer

up / forward

To bring something earlier = move it up / bring it forward. 'Prepone' is a logical word but does not exist abroad.

Exercise 8

One word is redundant — tap it.

Please revert back to me by Thursday.

Answer

Wrong word: back.

Corrected: Please get back to me by Thursday.

Revert, reply and return already contain 'back', so 'back' is redundant. And abroad, 'revert' means to go back to an earlier state.

Exercise 9

One word should be removed — find it.

Let us discuss about the budget tomorrow.

Answer

Wrong word: about.

Corrected: Let's discuss the budget tomorrow.

Discuss already contains 'about'. In the same family: enter the room, reach Delhi, order two teas, consider my request.

Exercise 10

One word sounds odd — tap it.

He is my cousin brother from Indore.

Answer

Wrong word: brother.

Corrected: He's my cousin from Indore.

In English 'cousin' doesn't distinguish boy from girl, so adding brother sounds odd. If necessary: 'my cousin — my uncle's son'.

Exercise 11

Match each habit to its international form.

A B Myself Ravi exactly the same I have a doubt right now same to same I'm Ravi now itself I have a question Answer

Myself Ravi — I'm Ravi; I have a doubt — I have a question; same to same — exactly the same; now itself — right now

All four are perfectly clear in India — they just need a second form for an ear abroad.

Exercise 12

Match each phrase to its problem.

A B prepone which station? it isn't clear pass out from college 'back' is redundant out of station the word doesn't exist abroad revert back it ends up meaning to faint Answer

prepone — the word doesn't exist abroad; pass out from college — it ends up meaning to faint; out of station — which station? it isn't clear; revert back — 'back' is redundant

Each habit has a different problem — sometimes the word doesn't exist, sometimes the meaning changes, sometimes one word is redundant.

Exercise 13

Build one clear email line — task, who and by when.

Words: approve / by / the / release / payment / you / so / we / can / invoice / Could / Friday

Answer

Could you approve the invoice by Friday so we can release payment

This is the formula: what to do, for whom, by when. There is no need for 'kindly', 'needful' or 'at the earliest'.

Exercise 14

Say your introduction aloud. 'I'm' should come out in a single sound at the start.

Answer

Say: Hi I am Ravi and I graduated in 2019

The first two lines of an interview are the most remembered. 'I'm' and 'graduated' are both here, and both are safe.

What to do next

Open your last five sent emails and search for just three words: kindly, revert, needful. Wherever you find them, write directly what has to be done and by when. In one go, your written English will move two steps ahead — and without "learning" anything.

docs.title: Chapter 14: Interjections
docs.text:
Interjection — the words of feeling

An interjection is a word that suddenly lets out a feeling — joy, pain, surprise, regret. It isn't part of the sentence; it stands apart from it, and if you remove it the meaning of the sentence doesn't change at all — only its voice is lost. Among the eight parts of speech it is the smallest, but in everyday conversation it does the most work.

In one line

An interjection is a word or short phrase that expresses sudden feeling and stands apart from the rest of the sentence. It does exactly the job that "arre, waah, haaye, achha, ohho" do in Hindi.

  • Wow! That was a brilliant catch. = What an amazing catch that was!
  • Ouch! That hurt. = A cry of sudden pain. (In Hindi we say "ssss" or "aai".)
  • Oh, I forgot my wallet at home. The feeling is mild, so use a comma — not an exclamation mark.

docs.title: 14.1 Where an interjection sits in a sentence
docs.text:
An interjection has no grammatical link with the rest of the sentence. It is not the subject, the verb or the object. So if you take it out, the sentence doesn't break.

Figure 14.1. An interjection stands outside the sentence, and the strength of the feeling decides the punctuation.

Five features of an interjection

1. Strong / sudden emotion — shows a sudden, strong feeling: joy, pain, fear, surprise. 2. Stands apart — stays separate from the rest of the sentence, often at the start. 3. Usually "!" — it is usually followed by an exclamation mark (a comma if the feeling is mild). 4. No grammatical link — no grammatical link to the subject, verb or object; take it out and the sentence is still fine. 5. Same word, different feelings — one word can carry different feelings on different occasions.

  • Oh! What a lovely surprise. "Oh" = surprise / happiness.
  • Oh! My knee hurts. The same "Oh" = pain.
  • Oh! I am so sorry to hear that. The same "Oh" = sorrow. The feeling comes not from the word but from the situation and the tone of voice.

docs.title: 14.2 Types — by feeling
docs.text:
School books teach ten (10) types of interjection. Each type has its English name here too, so you can match it directly with your textbook.

Type (feeling) Typical words Example In Hindi 1. Joy (happiness) Hurrah! Hurray! Yippee! Hurray! We won the match. Waah! (We won!) 2. Sorrow (sadness / regret) Alas! Oh! Ah! Alas! He could not make it. Haaye! (What a pity!) 3. Surprise (astonishment) Oh! Wow! What! Ah! What! You passed already? Arre! (Really?) 4. Pain (hurt) Ouch! Ah! Oh! Ouch! The tea is hot. Aai! Ssss! 5. Approval / Appreciation (praise) Bravo! Well done! Excellent! Bravo! What a performance. Shabaash! (Well done!) 6. Anger / Irritation (annoyance, frustration) Pooh! Bah! Bah! Another traffic jam. Uff! (That's too much!) 7. Greeting (saying hello) Hello! Hi! Hey! Hello! How are you? Namaste! (How are you?) 8. Attention (getting someone's notice) Hey! Look! Listen! Look! The train is coming. Arre! (Look!) 9. Calling (calling someone) O! Ho! Hey! Hey, Ravi! Come here. Aye Ravi! (Come here.) 10. Fear (being scared) Help! Oh! Ah! Help! There is a snake! Bachao! (Save me!)
  • Yippee! School is closed tomorrow. Joy — the bouncing happiness of children.
  • Well done! You topped the class. Approval — two words, but they do the job of one interjection.
  • O God, please help us! Calling — "O" survives today only in prayers and poetry; it is always a capital letter and goes straight before a name.

'Damn!' — a word of anger, but rude

You hear "Damn!" a lot in films, but it is considered rude. Never say it in class, at the office, or in front of elders. To show irritation, "Oh no!", "Ugh!" or "Come on!" are enough.

docs.title: More feelings in everyday speech
docs.text: Feeling Words Example In Hindi Agreement Yes! Sure! Indeed! Right! Indeed, that was clever. Bilkul! Sahi! Disgust Ugh! Yuck! Eww! Yuck! This milk has gone bad. Chhee! Thoo! Pausing / thinking Well… Um… Hmm… Er… Hmm, let me check. Hmm… Achha… A mistake Oops! Whoops! My bad! Oops! I sent the wrong file. Oho! (A mistake happened.) Relief Phew! Thank goodness! Phew! That was close. Uff! (We escaped.)

docs.title: Common interjections and how to use them
docs.text: Interjection When to say it Example Oh! surprise, pain, sorrow — all three Oh! I didn't know that. Ah! understanding, relief, mild pain Ah, now I understand. Wow! surprise + admiration Wow! What a view. Ouch! your own sudden pain Ouch! I cut my finger. Hurray! joy at a win Hurray! We are on holiday. Bravo! praising someone's work Bravo! Great speech. Hello! / Hi! meeting someone, answering the phone Hi! Good to see you. Hey! getting attention, calling (to equals) Hey! Wait for me. Help! fear, danger Help! I can't swim. Oops! a small mistake Oops! I dropped it. Phew! relief Phew! We made it. Alas! deep sorrow (bookish) Alas! The king was dead.

docs.title: 14.3 Punctuation — three fixed rules
docs.text:
Where to use a comma, where an exclamation mark

1. Strong feeling → exclamation mark, and the next word starts with a capital: Wow! That is amazing. 2. Mild feeling → comma, and the next word starts in lower case: Oh, it's you. 3. In the middle of a sentence → a comma on both sides: The result, alas, was disappointing.

One word, two punctuation marks — the meaning changes

Oh! You came. — surprise; it seems you weren't expecting it. Oh, you came. — a mild acknowledgement; it seems you knew. Here punctuation works like a volume control for the feeling.

No more than one exclamation mark

In a chat, "Wow!!!" is fine. In an email, an exam or any written work, use just one exclamation mark. Three don't make the point stronger — they make you sound less serious.

docs.title: 14.4 Interjection or something else — one word, two jobs
docs.text:
Many words can be an interjection and also an ordinary part of speech. You decide by checking whether the word is inside the sentence or outside it.

Word As an interjection In its normal role well Well, I am not sure. She sings well. (adverb) what What! You are leaving? What is your name? (pronoun) right Right, let's begin. Your answer is right. (adjective) indeed Indeed! I never expected that. It was indeed difficult. (adverb) my My! How you have grown. This is my bag. (possessive)

The test for spotting one

Take the word out and read the rest of the sentence. If what remains is complete and correct → it was an interjection. If the sentence is left incomplete → the word was part of the sentence. "Well, I am not sure" → "I am not sure" is complete. ✓ interjection. "She sings well" → "She sings" changes the meaning. ✗ not an interjection.

docs.title: 14.5 From Hindi to English — pairs for real conversation
docs.text:
We tend to carry Hindi interjections straight into English — "Arre, where were you?" It's understood, but it doesn't sound like English. Here are some useful pairs:

We say (in Hindi) In English When Arre! Hey! / Oh! / Come on! getting attention or mild surprise Achha? Really? / Is that so? on hearing something new Achha, theek hai Right. / Okay then. accepting what was said Waah! Wow! / Brilliant! praise Haaye! Oh no! / Alas! (old-fashioned) sorrow Uff / Chalo bach gaye Phew! relief Chhee! Yuck! / Ugh! disgust Hmm… dekhte hain Well… let me see. while thinking Oho, galti ho gayi Oops! My bad. a small mistake Arre nahi! Oh no! / No way! on hearing bad news

The truth about 'Alas', 'Hurrah' and 'Pooh' — old words

School books are full of Alas!, Hurrah! and Pooh!, but today's speech hardly uses them — they sound old-fashioned and theatrical. They are fine in exams and stories; in conversation, use the modern words below.

Old (bookish) Say today Feeling Alas! Oh no! / That's so sad. sorrow Hurrah! Yay! / Yes! / Woo-hoo! joy Pooh! / Bah! Ugh! / Come on! / Seriously? irritation O! / Ho! Hey! / Excuse me! calling

docs.title: 14.6 Office and formal places — where to hold back
docs.text:
Place Fine Not fine Chat with a friend Wow! Oops! Yay! Ugh! — Office email Well, Right, Indeed (with a comma) Yay! Yuck! Oops! Interview Well, … (to buy thinking time) Hmm… many times Exam writing in a story / dialogue in an essay or report

A useful point for interviews

Instead of answering a question at once, it is perfectly fine to say "Well, that's an interesting question…" — it buys you two seconds to think and makes you look prepared. But don't say it three times in one interview.

docs.title: 14.7 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
Mistakes that go with interjections

  • Wrong: Myself Ravi. Wow, nice to meet you!
  • Right: Hello! I am Ravi. Nice to meet you.

  • Why: Two things: "Myself Ravi" is wrong — the subject needs "I". And "Wow" sounds odd when you meet someone; it is meant for admiration. For a greeting, say "Hello" or "Hi".

  • Wrong: Oh! i forgot to call her.

  • Right: Oh! I forgot to call her.

  • Why: A new sentence begins after an exclamation mark, so the next word is a capital. With a comma, a small letter would be fine: Oh, I forgot…

  • Wrong: Dear Sir, Wow!!! Thank you for the offer.

  • Right: Dear Sir, Thank you very much for the offer.

  • Why: In a formal email, both an interjection and three exclamation marks feel heavy. To show happiness, use words: I am delighted to accept.

  • Wrong: Alas the news was bad.

  • Right: Alas, the news was bad.

  • Why: An interjection needs punctuation after it — a comma or an exclamation mark. Without anything, it melts into the sentence and the reader stumbles.

  • Wrong: Ouch, she don't know the answer.

  • Right: Oh no, she doesn't know the answer.

  • Why: "Ouch" is only for your own pain, not for someone else's trouble — for that use "Oh no". And "she" takes "doesn't", not "don't".

  • Wrong: Hey! Sir, can you discuss about my marks?

  • Right: Excuse me, Sir, could we discuss my marks?

  • Why: "Hey!" is for equals; with an elder or a teacher, say "Excuse me". And "about" doesn't go after "discuss".

  • Wrong: Yuck! This is my cousin brother's cooking.

  • Right: Hmm, this is my cousin's cooking — not my favourite.
  • Why: "Yuck" is quite harsh — saying it about someone's food in front of them is rude. And "cousin" is a complete word by itself — there is no need to add brother.

docs.title: 14.8 A short summary
docs.text:
Remember four things

1. An interjection stands outside the sentence — take it out and the sentence still works. 2. Strong feeling → ! and a capital next word. Mild feeling → , and a lower-case next word. 3. In formal writing, don't use it — show the feeling in words instead. 4. One exclamation mark is enough.

docs.title: 14.9 Practice — Interjections
docs.text:
Exercise 1

___! We finally won the trophy.

  • Hurray
  • Alas
  • Ouch
  • Yuck

Hint: You need a feeling of joy.

Answer

Hurray

Winning brings joy, and for joy we use Hurray / Yay / Wow. Alas is for sorrow, ouch for pain, and yuck for disgust.

Exercise 2

Which sentence is correctly punctuated?

  • Oh! I forgot my keys.
  • Oh! i forgot my keys.
  • Oh i forgot my keys.
  • Oh. i forgot my keys!

Hint: What follows an exclamation mark?

Answer

Oh! I forgot my keys.

A new sentence begins after an exclamation mark, so the next word is a capital. With a comma a small letter would be fine — 'Oh, I forgot'.

Exercise 3

'Well, I am not sure about that.' — what is 'Well' here?

  • interjection
  • adverb
  • adjective
  • conjunction

Hint: Take the word out and read the sentence.

Answer

interjection

Even without 'Well', 'I am not sure about that' is a complete sentence, so 'Well' stands outside it — an interjection. In 'She sings well' removing it would change the meaning; there it is an adverb.

Exercise 4

Which version is best for an office email?

  • I am delighted to accept the offer.
  • Wow!!! Thanks for the offer.
  • Yay! I accept.
  • Oops, I accept.

Hint: In formal places, feelings are shown in words.

Answer

I am delighted to accept the offer.

In formal writing, interjections and several exclamation marks feel heavy. Showing happiness in words sounds more professional.

Exercise 5

___! That water is boiling hot. (a word for pain)

Hint: What do you say at your own sudden pain?

Answer

Ouch

For sudden pain we say Ouch / Ow. Remember — it is only for your own pain; for someone else's trouble we say 'Oh no'.

Exercise 6

___, that was a close call. (a word for relief)

Hint: The sound of breathing out after an escape.

Answer

Phew

'Phew' shows relief — the Hindi 'uff' or 'chalo bach gaye'. It comes from the sound of letting out a breath.

Exercise 7

There is one mistake in this sentence — tap the wrong word.

Hey Sir can you discuss about my result?

Answer

Wrong word: about.

Corrected: Excuse me, Sir, could we discuss my result?

'about' doesn't go after 'discuss'. And 'Hey' is for equals — for a teacher or an elder, say 'Excuse me'.

Exercise 8

Find the wrong word.

Oh no she don't know about the meeting.

Answer

Wrong word: don't.

Corrected: Oh no, she doesn't know about the meeting.

'she' is third person singular, so it takes 'doesn't'. A comma was also needed after the interjection.

Exercise 9

There is one mistake — find it.

Myself Ravi and wow I am happy to be here.

Answer

Wrong word: Myself.

Corrected: Hello! I am Ravi, and I am happy to be here.

The reflexive pronoun 'myself' can't be a subject — you need 'I am'. And 'wow' sounds odd when meeting someone; say 'Hello' as a greeting.

Exercise 10

'Bravo! That was a brilliant speech.' — what type of interjection is 'Bravo'?

  • Approval / Appreciation
  • Joy
  • Surprise
  • Calling

Hint: Someone's work is being praised.

Answer

Approval / Appreciation

Bravo!, Well done!, Excellent! are words that praise someone's work (Approval / Appreciation). For your own happiness you use Hurray! or Yippee! (Joy).

Exercise 11

___! There is a snake under the bed! (a word for fear)

Hint: What do you shout to ask for help?

Answer

Help

For Fear, 'Help!' is the clearest interjection. 'Oh!' and 'Ah!' can show fear too, but 'Help!' tells people about the danger immediately.

Exercise 12

In conversation with a friend, what is more natural today instead of 'Hurrah!'?

  • Yay!
  • Alas!
  • Pooh!
  • Damn!

Hint: Hurrah is an old, bookish word.

Answer

Yay!

'Hurrah!', 'Alas!' and 'Pooh!' sound old-fashioned today. For joy people now say 'Yay!' or 'Yes!'. 'Damn!' is rude — don't use it.

Exercise 13

Which statement about interjections is WRONG?

  • It acts as the subject of the sentence
  • It shows a sudden feeling
  • It is often followed by '!'
  • One word can show different feelings

Hint: Remember the five features.

Answer

It acts as the subject of the sentence

An interjection has no grammatical link with the sentence — it is not a subject or an object. The other three are all its features.

Exercise 14

Match each interjection to its feeling.

A B Hurray! pain Alas! relief Ouch! disgust Phew! joy Yuck! sorrow Answer

Hurray! — joy; Alas! — sorrow; Ouch! — pain; Phew! — relief; Yuck! — disgust

You choose an interjection by the feeling, not by grammar. A word for the wrong feeling sounds odd — like saying 'Alas' to praise someone.

Exercise 15

Put the words in the right order — the interjection comes first.

Words: painting / is / beautiful / this / Wow

Answer

Wow this painting is beautiful

An interjection almost always comes at the start, because the feeling comes out first and the explanation follows. In writing, it is followed by a comma or an exclamation mark.

Exercise 16

Say this line aloud — stretch the 'Oh no' a little, as if you really feel sorry.

Answer

Say: Oh no I have missed the train

An interjection gets its effect more from the voice than from the word. Said flat, it sounds like acting; said with feeling, it sounds natural.

What to do next

Interjections aren't for memorising — they're for listening. While watching an English show, notice what people say when they are surprised or relieved — and try one new word the next day. With this, the eight parts of speech are complete; next comes the part about building sentences.

docs.title: Chapter 34: Interview & office English
docs.text:
Interview and office English

In an interview, structure matters more than English. People who get stuck do not have bad English — they do not have a pattern for their answer, so they think while they speak and get nervous. This chapter gives you ready patterns: your introduction, answers to common questions, the language of meetings, and email phrases. All of it is worth practising aloud.

The one real rule of interviews

An answer should be 30 to 60 seconds. Shorter = it looks like you did not prepare. Longer = you start to wander and your English gets tangled. Three or four sentences. That is all. Then stop and let the next question come.

docs.title: 34.1 Your introduction — a three-part pattern
docs.text:
"Tell me about yourself" is the first question and the one that goes wrong most often. People tell their whole life story — where they were born, how many brothers and sisters. The interviewer does not want that. They only need three things: what you do today → what you did before → what you want next.

Figure 34.1. This pattern works in every interview — fresher or 10 years of experience. Only the content inside changes; the structure stays the same.

A ready introduction — for someone with experience

  • Thanks for having me. I'm Ravi, and I currently work as a support engineer at a telecom company in Pune. Part 1 — now. "Thanks for having me" is a polite opening.
  • I've been there for about three years, mostly handling customer issues and billing problems. Part 2 — before. "for about three years" — "about" makes the voice sound natural.
  • Last year I also trained two new team members, which I really enjoyed. One solid example — this line sets you apart from the others.
  • Now I'm looking for a role where I can work more directly with clients, and that's why this job caught my eye. Part 3 — next, and why here. "caught my eye" = I noticed it and it interested me.

A ready introduction — for a fresher

  • Good morning. I'm Priya, and I finished my B.Com from Pune University this year. For a fresher, "now" means your studies.
  • During my final year I did a three-month internship at a small accounting firm, where I worked on GST filings. An internship, a project, part-time work — whatever you have, name one solid thing.
  • I'm comfortable with Excel and I'm learning Tally at the moment. "I'm comfortable with…" sounds better and more honest than "I know".
  • I'm looking for my first full-time role, and I'd like to start in a team where I can learn quickly. For a fresher, "wanting to learn" is the most honest and the best answer.

Five mistakes in introductions

  • Wrong: Myself Ravi Kumar.
  • Right: I'm Ravi Kumar.

  • Why: "Myself" is a pronoun, not a sentence. This is the mistake that gets noticed fastest.

  • Wrong: I am belonging to Jaipur.

  • Right: I'm from Jaipur.

  • Why: "Belong" does not take -ing. And "I'm from…" is short and natural.

  • Wrong: I have did my graduation in 2021.

  • Right: I graduated in 2021.

  • Why: "Graduation" is an event; "graduate" is the verb. Use the verb directly.

  • Wrong: I am having 4 years experience.

  • Right: I have four years of experience.

  • Why: "have", not "am having". And "of" goes in the middle.

  • Wrong: My father is a businessman and I have two sisters…

  • Right: No family details in the introduction at all.
  • Why: The interviewer wants an introduction to your work, not your life. Share it only if they ask.

docs.title: 34.2 Common interview questions — ready answers
docs.text:
The story pattern — for every 'example' question

Situation → your task → what you did → the result. Four sentences, in that order. Whenever you are asked "tell me about a time when…", just fill in this pattern. Do not forget the result — it is what completes the answer.

Question Ready answer Listen Why do you want to leave your current job? I've learnt a lot where I am, but the work has become quite repetitive. I'm looking for something with more responsibility. What are your strengths? I'm patient with people, which helps a lot in support work. I also stay calm when things go wrong. What is your weakness? I used to take on too much and then struggle with deadlines. I've started saying no more often, and planning my week on Monday. Why should we hire you? You need someone who can handle angry customers without losing patience. That's exactly what I've been doing for three years. Where do you see yourself in five years? I'd like to be leading a small team by then. For now my focus is on getting really good at the work itself. Tell me about a difficult situation at work. Last Diwali two people were on leave and our tickets doubled. I rearranged the queue by urgency and asked a colleague to help with calls. We cleared everything in two days. What are your salary expectations? Based on my experience and the market, I'm looking at somewhere between eight and ten lakhs. But I'm open to discussing it. Do you have any questions for us? Yes — could you tell me what a typical week looks like in this role? And how is the team structured?

The 'weakness' trap

"I have no weakness" or "I am a perfectionist" — every interviewer has heard both a thousand times, and both make it sound like you are not telling the truth. The right pattern: one real weakness + what you are doing to fix it. That sounds both honest and sensible.

You must ask questions at the end

The answer to "Do you have any questions?" should never be "No" — it makes you look uninterested. Keep two questions ready: What does a typical week look like in this role? What would you want me to achieve in the first three months?

docs.title: 34.3 If you get stuck in the interview
docs.text:
It will happen — it happens to everyone. There is no need to panic, just have a ready line come out.

Situation Line Listen You did not understand the question Sorry, could you rephrase that? You need a little time That's a good question. Let me think for a second. You do not know the answer I haven't worked on that, but I'd be happy to learn it. Your sentence got tangled Sorry, let me start that again. Checking you understood correctly Just to make sure I understood — you're asking about…? The interview is over Thank you for your time. I enjoyed talking to you.

Saying 'I do not know' does no harm

Lying does far more harm. "I haven't worked on that, but I'd be happy to learn it" is a solid, professional answer — and most interviewers like it.

docs.title: 34.4 The language of the office and meetings
docs.text:
Purpose Line Listen Starting to speak in a meeting Can I add something here? Sorry to interrupt, but I think there's an issue with the timeline. If I could just jump in for a second… Agreeing / disagreeing That makes sense to me. I see your point, but I'd do it slightly differently. I'm not sure that will work. Can I explain why? Time and work I'll have it ready by Thursday. I'm a bit stretched this week — could we push it to Monday? Let me check and get back to you in an hour. Asking for help and clarity Could you walk me through it once? Just to confirm — you want the report before the call, right? I'll need a bit of help with this part. Mistakes and apologies That was my mistake. I'll fix it today. Sorry for the delay — I got held up in another call. Let me look into it and come back with an answer. Ending a meeting So, to sum up — I'll send the draft and you'll review it by Friday. Shall we take this offline and discuss it after?

A full mini-dialogue — a team meeting

  • Manager: So, where are we on the client report? "Where are we on…" = what is the progress on that work?
  • You: I've finished the first half. The numbers for March are still pending from finance. First what is done, then what is stuck — and who it is stuck with.
  • Manager: Can you have it done by Thursday? = Will it be finished by Thursday?
  • You: If I get the numbers by tomorrow, yes. Otherwise Friday would be safer. Saying yes with a condition — "Friday would be safer" sounds very professional.
  • Manager: Fair enough. I'll chase finance today. "Fair enough" = OK, that is reasonable. "Chase" = to keep reminding someone.
  • You: Thanks. Just to confirm — you want the full report, not just the summary? "Just to confirm" shows you are paying attention. You can use this line every day.

docs.title: 34.5 Ready phrases for email
docs.text:
Purpose Phrase Opening (friendly) Hi Anita,Hope you're doing well. Opening (formal) Dear Mr Sharma,I hope this email finds you well. Giving the reason I'm writing to ask about… / I'm following up on my last email. Sending something Please find the report attached. / I've attached the file below. Asking for something Could you please share the figures for March? / Would you be able to review this by Friday? A gentle reminder Just a gentle reminder about the pending approval. Apologising for a delay Apologies for the delay in replying. Acknowledging a task Noted, I'll take care of it. / Thanks, that's clear now. Asking for more time Would it be possible to extend the deadline to Monday? Closing (friendly) Thanks,Ravi Closing (formal) Best regards,Ravi Kumar

Email lines you should drop

  • Wrong: Please do the needful and revert back at the earliest.
  • Right: Could you review this and let me know by Friday?

  • Why: Three problems: "do the needful" does not say what to do; "revert" means to go back, not to reply; and instead of "at the earliest" give a real date.

  • Wrong: Respected Sir, I beg to state that…

  • Right: Dear Mr Sharma, I'm writing to…

  • Why: This is very old, school-letter language. It sounds odd in today's office.

  • Wrong: Kindly intimate me the same.

  • Right: Please let me know.

  • Why: "Intimate" and "the same" are old office language. Short words sound more professional.

  • Wrong: Thanking you in advance for the same.

  • Right: Thanks in advance. / Thanks for your help.
  • Why: "For the same" simply has to go. Short lines read best in email.

docs.title: 34.6 Last preparation before the interview
docs.text:
The day before — five jobs

1. Say your 45-second introduction aloud 10 times. In front of a mirror. 2. Prepare answers to three questions: why you are leaving, a weakness, and one difficult situation. 3. Prepare two questions that you will ask. 4. Record your introduction on your phone and listen — wherever it sounds tangled, make it shorter. 5. On the day, speak slower than everyday speech. Nervousness makes you fast, and speed tangles your English.

docs.title: 34.7 Practice — Interview and office
docs.text:
Exercise 1

What is the right structure for 'Tell me about yourself'?

  • What you do now → what you did before → what you want next
  • Where you were born → studies → family
  • Family → hobby → job
  • Only your degree and marks

Hint: Three parts, three times.

Answer

What you do now → what you did before → what you want next

Three parts, about 15 seconds each. Mention family and village only when asked.

Exercise 2

How long should an interview answer be?

  • 30 to 60 seconds
  • 5 to 10 seconds
  • 3 to 4 minutes
  • As long as possible
Answer

30 to 60 seconds

A short answer shows lack of preparation; in a long answer you start to wander and your English gets tangled.

Exercise 3

What is the right pattern for 'What is your weakness?'

  • One real weakness + what you are doing to fix it
  • I have no weakness
  • I am a perfectionist
  • A weakness that is really a compliment
Answer

One real weakness + what you are doing to fix it

Honesty + good sense. Every interviewer has heard 'no weakness' and 'perfectionist' a thousand times.

Exercise 4

You are asked a technical thing you do not know. What do you do?

  • I haven't worked on that, but I'd be happy to learn it
  • Lie and say you know it
  • Go silent
  • Change the subject
Answer

I haven't worked on that, but I'd be happy to learn it

A lie gets caught later. Most interviewers like an honest answer.

Exercise 5

What is the worst answer to 'Do you have any questions for us?'

  • No, everything is clear
  • A question about the role
  • A question about the team
  • A question about the goals for the first three months
Answer

No, everything is clear

'No' makes you look uninterested. Keep two questions ready.

Exercise 6

What is the pattern for 'Tell me about a difficult situation'?

  • Situation → your task → what you did → result
  • Only the result
  • Who was to blame
  • Situation → whose fault it was

Hint: Four parts.

Answer

Situation → your task → what you did → result

Four sentences in that order. Do not forget the result — it is what completes the answer.

Exercise 7

Fix it: I have ___ years of experience. (four years)

Hint: A number in words, and not 'am having'.

Answer

four / 4

'I have four years of experience' — 'am having' is wrong, and 'of' goes in the middle.

Exercise 8

Confirming in a meeting: ___ to confirm — you want the full report?

Hint: The first word of the phrase, starting with 'J'.

Answer

Just / just

'Just to confirm…' is a line you can use at the office every day — it shows you are paying attention.

Exercise 9

Email: Please find the report ___.

Hint: The file is sent along with the email.

Answer

attached

'Please find the report attached' or 'I've attached the report'. Both are fine.

Exercise 10

There is a mistake in this sentence — tap the word.

Myself Ravi Kumar from Jaipur.

Answer

Wrong word: Myself.

Corrected: I'm Ravi Kumar, from Jaipur.

'Myself' is a pronoun, not a word to start a sentence with. In an interview this is noticed fastest.

Exercise 11

Find the wrong word.

I am belonging to a small town near Nashik.

Answer

Wrong word: belonging.

Corrected: I'm from a small town near Nashik.

'Belong' does not take -ing. And 'I'm from…' is short and natural.

Exercise 12

Tap the word in this email that should be dropped.

Please review this and revert at the earliest.

Answer

Wrong word: revert.

Corrected: Please review this and let me know by Friday.

'Revert' means to go back to an earlier state, not to reply. And instead of 'at the earliest' give a real date.

Exercise 13

Match each office situation to its line.

A B Starting to speak in a meeting I'm a bit stretched this week. Disagreeing, but politely That was my mistake. I'll fix it today. Too much work Can I add something here? Admitting a mistake I see your point, but I'd do it differently. Answer
