Starting to speak in a meeting — Can I add something here?; Disagreeing, but politely — I see your point, but I'd do it differently.; Too much work — I'm a bit stretched this week.; Admitting a mistake — That was my mistake. I'll fix it today.

A ready line for every situation. In a meeting there is no time to think — that is why memorising helps.

Exercise 14

Build the opening line of an interview.

Words: for / Thanks / having / me

Answer

Thanks for having me

A short, polite opening. After it, go straight to part 1 — what you do now.

Exercise 15

Introduction, part 1 — what you do now.

Answer

Say: I currently work as a support engineer at a telecom company

'currently' makes it clear this is about today. Speak slowly — this is the first impression.

Exercise 16

Introduction, part 2 — experience.

Answer

Say: I've been there for about three years, mostly handling customer issues

'for about three years' — 'about' makes your voice sound natural, not memorised.

Exercise 17

Introduction, part 3 — what you want next.

Answer

Say: Now I'm looking for a role where I can work more directly with clients

This part tells them why you are sitting here. Skipping it is the biggest mistake.

Exercise 18

Name your strength — without big words.

Answer

Say: I'm patient with people and I stay calm when things go wrong

It sounds solid and true. Much better than 'I am a hard worker'.

Exercise 19

Why you are leaving your job — without speaking badly of the old company.

Answer

Say: I've learnt a lot where I am but I'm looking for more responsibility

Never criticise the old place. Talk about what is ahead, not what is behind.

Exercise 20

You did not understand the question. Ask politely.

Answer

Say: Sorry, could you rephrase that

'Rephrase' = say it again in other words. This is perfectly fine in an interview.

Exercise 21

A technical question you cannot answer. Give an honest reply.

Answer

Say: I haven't worked on that but I'd be happy to learn it

Clear, professional and true. Much better than a lie.

Exercise 22

The question you will ask at the end.

Answer

Say: What does a typical week look like in this role

This question makes you look serious, and also gives you real information.

Exercise 23

The interview is over. The parting line.

Answer

Say: Thank you for your time. I enjoyed talking to you

Short and warm. The last impression is also remembered.

Exercise 24

Saying yes with a condition in a meeting.

Answer

Say: If I get the numbers by tomorrow yes. Otherwise Friday would be safer

A yes with a condition is better than a false yes. 'Would be safer' sounds very professional.

Exercise 25

You have too much work at the office. Ask for time.

Answer

Say: I'm a bit stretched this week. Could we push it to Monday

'A bit stretched' = under some pressure. 'Push it to' = move it later.

Exercise 26

Admit a mistake — without making excuses.

Answer

Say: That was my mistake. I'll fix it today

Two short sentences: you admit the mistake and give the fix. Much better than a long explanation.

What next?

Write your 45-second introduction today — no more than five sentences — and record it on your phone and listen. Wherever a sentence tangled as you spoke, make it shorter. Then say it 10 times. Before an interview, two chapters will help you most: Fluency and filler words (the cure for getting stuck) and Indian English habits (the mistakes that get noticed at once).

docs.title: Chapter 16: Modal verbs
docs.text:
Modals — can, should, must

In Hindi we add "sakna", "chahiye", "padega", "shayad" to a verb to show our mood. In English this job is done by small helping verbs called modals. They are the heart of everyday conversation — whether you want to ask politely, give advice or make a guess, you can't manage without modals.

In one line

A modal verb is a helping verb that adds ability, permission, advice, obligation or possibility to the main verb. The main verb tells you the action; the modal tells you what we think about the action.

  • I can swim. = I know how to swim. — ability
  • You should drink more water. = Drinking more water would be a good idea for you. — advice
  • It might rain in the evening. = Perhaps it will rain in the evening. — possibility

docs.title: 16.1 How a modal works — three fixed rules
docs.text:
The good news is that all modals work in the same way. Once you have these three rules firmly in your head, half your mistakes will stop by themselves — whichever modal it is.

Figure 16.1. A modal makes its own negatives and questions — there is no need to call in do .

The three rules for modals

1. After a modal, the verb is in its base form (V1) — no -s, no -ing, no "to". 2. A modal never changes itself — there is no "cans" or "musted". 3. A modal makes its own negatives and questions: can't go, Can you go?

Three modal-like verbs come with 'to'

ought to, have to, used to — here "to" is part of them: You ought to apologise. After any other modal there is no "to": You must to go.

docs.title: 16.2 Ability — can, could, be able to
docs.text:
"I can do this" — you say it every day: in job interviews, when filling in forms, with friends. What matters is choosing the right word as the time changes.

Time Word Example Now (present) can She can speak Tamil. Past, in general could I could run fast when I was young. Past, on one particular occasion was / were able to We were able to catch the last bus. Later (future) will be able to You will be able to drive in a month. In a perfect tense have been able to I haven't been able to sleep.

Ability

Use can for the present and could for the past. Where "can" doesn't fit — the future, the perfect, or after another modal — use be able to: will be able to.

No two modals together

You will can come. ✗ → You will be able to come. ✓ One modal per sentence. If you need another, take a form like "be able to" or "have to".

docs.title: 16.3 Permission and requests — how polite do you need to be?
docs.text:
The word you choose when asking shows how much respect you are giving the other person. "Can I…?" is fine with a friend, but with a boss or a stranger "Could you…?" sounds better.

Figure 16.2. The higher the step, the more polite the request. At the office and with strangers, the middle steps are the safest.

Permission and requests

Permission: Can I (casual) → Could I → May I (formal). Request: Can you → Could you → Would you mind + -ing. "May" is only for asking permission for yourself — there is no "May you…?".

  • Could you send me the file by evening? = Would it be possible for you to send the file by this evening? — perfect for the office.
  • Would you mind closing the window? = Is it a problem for you to close the window? — answering "No, not at all" means "Sure, I'll do it".

docs.title: 16.4 Advice and obligation — should, must, have to
docs.text:
"I should do it" and "I have to do it" are very different — one is advice, the other is a duty. English makes this difference clear too, and if you pick the wrong word you sound either too harsh or too weak.

Figure 16.3. Top: the need gets stronger. Bottom: in the negative, must and have to mean completely different things.

Advice and duty

should / ought to = advice. have to = a rule or a duty forced by the situation. must = a strong need. Note: mustn't = forbidden, but don't have to = not necessary.

  • You should see a doctor. = Seeing a doctor is a good idea — it is advice, and the choice is yours.
  • I have to wear a uniform at work. = The company requires it — the obligation comes from outside.
  • In the past: I had to wait for two hours. "must" has no past form — use "had to".

docs.title: 16.5 Possibility — from might to must, how sure are you?
docs.text:
When you make a guess, the modal shows how sure you are. "She might be at home" and "She must be at home" use different modals. Using them well makes your English sound thoughtful.

Figure 16.4. Certainty grows from left to right. can't and must are both firm conclusions — one a no , one a yes .

The certainty meter

might / could (perhaps) → may (it's possible) → should (it ought to be so) → must (it surely is). The firm opposite: can't — He can't be at home; I just saw him at the station.

The opposite of a 'must' guess is not 'mustn't'

She must be at work. (I'm sure she's at the office) → the opposite: She can't be at work. "She mustn't be at work" would mean she is forbidden to be at the office!

docs.title: 16.6 will, would, shall, need, used to
docs.text:
These five modals (or modal-like words) turn up every day, and each has its own special job. Look at them in one place, and you don't need to remember them separately.

Word Job Example will future, promise, instant decision I will call you tonight. would polite wish, imagination I would like a cup of tea. would an old habit (action) Dadi would tell us stories every night. shall an offer or suggestion with I / we Shall I open the window? need necessity You need to sign here. / You needn't worry. used to was true in the past, but not now I used to live in Patna.

used to vs be used to — two different things

used to + V1 = did it in the past: I used to wake up at 9. (not any more) be used to + -ing = am accustomed to it: I am used to waking up early. In the second one "to" is a preposition, so -ing follows. In questions: Did you use to…? (no -d)

docs.title: 16.7 Past modals — should have, could have, must have
docs.text:
Regret about the past, a missed chance, or a guess about something that already happened — all of these are said with modal + have + V3. The pattern sounds hard, but it comes up all the time in conversation.

Figure 16.5. All three arrows point back from today — we are standing in the present and speaking about yesterday.

Past modals

modal + have + V3: should have done = it was right to do it, but it wasn't done (regret), could have done = was able to do it, but didn't (missed chance), must have done = surely did it (a sure guess). "have" never becomes "has".

  • I should have studied harder. = Studying harder was the right thing to do, but I didn't. (regret)
  • The roads are wet. It must have rained last night. = It surely rained last night — a sure guess from the wet roads.

'should've' in speech

In conversation, should have sounds like "should've" (shud-uv). That is why many people write "should of" — which is wrong. In writing, always use have.

docs.title: 16.8 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
The most common Indian-English mistakes with modals

  • Wrong: Can you able to come tomorrow?
  • Right: Can you come tomorrow? / Will you be able to come?

  • Why: "can" and "able to" mean the same thing — using both is repetition. Pick one.

  • Wrong: You must to submit the form today.

  • Right: You must submit the form today.

  • Why: After a modal comes V1 directly, with no "to" in between. Only ought to, have to and used to have "to".

  • Wrong: May you help me with this?

  • Right: Could you help me with this?

  • Why: "May" is used only to ask permission for yourself (May I…?). To ask someone to do something, use Could you / Would you.

  • Wrong: I could not able to attend the meeting.

  • Right: I couldn't attend / I wasn't able to attend the meeting.

  • Why: The same repetition — "could" and "able" don't go together. For one particular occasion, "wasn't able to" is the most natural.

  • Wrong: You should have went to the doctor.

  • Right: You should have gone to the doctor.
  • Why: After "have" you always need V3 — gone, seen, done. "went" is V2, which doesn't belong here.

docs.title: 16.9 Practice — Modals
docs.text:
Exercise 1

She ___ speak four languages.

  • can
  • cans
  • can to
  • is can

Hint: Which form of the verb comes after a modal?

Answer

can

A modal never changes — no -s, no 'to', and no 'is' with it. Just 'She can speak'.

Exercise 2

You want to ask your boss politely: '___ you check my report, please?'

  • Could
  • May
  • Must
  • Shall
Answer

Could

A polite request to get someone to do something is Could you…? 'May you' is wrong — may is only for asking permission for yourself (May I…?).

Exercise 3

Tomorrow is a holiday, so you ___ come to the office.

  • don't have to
  • mustn't
  • can't
  • shouldn't have

Hint: It isn't forbidden — it just isn't necessary.

Answer

don't have to

It's a holiday, so coming in isn't necessary — 'don't have to'. 'mustn't' would mean coming in is forbidden, which isn't the point here.

Exercise 4

He has been working for 14 hours. He ___ be very tired.

  • must
  • might
  • can't
  • should have

Hint: A sure guess.

Answer

must

After 14 hours of work, being tired is almost certain. For a sure guess use 'must'.

Exercise 5

When I was a child, I ___ climb trees easily.

  • could
  • can
  • am able to
  • will be able to
Answer

could

This is a general ability in the past — so 'could', the past of 'can'.

Exercise 6

I missed the bus. I should have ___ earlier. (leave)

Hint: have + V3

Answer

left

The formula for a past modal is should + have + V3. The V3 of 'leave' is 'left'. It means leaving early was the right thing to do (but I didn't).

Exercise 7

Next year I will ___ able to vote.

Hint: Two modals can't go together.

Answer

be

'will can' is wrong because two modals can't be used together. Ability in the future = will be able to.

Exercise 8

Tap the wrong word.

Can you able to send the document today?

Answer

Wrong word: able.

Corrected: Can you send the document today?

'Can' and 'able to' both mean the same thing, so together they repeat. Drop 'able to', or say 'Will you be able to…?'

Exercise 9

One word is extra — find it.

You must to wear a helmet on the bike.

Answer

Wrong word: to.

Corrected: You must wear a helmet on the bike.

After 'must' comes V1 directly, with no 'to'. 'to' appears only with ought to, have to and used to.

Exercise 10

Match each modal to its job.

A B should perhaps, low certainty mustn't was true before, not now might advice used to forbidden Answer

should — advice; mustn't — forbidden; might — perhaps, low certainty; used to — was true before, not now

should = a good idea, mustn't = don't do it, might = perhaps, used to = an old habit that has stopped.

Exercise 11

Make a polite request.

Words: mind / door / Would / the / opening / you

Answer

Would you mind opening the door

After 'Would you mind' the verb takes -ing — opening. It is the most polite way to ask someone to do something.

Exercise 12

Say this line aloud — join 'should have' like 'should've'.

Answer

Say: I should have called you yesterday

Native speakers say 'should have' as 'shud-uv'. Joining it when you speak makes listening easier too, and fixes the formula (modal + have + V3) in your head.

What to do next

Tomorrow at the office or college, whenever you ask for something, say "Could you" instead of "Can you". And at the end of the day, write one "should have" sentence about yourself — something you should have done but didn't.

docs.title: Chapter 44: Normal → advanced verbs
docs.text:
Verb upgrades — one word instead of three

In English, the verb is the engine of the sentence. When the engine is weak — make better, get rid of, give permission — the whole sentence feels slack, even if the grammar is perfect. One precise verb does the work of two or three words, and the sentence at once sounds clear and educated. In this chapter: five upgrades in depth, then a full list of more than twenty, their rules, and the most important question — when not to use them.

In one line

Wherever two or three words together describe one action, there is often a single verb that describes the same action more clearly. Fewer words, more impact — this is the first rule of writing English.

docs.title: show clearly → demonstrate
docs.text:
Demonstrate does not only mean to show — it means to prove by doing or by giving evidence. That is why it fits in a lab, a class, a product demo and a report. If you are just pointing out a place with your finger, show is the right verb.

  • The trial demonstrated that the cheaper design works just as well. = The trial proved that the cheaper design works equally well.
  • Let me demonstrate the new feature before we discuss pricing. = Before we talk about pricing, let me show the new feature in action.

When not to

"Demonstrate me the way to the station" — this is odd. To point out a route, use show. Remember: demonstrate needs evidence or a process behind it.

docs.title: make better → enhance
docs.text:
Enhance means to make something that is already good even better. So you do not "enhance" something that is broken — you fix it. Something weak you improve. Enhance carries a feeling of adding polish on top.

  • Better lighting would really enhance these photos. = Better lighting would make these photos look even nicer.
  • We added search to enhance the reading experience. = We added search to make reading better.

Three different 'betters'

fix = repair something broken · improve = make something weak better · enhance = make something good even better. You do not say "enhance the bug" — a bug is fixed.

docs.title: get rid of → eliminate
docs.text:
Eliminate means to remove completely, leaving not even one. It is a heavy verb — it sounds good with numbers, process, risk and waste. You do not "eliminate" your old clothes; they are simply got rid of.

  • The new form eliminated almost all data-entry errors. = The new form removed almost every data-entry error.
  • We can eliminate two steps and still get the same result. = We can remove two steps and the result will stay the same.

docs.title: give permission → authorize
docs.text:
Authorize is not just "saying yes" — it carries authority. The one who authorizes must have official power: a manager, a bank, the government, a system. A mother who allows her child to go out lets him go — she does not authorize it.

  • Only the finance head can authorize a refund above fifty thousand. = Only the finance head can approve a refund of more than fifty thousand.
  • I'm not authorized to share those figures — let me check with my manager. = I do not have the authority to share those numbers — let me ask my manager.

A very useful line

"I'm not authorized to do that" works in interviews, support calls and the office — all three. It is a polite and professional way to say no, and it does not make you look at fault.

docs.title: take into account → consider
docs.text:
Consider does two jobs: (1) to think about something carefully and (2) to keep something in mind. In both, it is shorter and cleaner than take into account. Note: about never comes after consider.

  • We should consider the delivery cost before choosing a vendor. = We should keep the delivery cost in mind before choosing a vendor.
  • Have you considered doing it the other way round? = Have you thought about doing it the opposite way?

Two firm rules for consider

  • Wrong: Please consider about my request.
  • Right: Please consider my request.

  • Why: The thing comes straight after consider — no preposition.

  • Wrong: Have you considered to change the design?

  • Right: Have you considered changing the design?
  • Why: After consider, a verb always takes the -ing form, not the "to" form.

docs.title: 44.2 One weak verb, several right verbs
docs.text:
The biggest mistake is to always replace a weak phrase with one and the same big word. The truth is that every weak phrase opens in several directions — which one you choose depends on the meaning.

Figure 44.1. One slack phrase, four different meanings. Before choosing a word, ask: is the thing broken, weak, good, or slow?

docs.title: 44.3 The big upgrade table
docs.text:
It is not only the words here — the third column tells you where each upgrade fits. Without that column, this table is dangerous.

Slack phrase One verb Where it fits show clearly / prove by doing demonstrate Report, presentation, class, product demo make better (something already good) enhance Product, design, experience, taste get rid of (completely) eliminate Risk, waste, error, step, cost give permission (with authority) authorize Office, bank, payment, access take into account consider Everywhere — speaking and writing make smaller / cut down reduce Cost, time, size — very common make bigger / increase expand Business, team, scope find out determine Investigation, report, official writing put in place implement Office, software, policy say sorry formally apologize Email, customer support make sure ensure Email, process, instructions give out distribute Stock, salary, files look into examine / investigate Investigation, audit, problem keep up maintain Machine, record, standard cut down slowly taper Medicine, spending — a bit technical take part in participate Event, survey, training

docs.title: 44.4 Fifteen more upgrades — make, give, get, have, take
docs.text: These are the same "light verb + noun" phrases we use every day. Each has a real sentence (press 🔊) and the last column gives the register — because some of these words sound heavy or odd in speech.

docs.title: make ___ phrases
docs.text: Normal → Advanced Example Meaning When to use it make worse → aggravate Skipping physio will only aggravate the injury. To make something already bad even worse. Formal — injury, illness, quarrel, problem. In casual speech "make it worse" is better. make possible → enable The new app enables farmers to check prices instantly. To make something possible for someone. Neutral, very common in office and tech. Pattern: enable + someone + to + verb. make certain → ensure Please ensure that all files are backed up by Friday. To make certain that something happens. Email and instructions. In speech "make sure" is the natural one. make clear → elucidate The professor elucidated the theory with two simple diagrams. To open up a difficult idea and explain it clearly. Very bookish — research papers, lectures. In daily life say "explain" or "clarify". make use of → utilize The plant now utilizes waste heat to warm the offices. To put something to work. Technical/report. In 90% of cases plain "use" is better — "utilize" sounds heavy for no reason.

docs.title: give / get / find phrases
docs.text: Normal → Advanced Example Meaning When to use it give information → provide Could you provide details of the payment? To supply information or something else. Safe in the office and in email. Pattern: provide something, provide someone with something. give an example → exemplify This project exemplifies what a small team can do. To be a perfect example of something. Formal writing. In speech "is a great example of" is more natural. get involved → participate Over two hundred students participated in the survey. To take part in an activity. Neutral. Always participate in. Among friends "get involved" or "join in" is fine. find a solution → resolve The support team resolved the issue within an hour. To settle a problem. Office, support, disputes. Very useful. For a small thing "sort out" also works.

docs.title: have / come / reach / take / keep phrases
docs.text:
Normal → Advanced Example Meaning When to use it have an effect → influence Reviews strongly influence what people buy online. To have an effect on someone or something. Safe everywhere. Note: no on after influence — "influence people", but "have an influence on people". have a need → require This role requires three years of experience. To need something. Rules, job posts, instructions. In conversation use "need" — "I require water" sounds robotic. come to a decision → determine The committee will determine the final budget next week. To decide after careful thought. Official. In speech "decide" is more common. The other meaning of determine: to find out. reach an agreement → reconcile The mediator helped them reconcile their differences. To end a disagreement and bring two sides together. Reconcile = to settle relationships or differences, or to match accounts. For simply "we agreed" use reach a consensus or agree. take control → assume authority The deputy will assume authority while the director is away. To take over command officially. Very formal — notices, reports. In daily life and at the office use take charge: "She took charge of the project." keep safe → safeguard Strong passwords help safeguard your data. To protect from harm. Formal and policy language — data, rights, interests. For a child or a bag, "keep safe" is fine.

Where the simple verb wins

use > utilize · explain > elucidate · need > require · decide > determine · make sure > ensure · take charge > assume authority — all of this in conversation. Keep the heavy forms for reports, policies and formal emails. If you ask a friend "Can you elucidate?", they will laugh. Big verbs are for writing, not for the tea stall.

docs.title: 44.5 Three questions — before you upgrade
docs.text:
A bigger word is not always better. Before replacing any weak phrase, ask yourself three questions:

The upgrade test

1. Does the meaning stay the same? — "eliminate the poor" means something completely different. Changing a word can change the meaning. 2. Can the setting carry it? — at a tea stall, "Could you authorize one more cup?" sounds like a joke. 3. Can I say it comfortably? — if your tongue stumbles while speaking, that word is not yours yet.

The truth about interviews

An interviewer likes clear thinking more than big words. One right verb sounds good; three heavy verbs in every line make you look memorised. In one paragraph, one or two upgrades are plenty. Add spice only as much as the dish can take.

docs.title: 44.6 Mistakes people make with these verbs
docs.text:
Be careful

  • Wrong: He demonstrated me his new phone.
  • Right: He showed me his new phone.

  • Why: Demonstrate means to prove by doing or by evidence. To show a phone, simply use "show".

  • Wrong: Please enhance this broken link.

  • Right: Please fix this broken link.

  • Why: Something broken is fixed. Enhance is only for something that already works.

  • Wrong: My father authorized me to go to the party.

  • Right: My father let me go to the party.

  • Why: Authorize carries official authority. At home say "let", "allowed me to", or "gave me permission".

  • Wrong: We will eliminate the old sofa this weekend.

  • Right: We will get rid of the old sofa this weekend.

  • Why: For everyday objects, "get rid of" is the natural choice. Eliminate is for abstract things like risk, error and cost.

  • Wrong: Kindly consider about my application.

  • Right: Please consider my application.

  • Why: No preposition comes after consider — and "please" is more natural than "kindly".

  • Wrong: We implemented a new chair in the office.

  • Right: We got a new chair for the office.
  • Why: Implement is for processes, systems and policies — not for objects.

docs.title: 44.7 One paragraph, two versions
docs.text:
Below is a short office update. First the slack version, then the upgraded one. Notice that the second version is also shorter — that is the real benefit.

Before

We made the checkout page better and we got rid of two steps. The data shows clearly that people finish faster now. Before we do it on the live site, the manager has to give permission, and we should also take into account the extra server cost.

After

We enhanced the checkout page and eliminated two steps. The data demonstrates that people finish faster now. Before we go live, the manager has to authorize it, and we should also consider the extra server cost.

docs.title: 44.8 Practice — Verb upgrades
docs.text:
Exercise 1

In a report you want to say that the figures proved the point. Which verb?

  • demonstrate
  • enhance
  • authorize
  • maintain

Hint: Showing with evidence.

Answer

demonstrate

Demonstrate = to prove by doing or by evidence. This is what fits the language of reports and presentations.

Exercise 2

The website already works well, but we want to make it even better.

  • enhance
  • fix
  • eliminate
  • demonstrate
Answer

enhance

Making something good even better = enhance. If it were broken, it would be 'fix'.

Exercise 3

Which sentence is wrong?

  • We will eliminate the old sofa this weekend.
  • The new form eliminated most errors.
  • We eliminated two unnecessary steps.
  • This change eliminates the risk of double billing.

Hint: In one of them, a big word is in the wrong place.

Answer

We will eliminate the old sofa this weekend.

For an everyday object, use 'get rid of'. Eliminate goes with things like risk, error, step and cost.

Exercise 4

Only the finance head can ___ a refund above fifty thousand.

Hint: Giving permission with authority.

Answer

authorize / authorise

Authorize = to approve with official power. For permission at home use 'let' or 'allow'.

Exercise 5

Have you ___ changing the layout instead?

Hint: A one-word form of take into account.

Answer

considered

After consider, a verb takes -ing: considered changing, not 'considered to change'.

Exercise 6

One word here is unnecessary — find it.

Please consider about my application carefully.

Answer

Wrong word: about.

Corrected: Please consider my application carefully.

No preposition comes after consider. The same mistake happens with 'discuss about'.

Exercise 7

The verb has been chosen wrongly — tap it.

He demonstrated me his new bike yesterday.

Answer

Wrong word: demonstrated.

Corrected: He showed me his new bike yesterday.

Showing a bike is just 'show'. Demonstrate needs a process or evidence behind it.

Exercise 8

Match each slack phrase with its right one-word form.

A B get rid of completely consider give permission officially demonstrate take into account eliminate show by proving authorize Answer

get rid of completely — eliminate; give permission officially — authorize; take into account — consider; show by proving — demonstrate

Remember the real meaning of all four upgrades — not the word, but the feeling behind it.

Exercise 9

Choose the right 'better'.

A B to repair something broken enhance to make something weak better optimize to polish something good fix to make the best use of speed improve Answer

to repair something broken — fix; to make something weak better — improve; to polish something good — enhance; to make the best use of speed — optimize

The one Hindi idea of 'making better' becomes four different verbs in English. Choose by the condition of the thing.

Exercise 10

Build the upgraded line.

Words: all / eliminated / almost / errors / process / The / new / data / entry

Answer

The new process eliminated almost all data entry errors

This sentence is shorter and cleaner than 'got rid of almost all errors in data entry'.

Exercise 11

How many heavy verbs are fine in one paragraph?

  • One or two
  • One in every sentence
  • The more the better
  • At least five
Answer

One or two

Too many heavy verbs make writing look memorised. Clear thinking has more impact than big words.

Exercise 12

Two teams had an old disagreement. A mediator brought them together again. Which verb?

  • reconcile
  • aggravate
  • utilize
  • exemplify

Hint: Settling differences.

Answer

reconcile

Reconcile = to end a disagreement and bring people together (reconcile their differences). Aggravate is the opposite — it makes things worse.

Exercise 13

You are talking to a friend: 'We utilize this app for groceries.' What would sound more natural?

  • We use this app for groceries.
  • We elucidate this app for groceries.
  • We safeguard this app for groceries.
  • We require this app for groceries.
Answer

We use this app for groceries.

In daily life 'use' is the right verb. 'Utilize' is a technical-report word — in conversation it sounds heavy for no reason.

Exercise 14

Please ___ that the door is locked before you leave.

Hint: A one-word form of make certain.

Answer

ensure / make sure

Ensure = to make certain. Use ensure in instructions and email, 'make sure' in conversation — both are correct.

Exercise 15

One verb is far too heavy for this setting — find it.

Hey, can you elucidate where the washroom is?

Answer

Wrong word: elucidate.

Corrected: Hey, can you tell me where the washroom is?

Elucidate is a lecture and research word. To ask for directions use 'tell me' or 'show me'.

Exercise 16

Match each normal phrase with its advanced verb.

A B make worse safeguard make possible resolve keep safe aggravate find a solution enable Answer

make worse — aggravate; make possible — enable; keep safe — safeguard; find a solution — resolve

All four are useful in formal writing. In speech the simple forms are perfectly fine.

Exercise 17

Say this line. Stress the second part of 'authorized' — a-THO-rized.

Answer

Say: I am not authorized to share those figures

This line works on support calls and in the office, and it does not point at you as being at fault — only at the rule.

What to do next

Open one of your old emails and mark only the verbs. Wherever two or three words together describe one action, try putting in a single verb. This fifteen-minute exercise teaches more than any vocabulary list.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Nouns
docs.text:
Noun — the naming words

A noun is a word that gives the name of a person, place, thing or feeling. It is the foundation of every sentence — first there is someone, then that someone does something. Nouns have three parts that trip up Indian speakers the most: countable vs uncountable, making plurals, and where the apostrophe goes. All three are in this chapter.

In one line

A noun is a word that names a person, place, thing, animal, or idea. If you can name it, it is a noun.

  • My brother works in Chennai. = My brother has a job in Chennai. (a person + a place)
  • Honesty is the best policy. Honesty is a noun too — you cannot touch it, but it has a name.
  • The team won two matches. The name of a group is a noun, and so is the name of an object.

docs.title: 5.1 Types of noun — a map
docs.text:
Nouns are divided in two ways, and both divisions work together. First by kind of name (proper, common, collective, abstract, material), and then by counting (countable, uncountable). One noun will appear in both lists — for example "water" is common and also uncountable.

Figure 5.1. The noun tree — five branches on top by kind of name, two below by counting.

docs.title: 5.2 The five kinds, in a little more detail
docs.text:
Type Meaning Examples Note Proper The own name of one particular thing Ravi, Ganga, India, Diwali, Toyota Always starts with a capital letter Common The general name of a whole class boy, river, country, festival, car Small letter, and takes a/an/the Collective One name for a group of many things team, family, crowd, class, herd Looks like one, means many Abstract Something you cannot touch — a feeling, quality, state honesty, anger, childhood, freedom Often uncountable Material The substance something is made of gold, cotton, rice, water, iron Uncountable, so not "a gold"

Collective noun — singular or plural?

When the whole group acts together, use singular: The team is playing well. When the members of the group act separately, plural is fine too: The team are arguing among themselves. In India the first form is more common — when in doubt, use singular.

docs.title: Quick guide — all the types at a glance
docs.text:
The five kinds by name were above. Nouns are also looked at in two more ways — can you count it or not (countable / uncountable), and how many words it is made of (compound).

Type Question to ask Examples Proper A special name for one thing? (capital) Ravi, Delhi, Ganga Common A general name for a whole class? boy, city, river Collective The name of a group? team, army, herd Material What is it made of? gold, wood, cotton Abstract Can't touch it — a feeling, quality, state? love, honesty, childhood Countable Can you count it? (a / an, plural) a pen, two pens Uncountable Can't count it? (no a / an, no plural) water, advice, furniture Compound Two or more words together making one name? toothpaste, bus stop, mother-in-law

Three forms of compound noun

Joined into one word — toothbrush, classroom, sunlight Written as separate words — bus stop, ice cream, post office With a hyphen — mother-in-law, passer-by, well-wisher Which form is correct is shown by the dictionary — it comes from habit, not from a rule.

docs.title: 5.3 Countable and Uncountable — this is the biggest trouble
docs.text:
In Hindi we say "ek paani", "do advice" and people understand. In English that doesn't work. Some nouns are a heap in English eyes, not pieces — and a heap is not counted, it is measured.

Countable Uncountable a / an a book, an apple ✗ a water, ✗ an advice Plural books, apples ✗ waters, ✗ advices How many? many, few, a few, number of much, little, a little, amount of Counting two books two glasses of water Verb These books are new. This water is cold.

These nouns are uncountable — never make a plural of them

information, advice, furniture, luggage, equipment, machinery, stationery, news, work, bread, rice, money, traffic, scenery, knowledge, progress, homework, research, hair (all the hair on your head). As soon as you add -s to these, the sentence becomes wrong.

When you need to count, put a measuring word in front — this is the real way:

Wrong Right two informations two pieces of information many advices a lot of advice / several pieces of advice three furnitures three pieces of furniture two breads two slices / loaves of bread four luggages four bags of luggage a news a piece of news / some news

Some nouns are both — and the meaning changes

Word Uncountable Countable hair her hair is long (all the hair) two hairs in my food (single strands) time I have no time (time in general) three times (occasions) paper I need paper (the material) today's paper (a newspaper) water drink water (the liquid) the waters of the Ganga (literary) experience he has experience (skill from doing) a strange experience (one event)

docs.title: 5.4 Rules for making plurals
docs.text:
Most of the time you just add -s. But in eight places it is a little different. Look at the table once, and most of the work is done.

How the word ends What to do Example Normal + s book → books, pen → pens -s, -ss, -sh, -ch, -x, -z + es bus → buses, box → boxes, watch → watches consonant + y y → ies city → cities, baby → babies vowel + y + s (the y stays) boy → boys, day → days -f, -fe (in some) f → ves leaf → leaves, knife → knives, wife → wives -o (in some) + es mango → mangoes, hero → heroes, potato → potatoes -o (foreign words) + s photos, pianos, radios, zoos Completely different (irregular) learn by heart man → men, child → children, tooth → teeth

docs.title: Plurals that follow no rule
docs.text:
Singular Plural Singular Plural man men woman women child children person people tooth teeth foot feet mouse mice goose geese ox oxen louse lice sheep sheep deer deer fish fish series series criterion criteria analysis analyses

These are always plural

trousers, jeans, scissors, spectacles, glasses, clothes, goods, thanks, surroundings, premises, scales — they have no singular. To talk about one, say: a pair of trousers. Not "My trouser is dirty" — "My trousers are dirty".

Plural of a compound noun

The -s goes on the main word, not at the end: brothers-in-law, passers-by, *Commanders-in-Chief. But in today's English you may also hear son-in-laws* — in an exam, write the traditional form.

docs.title: 5.5 Possessive — where the apostrophe goes
docs.text:
Hindi has "ka, ki, ke". English has 's or of. The rule is simple — first check whether the noun is singular or plural, and whether the plural already ends in -s.

Figure 5.2. One question — does it end in -s? — and the place of the apostrophe is decided. Situation Rule Example Singular noun + 's my sister's phone Plural ending in -s just ' the students' hostel Irregular plural + 's the children's books, men's shoes Two people, one thing 's on the last one Ram and Shyam's shop (one shop shared) Two people, separate things 's on both Ram's and Shyam's shops (two shops) A lifeless thing use of the roof of the house Time / measure 's works a day's work, two weeks' notice

its vs it's — 90% of people get this wrong

  • Wrong: The dog wagged it's tail.
  • Right: The dog wagged its tail.
  • Why: its = belonging to it (possessive). it's = it is. Test: put "it is" into the sentence and read it — if it sounds like nonsense, remove the apostrophe.

docs.title: 5.6 Where a noun sits in a sentence
docs.text: Job Example Meaning Subject Ravi called me. the doer Object I called Ravi. what the action fell on Indirect object I gave Ravi a pen. who it was for Complement He became a doctor. says more about the subject After a preposition She sat on the chair. object of a preposition Addressing someone Sir, may I come in? the person being called

docs.title: 5.7 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
The most common Indian-English mistakes with nouns

  • Wrong: She is one of my friend.
  • Right: She is one of my friends.

  • Why: "One of" means one out of many. When there are many, the noun must be plural. First make the group (my friends), then pick one from it (one of).

  • Wrong: Please give me some informations.

  • Right: Please give me some information.

  • Why: Information is uncountable — English sees it as a heap, not pieces. To count it, say two pieces of information.

  • Wrong: He gave me many good advices.

  • Right: He gave me a lot of good advice.

  • Why: Advice has no plural, and it doesn't go with "many" either — use "much" or "a lot of". Remember: advice is the noun, advise is the verb.

  • Wrong: She is my cousin sister.

  • Right: She is my cousin.

  • Why: "Cousin" is a complete noun — you don't need to add brother or sister. If you want to be specific, say: She is my cousin — my uncle's daughter.

  • Wrong: I bought two new furnitures.

  • Right: I bought two new pieces of furniture.

  • Why: Furniture means the whole stock, not single items. To name one item, use its name: a table, a sofa.

  • Wrong: My all luggages are in the car.

  • Right: All my luggage is in the car.

  • Why: Two mistakes together: luggage is uncountable (no plural), and the order is "all my", not "my all". With an uncountable noun the verb is singular too — is.

  • Wrong: The peoples of my village are very kind.

  • Right: The people of my village are very kind.

  • Why: "People" is already a plural — the plural of person. "Peoples" is used only when you mean different nations or ethnic groups: the peoples of Asia.

  • Wrong: I have two womens in my team.

  • Right: I have two women in my team.
  • Why: "Women" is already plural. You never add -s again to an irregular plural — not "childrens", not "mens", not "teeths".

docs.title: 5.8 A short thing to remember
docs.text:
Three questions for every noun

1. Can it be counted? → if yes, a/an and a plural; if no, no a/an and a singular verb. 2. Whose is it? → if it ends in -s, just ', otherwise 's. 3. One or many? → change the verb to match.

docs.title: 5.9 Practice — Nouns
docs.text:
Exercise 1

She is one of my ___ from college.

  • friends
  • friend
  • friend's
  • friends'

Hint: After 'one of' comes a group.

Answer

friends

'One of' means one out of many — so the group must be plural. First the group (friends), then one is picked from it.

Exercise 2

I need some ___ about the admission process.

  • information
  • informations
  • an information
  • informations'

Hint: This noun is uncountable.

Answer

information

Information is uncountable — English sees it as a heap, so it takes neither -s nor a/an. To count it, say 'two pieces of information'.

Exercise 3

Which plural is correct?

  • children
  • childrens
  • childs
  • childrens'
Answer

children

The plural of child is children — it is irregular. You don't add -s to an irregular plural, so 'childrens' is always wrong.

Exercise 4

The ___ hostel is behind the library. (the hostel of many students)

  • students'
  • student's
  • students
  • students's

Hint: The plural already ends in -s.

Answer

students'

The plural 'students' already ends in -s, so only the apostrophe is added — no second s. For one student it would be student's.

Exercise 5

The dog wagged ___ tail happily.

Hint: You need a possessive, not 'it is'.

Answer

its

'its' is the possessive — belonging to it. 'it's' means 'it is', and 'the dog wagged it is tail' would be nonsense.

Exercise 6

Three ___ of furniture arrived yesterday. (a counting word)

Hint: To count an uncountable noun you need a word in between.

Answer

pieces

Furniture is uncountable, so you can't count it directly. You put a measuring word — pieces — in between.

Exercise 7

There is one mistake in this sentence — tap the wrong word.

She is my cousin sister from Nagpur.

Answer

Wrong word: sister.

Corrected: She is my cousin from Nagpur.

In English 'cousin' is a complete word — you don't need to add sister or brother. This habit comes from the Hindi 'cousin behen'.

Exercise 8

Find the wrong word.

He gave me many advices about the exam.

Answer

Wrong word: advices.

Corrected: He gave me a lot of advice about the exam.

Advice is uncountable — it has no plural, and 'many' doesn't go with it. It takes 'much' or 'a lot of'.

Exercise 9

One word is wrong — find it.

My trouser is lying on the bed.

Answer

Wrong word: trouser.

Corrected: My trousers are lying on the bed.

Trousers is always plural, because it has two legs. That is why the verb is 'are' too. To talk about one, say 'a pair of trousers'.

Exercise 10

'Toothpaste', 'bus stop' and 'mother-in-law' — what kind of noun are all three?

  • Compound
  • Collective
  • Abstract
  • Material

Hint: How many words are they made of?

Answer

Compound

When two or more words together make one name, it is a compound noun — whether joined (toothpaste), separate (bus stop), or hyphenated (mother-in-law).

Exercise 11

Which noun is uncountable?

  • luggage
  • bag
  • suitcase
  • ticket

Hint: It doesn't take 'a', and it has no plural.

Answer

luggage

'luggage' is uncountable — not 'a luggage' or 'luggages'. To count, say 'two pieces of luggage' or 'two bags'. The other three are countable.

Exercise 12

Match each noun to its type.

A B Mumbai abstract noun crowd material noun kindness common noun cotton proper noun chair collective noun Answer

Mumbai — proper noun; crowd — collective noun; kindness — abstract noun; cotton — material noun; chair — common noun

A special name is proper, a group is collective, a feeling or quality is abstract, a substance is material, and the general name of a class is common.

Exercise 13

Put the words in the right order — it uses a possessive.

Words: phone / is / the / My / sister's / on / table

Answer

My sister's phone is on the table

The possessive 's comes right after the owner, and the thing owned comes right after that — sister's phone.

Exercise 14

Say this line aloud. Make the -s at the end of 'friends' clearly heard.

Answer

Say: She is one of my closest friends

We often swallow the final -s, so it sounds like 'one of my friend'. Push the -s out on purpose — that is the fix.

What next?

Write ten sentences from your day and draw a line under every noun — then ask "is it countable?". In two days the uncountable list will stick in your head. The next chapter is Pronoun — the shortcut for a noun.

docs.title: Chapter 31: Numbers, dates, time & money
docs.text:
Number, date, time, paise

Saying numbers seems easy — until an auto driver hears "fifteen" instead of "fifty", or a foreign client hears "twelve lakh" and goes quiet. In this chapter you will learn to say numbers, money, years, dates, times and phone numbers clearly and correctly — and how to turn lakh-crore into million. Press 🔊 on every line and repeat it aloud.

In one line

-teen: stress at the end, -ty: stress at the start · hundred and · 10 lakh = 1 million · twenty twenty-six · quarter past / half past / quarter to. One small slip with a number = wrong money, wrong train, wrong day.

docs.title: 31.1 13 or 30? — the most expensive confusion
docs.text:
thirteen and thirty, fifteen and fifty — they are different in writing, but Indian speakers often say them the same way. The difference is in two things: where the stress is, and whether the ending is long or short.

Figure 31.1. The big box = the stressed part. In -teen the last part is big and long; in -ty the first part is big and the ending stops short. -teen Listen -ty Listen 13 thirTEEN 30 THIRty 14 fourTEEN 40 FORty 15 fifTEEN 50 FIFty 16 sixTEEN 60 SIXty 18 eighTEEN 80 EIGHty
  • She's fifteen, not fifty! = She is 15 years old, not 50!
  • Platform thirteen, please. = Asking for platform number 13.

If in doubt, break it up

With important numbers like money or a platform, confusion is possible, so make it clear: "Fifteen — one five." or "Fifty — five zero." Native speakers do exactly this on the phone.

docs.title: 31.2 Above 100 — hundred, thousand and "and"
docs.text:
In British and Indian English, and comes after hundred: a hundred and twenty. American English often leaves out the "and". And one firm rule: with a number, hundred / thousand / million never take a plural.

Number Say Listen 100 a hundred / one hundred 120 a hundred and twenty 305 three hundred and five 999 nine hundred and ninety-nine 1,500 one thousand five hundred / fifteen hundred 4,250 four thousand two hundred and fifty 70,000 seventy thousand

✗

There were three hundreds people at the wedding.

✓

There were three hundred people at the wedding.

hundreds of people

thousands of rupees

  • Hundreds of people were waiting at the station. = A very large crowd (we don't know the exact number) was waiting.

docs.title: 31.3 Lakh, crore and million — the bridge between two worlds
docs.text:
In India we think in lakh and crore, and in Indian English these are perfectly good words. But a foreign client, an international exam (IELTS) or a global meeting needs thousand, million, billion. The commas go in different places too: Indian 1,25,000 = international 125,000.

Figure 31.2. Remember two magic pairs: 10 lakh = 1 million and 1 crore = 10 million . Everything else follows from these. Amount Indian English International ₹1,25,000 one lakh twenty-five thousand a hundred and twenty-five thousand ₹8,50,000 eight and a half lakh eight hundred and fifty thousand ₹25,00,000 twenty-five lakh two and a half million ₹3,00,00,000 three crore thirty million ₹1,500 crore fifteen hundred crore fifteen billion
  • The bike costs one lakh twenty-five thousand rupees. = The bike costs ₹1,25,000. (Use this when talking within India.)
  • That's about a hundred and twenty-five thousand rupees. = The same amount, said for a foreign friend.
  • Our app has two and a half million users — that's twenty-five lakh. = Our app has 25 lakh users, said both ways.
  • The film made three hundred crore — about thirty-six million dollars. = The film earned 300 crore rupees, which is roughly 36 million US dollars.

✗

My salary is twelve lakhs per annum. (to a US client)

✓

My salary is about 1.2 million rupees a year — roughly fourteen thousand dollars.

docs.title: 31.4 Decimals, fractions and percentages
docs.text:
After the decimal point, say each digit separately: 3.14 = "three point one four", not "three point fourteen". Say 0 as "zero" (in British English also "nought"); and 0.5 can simply be "point five".

Written Say Listen 2.5 two point five 3.14 three point one four 0.75 zero point seven five ½ a half 1½ one and a half ⅓ · ⅔ a third · two thirds ¼ · ¾ a quarter · three quarters 50% fifty per cent 7.5% seven point five per cent
  • One and a half kilos of tomatoes, please. = Please give me 1.5 kg of tomatoes (in Hindi: "dedh kilo").
  • Two thirds of the class passed with distinction. = 2 out of every 3 students got a distinction.
  • Prices went up by twelve per cent this year. = Prices rose by 12% this year.

Small points

British/Indian spelling is per cent, American is percent — they sound the same. One and a half hours (plural), but half an hour. And "dedh" = one and a half, "dhai" = two and a half.

docs.title: 31.5 Money and prices
docs.text:
We write ₹250 or Rs 250 — the symbol first; but we say "two hundred and fifty rupees" — rupees after the number. In shops and markets a short form is common too: ₹499 = "four ninety-nine".

Written Say Listen ₹50 fifty rupees ₹499 four hundred and ninety-nine rupees / four ninety-nine ₹2.50 two rupees fifty (paise) ₹1,200 one thousand two hundred / twelve hundred $3.99 three ninety-nine / three dollars ninety-nine cents £15 fifteen pounds
  • How much is this kurta? — It's eight hundred rupees. = Asking the price, and hearing that it is ₹800.
  • Could you do it for six fifty? = Can you lower the price to ₹650? (bargaining)
  • The bill comes to two thousand three hundred and forty rupees. = The total bill is ₹2,340.
  • Can you split it? That's about six hundred each. = Let's share the bill — about ₹600 per person.

✗

It costs rupees two hundred.

✓

It costs two hundred rupees.

after

'k' is informal only

With friends "fifteen k" (15,000) is fine. In an office email or an interview, say it in full: fifteen thousand. For salary, say "twelve lakh a year" or "twelve lakh per annum", not "12 LPA".

docs.title: Years — in pairs of digits
docs.text:
Years are usually said in two parts: 19|98 = nineteen ninety-eight. Only 2000 to 2009 use "two thousand (and) …". After 2010 both ways work, but twenty twenty-six is more common.

Year Say Listen 1947 nineteen forty-seven 1900 nineteen hundred 2000 the year two thousand 2005 two thousand and five (US: two thousand five) 2026 twenty twenty-six 1990s the nineties

docs.title: Ordinal numbers — first, second, third
docs.text:
Dates are always said as ordinals: the fifth, not "the five". Watch out for 11/12/13 (eleventh, twelfth, thirteenth) and for 21/22/23 (twenty-first, twenty-second, twenty-third).

Number Ordinal Listen 1st · 2nd · 3rd first · second · third 5th · 8th · 9th fifth · eighth · ninth 11th · 12th · 13th eleventh · twelfth · thirteenth 20th · 21st · 22nd twentieth · twenty-first · twenty-second 30th · 31st thirtieth · thirty-first

docs.title: Dates — British or American?
docs.text:
Style Written Spoken British / Indian 5 May 2026 the fifth of May, twenty twenty-six American May 5, 2026 May fifth, twenty twenty-six India/UK number 05/06/2026 5 June US number 05/06/2026 May 6
  • My birthday is on the twenty-first of October. = My birthday is on 21 October.
  • The exam is on March the third. = The exam is on 3 March.
  • I was born in two thousand and five. = I was born in 2005.
  • India became independent on the fifteenth of August, nineteen forty-seven. = India became independent on 15 August 1947.

✗

The meeting is on five May.

✓

The meeting is on the fifth of May. / on May fifth.

on

in

Prepositions — the linking words

The 05/06 trap

For a US client, 05/06 = 6 May; for you it is 5 June. In international emails always write the month as a word: 5 June 2026. Problem solved.

docs.title: 31.7 Telling the time — from o'clock to "7 sharp"
docs.text:
There are two ways: digital (seven fifteen) — easy and always correct; and past / to (quarter past seven) — very common in everyday talk. You need to understand both.

Time past / to Digital Listen 7:00 seven o'clock seven 7:05 five past seven seven oh five 7:15 quarter past seven seven fifteen 7:30 half past seven seven thirty 7:40 twenty to eight seven forty 7:45 quarter to eight seven forty-five

past and to

For the first 30 minutes: minutes + past + the current hour. For the last 30: minutes + to + the next hour. 15 = quarter, 30 = half. If in doubt, say it digitally: seven forty-five is never wrong.

Hindi Time English sawa saat 7:15 quarter past seven saadhe saat 7:30 half past seven paune aath 7:45 quarter to eight dedh baje 1:30 half past one dhai baje 2:30 half past two
  • The meeting starts at ten sharp. = The meeting starts at exactly ten — not even one minute late.
  • Let's meet around six. / Let's meet at six-ish. = Let's meet at about six — the exact time doesn't matter.
  • My flight is at eleven forty-five p.m. = My flight is at 11:45 at night.
  • The train departs at nineteen hundred hours. = The train leaves at 19:00 (7 p.m.). The 24-hour clock is used in announcements.
  • What time is it? — It's half past four. = Asking the time, and hearing that it is 4:30.

✗

I'll come at 7 o'clock in the evening p.m.

✓

I'll come at 7 p.m. / at seven in the evening.

seven o'clock

British 'half seven'

In the UK people say "half seven" and mean 7:30 (half past seven). Not 6:30!

docs.title: Phone numbers — one digit at a time, in groups
docs.text:
Say each digit of a phone number separately, in small groups, with a slight pause between groups. Two identical digits = double, three = triple. Say 0 as "oh" or "zero" — both are fine.

  • 98450 22301 → nine eight four five oh, double two three oh one. = Two groups of five digits.
  • My extension is triple four. = My extension is 444.
  • Sorry, was that five oh or five four? = Checking again: was it 50 or 54?

docs.title: Measurements, temperature and scores
docs.text:
Written Say Listen 5'8" five foot eight / five feet eight inches 70 kg seventy kilos 12 km twelve kilometres 2 BHK, 1,100 sq ft a two B-H-K, eleven hundred square feet 38°C thirty-eight degrees (Celsius) −5°C minus five degrees 250/3 (cricket) two fifty for three 2–0 (football) two nil / two-zero
  • It was forty-four degrees in Nagpur yesterday! = Yesterday's temperature in Nagpur was 44°C!
  • I'm five foot six and I weigh about sixty kilos. = My height is 5'6" and my weight is about 60 kg.

✗

The office is 12 kms from here. / It's 38 degree.

✓

The office is 12 km (twelve kilometres) from here. / It's 38 degrees.

docs.title: 31.9 In real life — booking a cab and paying a bill
docs.text:
Ankit is booking a cab to the airport, and later paying a bill at a shop. Listen to every line and repeat it — pay special attention to the numbers.

Who What they say Listen Agent What time is your flight, sir? Ankit It's at six forty-five a.m. on the thirteenth. Agent Sorry — the thirteenth or the thirtieth? Ankit The thirteenth. One three. Agent Then the driver will pick you up at four sharp. The fare is eight hundred and fifty rupees. Ankit Great. My number is nine eight one oh, double seven, four five two six. Cashier That's one thousand two hundred and forty, sir. Card or UPI?

The daily 3-minute drill

Whatever number you see on the way — a car plate, a price in a shop, the time on a clock — say it in English in your head. "Seven forty-five… quarter to eight." Within a week, saying numbers will be a job for your tongue, not your brain.

docs.title: 31.10 Practice — Numbers, dates, time & money
docs.text:
Exercise 1

When is the meeting?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

The meeting has been moved to the thirteenth of March.

  • 13 March
  • 30 March
  • 3 March
  • 13 May
Answer

13 March

thir-TEEN — the stress is at the end, with a long 'ee'. For 30 it would be THIR-tieth.

Exercise 2

How much does the driver want?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

That will be fifty rupees, please.

  • ₹15
  • ₹50
  • ₹500
  • ₹5
Answer

₹50

FIF-ty: stress at the start, short ending. In fifteen the stress would be on 'teen'.

Exercise 3

What time does the flight leave?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

My flight leaves at a quarter to nine.

  • 8:45
  • 9:15
  • 8:15
  • 9:45
Answer

8:45

quarter to nine = fifteen minutes before nine = 8:45 (paune nau).

Exercise 4

What is the price of the flat?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

The flat costs one crore twenty lakh rupees.

  • ₹1,20,00,000
  • ₹12,00,000
  • ₹1,20,000
  • ₹1,02,00,000
Answer

₹1,20,00,000

1 crore + 20 lakh = 1,20,00,000 (= 12 million).

Exercise 5

How many users is that in lakh?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Our app now has about one point five million users.

  • 15 lakh
  • 1.5 lakh
  • 150 lakh
  • 1.5 crore
Answer

15 lakh

1 million = 10 lakh, so 1.5 million = 15 lakh.

Exercise 6

What is Kavya's number?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Hi, it's Kavya. Please call me back on nine eight four five oh, double two, three oh one.

  • 98450 22301
  • 98450 23011
  • 98405 22301
  • 98450 22310
Answer

98450 22301

oh = 0, double two = 22. In a phone number, every digit is said separately.

Exercise 7

When does the train leave?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Train number one two nine five one will depart from platform four at nineteen hundred hours.

  • 7 p.m.
  • 9 p.m.
  • 7 a.m.
  • 9 a.m.
Answer

7 p.m.

Nineteen hundred hours = 19:00 = 7 in the evening. Announcements use the 24-hour clock.

Exercise 8

Which platform?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Train number one two nine five one will depart from platform four at nineteen hundred hours.

  • 4
  • 14
  • 19
  • 1
Answer

4

platform four. 12951 is the train number, and 19 is part of the time.

Exercise 9

Write what you hear. (Numbers can be digits or words — both are accepted)

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

The tickets cost two hundred and fifty rupees each.

two hundred and fifty = 250. Rupees comes after the number.

Exercise 10

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

My birthday is on the twenty-first of October.

Dates are said as ordinals: twenty-first (21st).

Exercise 11

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

I was born in two thousand and five.

2000–2009: two thousand (and) five.

Exercise 12

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

The shop opens at half past ten.

half past ten = 10:30 (saadhe das).

Exercise 13

How do people usually say the year 2026?

  • twenty twenty-six
  • two zero two six
  • twenty hundred twenty-six
  • two thousand twenty-six hundred
Answer

twenty twenty-six

Years are said in two pairs: 20|26 = twenty twenty-six. ('two thousand and twenty-six' is also correct, but less common.)

Exercise 14

A US client asks your budget. ₹1,25,000 in international English is…

  • a hundred and twenty-five thousand rupees
  • twelve lakh fifty thousand rupees
  • one million two hundred and fifty thousand rupees
  • twelve thousand five hundred rupees
Answer

a hundred and twenty-five thousand rupees

1,25,000 = 125,000 = a hundred and twenty-five thousand.

Exercise 15

An American email says the deadline is 05/06. What date do they mean?

  • 6 May
  • 5 June
  • 5 May
  • 6 June
Answer

6 May

US style is month/day. That is why you should write the month as a word in international emails.

Exercise 16

7:45 = a quarter ___ eight.

Hint: The next hour is coming.

Answer

to

After 30 minutes: minutes + to + the next hour.

Exercise 17

Tap the wrong word.

There were three hundreds people at the wedding.

Answer

Wrong word: hundreds.

Corrected: There were three hundred people at the wedding.

With a number, hundred stays singular: three hundred people.

Exercise 18

Match the ordinals.

A B 1st twelfth 3rd twenty-first 12th first 21st third Answer

1st — first; 3rd — third; 12th — twelfth; 21st — twenty-first

1, 2, 3 and the numbers ending in them (21, 22, 23) are special; 12 = twelfth.

Exercise 19

Say it aloud — make the difference between thir-TEEN and THIR-ty clear.

Answer

Say: The train leaves from platform thirteen, not thirty

thir-TEEN: stress at the end, long 'ee'. THIR-ty: stress at the start, short ending.

What to do next

Say your phone number, your birthday and last month's electricity bill aloud in English — three times. Then use these numbers in a real call in the Phone and video calls chapter, and listen in Native speed English to hear how words join together when people speak fast.

docs.title: Chapter 33: Phone & video calls
docs.text:
Phone and video calls — talking without seeing a face

In a face-to-face talk, your hands, eyes and smile help you. On the phone there is only your voice — that is why English feels hardest there. The good news is that phone English is very fixed: the same few sentences come up again and again. Memorise those sentences and half the nervousness is gone. This chapter covers everything from answering a call to "You're on mute" — with a 🔊 on every line.

docs.title: 33.1 Answering and making a call
docs.text:
The first ten seconds of a call decide how the rest will go. The other person needs three things at once: who you are, where you are from, and why you called.

Figure 33.1. Every call follows this map — whether you make the call or answer it. The question in the middle ( Are they free? ) decides which path you take.
  • Hello, Priya speaking. Saying your name when you pick up — the clearest way at the office.
  • Good morning, Sharma Traders. How can I help you? When you answer a company phone.
  • Hi, this is Arjun from BlueLeaf Design. On the phone, your name = "This is…", not "I am…".
  • Could I speak to Ms Rao, please? When you want to talk to one particular person.
  • I'm calling about the invoice you sent last week. "I'm calling about…" = the topic you are calling for.
  • Is this a good time to talk? = Can you talk now? A polite question, especially on a mobile.

The first ten seconds

Greeting + name + purpose: "Hi, this is Arjun from BlueLeaf. I'm calling about the invoice." On the phone, always give your name with "This is…" — not "I am Arjun this side".

docs.title: 33.2 Who is calling — asking, holding, taking a message
docs.text:
If you answer the office or home phone and the call is for someone else, you have three jobs: ask the caller's name, ask them to hold, or take a message. For all three there are soft lines in place of a blunt "Who are you?".

You want to English line Listen Ask who is calling May I ask who's calling? Ask them to wait a minute Could you hold on a moment, please? Connect the call I'll put you through. Say the person is not available I'm afraid she's in a meeting right now. Offer to take a message Can I take a message? Ask them to call you back Could you ask her to call me back? Wrong number Sorry, I think you have the wrong number.

A soft question, a clear job

Say "May I ask who's calling?" in place of "Who are you?". And before giving bad news, add "I'm afraid…" — "I'm afraid he's not in today." "I'm afraid" does not mean fear here; it means "I'm sorry to say, but…".

Mini-dialogue — the office reception

Situation: you are at reception. A call comes in for your manager, Ms Rao, but she is in a meeting.

  • You: Good afternoon, Zenith Travels. How can I help you? Greeting + company + an offer to help.
  • Caller: Hi, could I speak to Ms Rao, please? The caller did not give a name — now you have to ask.
  • You: Of course. May I ask who's calling? Not "Who are you?" — this is the soft way.
  • Caller: It's Karan Mehta from Skyline Hotels. On the phone, "It's…" and "This is…" are both correct.
  • You: Thank you, Mr Mehta. I'm afraid she's in a meeting right now. Can I take a message? Bad news with "I'm afraid", and a solution straight away.
  • Caller: Yes, could you ask her to call me back before five? The message: call back before five o'clock.
  • You: Sure. I'll make sure she gets the message. A line that gives reassurance.

docs.title: 33.3 Could not hear, did not understand
docs.text:
Half the problems on the phone are not about English — they are about the network. The fear is that asking again will seem rude — but saying "yes, yes" while guessing costs far more. Spot the problem, and say its line.

Figure 33.2. First spot the problem, then say its line. And for any date, time, number or name — repeat it in your own words to be sure.
  • Sorry, could you repeat that? The most useful line. Even "Sorry?" alone works — let your voice rise.
  • Sorry, I didn't catch your name. "catch" = to hear and take in — I could not hear the name.
  • Sorry, you're breaking up. Can I call you back? = Your voice is cutting out — I will call you again.
  • Could you speak a little more slowly, please? = A little slower, please. Nobody minds.
  • Just to confirm, you said Thursday at three? = Let me make sure: Thursday, 3 o'clock? Misunderstandings stop here.

Ask, do not guess

When you do not understand, do not say "What?" or "Haan?" — say "Sorry, could you repeat that?" And repeat every important date, time and number with "Just to confirm…". A "yes, yes" said while guessing is the most expensive mistake.

docs.title: 33.4 Spelling names and numbers
docs.text:
On the phone B, D, P, V and T sound alike; so do M and N, and F and S. So, with each letter, add a word that is easy to recognise. This list is used all over the world — memorise it, or at least the letters of your own name.

Figure 33.3. Everyday words like B for Bombay also work in India — as long as the word is clear and well known. On an international call, the list above is the safest.
  • My surname is Rawat. That's R for Romeo, A for Alpha, W for Whiskey, A for Alpha, T for Tango. Start the spelling with "That's…" and pause a little after each letter.
  • My number is nine eight two zero one, four five six seven eight. Say the number in groups of 5 + 5, with a pause in between. Nobody can write ten digits in one breath.
  • That's double seven, not one seven. "77" = double seven. Common in India and the UK; Americans say "seven seven".
  • My email is priya dot sharma at gmail dot com. . = dot, @ = at, _ = underscore, - = hyphen or dash, / = slash.

How to spell

Letter + for + word: "S for Sierra, H for Hotel." Say numbers in groups (98201 · 45678), and in an email say dot, at, underscore. Practise the spelling of your own name, surname and email aloud once today.

docs.title: 33.5 Leaving a voicemail
docs.text:
After the beep, many people panic and hang up, or say anything without a pause. A voicemail is a short script — thirty seconds, five parts. If you have planned it, it is easy.

Figure 33.4. Step 4 is the most important — the listener is looking for a pen, so say the number twice.
  • Hi, this is Neha Kapoor from Zenith Travels. Name + company.
  • I'm calling about your booking for Goa next month. The reason for the call — in one line.
  • Could you call me back to confirm the dates? What you want them to do — in clear words.
  • My number is nine eight two zero one, four five six seven eight. Again, nine eight two zero one, four five six seven eight. The number twice, and slowly on purpose.
  • Before six today would be great. Thanks, bye! By when + thanks. That is all — the thirty seconds are up.

The voicemail pattern

Name → reason → what you need → number (twice, slowly) → by when + thanks. No more than thirty seconds. Have the first line ready in your mind before the beep — "Hi, this is…"

docs.title: 33.6 Video call — "You're on mute"
docs.text:
A video call brings three new troubles — mute, camera and screen share. And English has completely ready lines for each, which come up in every meeting. Learn to recognise them as soon as you hear them.

Figure 33.5. The three most common lines in one picture — mic, screen and a frozen video. Understand them the moment you hear them. Situation English line Listen At the start Can everyone hear me OK? Someone's mic is off Sorry, I think you're on mute. Your own mic was off Sorry, I was on mute. You want to show your screen Let me share my screen. Checking they can see it Can you see my screen? The video froze You froze for a second there. Two people spoke at once Sorry, go ahead. Weak internet I'll turn my camera off. My connection is a bit weak.

Four rules for video calls

Mute when you are not speaking. Keep the camera at eye level. Join two minutes early. In a big meeting, say your name before you speak: "This is Ravi — quick question." And if two people start together: "Sorry, go ahead." — let the other person go first.

docs.title: 33.7 Ending the call
docs.text:
If "bye" comes suddenly on the phone, it feels like you hung up on them. Close with three things: what was agreed, the next step, and thanks. Then bye — and wait a moment after bye before you put the phone down.

  • So, just to sum up, you'll send the report by Friday. What was agreed — repeat it in one line.
  • I'll send you an email with the details. The next step — from your side.
  • Is there anything else I can help you with? = Anything more? Use it when you are the one helping.
  • Thanks for your time. Talk to you soon. Bye! Thanks + we'll talk soon + bye.

Mini-dialogue — the end of a call with a vendor

Situation: you talked to the printer company about an order. Now you are wrapping up the call.

  • You: Great. So, just to confirm, the delivery is on Tuesday morning? What was agreed — make sure of it.
  • Vendor: That's right, between nine and eleven. "That's right" = yes, correct.
  • You: Perfect. Could you send me the invoice by email? The next step, from their side.
  • Vendor: Sure, I'll send it this afternoon. Anything else? "Anything else?" — now the signal that the call is ending.
  • You: No, that's everything. Thanks for your help. = That is all. Clear and polite.
  • Vendor: You're welcome. Have a good day! A warm ending.
  • You: You too. Bye! Wait one second after bye, then put the phone down.

docs.title: 33.8 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
You hear these lines every day in India, and people in the country understand them. But on a call with a client, an interview or someone abroad, the same lines sound "translated" at once.

Common phone mistakes

  • Wrong: Hello, I am Rahul this side.
  • Right: Hi, this is Rahul from Infotech.

  • Why: A translation of the Hindi "is taraf se Rahul". On the phone, your name = "This is…" or "It's…"

  • Wrong: Who is speaking? / Who are you?

  • Right: May I ask who's calling?

  • Why: A blunt "Who are you?" sounds very rude. At the office, always use the soft question.

  • Wrong: Am I audible?

  • Right: Can you hear me OK?

  • Why: "Audible" is a correct word, but only Indian English uses it in this question. Everywhere else it is "Can you hear me?"

  • Wrong: Your voice is cutting.

  • Right: You're breaking up. / The line is bad.

  • Why: A translation of "awaaz kat rahi hai". In English a voice "breaks up".

  • Wrong: (Picking up the phone) Tell me.

  • Right: Hi Rahul! How can I help? / Hi, what's up?
  • Why: A translation of "haan, bolo" — in English it sounds like an order. Greeting first, then the question.

docs.title: 33.9 Practice — Phone and video calls
docs.text:
Exercise 1

You are at reception and need to know the caller's name. Which is the most polite line?

  • May I ask who's calling?
  • Who are you?
  • Who is speaking there?
  • Tell your name first.
Answer

May I ask who's calling?

'May I ask…' is a soft question. 'Who are you?' sounds rude and suspicious on the phone.

Exercise 2

The network is bad and the other person's voice keeps breaking. What do you say?

  • Sorry, you're breaking up.
  • Your voice is cutting.
  • Am I audible?
  • What? What?
Answer

Sorry, you're breaking up.

In English a phone voice 'breaks up'. 'Your voice is cutting' is a word-for-word translation from Hindi.

Exercise 3

How do you say '_' in an email address over the phone?

  • underscore
  • dash
  • slash
  • dot
Answer

underscore

_ = underscore, - = hyphen or dash, / = slash, . = dot. If the email goes wrong, the whole job gets stuck.

Exercise 4

Hi, ___ is Arjun from BlueLeaf Design.

Hint: The word for giving your name on the phone — not 'I am'.

Answer

this

On the phone: 'This is Arjun' or 'It's Arjun'. The other person cannot see you, so 'this'.

Exercise 5

Sorry, could you ___ that, please? The line is bad.

Hint: Say it again.

Answer

repeat / say

'Could you repeat that?' — the most useful line when you cannot hear. Better than guessing.

Exercise 6

One word in this video-call line is Indian English — tap it.

Hi everyone, am I audible?

Answer

Wrong word: audible.

Corrected: Hi everyone, can you hear me?

'Am I audible?' is only said in India. Everywhere else: 'Can you hear me?'

Exercise 7

Put the words in the right order — you want to speak to one particular person.

Words: to / Could / speak / Ms / I / Rao / please

Answer

Could I speak to Ms Rao please

Could I + verb… — the most polite pattern for a request.

Exercise 8

Match each line to its meaning.

A B You're on mute. she is not here, do you want to leave a message? I'll put you through. your video got stuck Can I take a message? your mic is off You froze. I am connecting your call Answer

You're on mute. — your mic is off; I'll put you through. — I am connecting your call; Can I take a message? — she is not here, do you want to leave a message?; You froze. — your video got stuck

These four lines are so common that you should understand them the moment you hear them — without translating.

Exercise 9

You could not hear the other person. Say this line.

Answer

Say: Sorry, could you repeat that

Join 'could you' together — 'kud-ju'. Starting with 'Sorry' makes the line softer.

Exercise 10

A colleague is talking in a meeting but there is no sound. Tell them.

Answer

Say: You're on mute

'You're' = 'yor'. Three words, one breath — and smile as you say it.

Exercise 11

You have shared your screen. Now ask.

Answer

Say: Can you see my screen

A yes/no question — the voice rises on 'screen'.

What next?

Today say the spelling of your name, surname and email, with the "for" words, aloud three times. The next time you call customer care, use at least one line from this chapter.

docs.title: Chapter 40: Phrasal verbs
docs.text:
Phrasal verbs — two words, a new meaning

A phrasal verb is a verb + a small word (up, off, out, after…) that together make a completely new meaning. Give = to hand over. Up = in the upward direction. But give up = to stop trying. This is why you can know every word and still not understand English — and it is why learning phrasal verbs is one of the most rewarding things you can do for your vocabulary. Native speakers use them more than big words.

In one line

Remember a phrasal verb as one word — do not try to work out the meaning by adding up the parts. Don't think of "look after" as look + later; just remember it as "take care of".

docs.title: 40.1 The personality of the small word
docs.text:
Every particle (up, off, out…) carries a feeling that shows up in almost every phrasal verb it is part of. Once you understand that feeling, you can start guessing new phrasal verbs on your own.

Figure 40.1. Eight particles, the feeling each one carries, and three common phrasal verbs for each.

docs.title: 40.2 Separable vs inseparable — the real rule
docs.text:
This part causes the most mistakes. The question is: does the object (the thing the action is done to) come before the particle or after it?

Three kinds of phrasal verbs

A. Separable — the object can go in the middle or after: Turn down the offer ✓ · Turn the offer down ✓ B. Inseparable — the object always comes after the particle: Look after the baby ✓ · Look the baby after ✗ C. No object — nothing follows: Please carry on. · Don't give up.

The firm pronoun rule — never forget it

With a separable phrasal verb, when the object is it, him, her, them, us, me, it must go in the middle. There is no choice here. ✓ Turn it down. · ✗ Turn down it. ✓ Pick her up at six. · ✗ Pick up her at six. ✓ Put it off till Monday. · ✗ Put off it till Monday. A pronoun is short and light — it cannot trail behind, so it sits in the middle.
