One more easy clue: if a phrasal verb is already followed by a preposition (get along with, run out of), it is always inseparable.

docs.title: 40.3 By group — eleven essential phrasal verbs
A. With people — relationships and care
docs.text:
Phrasal verb Meaning Type look after take care of Inseparable get along (with) have a good relationship Inseparable bring up raise a child; or mention a topic Separable
  • Can you look after my bag for ten minutes? = Can you watch my bag for ten minutes?
  • I get along with almost everyone on the team. = I have a good relationship with almost everyone on the team.
  • She brought up the budget issue at the end of the call. = She mentioned the budget issue at the end of the call.
  • He was brought up by his grandparents in Nagpur. = His grandparents raised him in Nagpur.

An interview line

"I get along well with people from different teams." Sounds more natural, and more honest, than "I am a good team player".

docs.title: B. Starting, continuing and finishing
docs.text:
Phrasal verb Meaning Type give up stop trying; quit (a habit) Separable / no object carry on continue No object (or "with") run out of have none left (stock) Inseparable
  • Don't give up now — you're two days from finishing. = Don't stop trying now — only two days are left.
  • He gave up sugar in January and hasn't looked back. = He quit sugar in January and has never gone back to it.
  • Sorry to interrupt — please carry on. = Sorry for interrupting — please continue.
  • We've run out of milk again. = We have no milk left, again.

run out of — two mistakes

  • Wrong: The milk run out.
  • Right: We've run out of milk. / The milk has run out.

  • Why: When you say what is missing, "of" is needed. Without "of", only the thing itself can be the subject.

  • Wrong: I am running out from time.

  • Right: I'm running out of time.
  • Why: Always "out of" — never "out from".

docs.title: C. Decisions and work — office phrasal verbs
docs.text:
Phrasal verb Meaning Type put off postpone, delay Separable turn down refuse (an offer, a request); lower the volume Separable sort out solve, fix, organise Separable
  • Let's put the review off until Thursday. = Let's postpone the review until Thursday.
  • She turned down the offer — the pay was good but the city wasn't. = She refused the offer — the salary was good, but she did not like the city.
  • Give me an hour and I'll sort it out. = Give me an hour and I will fix everything.

'I'll sort it out' — pure gold

When something goes wrong at the office, these three words build more trust than anything else. You do not need to say more.

docs.title: D. Chance and learning
docs.text:
Phrasal verb Meaning Type come across find by chance; or give an impression Inseparable pick up lift; collect someone; learn casually Separable
  • I came across an old photo of us while clearing my desk. = I found an old photo of us by chance while clearing my desk.
  • He comes across as shy, but he isn't. = He seems shy, but he is not.
  • Can you pick the kids up at four? = Can you collect the kids at four?
  • She picked up Tamil just by living there. = She learned Tamil simply by living there.

'comes across as' — very useful

A gentle way to give an opinion about someone: "The email comes across as a bit harsh." You are not saying it is bad — only that it seems that way. At work, that difference matters.

docs.title: 40.4 At a glance — the full list
docs.text: Phrasal verb Meaning Separable? With a pronoun give up stop trying / quit Yes give it up look after take care of No look after her pick up lift / collect / learn Yes pick it up put off postpone Yes put it off turn down refuse / lower the volume Yes turn it down come across find by chance / seem No come across it carry on continue No object carry on run out of have none left No run out of it sort out solve Yes sort it out get along (with) have a good relationship No get along with him bring up raise / mention Yes bring it up

docs.title: 40.5 The most common mistakes
docs.text:
Pay attention

  • Wrong: Please turn down it, the music is too loud.
  • Right: Please turn it down, the music is too loud.

  • Why: With a separable phrasal verb, a pronoun (it, him, her, them) must go in the middle.

  • Wrong: She will look the baby after.

  • Right: She will look after the baby.

  • Why: Look after is inseparable — the object never goes in the middle, even a pronoun: look after her.

  • Wrong: I gave up from the exam.

  • Right: I gave up on the exam.

  • Why: To lose hope in something = give up on. There is no "give up from".

  • Wrong: We are running out from seats.

  • Right: We are running out of seats.

  • Why: Always "out of". Remember the pair as if it were one word.

  • Wrong: Let's prepone the meeting to Monday.

  • Right: Let's move the meeting up to Monday.

  • Why: "Prepone" is only understood in India. To make something earlier = move up / bring forward. To make it later = put off / push back.

  • Wrong: I get along my manager very well.

  • Right: I get along with my manager very well.

  • Why: With a person, "with" is needed. Without "with", it means "I am managing".

  • Wrong: He came across very rude.

  • Right: He came across as very rude.
  • Why: When the meaning is "seemed", "as" is needed. Without "as", it means "met by chance".

docs.title: 40.6 A short conversation — seven phrasal verbs together
docs.text:
Read it aloud twice

A: We've run out of chairs, and I've still got forty forms to sort out. B: Don't give up — I'll pick some up from the store room. Should we put the briefing off by an hour? A: Good idea. Can you bring that up with Meera? She gets along with the facilities team. B: Done. You carry on with the forms.

docs.title: 40.7 Practice — Phrasal verbs
docs.text:
Exercise 1

The music is too loud. Which sentence is correct?

  • Please turn it down.
  • Please turn down it.
  • Please turn down.
  • Please it turn down.

Hint: Where does the pronoun go?

Answer

Please turn it down.

Turn down is separable, and the pronoun (it) must go in the middle. 'Turn down it' is never correct.

Exercise 2

Which phrasal verb is inseparable — the object never goes in the middle?

  • look after
  • put off
  • sort out
  • bring up
Answer

look after

Look after is inseparable: look after her ✓, look her after ✗. The other three are separable.

Exercise 3

What does 'He comes across as shy' mean?

  • He seems shy
  • He meets shy people
  • He has become shy
  • He is not shy
Answer

He seems shy

'Come across as' = seem, give an impression. Note that 'as' is needed.

Exercise 4

You want to make a meeting earlier, not later. What do you say?

  • Let's move the meeting up.
  • Let's prepone the meeting.
  • Let's put the meeting off.
  • Let's turn the meeting down.

Hint: 'Prepone' is not understood outside India.

Answer

Let's move the meeting up.

Making it earlier = move up / bring forward. Put off means the opposite (postpone), and turn down means refuse.

Exercise 5

We've run ___ of printer paper again.

Hint: This pair never changes.

Answer

out

Always 'run out of' — 'run out from', or just 'run out' + a thing, is wrong.

Exercise 6

I ___ along with everyone on my team.

Hint: Have a good relationship.

Answer

get

Get along with = have a good relationship. With a person, 'with' is needed.

Exercise 7

She ___ up the budget problem right at the end of the call.

Hint: Mention a topic.

Answer

brought

Bring up has two meanings: raise a child, and mention a topic. Here it is the second one.

Exercise 8

The word order in this sentence is wrong — tap the wrong word.

She will look the baby after this evening.

Answer

Wrong word: after.

Corrected: She will look after the baby this evening.

Look after is inseparable — the object comes after the particle, never in the middle.

Exercise 9

One word is wrong — find it.

I finally gave up from trying to fix the printer.

Answer

Wrong word: from.

Corrected: I finally gave up on trying to fix the printer.

To lose hope = give up on. There is no 'give up from' in English.

Exercise 10

Match each phrasal verb with its meaning.

A B put off solve turn down find by chance sort out postpone come across refuse Answer

put off — postpone; turn down — refuse; sort out — solve; come across — find by chance

All four are used at the office every day. Note: the first three are separable, come across is not.

Exercise 11

Match each particle with its core feeling.

A B up continue off moving together on completely, finished along apart, moving away Answer

up — completely, finished; off — apart, moving away; on — continue; along — moving together

Once you understand the feeling of the particle, half the meaning of a new phrasal verb guesses itself.

Exercise 12

Build the sentence — watch the pronoun.

Words: hour / it / an / out / sort / Give / I / and / me / will

Answer

Give me an hour and I will sort it out

'Sort it out' — the pronoun goes in the middle. 'Sort out it' is wrong.

Exercise 13

Build the sentence.

Words: four / you / Can / pick / kids / at / up / the

Answer

Can you pick the kids up at four

With a separable phrasal verb, a noun can go in the middle or after: 'pick up the kids' is also correct.

Exercise 14

Say this line. The three words of 'sort it out' join together and flow as one.

Answer

Say: Don't worry I will sort it out

This is the most trusted line when something goes wrong at the office. When speaking, 'sort-it-out' comes out like a single wave.

What to do next

Don't memorise all eleven phrasal verbs at once. Pick just three today — sort out, get along with, put off — and use them in sentences from your real life (your work, your people, your names). The sentence that is yours is the one you remember.

docs.title: Chapter 45: Precise adjectives
docs.text:
Choosing the right adjective — give "very" a holiday

Very is the hardest-working and most useless word in English. It tells you nothing — it just raises the volume. When you hear very hot, you cannot tell whether it is 43 degrees or 33. But the moment you hear sweltering, you can feel the sweat. This chapter has just one aim: wherever you say very + adjective, learn to use one precise word — and know where that word fits and where it does not.

In one line

very + adjective means you have not found the right word yet. Find it, and the "very" disappears by itself. One right word is always stronger than two slack words.

docs.title: very upset → distraught
docs.text:
Distraught means so sad or distressed that the person cannot cope — hands shaking, unable to finish a sentence. It is a very heavy word. If you miss a train you are annoyed or upset — not distraught. If a child goes missing, then distraught.

  • She was distraught when she heard about the accident. = She was completely broken when she heard about the accident.

Odd in casual chat

Writing "I'm distraught, the cafe was closed" to a friend on WhatsApp would sound like a joke. There, gutted (casual, disappointed), annoyed or even bummed will do. Using a big word for a small matter turns it into a joke.

docs.title: very hot → sweltering
docs.text:
Sweltering is for heat that is sticky and suffocating — Mumbai in May, or a crowd in a closed room. Remember: it is only for weather and places. Never for tea — tea is scalding or piping hot.

  • It was sweltering on the platform — no fan, no breeze. = The platform was unbearably hot and sticky — no fan, no breeze.

Three different words for heat

sweltering = sticky heat (weather) · scorching = sun that burns the skin · scalding = hot water or tea that can burn you.

docs.title: very rude → boorish
docs.text:
Boorish means coarse, ill-mannered, with no thought for others — talking loudly, interrupting, pushing into a queue. This word is a bit bookish, and is heard less in speech. In writing, in a review, or when writing a complaint about someone, it is very strong. In ordinary conversation, obnoxious or incredibly rude sounds more natural.

  • His boorish behaviour at the dinner embarrassed everyone. = His coarse, rude behaviour at the dinner embarrassed everyone.

docs.title: very big → mammoth
docs.text:
Mammoth (from the ancient woolly elephant) means enormous and hard to handle. It mostly goes with a job, project, task, effort — it speaks about scale more than size.

  • Shifting the whole office in one weekend was a mammoth task. = Moving the whole office in one weekend was a huge job.

Four forms of 'big'

mammoth = a big job or scale · colossal = huge to look at (building, statue) · vast = stretching far (a field, an ocean, a difference) · hefty = heavy (a bill, a fine, a book).

docs.title: very hungry → ravenous
docs.text:
Ravenous means desperate with hunger, ready to eat anything. The good news is that, though heavy, this word also works in casual talk — with humour and exaggeration. Starving is its more common form.

  • We skipped lunch, so by eight we were ravenous. = We missed lunch, so by eight o'clock we were extremely hungry.

docs.title: 45.2 The intensity ladder — where do you stand
docs.text:
Adjectives climb a ladder. The mistake happens when we take the top word and stick it on a bottom-rung situation. Look closely at the picture below — this is what stops overcorrection.

Figure 45.1. Three rungs: mild, ordinary, and strongest. If the matter is small, choose the lower word — otherwise your English sounds fake, not natural.

docs.title: 45.3 The big swap table
docs.text:
The third column is again the most important. Remembering the word is easy; remembering where it belongs is the real skill.

very + … One word When it is fine, when it is not very upset distraught Only for deep shock. For small disappointment it sounds like a joke. very hot (weather) sweltering For heat and places. Never for food or tea. very rude boorish Strong in writing and complaints. In speech obnoxious is natural. very big (a job) mammoth Task, project, effort. For a room or a book use large. very hungry ravenous Also works in casual talk, even as a joke. very tired exhausted Safe everywhere — office, doctor, friends. very cold freezing Very common and perfectly natural. The first choice in daily life. very happy thrilled For good news. Good in email too: "I'm thrilled to…" very scared terrified Works everywhere. Petrified is even stronger. very surprised astonished A little formal. In casual talk stunned. very dirty filthy Everyday. Clothes, a room, hands — all fine. very tasty delicious Everywhere. Mouth-watering is for before you taste it. very boring tedious For work and processes. For a film use dull. very important crucial Strong and clear in both office talk and writing. very interested keen Gold in interviews: "I'm keen to learn." very expensive exorbitant In complaints or reports. In casual talk pricey. very poor (quality) shoddy For work and goods. Not for people. very busy (a place) bustling Market, station, city. For a person use swamped.

docs.title: 45.4 Fourteen more one-word swaps
docs.text: This list is in two parts. You can use the first group from today. The second group is bookish or rare — recognise them when reading, use them occasionally in writing, but be careful in speech. Press 🔊 on every line.

docs.title: Useful every day
docs.text: very + … → one word Example Meaning When to use it very wet → drenched We got drenched walking back from the station. Completely wet, wet enough to wring out. Everywhere, very natural. Soaked is similar. very angry → incensed Residents were incensed by the sudden fare hike. Anger that flares up over something unfair. Strong in news and writing. In speech furious is more common. very happy → jubilant The jubilant crowd danced outside the stadium. Joy that bursts out after a win or a success. For crowds, teams, celebrations. For quiet happiness on your own use delighted. very scared → terror-stricken The terror-stricken passengers ran for the exits. Frozen and numb with terror. Very heavy — an accident, a fire, an attack. In speech terrified is enough. very friendly → affable Our new manager is affable and easy to talk to. Pleasant and easy to talk to. In praise — a reference letter, a review. A little formal; for a friend say really friendly. very empty → desolate After midnight the highway looked desolate. Deserted and bleak — empty and sad. For places (a road, a village, a field). It carries sadness — an empty box is not desolate. elegant → sophisticated She has a sophisticated taste in music. Refined and worldly; or (of a machine) very advanced. Safe everywhere. Elegant = graceful simplicity; sophisticated = knowledge and refinement. talented → consummate He is a consummate professional — always prepared. Completely skilled at what you do, an expert. Only before a noun: a consummate professional / musician. People do not say "He is consummate" on its own.

docs.title: Bookish or rare — recognise them, use with care
docs.text:
very + … → one word Example Meaning When to use it very tired → enervated The long heatwave left everyone enervated. With the strength drained out of you, weakened. Literary and rare. Don't be fooled — it does not mean energized, it means the opposite. In speech say drained. very wise → sagacious Her sagacious advice saved the company. Far-sighted, with deep understanding. Very bookish — it would sound odd in speech. Wise or shrewd is more natural. very rich → opulent They stayed in an opulent palace hotel in Udaipur. Royal, full of wealth and grandeur. For things and lifestyles (a hotel, a wedding, an interior). For a person use wealthy or affluent. very funny → jocular He kept the meeting light with his jocular remarks. Joking, in a light-hearted way. Formal/literary — for a person or a tone. If a joke or a film is very funny, say hilarious. very confused → nonplussed I was nonplussed when he suddenly resigned. So surprised and puzzled that you don't know what to say. True meaning: confused, stumped. But in American speech people also use it to mean "unbothered", the opposite — so it can cause misunderstanding. To be clear, say baffled. very noisy → cacophonous The cacophonous traffic made it hard to think. Harsh, ear-splitting, tuneless noise. A writing word, rare in speech. In daily life say deafening or really loud.

Three traps in this list

enervated ≠ energized — it means drained of energy, not full of it · opulent is for things; a person is wealthy / affluent · jocular describes a person's manner — a joke is hilarious. Using a rare word with the wrong meaning sounds much worse than using a simple word.

docs.title: 45.5 Three rules that save you
docs.text:
a) Never 'very' + the strongest word

Exhausted, freezing, terrified, delicious — these are already at the top. Putting "very" in front is like saying "completely completely". ✗ very exhausted · ✓ utterly exhausted or just exhausted. If you must add force, use 'absolutely', 'utterly', 'completely'.

b) Words for people and for things are different

A place is bustling, a person is swamped. Work is shoddy, a person is careless. Before you pick a word, check what it is used for.

c) One strong word per sentence

✗ It was a sweltering, mammoth, tedious day. — three strong words together, and the effect is zero. ✓ It was a sweltering day, and the work was tedious.

docs.title: 45.6 The mistakes people really make
docs.text:
Pay attention

  • Wrong: The tea was sweltering, I burnt my tongue.
  • Right: The tea was scalding, I burnt my tongue.

  • Why: Sweltering is only for weather and places. For a hot liquid that burns, use scalding.

  • Wrong: I was distraught because the shop was closed.

  • Right: I was annoyed because the shop was closed.

  • Why: Distraught is for deep shock. Using it for a small matter makes you sound over-dramatic.

  • Wrong: He is a very exhausted man today.

  • Right: He is exhausted today.

  • Why: Exhausted is already at the top — "very" is useless. For more force say "utterly exhausted".

  • Wrong: The market was very swamped on Sunday.

  • Right: The market was bustling on Sunday.

  • Why: A person is swamped (buried in work), a place is bustling (full of crowds).

  • Wrong: My room is mammoth dirty.

  • Right: My room is filthy.

  • Why: Mammoth is not an adverb — it cannot take the place of "very". For dirt there is one word: filthy.

  • Wrong: She was very keen interested in the role.

  • Right: She was keen to take on the role.
  • Why: Keen itself means "very interested" — the two do not go together.

docs.title: 45.7 One paragraph, two versions
docs.text:
Before — five 'very'

It was a very hot day. The road was very dirty, the auto driver was very rude, and by the time I reached the office I was very tired. The meeting was very boring, but the news at the end made me very happy.

After — not a single 'very'

It was a sweltering day. The road was filthy, the auto driver was obnoxious, and by the time I reached the office I was exhausted. The meeting was tedious, but the news at the end left me thrilled.

docs.title: 45.8 Practice — Precise adjectives
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Mumbai in May — sticky, suffocating heat. Which word?

  • sweltering
  • scalding
  • piping hot
  • warm

Hint: A special word for weather.

Answer

sweltering

Sweltering = sticky, heavy heat, only for weather and places. Scalding is for hot liquid.

Exercise 2

Which sentence is wrong?

  • I was distraught because my pen stopped working.
  • She was distraught after the accident.
  • He was distraught when his dog went missing.
  • They were distraught at the news.
Answer

I was distraught because my pen stopped working.

Distraught is for deep shock. Saying it about a pen that stopped working is over-dramatic — 'annoyed' is right there.

Exercise 3

Moving the whole office in a single weekend — what kind of job was it?

  • a mammoth task
  • a colossal task
  • a hefty task
  • a vast task
Answer

a mammoth task

Mammoth is for jobs and scale. Colossal is for things that look huge, hefty for a heavy bill or fine, vast for a field that stretches far.

Exercise 4

Why is 'very exhausted' wrong?

  • Exhausted is already the strongest word
  • Exhausted is not an adjective
  • Exhausted is only used in writing
  • -ed words cannot follow 'very'

Hint: How strong is the word already?

Answer

Exhausted is already the strongest word

A word that is already 'at the top' does not need 'very' in front of it. For more force add 'utterly' or 'absolutely'.

Exercise 5

We skipped lunch, so by eight we were ___.

Hint: One word for very hungry.

Answer

ravenous / starving

Ravenous = desperate with hunger. Though heavy, it works in casual talk too.

Exercise 6

The Sunday market was ___ with shoppers.

Hint: A word for places, not for people.

Answer

bustling

A place is bustling (full of crowds), a person is swamped (buried in work).

Exercise 7

One word is in the wrong place — find it.

Careful, the soup is sweltering hot.

Answer

Wrong word: sweltering.

Corrected: Careful, the soup is scalding hot.

Sweltering is only for weather and places. For hot food or drink that burns, use scalding.

Exercise 8

One word is useless — tap it.

I am very freezing in this room.

Answer

Wrong word: very.

Corrected: I am freezing in this room.

Freezing is already at the top, so 'very' is not needed.

Exercise 9

Match each quality with its strongest word.

A B very hungry distraught very rude mammoth very upset ravenous very big a task boorish Answer

very hungry — ravenous; very rude — boorish; very upset — distraught; very big a task — mammoth

Remember: these are all top-of-the-ladder words — don't use them for small matters.

Exercise 10

Match each word with its right use.

A B bustling work — poor quality swamped a price — extremely high shoddy a place — full of crowds exorbitant a person — buried in work Answer

bustling — a place — full of crowds; swamped — a person — buried in work; shoddy — work — poor quality; exorbitant — a price — extremely high

Each strong adjective goes with one kind of thing. Using it on the wrong thing makes the sentence sound odd.

Exercise 11

Build the sentence without 'very'.

Words: tedious / the / was / sweltering / and / meeting / day / a / was / It

Answer

It was a sweltering day and the meeting was tedious

One strong word per sentence, each in its place. Stuffing in three strong words together kills the effect.

Exercise 12

You had no umbrella in the rain — wet enough to wring out your clothes. Which word?

  • drenched
  • desolate
  • opulent
  • affable
Answer

drenched

Drenched = completely wet. It is an everyday, perfectly natural word — it works in any setting.

Exercise 13

'The heat left us enervated.' What does this mean?

  • The heat drained all our strength
  • The heat filled us with energy
  • The heat made us angry
  • The heat made us scared

Hint: The word looks like 'energy', but it is a trap.

Answer

The heat drained all our strength

Enervated = weakened, with no strength left. It is the opposite of 'energized' — and it is a bookish word; in speech 'drained' is better.

Exercise 14

This word is for things or lifestyles, not for people — find it.

My uncle is an opulent businessman from Surat.

Answer

Wrong word: opulent.

Corrected: My uncle is a wealthy businessman from Surat.

Opulent is for a hotel, a wedding, a palace. A rich person is wealthy or affluent.

Exercise 15

When India won the final, the crowd outside was ___.

Hint: very happy — celebration joy, one word.

Answer

jubilant / ecstatic / elated / overjoyed

Jubilant = joy that bursts out after a win, especially for a crowd or a team.

Exercise 16

Match each very + adjective with its one-word form.

A B very angry sagacious very friendly cacophonous very wise incensed very noisy affable Answer

very angry — incensed; very friendly — affable; very wise — sagacious; very noisy — cacophonous

Incensed and affable are comfortable in writing. Sagacious and cacophonous are rare — recognise them, speak them less.

Exercise 17

Say this line. Stress the first part of 'ravenous' — RA-ve-nus.

Answer

Say: We skipped lunch so by eight we were ravenous

It has three parts, but only the first takes stress. The word is not hard to say — it only needs a little practice.

What to do next

A one-week challenge: whenever you are about to say "very", pause for a moment and think — what single word could replace it? If no answer comes, go ahead and say "very"; no harm done. But that one-moment pause is what grows your vocabulary.

docs.title: Chapter 12: Prepositions
docs.text:
Preposition — the words that show relationships

A preposition is a small word that shows the relationship between one thing and another — where it is, when it is, how it happens. In Hindi this job is done by "me, par, se, tak, ke paas", and that is where the biggest confusion starts: one Hindi word can turn into three different prepositions in English.

In one line

A preposition is a word placed before a noun or pronoun to show its relationship with another word in the sentence. A word that comes before a noun and shows how it is related to something else.

  • The book is on the table. = The book is resting on top of the table.
  • She went to school. = School was her destination.
  • The cat is under the chair. = The cat is below the chair.

docs.title: 12.1 Prepositions of place — in one picture
docs.text:
The easiest trick is to remember these not as words but as a picture. Look at the picture below carefully once — and you won't be confused again.

Figure 12.1. Orange ball = the thing being talked about. Box = the thing it is compared to.

From big to small

When giving a place, remember the order — in → on → at: in the country → in the city → on the street → at the address. The bigger the place, the more likely "in"; the more exact the point, the more likely "at".

docs.title: 12.2 Prepositions of time — at, on, in
docs.text:
The same three words are used for time, and the rule is the same: from specific to big.

Preposition When Examples at Exact time at 6 o'clock · at noon · at midnight · at night on Day / date on Monday · on 15 August · on my birthday · on Diwali in Month, year, season, longer periods in July · in 2026 · in winter · in the morning

All three in one sentence: The meeting is at 4 pm on Monday in July.

docs.title: Other time prepositions
docs.text:
Word Meaning Example before earlier than before lunch after later than after school during throughout a period during summer since from a starting point since Monday for how long (duration) for two hours until / till up to a point in time until evening

since vs for — this is caught very often

  • Wrong: I am working here since three years.
  • Right: I have been working here for three years.
  • Why: for = how long (duration) → for three years. since = starting from when (a point) → since 2023.

docs.title: 12.3 The eight types of preposition
docs.text:
Besides place and time, prepositions show other relationships too. Each type answers one question:

Type Question Common words Example 1. Place Where? in, on, at, under, near, behind, beside, between The pen is in the box. 2. Time When? at, on, in, before, after, since, for, during I wake up at six. 3. Direction / Movement Where to? to, into, onto, from, through, across, towards, along She walked into the room. 4. Manner / Instrument How? With what? by, with, in, on He wrote it with a pen. · We went by bus. 5. Agent Who did it (in the passive)? by The poem was written by Tagore. 6. Purpose What for? for, to He went for vegetables. 7. Possession Whose? Who has it? of, with The colour of the sky is blue. · a girl with long hair 8. Source Where from? from, of, out of We get milk from cows.

docs.title: Eight direction words — which way are we going
docs.text:
Prepositions of direction go with verbs of moving, going and coming (go, walk, run, jump, come). Note — here the thing is not still; it is moving.

Word Meaning Example to as far as the destination (towards it, and arriving) She goes to school. into from outside to inside He jumped into the pool. onto from below to on top, onto a surface The cat climbed onto the roof. from the starting point I came from Patna. through passing inside something, from one end to the other The train went through a tunnel. across from one side to the other, over the surface They swam across the river. towards in the direction of (not necessarily arriving) The dog ran towards me. along following the length of something, beside it We walked along the beach.
  • The children ran towards the gate. = They ran in the direction of the gate — we don't know if they got there.
  • There are shops along the road. = The shops stand all the way down the length of the road.

to vs towards — a small difference

to = arriving at the destination — He walked to the station. (he got there) towards = only the direction — He walked towards the station. (he was heading that way) British English uses "towards", American English often uses "toward" — both are correct.

across vs through vs along

across = over a surface, from one side to the other — across the road through = passing inside something — through the forest along = following the length, not crossing — along the river

docs.title: 12.4 Important differences — five pairs that always cause confusion
docs.text:
in vs into

in = position (already inside) — He is in the room. into = movement (from outside to inside) — He walked into the room.

between vs among

between = two things — The pen is between Ram and Shyam. among = more than two — He was sitting among his friends.

beside vs besides

beside = next to — Sit beside me. besides = in addition to — Besides English, I know Hindi.

on vs onto

on = position — The book is on the table. onto = movement — The cat jumped onto the table.

by vs with

by = the doer (agent) or the means (bus, train, email) — The letter was written by Ravi. · I came by train. with = a tool held in the hand — He cut the cake with a knife. Trick: a person or a means of travel → by; a tool in your hand → with. "Written by a pen" is wrong — it is "written with a pen".

docs.title: 12.5 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
The most common preposition mistakes

  • Wrong: Let us discuss about the plan.
  • Right: Let us discuss the plan.

  • Why: No preposition comes after "discuss". Same with enter the room, not "enter into".

  • Wrong: He is good in English.

  • Right: He is good at English.

  • Why: Being skilled at something = good at. Remember: good at maths, good at cricket.

  • Wrong: I will reach at Delhi tomorrow.

  • Right: I will reach Delhi tomorrow.

  • Why: "Reach" is followed directly by the place. But "arrive" takes a preposition: arrive in Delhi.

  • Wrong: She is married with a doctor.

  • Right: She is married to a doctor.

  • Why: Marriage is always "married to".

  • Wrong: I am afraid from dogs.

  • Right: I am afraid of dogs.

  • Why: Fear is always "afraid of".

  • Wrong: Please explain me this.

  • Right: Please explain this to me.
  • Why: After "explain" comes the thing first, then "to" + the person.

docs.title: 12.6 An easy way to remember
docs.text:
Before choosing a preposition, ask yourself one question — the answer tells you which box to take the word from.

Figure 12.2. Question first, then the word: Where? → place, When? → time, Where to? → direction, How / with what? → manner, Why / for what? → purpose.

The most common prepositions — learn these first

of · in · to · for · with · on · at · from · by · about · into · through · over · under · after · before · between · among · during · without · against · around · near · behind · across · along · towards · since · until · like The first ten (of to about) appear on almost every page of English — get those right and you've won half the battle.

docs.title: 12.7 Practice — Prepositions
docs.text:
Exercise 1

The class starts ___ 9 am.

  • at
  • on
  • in
  • for

Hint: Which one is for an exact time?

Answer

at

Use 'at' with an exact time — at 9 am, at noon, at midnight.

Exercise 2

My birthday is ___ December.

  • at
  • on
  • in
  • to
Answer

in

Use 'in' with months — in December, in 2026, in winter.

Exercise 3

The medical store is ___ the bank and the school.

  • between
  • among
  • near
  • beside

Hint: There are two things.

Answer

between

In the middle of two things = between. With more than two it would be 'among'.

Exercise 4

There is one mistake in this sentence — tap that word.

Let us discuss about the budget tomorrow.

Answer

Wrong word: about.

Corrected: Let us discuss the budget tomorrow.

'Discuss' isn't followed by 'about' — the thing comes straight after it.

Exercise 5

Find the wrong word.

She is very good in mathematics.

Answer

Wrong word: in.

Corrected: She is very good at mathematics.

Being skilled in a subject = good at.

Exercise 6

I have been waiting ___ two hours.

Hint: Is it a duration or a point in time?

Answer

for

How long = for. If it were 'since 3 o'clock', that would be a point in time.

Exercise 7

The keys are ___ the table.

Hint: They are lying on top of the table.

Answer

on

On a surface = on.

Exercise 8

The dog ran ___ me, but stopped halfway.

  • towards
  • into
  • onto
  • at

Hint: You need the direction, not arriving.

Answer

towards

'towards' shows only the direction — heading that way, without necessarily arriving. 'to' would suggest it got there.

Exercise 9

We took a long walk ___ the beach. (following its edge)

Hint: Walking beside something long.

Answer

along

Walking beside something long (a road, river, beach) = along. To cross it, it would be 'across'.

Exercise 10

He opened the lock ___ a hairpin.

  • with
  • by
  • from
  • of

Hint: A tool held in the hand.

Answer

with

Use 'with' for a tool (instrument) — with a key, with a knife. 'by' is for the doer (agent) or a means of travel: by Ravi, by bus.

Exercise 11

Which type of preposition answers the question 'Where to?'

  • Direction / Movement
  • Place
  • Time
  • Purpose

Hint: Look at the grid you learned.

Answer

Direction / Movement

Where? = place, When? = time, Where to? = direction (to, into, through, across, towards, along), How? = manner, Why? = purpose.

Exercise 12

Match each preposition to its meaning.

A B into right next to among in addition to beside moving from outside to inside besides in the middle of more than two Answer

into — moving from outside to inside; among — in the middle of more than two; beside — right next to; besides — in addition to

into = movement, among = between more than two, beside = next to, besides = in addition to.

Exercise 13

Put the words in the right order.

Words: stop / shop / The / is / to / bus / the / next

Answer

The shop is next to the bus stop

Subject + verb + prepositional phrase — that is the straightforward English order.

Exercise 14

Now say this line aloud — join 'next to' together.

Answer

Say: The shop is next to the bus stop

When spoken, 'next to' sounds almost like one word — 'nekstu'.

What to do next

Prepositions come from listening, not from memorising. From today, whenever you hear English, notice where the small words fall. You'll see the difference in a week.

docs.title: Chapter 35: Presenting & storytelling
docs.text:
Giving a presentation — beginning, middle, end

A college seminar, a Monday office meeting or a client pitch — standing up and speaking English in front of everyone is the biggest fear. But a good presenter's English is not the most fancy; their structure is the clearest. The listener knows at every moment where we are and where we are going. This chapter gives you that structure — ready-made lines, a story pattern, a way to handle questions, and tips for managing nerves.

docs.title: 35.1 The structure of a presentation — open, signpost, body, close
docs.text:
A listener cannot turn the page back — whatever has gone by is gone. That is why structure in spoken English matters even more than in writing. The old rule is still the most useful: tell them what you will tell them, tell them, then tell them what you told them.

Figure 35.1. Open and Close are short, the Body is long. The small pills in between — signposts — tell the listener that one part has ended and a new one has begun.

The structure

Open → Signpost → Body → Close. Say what you will say, say it, then say what you said. In the Body, no more than three points, and one example with each point. People remember three points; with seven points everyone forgets.

docs.title: 35.2 The opening — the first thirty seconds
docs.text:
In the first thirty seconds the listeners decide whether to look at their phones or at you. Do not waste that time on a "mic check" and "sorry" — go straight to a hook, then introduce yourself.

  • Good morning, everyone. Thanks for being here. Greeting + thanks — a clear, warm start.
  • Let me start with a quick question. How many of you checked your phone in the last ten minutes? Hook: a question. People raise their hands — and wake up.
  • Here's a number that surprised me: we lose three customers every single day. Hook: a surprising number.
  • I'm Neha, and I lead the design team at Brightline. Introduction — one line, that is all. Not your whole resume.
  • Today, I'm going to talk about how we can fix that. Today's topic — "talk about", not "talk on the topic of".
  • I'll take about fifteen minutes, and there'll be time for questions at the end. How long it will take and when questions come — the listener feels relieved.

Hook first, introduction later

Begin with a question, a number, or a one-line story. Never with "Sorry, I'm not a good speaker" or "Am I audible?". If you apologise, the listener thinks you are weak — before you have even spoken.

docs.title: 35.3 Signposting — showing the listeners the way
docs.text:
The listeners are following your voice, not your slides. Signposts are short phrases that work like road signs: now we are here, now we are turning here.

Figure 35.2. The road = your presentation. Without signs the listener gets lost, however good your English is. Purpose Signpost Listen Giving the map I've divided this talk into three parts. The first point Let's start with the problem. Moving on That brings me to my second point. An example Let me give you an example. Linking back As I mentioned earlier, cost is the big issue. Stressing a point The key point here is this. Wrapping up So, to sum up, we need three things.

A sign at every turn

A signpost before every new part: "Moving on…", "That brings me to…", "Let me give you an example.", "To sum up…" Pause for a moment after a signpost — the listener turns with you, then you move on.

docs.title: 35.4 Telling a story — a short arc
docs.text:
People forget numbers and bullet points by evening; a story is remembered for weeks. Every good short story climbs one hill — a calm start, a problem, an attempt, a turn, a result and a lesson.

Figure 35.3. The top of the hill = the turning point, where everything changed. Slow your voice there and pause for a moment.
  • Last year, our app had about ten thousand users. Situation — everything was going well.
  • Then, in March, half of them suddenly stopped using it. Problem — this is where the story comes alive.
  • We tried discounts, new features, even a new logo. Nothing worked. Attempt — pause after "Nothing worked".
  • Then we called twenty users, and we realised the login was too slow. Turning point — "we realised" = we understood it.
  • We fixed the login in two weeks, and people started coming back. Result.
  • What I learnt was simple: ask your users before you guess. Lesson — this is the line people take home.

The story pattern

Situation → Problem → Attempt → Turning point → Result → Lesson. Under a minute, in the past tense, and always with a lesson at the end. A story without a lesson is just an anecdote; the lesson makes it proof of your point.

docs.title: 35.5 The ending — what stays in the mind
docs.text:
We are often weakest at the end — we get tired and say "that's all" and run. But the listener remembers the last line best. Write it out in advance.

  • So, to sum up, we covered three things: the problem, the plan, and the cost. Summary — the three points again, in one line.
  • If you remember just one thing from today, remember this: speed matters more than features. One takeaway — pause after "remember this".
  • So my request is simple: let's run a two-week trial. If you need something — ask for it clearly.
  • Thank you. I'm happy to take any questions. Use this line in place of "That's all from my side".

The ending formula

Summary + one takeaway + thanks. In place of "That's all from my side": "Thank you. I'm happy to take questions." Write the last line in advance and learn it by heart — it will come out even when you are nervous.

docs.title: 35.6 Questions and answers — when you know, and when you do not
docs.text:
People are most afraid of Q&A, because there is no script. But an answer also has a pattern — and the most important thing: if you do not know, do not make it up.

Figure 35.4. Repeating the question has two benefits: everyone has heard the question, and you get three seconds to think.
  • That's a really good question. Only sometimes — if you say it for every question, it will sound hollow.
  • If I understand correctly, you're asking about the timeline. Repeating the question — "if I have understood you right…"
  • I don't have that number with me, but I'll email it to you today. When you do not know — honesty + a promise.
  • Can I come back to that at the end? For when a question comes in the middle and answering now would break your flow.
  • Does that answer your question? A check after the answer — a polite way to close the door.

If you do not know, do not make it up

A bare "I don't know" sounds weak, and a made-up answer is worse. "I don't have that right now, but I'll get back to you by Friday" — honest and strong at once. And if you made the promise, do send the email by Friday.

Mini-dialogue — questions after a presentation

Situation: you proposed a trial of new software. Your manager has two questions — you know the answer to one, and not the other.

  • Manager: How long will the trial take? = How long will the trial run?
  • You: So you're asking about the timeline. It'll take about two weeks. Repeat + a short answer.
  • Manager: And what will it cost us? Now the hard question — you do not have the exact number.
  • You: I don't have the exact figure with me, but I'll email it to you this afternoon. Honesty + a promise, with a time.
  • Manager: That's fine. Thanks, Neha. A far better effect than a made-up number.
  • You: Thank you. Does anyone else have a question? Open the door for the next question.

docs.title: 35.7 Nerves, voice and pace
docs.text:
Everyone gets nervous — even great speakers. The only difference is that prepared people handle it. And the first effect of nerves is on your pace: we start to speak fast.

Figure 35.5. When the heartbeat slows, the voice also becomes slower and deeper. It is a one-minute job.

Five things for nerves

1. Learn the first three lines by heart — if the start goes well, the rest follows. 2. Practise at least three times standing up, aloud — reading in your head is not practice. 3. Three rounds of box breathing before you go. 4. Find two or three smiling faces in the audience and talk to them. 5. If you get stuck on a word, do not fill with "umm" — stay silent for a moment. Silence feels much longer to you than it is.

Pace and stress: whatever feels "slow" to you is exactly right for the listener. A short pause at each comma, a full breath at each full stop, and stress on the important word. Listen:

  • Last year / we lost / our biggest client. // Today / I'll show you / how we won them back. / = a short pause, // = a full breath. Stress the bold words. The voice falls at the end of a statement.

docs.title: 35.8 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
Most of these mistakes have come down from the college seminar — everyone heard them, everyone repeated them. Catch them once, and your presentation will sound more professional at once.

Common presentation mistakes

  • Wrong: Myself Neha and today I will be presenting on the topic of sales.
  • Right: Hi, I'm Neha. Today I'll talk about our sales.

  • Why: "Myself…" is not how you introduce yourself, and "presenting on the topic of" is heavy. Short and direct.

  • Wrong: I will explain about the new process.

  • Right: I'll explain the new process.

  • Why: "Explain" and "discuss" do not take "about". "Talk about" does.

  • Wrong: Any doubts?

  • Right: Any questions?

  • Why: In Indian English "doubt" = question. In the rest of the world "doubt" = disbelief — "Any doubts?" sounds like "does anyone doubt me?"

  • Wrong: That's all from my side.

  • Right: Thank you. I'm happy to take questions.

  • Why: A translation of "meri taraf se itna hi" — it makes the ending flat. End with a summary and a warm thank-you.

  • Wrong: As you can see in this slide…

  • Right: As you can see on this slide…
  • Why: A slide, a screen and a page are all surfaces — on the slide, on the screen, on page 5.

docs.title: 35.9 Practice — Presentations
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Which is the best way to start a presentation?

  • Let me start with a quick question.
  • Sorry, I am not a good speaker.
  • Am I audible to all?
  • Myself Neha, I will present.
Answer

Let me start with a quick question.

Hook first — a question, a number or a story. Starting with an apology or a mic check wastes the first thirty seconds.

Exercise 2

The first point is over and you move to the second. Which is the right signpost?

  • That brings me to my second point.
  • Now second point is coming.
  • Next is the next point.
  • Please see second.
Answer

That brings me to my second point.

'That brings me to…' tells the listener clearly that one part has ended and a new one has begun.

Exercise 3

In Q&A you get a question you do not know the answer to. What is the best reply?

  • I don't have that figure now, but I'll email it to you today.
  • (Guess any number)
  • That question is not relevant.
  • (Stay silent and move to the next slide)
Answer

I don't have that figure now, but I'll email it to you today.

Honesty + a promise. If a made-up answer is caught, trust in the whole presentation is lost.

Exercise 4

So, to sum ___, we need more time and a bigger team.

Hint: The signpost for the ending — 'to wrap up'.

Answer

up

'To sum up' = in short. The most common signpost for an ending.

Exercise 5

Let me give you an ___. Last month, two clients left.

Hint: A sample case.

Answer

example

'Let me give you an example' — an example after a point, so the idea lands on the ground.

Exercise 6

One preposition in this line is wrong — tap it.

As you can see in this slide, sales went up.

Answer

Wrong word: in.

Corrected: As you can see on this slide, sales went up.

A slide is a surface — on the slide, on the screen, on page 5.

Exercise 7

Put the words in order — give the audience the map.

Words: have / I / talk / parts / divided / three / into / this

Answer

I have divided this talk into three parts

Present perfect (have divided) + 'into three parts' — the line for giving a roadmap at the start.

Exercise 8

Match each story line to its part of the arc.

A B Last year, we had ten thousand users. Turning point Then half of them suddenly left. Lesson Then we realised the login was slow. Situation What I learnt was simple: ask first. Problem Answer

Last year, we had ten thousand users. — Situation; Then half of them suddenly left. — Problem; Then we realised the login was slow. — Turning point; What I learnt was simple: ask first. — Lesson

It starts with the situation, the problem brings tension, the turning point is the turn, and the lesson is the end — this is the arc.

Exercise 9

Say the first line of a presentation — with a smile.

Answer

Say: Good morning, everyone. Thanks for being here

A short pause after 'everyone'. Join 'Thanks for' together — 'thanks-fer'.

Exercise 10

Now say a signpost.

Answer

Say: That brings me to my second point

Stress 'second' — so the listener knows a new part has begun.

Exercise 11

The end of a presentation — in place of 'That's all from my side'.

Answer

Say: Thank you. I'm happy to take questions

A full breath after 'Thank you'. Let your voice fall at the end, and keep your eyes on the audience.

What next?

Make a two-minute presentation on your work or studies — one hook, three points, one short story, one ending. Record it on your phone, listen once, and fix just one thing: pace.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Pronouns
docs.text:
Pronoun — the words that take a noun's place

A pronoun is a word that takes the place of a noun, so that you don't have to say the same name again and again. They are small words — I, me, my, he, him, who, this — but mistakes in them are the easiest to hear. "Myself Ravi", "Me and my friend went", "Between you and I" — all three are pronoun mistakes, and all three will be fixed in this chapter.

In one line

A pronoun is a word used in place of a noun. A word that stands in place of a noun is a pronoun. The noun it replaces is called the antecedent.

  • Priya lost her keys, so she called me. "she" = Priya. Say the name once, then use a pronoun — this is natural English.
  • This is mine, and that is yours. = This one belongs to me, and that one belongs to you. The whole idea is said without any noun.

docs.title: 8.1 Personal pronouns — the whole table in one place
docs.text:
This is the most important table. Once you understand its columns, the confusion over I/me, he/him, we/us is finished. A column means where the pronoun sits in the sentence.

Who Subject(the doer) Object(what the action fell on) Possessive adj.(with a noun) Possessive pron.(on its own) Reflexive(oneself) The speaker (main) I me my mine myself The listener (tum / aap) you you your yours yourself / yourselves A boy or man (wo) he him his his himself A girl or woman (wo) she her her hers herself A thing (wo) it it its — itself The speaker and others (hum) we us our ours ourselves Several people (wo log) they them their theirs themselves Figure 8.1. The form of a pronoun is decided by its place — subject before the verb, object after the verb.

docs.title: 8.2 I or me? — a one-second test
docs.text:
The biggest confusion comes when there are two people: "Ravi and I" or "Ravi and me"? You don't need to remember a rule — take the other person out and read it again.

The take-it-out-and-listen test

Ravi and __ went to the market. → take out "Ravi and" → "I went to the market." ✓ ("Me went" sounds wrong) → so it is Ravi and I. She invited Ravi and __. → take out → "She invited me." ✓ ("She invited I" sounds wrong) → so it is Ravi and me. Your ear tells you the answer — just remove the other name from the middle.

Three mistakes you hear every day

  • Wrong: Me and my friend went to the mall.
  • Right: My friend and I went to the mall.

  • Why: Two things: it is the subject, so "I" — and for politeness the other person's name comes first. Test: "Me went" — it sounds wrong.

  • Wrong: Between you and I…

  • Right: Between you and me…

  • Why: "Between" is a preposition, and after a preposition the object list always comes — me, him, her, us, them. People get it wrong because they think "I" sounds more correct.

  • Wrong: He is taller than me. (fine in speech)

  • Right: He is taller than I am. (better in writing)
  • Why: The full sentence is "than I am tall" — so in formal English it is "than I". In speech "than me" is common, but in an exam or an email write "than I am".

docs.title: 8.3 Possessive — the difference between my and mine
docs.text:
There are two lists: one that comes with a noun, and one that stands alone.

With a noun Example On its own Example my This is my pen. mine This pen is mine. your your seat yours The seat is yours. his his bike his The bike is his. her her bag hers The bag is hers. our our house ours The house is ours. their their car theirs The car is theirs.

These never take an apostrophe

its, hers, ours, yours, theirs — adding an apostrophe to these five is always wrong. They are possessive by themselves and don't need an apostrophe to help them. ✗ her's, ✗ our's, ✗ their's, ✗ it's (for the possessive)

docs.title: 8.4 Reflexive pronouns — when the action turns back on the doer
docs.text:
The -self / -selves pronouns are used when the doer and the one the action falls on are the same person.

  • She hurt herself while cooking. The one who got hurt is the one who was working — so herself.
  • I made this cake myself. Here "myself" adds emphasis — nobody else did it, I did. This use is called emphatic (see below).
  • The children behaved themselves at the wedding. There are many children, so -selves.

docs.title: Emphatic pronouns — the same words, a different job
docs.text:
myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves — when these same words come only to add emphasis, they are called emphatic pronouns. They usually come right after a noun or pronoun, or at the end of the sentence. In Hindi they are "khud", "swayam", "apne aap".

  • I myself saw the accident. = I saw it with my own eyes — I didn't hear it from someone.
  • She herself cooked the whole dinner. = She cooked it personally — not a cook.
  • The Principal himself gave us the prizes. = The Principal gave them in person — which made the event feel more important.
Reflexive Emphatic Job turns back on the doer (it is the object) only adds emphasis — "personally, nobody else" If you remove it? the sentence becomes unfinished / wrong the sentence is still complete, only the emphasis goes Position after the verb or a preposition right after the subject, or at the end Example She hurt herself. She herself called me.

Remove-it test — reflexive or emphatic?

He cut himself. → "He cut." is unfinished → reflexive. He himself cut the cake. → "He cut the cake." is complete → emphatic. An emphatic pronoun also never stands alone in the subject's place — "Himself cut the cake" is wrong. The subject first, then the emphasis.

'Myself Ravi' — the best-known Indian English mistake

  • Wrong: Myself Ravi Kumar, from Lucknow.
  • Right: I am Ravi Kumar, from Lucknow.

  • Why: A reflexive pronoun can never be a subject — to stand in front of one, you first need a normal subject (I). "Myself" creeps in from translating the Hindi "main Ravi" word for word. In an interview this is caught within the first three seconds.

  • Wrong: My friend and myself attended the class.

  • Right: My friend and I attended the class.

  • Why: Here you need the subject — I. "Myself" would be used only if I had done something to myself.

  • Wrong: Please send the file to myself.

  • Right: Please send the file to me.
  • Why: After a preposition comes an object pronoun — to me. In an office email "to myself" sounds formal but is wrong.

docs.title: 8.5 Demonstrative pronouns — this, that, these, those
docs.text:
These four words work like a pointing finger — this one, that one.

Near Far One this that Many these those
  • This is my seat, and those are theirs. = This is my seat, and those seats over there belong to them.

Pronoun or adjective?

If a noun comes right after it, it is an adjective — this book. If it stands alone, it is a pronoun — This is good. Identify it by its job, not by the word.

docs.title: 8.6 Relative pronouns — who, whom, which, that, whose
docs.text:
These join two sentences into one, and slip a small piece of information into the middle. Without them English would sound very choppy.

Word Used for Example who a person — subject The man who called is my uncle. whom a person — object (formal) The man whom I met is a doctor. whose belonging to (possession) The boy whose bag was lost is crying. which a thing / an animal The phone which I bought is heavy. that both — for essential information The book that you lent me is great.

who or whom — a small trick

If the answer would be he, use who; if the answer would be him, use whom. Both "him" and "whom" have an "m" — remember that pair. __ called? → He called. → Who called? You met __? → I met him. → Whom did you meet?

docs.title: 8.7 The other types — one line each
docs.text:
Type Words Example Interrogative (questions) who, whom, whose, which, what What is your name? Indefinite (not specific) someone, anyone, everyone, nobody, something, all, few, many Someone is knocking. Reciprocal (one to the other) each other, one another They love each other. Emphatic (emphasis) myself, herself, themselves… (after the subject) I myself checked it. Distributive (one by one) each, either, neither Each of the boys has a bat.

Indefinite pronouns and the verb

everyone, everybody, someone, nobody, each, either, neither — these all look like "many", but in grammar they are singular. ✓ Everyone is ready. ✗ Everyone are ready. ✓ Neither of them knows the answer.

docs.title: 8.8 It must be clear whose place a pronoun takes
docs.text:
A pronoun does its job only when the listener knows whose place it is taking. If there are two people, a pronoun can confuse:

✗

Ravi told Mohan that he had failed. (who failed — Ravi or Mohan?)

✓

Ravi told Mohan, "You have failed." (or) Ravi admitted to Mohan that he himself had failed.

docs.title: 8.9 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
Common Indian-English pronoun mistakes

  • Wrong: Myself Ravi, and myself working in an IT company.
  • Right: I am Ravi, and I work in an IT company.

  • Why: A reflexive pronoun can't be a subject, and the verb was missing too. A safe formula for an introduction: "My name is ___ . I am from ___ . I work as ___ ."

  • Wrong: She is my cousin sister, and she don't speak Hindi.

  • Right: She is my cousin, and she doesn't speak Hindi.

  • Why: "Cousin" is a complete word by itself. And "she" is third person singular, so the helping verb is "does" — she doesn't.

  • Wrong: I am having a car, and it's colour is red.

  • Right: I have a car, and its colour is red.

  • Why: Two mistakes: "have" is not put in the continuous when it means possession, and the possessive "its" takes no apostrophe. "it's" is only the short form of "it is".

  • Wrong: Me and my brother are going to Goa.

  • Right: My brother and I are going to Goa.

  • Why: It is the subject, so you need "I" — "Me am going" sounds wrong, doesn't it? Putting the other name first is politeness.

  • Wrong: Everyone have submitted their forms.

  • Right: Everyone has submitted their forms.

  • Why: "Everyone" looks like many people, but in grammar it is singular — so "has". Using "their" after it is perfectly fine in today's English.

  • Wrong: One of my friend gave I a gift.

  • Right: One of my friends gave me a gift.

  • Why: After "one of" comes a plural noun, and after the verb an object pronoun — me, not I.

  • Wrong: The two brothers help themself.

  • Right: The two brothers help each other.
  • Why: "themself" is not a word. And the meaning has changed too — to help one another you need "each other"; "themselves" would mean each helps his own self.

Three firm rules, that's all

1. Before the verb → I, he, she, we, they. After a verb or preposition → me, him, her, us, them. 2. A -self word never becomes a subject. 3. its, hers, ours, yours, theirs never take an apostrophe.

docs.title: 8.10 Practice — Pronouns
docs.text:
Exercise 1

___ and I went to the station together.

  • My sister
  • Me
  • Myself
  • Mine

Hint: Use the take-it-out-and-listen test.

Answer

My sister

There are two people in the subject, and 'I' is already in the right form. For politeness the other person's name comes first — 'My sister and I'.

Exercise 2

This is a secret between you and ___.

  • me
  • I
  • myself
  • mine

Hint: What part of speech is 'between'?

Answer

me

'Between' is a preposition, and after a preposition the object pronoun always comes — me, him, her, us, them. 'I' sounds more correct but is wrong.

Exercise 3

Which is the correct way to introduce yourself?

  • I am Ravi from Patna.
  • Myself Ravi from Patna.
  • Myself is Ravi from Patna.
  • Me Ravi from Patna.
Answer

I am Ravi from Patna.

The reflexive pronoun 'myself' can't be a subject, and a sentence needs a verb. 'I am ___' has both.

Exercise 4

The girl ___ bag was stolen is in my class.

  • whose
  • who
  • whom
  • which

Hint: Whose bag? — possession.

Answer

whose

'Whose' shows possession — belonging to. 'Who' is for a subject and 'whom' for an object, but here we need to say who owns the bag.

Exercise 5

She cut ___ while chopping onions. (she herself)

Hint: The doer and the one the action fell on are the same person.

Answer

herself

The one who got hurt is the one who was working, so you need a reflexive pronoun — herself. With 'her' it would be some other girl.

Exercise 6

The dog hurt ___ paw. (possessive)

Hint: Does it take an apostrophe or not?

Answer

its

The possessive 'its' takes no apostrophe. 'it's' means 'it is', and 'the dog hurt it is paw' is nonsense.

Exercise 7

Tap the wrong word in this sentence.

Please send the report to myself by evening.

Answer

Wrong word: myself.

Corrected: Please send the report to me by evening.

After the preposition 'to' comes an object pronoun — me. 'Myself' would be used if I were sending something to myself, which is not what is happening here.

Exercise 8

Find the wrong word.

Everyone have finished their homework.

Answer

Wrong word: have.

Corrected: Everyone has finished their homework.

'Everyone' looks like many people but is singular in grammar, so 'has'. Using 'their' after it is fine in today's English.

Exercise 9

One word is wrong.

Me and Rohit watched the match yesterday.

Answer

Wrong word: Me.

Corrected: Rohit and I watched the match yesterday.

A subject needs 'I' — 'Me watched' sounds wrong. Take Rohit out and read it, and your ear will tell you.

Exercise 10

In which sentence is 'herself' an EMPHATIC pronoun?

  • She herself solved the puzzle.
  • She hurt herself.
  • She looked at herself in the mirror.
  • She introduced herself.

Hint: Take it out — is the sentence still complete?

Answer

She herself solved the puzzle.

'She solved the puzzle' is complete even without it — 'herself' was only adding emphasis, so it is emphatic. In the other three the action turns back on her — reflexive.

Exercise 11

The Prime Minister ___ opened the new bridge. (personally, for emphasis)

Hint: Prime Minister — he.

Answer

himself

To add emphasis, put an emphatic pronoun right after the subject — himself. The sentence is complete even without it.

Exercise 12

Match each pronoun to its type.

A B himself relative those indefinite which possessive somebody reflexive theirs demonstrative Answer

himself — reflexive; those — demonstrative; which — relative; somebody — indefinite; theirs — possessive

A reflexive has -self/-selves, a demonstrative points, a relative joins two sentences, an indefinite talks about an unknown person, and a possessive shows ownership.

Exercise 13

Make the sentence in the right order — it has both a subject and an object pronoun.

Words: notebook / She / me / gave / old / her

Answer

She gave me her old notebook

The order is: subject pronoun (She) + verb (gave) + who received it (me) + what was given (her old notebook). The object pronoun always comes after the verb.

Exercise 14

Say this introduction aloud — build the habit of 'I am' instead of 'myself'.

Answer

Say: I am Ravi and I work in Pune

In an interview the first line becomes your identity. Once you are used to starting with 'I am', 'Myself Ravi' will never leave your mouth.

What next?

From today, whenever you feel like saying "myself", stop and think — "do I need I here, or me?" In two days the habit will change. The next chapter is Verb — the heart of the sentence.

docs.title: Chapter 26: Pronunciation
docs.text:
Fix your pronunciation

You do not need to change your accent — there is nothing wrong with an Indian accent. What needs fixing is the six or seven sounds that come out from the wrong place, because those are the sounds that make people misunderstand some words. This chapter gives clear instructions for each sound: where the lips go, where the tongue goes, and whether it is voiced or just air. Read, and do it right away. Reading and then leaving it is useless.

The three-step method — the same for every sound

1. Press 🔊 and listen. 2. Read the instructions and put your mouth in that position — with no voice, just the position. 3. Now make the sound, slowly, five times. Speaking fast is not the goal. Speaking clearly is the goal. Speed comes by itself.

docs.title: 26.1 V and W — the biggest battle
docs.text:
Hindi has only one "व". English has two completely different sounds, and each one uses a different mouth shape. Fix just this one thing and your English will sound clearer at once — because these sounds come up a hundred times a day.

V — how to make it

Put your upper teeth on your lower lip — press lightly, as if you were biting the lip, but very gently. Now make a sound from the throat: vvvvv. The air rubs out between the teeth and the lip. The lips are not round. Put a finger on your throat — you should feel a vibration.

W — how to make it

The teeth do not touch anything. Make both lips round — as if you were about to say "oo", or about to blow out a candle. Then start the sound from that round shape and open your lips as you go: oo-wet. W is a gliding sound, not a rubbing sound.

Figure 26.1. The easiest way to check: look in a mirror. When you say V, your upper teeth should be visible. When you say W, they should not.

docs.title: Minimal pairs — V versus W
docs.text:
Play both, hear the difference, then say them yourself. This is the real test.

V Listen W Listen Meaning vet wet animal doctor / not dry vine wine a climbing plant / an alcoholic drink vest west undershirt / the direction veil whale a face covering / a huge sea animal verse worse a line of poetry / more bad vary wary to change / careful
  • We were very worried about the weather. Three W sounds and one V in the same line. Teeth on the lip for "very", round lips for the other three.
  • The vet gave the dog water. Teeth for "vet" and "gave"; round lips for "water". Both sounds in one sentence.

Careful — the opposite mistake happens too

Many people try so hard to fix V that they use their teeth everywhere — "vater" for "water", "vindow", "ve are". This sounds even stranger than the first mistake. The rule is simple: where the spelling has W, say W. Where it has V, say V.

docs.title: 26.2 TH — two sounds, one position
docs.text:
For TH the tongue has to come out a little — this feels odd to many people, but it is correct. Hindi "थ" and "ध" are both made behind the teeth; English TH is made between the teeth.

TH — step by step

1. Put the thin tip of your tongue just out past your upper front teeth — only 2-3 millimetres, do not let the tongue hang out. 2. Let the teeth touch the tongue lightly. 3. Now blow air out: thhh — this is the think TH (air only). 4. Keep the same position, but now add voice from the throat: dhhh — this is the this TH (vibration).

A sure test

Hold your hand in front of your mouth. Say "think" — you should feel a puff of air. If you do not, you are saying "tink" or "sink", not "think".

TH (air only) Listen What comes out by mistake Listen think sink (basin) three tree (a plant) thin tin (a metal can) thank tank (water tank) mouth mouse (the animal) path pass TH (with vibration) Listen Note this, that, these, those The four most common words, every day — work on these first. the Not "da" — tongue between the teeth, then a light "uh". they, them, their "de, dem, der" is the most common Indian pattern. Put your tongue out. mother, father, brother, other The TH in the middle of a word is the one most often dropped.
  • I think this is the third thing. Four TH sounds in one line — two with air only (think, third, thing) and two with vibration (this, the).
  • My brother and my mother both thanked them. A drill for the TH in the middle of words. Say it slowly — tongue out on every TH.

docs.title: 26.3 P and F — Hindi "फ" sits in the middle
docs.text:
Hindi "फ" is made with both lips. English F is made with the teeth and lip. That is why "coffee" sometimes sounds like "copy", and "phone" sometimes sounds like "pone".

F vs P — the difference in position

P: close both lips completely, hold the air back, then release it suddenly — pop! You feel a push of air. F: upper teeth on the lower lip (exactly like V), but with no voice — just a long, thin stream of air: ffff. The lips do not close, and the air never stops.

P Listen F Listen Meaning pan fan a cooking pan / a ceiling fan pin fin a pin / a fish's fin copy coffee to copy / the drink pool fool a pond or swimming pool / a silly person supper suffer the evening meal / to feel pain or trouble
  • Please put the fan near the phone. Both lips for "please" and "put"; teeth and lip for "fan" and "phone". All three in one line.

docs.title: 26.4 S and SH — how far back the tongue goes
docs.text:
S vs SH

S: the tongue tip is just behind the upper teeth, the lips are wide (like a slight smile). Thin, sharp air: ssss — like a snake. SH: move the tongue back a little (towards the roof of the mouth) and round the lips, pushing them forward. Thick, heavy air: shhh — like asking someone to be quiet.

S Listen SH Listen Meaning sea she the ocean / that woman sip ship a small mouthful of a drink / a big boat save shave to rescue or keep / to cut off hair sort short to arrange in groups / not long seat sheet a place to sit / a bed sheet or sheet of paper

docs.title: 26.5 Z and J — a buzz vs a jerk
docs.text:
/z/ does not exist in Hindi, so we say either "s" or "j". Both are wrong.

Z vs J — one continuous, one sudden

Z: exactly the same position as /s/ — tongue behind the teeth — but add the throat vibration. The sound keeps going: zzzzzz, as long as your breath lasts. J: press the tongue against the roof of the mouth to stop the air, then release it suddenly — there is a jerk. You cannot stretch the sound. Test: you can stretch "zzzz" for 5 seconds. You cannot stretch "j".

Z Listen J / S Listen Note zoo Jew Z can be stretched, J is a jerk buzz bus to hum like a bee / a bus prize price a reward / what something costs — used every day eyes ice what you see with / frozen water rise rice to go up / the grain

A small rule that helps a lot

The plural and third-person "s" is very often /z/, not "s": dogs = dogz, jobs = jobz, plays = playz, comes = comz, is = iz, was = woz. If the sound before it has a throat vibration, the "s" becomes /z/ too.

docs.title: 26.6 "school" — not "iskool"
docs.text:
Hindi words do not start with two consonants, so our tongue adds a small "i" in front to make it easier. The cure is simple, and it works in 5 minutes:

The three-step cure

Step 1: Say just ssssssss for 3 seconds — no vowel. Step 2: Without breaking the breath, add the rest: sssss-kool. Step 3: Slowly make the "sss" shorter: sss-kool → ss-kool → school. The real trick is not to break the breath in the middle. Breath broken = an "i" sneaks in.

Wrong Right Listen iskool school istation station istudy study ispeak / isport speak / sport istreet street iskin skin filim film pleeze / pilees please
  • I study at a school near the station. Three "s" clusters — study, school, station. Not a single "i" added.
  • The street is small but the sky is clear. street, small, sky — all three have joined consonants. Do not break the breath.

docs.title: 26.7 Silent letters — not said at all
docs.text: Word Silent letter Say it like Listen know, knife, knock K no, naif, nok write, wrong W rait, rong thumb, climb, bomb B tham, klaim, bom talk, walk, calm, half L tok, wok, kaam, haaf Wednesday D + the middle e WENZ-day vegetable the middle e VEJ-tuh-bul (three parts, not four) comfortable the middle o KUMF-tuh-bul business the middle i BIZ-nis receipt P ri-SEET island, aisle S AI-land, ail

docs.title: 26.8 Ten words Indian speakers mispronounce most
docs.text:
Fix them once, fix them for life

Word Common mistake Right Listen determine de-ter-MINE di-TER-min develop DEV-lup di-VEL-up jewellery joo-la-REE JOOL-ri mischievous mis-CHEE-vi-us MIS-chi-vus pronunciation pro-NOUN-ciation pruh-nun-si-AY-shun often OFF-ten (strong T) OF-un (T almost silent) salmon SAL-mon SAM-un (silent L) colonel ko-lo-NEL KER-nul schedule SHED-yool / ske-DYOOL SKEJ-ool (US) / SHED-yool (UK) — both are fine February FEB-u-ary FEB-roo-ri

docs.title: 26.9 Today's drill — a one-week plan
docs.text: Day Focus Drill line Mon V / W We were very worried about the weather. Tue TH I think this is the third thing. Wed P / F Please put the fan near the phone. Thu S / SH She sells sheets by the sea. Fri Z The prize is zero rupees. Sat s- clusters I study at a school near the station. Sun All together Three of those women work in a very small school.

docs.title: 26.10 Practice — Pronunciation
docs.text:
Exercise 1

When you say W, where are your teeth?

  • They touch nothing — the lips are round
  • Upper teeth on the lower lip
  • Tongue between the teeth
  • Both lips closed

Hint: What would you see in a mirror?

Answer

They touch nothing — the lips are round

W does not use the teeth. The moment the teeth touch the lip, it turns into V.

Exercise 2

When you say 'think' with your hand in front of your mouth, what should you feel?

  • A puff of air
  • Nothing
  • Only a throat vibration
  • A push from the lips
Answer

A puff of air

For /θ/ the air comes out between the teeth and the tongue. No air = you said 'tink' or 'sink'.

Exercise 3

What is the difference between English F and Hindi 'फ'?

  • F uses teeth on the lip; 'फ' uses both lips
  • There is no difference
  • F puts the tongue between the teeth
  • F has a throat vibration
Answer

F uses teeth on the lip; 'फ' uses both lips

That is why 'coffee' sometimes sounds like 'copy'. F has the same position as V, just with no voice — only air.

Exercise 4

What is the easiest test to tell Z and J apart?

  • You can stretch Z for 5 seconds, but not J
  • J has a throat vibration, Z does not
  • Z has round lips
  • J puts the tongue between the teeth

Hint: You can stretch one sound but not the other.

Answer

You can stretch Z for 5 seconds, but not J

Z is a continuous buzz; J is a jerk where the air stops first.

Exercise 5

What sound is the last 's' of 'dogs' really?

  • /z/ — dogz
  • /s/ — dogs
  • It is silent
  • /sh/
Answer

/z/ — dogz

The sound before it (g) has a throat vibration, so the 's' becomes /z/ too: jobz, playz, comz.

Exercise 6

What is the right way to lose the 'iskool' habit?

  • Stretch 'sss', then add 'kool' without breaking the breath
  • Say 'school' faster
  • Say 'i' first, then drop it
  • Keep the 'k' silent
Answer

Stretch 'sss', then add 'kool' without breaking the breath

A vowel sneaks in the moment the breath breaks. Join it in one breath: sss-kool, then make it shorter.

Exercise 7

One word in this sentence is written with a wrong pronunciation — tap it.

My brother studies in a iskool near my house.

Answer

Wrong word: iskool.

Corrected: My brother studies in a school near my house.

school — starts straight with 's'. The extra 'i' in front is a Hindi habit.

Exercise 8

Find the word that is written wrongly.

We are going to see a filim tonight.

Answer

Wrong word: filim.

Corrected: We are going to see a film tonight.

film — 'l' and 'm' together, with no 'i' in between. Say it slowly: fi-lm.

Exercise 9

Match the minimal pairs to their meanings.

A B vet the number 3 wet a tall plant three animal doctor tree not dry Answer

vet — animal doctor; wet — not dry; three — the number 3; tree — a tall plant

One sound of difference, and the whole meaning changes. That is why these pairs need practice.

Exercise 10

Match each word to how it sounds with its silent letter.

A B know wok thumb ri-seet walk no receipt tham Answer

know — no; thumb — tham; walk — wok; receipt — ri-seet

K, B, L and P — all four are silent. You do not have to say every letter that is written.

Exercise 11

V and W together. Look in the mirror — where should you see the teeth?

Answer

Say: We were very worried about the weather

On 'very', upper teeth on the lower lip. On 'we, were, worried, weather', round lips and no teeth.

Exercise 12

TH drill. Tongue out between the teeth.

Answer

Say: I think this is the third thing

think, third, thing = air only. this, the = throat vibration. The position is the same for both.

Exercise 13

V and F — both use teeth on the lip, but one has voice.

Answer

Say: Very few of my friends have a van

very, have, van have vibration (V). few, friends have air only (F).

Exercise 14

The S and SH difference. Move the tongue back and round the lips for SH.

Answer

Say: She sells sheets by the sea

She, sheets have SH (round lips). sells, sea have S (wide lips, thin air).

Exercise 15

/z/ drill. Put a finger on your throat while you speak.

Answer

Say: The prize is zero rupees

prize, is, zero, rupees — all four have /z/. If you said 'price', the meaning changed.

Exercise 16

Joined consonants — do not add any 'i' at all.

Answer

Say: I study at a school near the station

study, school, station — all start straight with 's'. Join them in one breath.

Exercise 17

The final exam — all the sounds together.

Answer

Say: Three of those women work in a very small school

Three (air TH), those (voiced TH), women (W), very (V), small and school (s- clusters). Say it slowly and say all of it.

What next?
