One thing to remember: even when your sounds are right, if you say every word with equal force, your English will still sound robotic. The next chapter — Rhythm and stress — is the part that gives you the real "fluent" feeling.

docs.title: Chapter 47: Punctuation
docs.text:
Punctuation — small marks, big difference

When we speak, we breathe, pause and raise our voice — and that makes the meaning clear to the listener. In written English, punctuation marks do this job. It is not only about "writing beautifully": move a comma and the meaning changes, and put an apostrophe in the wrong place and the reader notices at once. The good news — there are only a few rules, and they are all in this chapter.

In one line

Punctuation marks tell the reader where to pause, where to stop, and how to read. Punctuation marks are traffic signs for the reader — where to slow down, where to stop, and where there is a question.

docs.title: 47.1 How long to pause — think of a road
docs.text:
First, understand how long each mark makes you pause. This one picture clears up half the confusion.

Figure 47.1. Four marks, four lengths of break. Orange = a light pause, red = a full stop.

docs.title: 47.2 Full stop — the most important and the most ignored
docs.text:
In Hindi we use "।"; in English it is a small dot. A long WhatsApp message with no full stops reads like one long breath, and the reader gets tired.

  • I called him twice. He did not pick up. I will try again tomorrow. Three short sentences — easy to read. Squeezing them into one long sentence makes the message confusing.

A full stop also appears in short forms — Dr. Sharma, Mr. Khan, a.m., p.m., etc. — but in today's English names like UK, USA, NGO, IIT are written without dots.

docs.title: 47.3 Comma — seven real jobs
docs.text:
Job Example In a list I bought rice, dal, oil and sugar. After an opening phrase After the meeting, we went for tea. Joining two complete sentences with and/but/so I called him, but he did not answer. Extra information in the middle My uncle, who lives in Surat, is a tailor. When calling someone Ravi, please close the window. After yes / no Yes, I understand. In dates and addresses She was born on 14 March, 1998, in Kanpur.

A comma changes the meaning

My brother, who lives in Pune, is a doctor. I have only one brother — and he lives in Pune (extra information). My brother who lives in Pune is a doctor. I have several brothers — the one who lives in Pune is a doctor (essential information).

Comma splice — a comma can't join two sentences

  • Wrong: It was raining, we stayed at home.
  • Right: It was raining, so we stayed at home.
  • Why: A comma is not enough to join two complete sentences. Either use a full stop, or bring in a joining word such as and / but / so / because after the comma, or use a semicolon.

docs.title: 47.4 Semicolon and colon — used less, but useful
docs.text: Mark Job Example ; Two complete sentences that are closely linked in meaning The road was blocked; we had to take a longer route. : A list is coming next Bring three things: a pen, a notebook and your ID card. : A reason or explanation is coming next There was one problem: nobody had the keys.

docs.title: 47.5 Apostrophe — two jobs, three mistakes
docs.text:
The apostrophe ( ' ) does only two jobs: it shows whose something is, or it shows a missing letter. The third job — making a plural — it never does.

Figure 47.2. Green = the right place. Red = the mistake you see everywhere, from shop boards to office emails.

docs.title: its vs it's — the costliest confusion
docs.text:
Form Meaning Example it's it is / it has It's raining. · It's been a long day. its belonging to it (possessive) The dog hurt its leg.

A sure test

Wherever you see "it's", read it as "it is". If the sentence still makes sense, the apostrophe is right; if not, you need "its". The same test works for your's/yours, their's/theirs — possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe: yours, hers, ours, theirs, its.

docs.title: 47.6 Capital letters — eight sure situations
docs.text:
Situation Example The first letter of a sentence The bus was late. "I" is always a capital Ravi and I went together. Names of people Anita Sharma Places, countries, rivers, cities Mumbai, India, the Ganga Days, months, festivals Monday, August, Diwali Languages and nationality words Hindi, English, Indian Names of organisations, books and films Delhi University, The Guide Titles when used with a name Dr. Verma, Prime Minister Nehru

Where capitals are NOT used

Seasons (summer, winter), subjects (science, history — unless it is the official name of a subject), directions (north, south), and common nouns (school, bank, doctor — when no particular one is named). I go to school in the summer. ✓ I go to School in the Summer. ✗

docs.title: 47.7 Quotation marks — someone's exact words
docs.text:
When you write someone's words exactly as they were said, you use quotation marks. Remember two things: the first letter of what was said is a capital, and the punctuation inside goes inside the quotes.

  • She said, "I will call you tomorrow." A comma after "said", a capital letter at the start of the speech, and the full stop inside the quotes.
  • "Where are you going?" he asked. When the question comes first, the question mark goes inside the quotes, and "he" is lowercase.

docs.title: 47.8 Question mark and exclamation mark
docs.text:
Mark When Example ? A direct question Have you eaten? . A reported question, or a polite question that is really a request He asked where I lived. · Could you pass the salt. ! Strong feeling — joy, surprise, warning What a match! · Watch out!

One is enough

Thank you so much!!! → Thank you so much! Three exclamation marks do not make the feeling three times stronger — they just look unpolished. In a professional email, use no more than one or two exclamation marks.

docs.title: 47.9 Hyphen and dash
docs.text: Mark Job Example - hyphen Joining two words to make one adjective a well-known singer · a five-year plan - hyphen Number words twenty-one, sixty-five — dash A thought added suddenly He agreed — after an hour of arguing.

docs.title: 47.10 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
Top punctuation mistakes

  • Wrong: Fresh Mango's available here.
  • Right: Fresh mangoes available here.

  • Why: An apostrophe is never used to make a plural. This mistake is seen most on shop boards.

  • Wrong: The company has lost it's way.

  • Right: The company has lost its way.

  • Why: "It is lost it is way" doesn't make sense — so no apostrophe. You need the possessive "its".

  • Wrong: Please send the file , I need it today.

  • Right: Please send the file. I need it today.

  • Why: These are two separate sentences. A comma can't join them — use a full stop (or add "as" / "because").

  • Wrong: Respected Sir ,

  • Right: Dear Sir,

  • Why: No space before a punctuation mark, one space after. Also, in English emails today "Dear Sir" is normal — "Respected Sir" is old-fashioned official language.

  • Wrong: she lives in mumbai and speaks marathi.

  • Right: She lives in Mumbai and speaks Marathi.

  • Why: The first letter of the sentence, the city name and the language name — all three are capitals.

  • Wrong: My brothers bike is new. (about one brother)

  • Right: My brother's bike is new.

  • Why: To show "whose", the apostrophe is necessary. Without it the meaning becomes "my several brothers".

  • Wrong: He said that "he was busy".

  • Right: He said that he was busy.
  • Why: Quotes are not used in a reported sentence with "that". Use quotes only when the words are written exactly as spoken.

Three habits that improve your writing at once

1. One idea in one sentence. If it is getting long, put in a full stop. 2. Before using an apostrophe ask — "whose?" or "which letter is missing?" If neither, no apostrophe. 3. No space before a mark, one space after it.

docs.title: 47.11 Practice — Punctuation
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Which sentence is correct?

  • The cat licked it's paw.
  • The cat licked its paw.
  • The cat licked its' paw.
  • The cat licked it is paw.

Hint: it's = it is. Try the test.

Answer

The cat licked its paw.

Here the meaning is 'the cat's paw' — possessive. 'It is paw' makes no sense, so there is no apostrophe.

Exercise 2

Choose the correct form: the common room of the boys

  • boy's common room
  • boys's common room
  • boys' common room
  • boys common room

Hint: 'boys' already ends in s.

Answer

boys' common room

A plural noun ending in s takes only an apostrophe — boys'. For one boy it would be boy's.

Exercise 3

Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

  • It was late, we went home.
  • It was late we went home.
  • It was late, so we went home.
  • It was late; so we went home.

Hint: Are both parts complete sentences?

Answer

It was late, so we went home.

A comma alone cannot join two complete sentences (a comma splice). You need a joining word like 'so' after the comma, or a full stop.

Exercise 4

Which of these words does NOT need a capital letter?

  • monday
  • diwali
  • summer
  • marathi

Hint: Think about seasons and directions.

Answer

summer

Days (Monday), festivals (Diwali) and languages (Marathi) take capitals, but seasons (summer, winter) are written with a small letter.

Exercise 5

The mark that joins two closely linked complete sentences is called a ___.

Hint: A longer pause than a comma, shorter than a full stop.

Answer

semicolon

A semicolon ( ; ) joins two complete sentences whose meanings are linked — 'The road was blocked; we took another route.'

Exercise 6

The mark that opens a list that follows is called a ___.

Hint: Two dots, one above the other.

Answer

colon

A colon ( : ) opens a list or an explanation — 'Bring three things: a pen, a notebook and your ID.'

Exercise 7

Names of languages, cities and days always begin with a ___ letter.

Hint: Big or small?

Answer

capital

English, Mumbai, Monday — proper names always begin with a capital letter. But seasons and directions take small letters.

Exercise 8

One word in this sentence is written wrongly — tap it.

We sell fresh mango's and bananas.

Answer

Wrong word: mango's.

Corrected: We sell fresh mangoes and bananas.

An apostrophe is never used to make a plural. 'Mangoes' is the correct form.

Exercise 9

Find the wrong word.

My father works in a bank and he speaks english fluently.

Answer

Wrong word: english.

Corrected: My father works in a bank and he speaks English fluently.

The name of a language always begins with a capital letter — English, Hindi, Marathi, Tamil.

Exercise 10

One word is wrong — catch it.

The company changed it's name last year.

Answer

Wrong word: it's.

Corrected: The company changed its name last year.

Here the meaning is 'the company's name'. 'It is name' makes no sense, so the apostrophe has to go — 'its'.

Exercise 11

Put the words in the correct order (the comma will find its own place).

Words: meeting / the / After / for / we / out / tea / went

Answer

After the meeting we went out for tea

In writing there is a comma after the opening phrase — 'After the meeting, we went out for tea.' A phrase at the start is followed by a comma.

Exercise 12

Match each mark with its job.

A B , a list or explanation follows ; whose, or a missing letter : strong feeling ' short pause, lists and phrases ! two linked complete sentences Answer

, — short pause, lists and phrases; ; — two linked complete sentences; : — a list or explanation follows; ' — whose, or a missing letter; ! — strong feeling

The comma is the lightest break, the semicolon joins two sentences, the colon opens what comes next, the apostrophe shows possession or a contraction, and the exclamation mark shows feeling.

Exercise 13

Now say this line aloud — pause lightly where the commas are.

Answer

Say: After the meeting we had tea and then we went home

In writing there would be two commas here — 'After the meeting, we had tea, and then we went home.' When speaking, you pause lightly in the same two places. Punctuation is really a map of your breathing.

What to do next

The best practice: read what you wrote aloud. Wherever you want to take a breath, you need a comma. Wherever the idea is complete, you need a full stop. Your ear knows more than your grammar does — listen to it.

docs.title: Chapter 18: Questions & question tags
docs.text:
Asking questions — the order changes, not the words

In Hindi, asking a question is very easy: "Tum ja rahe ho." and "Tum ja rahe ho?" — the words are the same, only the tone changes. This does not work in English. In English, to make a question you have to change the word order — the helping verb comes in front of the subject. That is why "Where you are going?" sounds wrong to the ear, and "Where are you going?" sounds just right.

In one line

In an English question, the helping verb comes before the subject. The helping verb (am/is/are/was/were/do/does/did/have/has/will/can…) moves in front of the subject. That is the whole rule.

docs.title: 18.1 The question machine — in one picture
docs.text:
Look below: there is a plain statement, and two kinds of questions made from it. Notice how the helping verb jumps in front of the subject.

Figure 18.1. Orange box = the helping verb. It jumps in front of the subject. Pink dotted box = the WH-word, which always sits at the very front.

docs.title: (a) When the sentence already has a helping verb
docs.text:
Just bring it to the front. Nothing needs to be added.

Statement Question She is ready. Is she ready? They were late. Were they late? He has finished. Has he finished? You can swim. Can you swim? It will rain. Will it rain?

docs.title: (b) When there is no helping verb — bring in do / does / did
docs.text:
In the Present Simple and Past Simple the helping verb is hidden. When you make a question, it comes out — and the main verb goes back to V1.

Statement Question Notice You play cricket. Do you play cricket? I/you/we/they → do She plays cricket. Does she play cricket? the -s moved into "does" He went home. Did he go home? the past moved into "did", verb is V1

The tense shows in only one place

Does she plays? ✗ · Does she play? ✓ Did you went? ✗ · Did you go? ✓ do/does/did has already done the tense job — the main verb stays plain.

docs.title: (c) "am / is / are" is a helping verb by itself
docs.text:
• Are you free tomorrow? Are you free tomorrow? — you never say "Do you are free".
  • Is this seat taken? Is anyone sitting here already?

docs.title: 18.3 WH-words — when "yes/no" is not enough
docs.text:
The WH-word always comes first, and after it the order is the same as in a yes/no question: WH + helping + subject + verb.

WH-word What it asks Example What a thing / an action What do you want? Who a person (subject) Who called you? Whom a person (object) Whom did you call? Whose whose it is Whose bag is this? Which which one from given options Which shirt do you like? When time When does the bus leave? Where place Where are you going? Why reason Why did she leave early? How manner / condition How did you come? How much how much (uncountable) How much sugar do we need? How many how many (countable) How many brothers do you have? How long how much time / how long How long have you worked here? How often how many times How often do you exercise? How far how much distance How far is the station?

Questions about the subject — no do/does/did here

If the WH-word itself is the subject (who did it? what happened?), there is no need to change the order — because the subject is already at the front. Who broke the window? "Who did break the window?" is wrong. Who broke the glass — "Who broke". What happened yesterday?

docs.title: 18.4 Question tags — "right?"
docs.text:
In Hindi we add "na?", "hai na?", "theek hai?" at the end of a sentence. English does the same, but the tag is the opposite of the sentence: a negative tag after a positive sentence, and a positive tag after a negative sentence.

Sentence Tag Full form Positive negative You are tired, aren't you? Negative positive She doesn't smoke, does she? Positive, past negative He came late, didn't he? Positive, perfect negative They have left, haven't they? Positive, modal negative You can drive, can't you?

Three steps to make a tag

1. Pick up the helping verb (if there is none, bring in do/does/did). 2. Flip it — positive → negative, negative → positive. 3. Turn the subject into a pronoun — Ravi → he, my sisters → they, this book → it.

docs.title: Four special tags you must remember
docs.text:
Sentence Tag Why I am late, … aren't I? "amn't" does not exist in English Let's go, … shall we? Let's = a suggestion Open the door, … will you? used with an order / request Nobody came, … did they? the pronoun for nobody / everybody is "they" There is a problem, … isn't there? "there" takes the place of the subject

'isn't it?' does not work everywhere

  • Wrong: You are coming tomorrow, isn't it?
  • Right: You are coming tomorrow, aren't you?

  • Why: The helping verb and the pronoun of the tag must come from the sentence. "Isn't it" is only right when the subject is "it" — It is cold, isn't it?

  • Wrong: He finished the work, no?

  • Right: He finished the work, didn't he?
  • Why: Hindi "na?" does not turn directly into "no?" — you have to build the full tag.

docs.title: 18.5 Polite questions — the order goes back to normal
docs.text:
When a question sits inside another sentence (a polite or indirect question), the inner part is written like a normal statement. Many people get this wrong.

Direct question Polite form Where is the station? Could you tell me where the station is? What time does it start? Do you know what time it starts? Why did he leave? I wonder why he left. Can I sit here? Would you mind if I sat here?
  • Could you please tell me where the ticket counter is? Notice: not "where is the ticket counter", but "where the ticket counter is".

docs.title: 18.6 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
Top question mistakes

  • Wrong: Where you are going?
  • Right: Where are you going?

  • Why: The helping verb "are" must come before the subject "you". Copying the Hindi word order is the most common mistake here.

  • Wrong: Why you did not come yesterday?

  • Right: Why didn't you come yesterday?

  • Why: WH + helping + subject + verb. "Didn't" first, "you" after it.

  • Wrong: What is your good name?

  • Right: May I know your name? / What's your name?

  • Why: "Good name" is a word-for-word translation of the Hindi "shubh naam" — English speakers don't say it. To sound polite, "May I know your name?" is best.

  • Wrong: Does she knows the answer?

  • Right: Does she know the answer?

  • Why: "Does" has taken the -s, so the main verb stays without -s.

  • Wrong: Tell me where is the office.

  • Right: Tell me where the office is.

  • Why: Inside an indirect question the order stays normal — the helping verb goes to the back.

  • Wrong: He is your brother, isn't it?

  • Right: He is your brother, isn't he?

  • Why: Take the pronoun from the sentence. The subject is "he", so the tag also has "he".

  • Wrong: What you do?

  • Right: What do you do?
  • Why: This is the standard question for asking someone's job, and "do" appears twice in it — once as the helping verb, once as the main verb.

docs.title: 18.7 A small map
docs.text: Type of question Order Yes / No HELPING + subject + verb + rest? WH (about the object) WH + HELPING + subject + verb? WH (about the subject) WH + verb + rest? (no do/does/did) Question tag Sentence + opposite helping verb + pronoun? Indirect / polite Polite opening + WH + subject + verb

docs.title: 18.8 Practice — Questions and question tags
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Which one is correct?

  • Where you are going?
  • Where are you going?
  • Where you going are?
  • Where going you are?

Hint: Where does the helping verb sit?

Answer

Where are you going?

The order is WH + helping + subject + verb. 'Are' must come before 'you'.

Exercise 2

___ she live in Delhi?

  • Do
  • Does
  • Did
  • Is

Hint: Present Simple, subject 'she'.

Answer

Does

With he/she/it we use 'Does'. And remember — the verb after it has no -s: 'Does she live', not 'lives'.

Exercise 3

You have finished the project, ___ ?

  • isn't it
  • haven't you
  • have you
  • didn't you

Hint: The sentence is positive, so what will the tag be?

Answer

haven't you

Positive sentence → negative tag. The helping verb is 'have' and the subject is 'you', so 'haven't you'.

Exercise 4

___ broke this glass?

  • Who did
  • Whom did
  • Who
  • Who does

Hint: Here the WH-word is itself the subject.

Answer

Who

When the WH-word is the subject, there is no do/does/did — 'Who broke this glass?' The verb follows directly.

Exercise 5

___ you like some tea?

Hint: The polite word for offering.

Answer

Would / would

'Would you like…?' is the polite way to offer something. It sounds more polite than 'Do you want'.

Exercise 6

How ___ brothers do you have?

Hint: Can brothers be counted or not?

Answer

many

Use 'how many' for countable things and 'how much' for uncountable ones. Brothers can be counted.

Exercise 7

Let's start the meeting, ___ we?

Hint: This is a special tag.

Answer

shall

'Let's' always takes the tag 'shall we?' — this one you have to remember.

Exercise 8

There is one mistake in this question — tap the wrong word.

Does your sister knows my address?

Answer

Wrong word: knows.

Corrected: Does your sister know my address?

'Does' has taken the -s into itself, so the main verb stays plain — 'know', not 'knows'.

Exercise 9

Find the wrong word.

Please tell me where is the railway station.

Answer

Wrong word: is.

Corrected: Please tell me where the railway station is.

Inside an indirect question the order stays normal. 'Is' has to move after the subject.

Exercise 10

There is a mistake in the tag — catch it.

She writes poems, isn't she?

Answer

Wrong word: isn't.

Corrected: She writes poems, doesn't she?

The sentence is in the Present Simple, where the hidden helping verb is 'does' — so the tag is 'doesn't she'. 'Isn't' would be right only if the sentence had 'is'.

Exercise 11

Put the words in the correct order to make a question.

Words: been / city / in / have / you / this / long / How / living

Answer

How long have you been living in this city

How long + helping verbs (have been) + subject (you) + main verb (living). 'How long you are living' is the wrong order.

Exercise 12

Match each meaning with the correct WH-word.

A B Asking about distance Whose Asking how many times Which Asking who owns it How much Choosing from given options How far Asking the amount of sugar How often Answer

Asking about distance — How far; Asking how many times — How often; Asking who owns it — Whose; Choosing from given options — Which; Asking the amount of sugar — How much

How far = distance, how often = number of times, whose = who owns it, which = choosing from options, how much = the amount of an uncountable thing.

Exercise 13

Now say this question aloud — your voice should rise at the end.

Answer

Say: Could you please tell me where the bus stop is

This is one of the most useful sentences — at a station, at a shop, anywhere. Remember — 'where the bus stop is', not 'where is the bus stop', because this is an indirect question.

What to do next

From today, whenever you ask a question, pause for one second in your mind, find the helping verb and put it first. At the start this will feel slow — but this one habit makes your English clearer straight away.

docs.title: Chapter 56: Real-world listening
docs.text:
Real-world English — from announcements to interviews

A station announcement is made only once. A newsreader doesn't stop. In a lecture the professor talks for 40 minutes, and in an ad the most important thing is said the fastest. In real-world listening you cannot catch everything — and you don't need to. What you need is a strategy: predict first, then key words, signposts, numbers, and good notes. This chapter has six real formats (all invented, but just like the real thing) — each with its own rules.

docs.title: 56.1 Four listening strategies
docs.text:
An advanced listener doesn't hear faster — they listen smart. They know what to wait for. This cycle works for every format:

Figure 56.1. Predict → Gist → Detail → Check. The cycle turns again with every new recording. The three things in the middle help you at every step.

Predict first, then listen

Before you listen, spend 10 seconds thinking: who is speaking, why, and which words are likely? Announcement = train, platform, minutes. Forecast = degrees, rain, wind. A brain that is already waiting can catch even fast English.

docs.title: Signposts — words that show where the talk is going
docs.text: Signpost What it tells you However / But the opposite is coming — pay attention! On the other hand the other side, a comparison For example an example — the main point has already been made In other words the same point, in simpler words So / As a result a result Finally / To sum up the last point / a summary

docs.title: Numbers and names
docs.text:
• Gate thirteen, not gate thirty. thir-TEEN (stress at the back, long "n") vs THIR-ty (stress at the front). The wrong gate = a missed flight.
  • That's Varghese, V-A-R-G-H-E-S-E. Names are often spelt out. Be sure of the letter sounds: G (jee) vs J (jay), E (ee) vs I (eye).
  • The fourteen thirty train — that's 2:30 p.m. At stations and airports the 24-hour clock is used: fourteen thirty = 2:30 in the afternoon. (See: Number, date, time, paise.)

docs.title: 56.2 How to take notes
docs.text:
For a lecture, interview or news item, never write full sentences in your notes. Only key words, numbers and symbols. Divide the page into three parts:

Figure 56.2. Left: signposts and questions (the structure). Right: facts and numbers. Bottom: a one-line summary — write it after listening. Symbol Meaning ↑ / ↓ rise / fall (prices ↑, temp ↓) → result, leads to, changes into = / ≠ means / is different from b/c · w/ · w/o because · with · without ~ · approx. about, roughly

Notes = words + numbers + symbols

If you write full sentences, you'll miss the next one. Write nouns and numbers, and use ↑ ↓ → in place of verbs. "Fuel costs will be cut by nearly 40%" → fuel cost ↓ ~40%.

docs.title: 56.3 Railway and airport announcements
docs.text:
Announcements always follow the same structure: get your attention → which train/flight → what has changed → what you have to do. The language is very formal (passengers are requested to…), and echoes make words blurry. So predict: the number, the platform/gate, the time.

Phrase Meaning scheduled to depart the planned time of leaving running late by is delayed by this much foot overbridge a bridge for walking over the tracks (FOB) final boarding call the last call to get on the flight proceed to (formal) go to

🎧 Listen to two announcements

  • Railway station — Pune Junction There are two changes — catch both.
  • Airport — final boarding call "immediately" twice — time is running out.
Transcript

Railway: Attention, please. Train number 12794, the Deccan Pearl Express from Pune to Hyderabad, scheduled to depart at 14:30, is running late by approximately 45 minutes. This train will now depart from platform number 6, instead of platform number 2. Passengers are requested to use the foot overbridge to reach platform 6. Please do not cross the railway tracks. We regret the inconvenience caused.

Airport: Good evening, ladies and gentlemen. This is the final boarding call for SkyIndus flight SI 712 to Kochi. Passengers on this flight are requested to proceed immediately to gate number 23, where boarding is about to close. Passenger Shalini Varghese, travelling to Kochi, please report to gate 23 immediately. Thank you.

  • This train will now depart from platform number six, instead of platform number two. The train will now leave from platform 6, not 2. The old information comes after "instead of" — the new number comes first.
  • We regret the inconvenience caused. We are sorry for the trouble. When you hear this line, the announcement is over — no new information is coming.

A common mistake with announcements

  • Wrong: "…platform six, instead of platform two" → I go to platform 2 (I remembered the last number).
  • Right: The new platform = 6. The number after "instead of" is the old one.
  • Why: The ear remembers the last word. So stop and think at words like "instead of / not / no longer": which is the new one and which is the old one?

docs.title: 56.4 The weather forecast
docs.text:
A forecast always has three things: what will happen (rain, sun, wind), when (tonight, by tomorrow morning, the weekend) and how much (degrees, km per hour). At the end there is often a piece of advice. Listen: how much will the temperature fall, and what were the fishermen told?

Phrase Meaning humid damp and sticky air (HYOO-mid) relief is on the way something better is coming soon showers light rain that lasts a short time are advised not to advice: please don't (a warning)

🎧 Listen to the forecast

  • Weather — Mumbai and the Konkan coast For your notes: today → tomorrow → weekend. One or two words for each.
Transcript

Here's the weather for Mumbai and the Konkan coast. After two very hot and humid days, relief is finally on the way. Light showers are expected in the city tonight, and by tomorrow morning the rain will become heavier, especially in the northern suburbs. Temperatures will drop from 34 degrees to around 29. Winds from the south-west may reach 50 km per hour along the coast, so fishermen are advised not to go out to sea until Thursday. However, the weekend looks brighter, with sunshine returning on Saturday. If you're commuting tomorrow, leave a little early and carry an umbrella.

  • Winds may reach fifty kilometres per hour, so fishermen are advised not to go out to sea. The wind could be as fast as 50 km/h, so fishermen are told to stay out of the sea. The reason (strong wind) → "so" → the advice.
  • However, the weekend looks brighter. But the weekend looks better. "However" = the forecast turns the other way — sunshine after the rain.

docs.title: 56.5 A news bulletin
docs.text:
In news, the most important point is in the first sentence (who, what, when) — the other sentences add detail. Each new item starts with "In other news…" or "And finally…". This bulletin is invented — the city and events are made up. Listen: what is the first story about, and what are people unhappy about?

Phrase Meaning announced made something public officially officials say the information comes from authorities (the source) commuter groups organisations of people who travel to work daily rice husk the outer covering of rice grains represent to speak or compete on behalf of a country or group

🎧 Listen to the bulletin (2 stories)

  • Story 1 — electric buses After "However" comes the other side — the criticism.
  • Story 2 — science prize "proud, but not surprised" — the teacher already believed in the children.
Transcript

Good evening, and here are tonight's main stories. The city of Ambarpur will get 200 new electric buses by the end of this year, the transport department announced today. Officials say the buses will cut fuel costs by nearly 40% and reduce air pollution on the busiest routes. However, some commuter groups have asked why ticket prices are not coming down as well. The first 50 buses are expected on the roads in August.

In other news, four students from a government school in Ranchi have won first prize at a national science fair. Their project, a low-cost water filter made from clay and rice husk, costs less than ₹300 to build. The students will now represent India at an international competition next spring. Speaking to reporters, their teacher said she was proud, but not surprised.

  • The buses will cut fuel costs by nearly forty percent. The buses will reduce fuel costs by almost 40%. "nearly" = a little less (38–39%); "over" would mean more. In notes: fuel ↓ ~40%.
  • Some commuter groups have asked why ticket prices are not coming down as well. Some passenger groups are asking why tickets aren't getting cheaper too. News often reports a "complaint" in the form of a question like this.

The first sentence of a news item = the whole story

For the gist, listen carefully to the first sentence of each item — the who, what and when are all there. The other sentences add numbers and opinions. "In other news" = a new topic, a new block in your notes.

docs.title: 56.6 Part of a lecture — the story of the PIN code
docs.text:
A lecture is long, so the lecturer (here the invented Dr Meenakshi Rao) gives the map herself: Today I want to talk about… So, how does it work? For example… Finally… In other words…. These signposts become the headings in your notes (see the template above). Listen: why was the PIN code introduced, and what does the first digit show?

Phrase Meaning stands for is the short form of (an abbreviation) digit a single number symbol (0–9) narrows it down makes the choice smaller and more exact sorting district the area where the post is sorted I'd argue that my opinion, with reasons, is that

🎧 Listen to the lecture (2 parts)

  • Part 1 — why? "Why? Well, …" — the lecturer asks a question and answers it herself. The answer = a key point.
  • Part 2 — how? The last question is a trailer for the next part — write "GPS? → next" in your notes.
Transcript

Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about something you write almost every week, but probably never think about: the PIN code. PIN stands for Postal Index Number, and it was introduced in India in 1972. Before that, letters were often delayed or lost. Why? Well, many towns had similar names, and letters were addressed in many different languages. So the postal department needed a system that worked in numbers, not words.

So, how does it work? A PIN code has six digits, and each part has a job. The first digit tells you the region. For example, 1 covers Delhi and much of the north, while 6 covers Tamil Nadu and Kerala. The second digit narrows it down to a sub-region, and the third shows the sorting district. Finally, the last three digits point to the individual post office. In other words, the number moves from big to small, just like an address. Now, you might ask: do we still need PIN codes in the age of GPS? I'd argue that we do, and here's why.

  • One covers Delhi and much of the north, while six covers Tamil Nadu and Kerala. 1 is for Delhi and much of the north, whereas 6 is for Tamil Nadu and Kerala. Here "while" is not about time; it shows a contrast (whereas).
  • In other words, the number moves from big to small, just like an address. That is, the number goes from large areas to small ones, like an address. "In other words" = a summary — this line should go into your summary.

A mistake in lecture notes

  • Wrong: Notes: "For example, one covers Delhi and much of the north…" (kept writing the full sentence, missed the next point)
  • Right: Notes: "1st = region (eg 1 = N, 6 = TN/KL)"
  • Why: What comes after "For example" is an example, not the main point. Write the example briefly, and make sure you get the main point (first digit = region).

docs.title: 56.7 An interview — questions and answers
docs.text:
In a radio interview the host asks a question and the guest answers with a story. The real answer often comes not at the start but at the end — "That's when I realised…", "For me, that was the moment…". This interview is invented: Kamla ji runs a mobile library in a village. Listen: how did it start, and when did she feel the work was succeeding?

Phrase Meaning by accident without planning, by chance access the ability to reach or get something convincing making someone believe or agree a waste of time time spent without any benefit

🎧 Listen to the interview (2 parts)

  • Part 1 — the beginning Questions end with a "?" — the answer starts right there.
  • Part 2 — difficulties and success "But the bigger challenge…" — the first answer (money) was not the real answer.
Transcript

Host: Kamla ji, thank you for joining us. Your mobile library now visits forty villages. How did it all start?

Kamla: Thank you for having me. Honestly, it started by accident. In 2019, I gave my old books to a school near my village, and within a week, the children had read all of them. They kept asking for more. That's when I realised the problem wasn't interest. It was access.

Host: And the library is actually a bus, isn't it?

Kamla: Yes, an old school bus. We removed the seats, added shelves, and painted it bright yellow, so children can see it coming from far away.

Host: What has been the biggest challenge?

Kamla: Money, of course. Fuel is expensive, and books get damaged. But the bigger challenge was convincing some parents that story books are not a waste of time.

Host: And has that changed?

Kamla: Slowly, yes. Last year, three mothers asked if they could borrow books for themselves. For me, that was the moment I knew it was working.

  • The problem wasn't interest. It was access. The problem was not a lack of interest, but a lack of access to books. Inference: the children wanted to read; they simply had no books.
  • Three mothers asked if they could borrow books for themselves. Three mothers asked to borrow books for themselves. Parents who once thought books were a "waste of time" now want to read — that is the success.

docs.title: 56.8 An advertisement — the language of selling
docs.text:
Listening to an ad is a different skill: you don't just understand, you also have to judge. An ad has questions (Tired of…?), best-of words (quietest), commands (Order today), time pressure (before Sunday) and "everyone is buying" (thousands of families). And the most important part — the terms and conditions — comes last and fastest. This product is invented.

Technique In the ad Effect Rhetorical question Tired of sleepless nights? reminds you of a pain Superlative the quietest fan we have ever made makes it seem the best "up to" save up to 50% a maximum — not guaranteed Urgency Order before Sunday a quick decision Social proof Thousands of families… everyone is buying it

🎧 Listen to the ad

  • Radio ad — CoolNest Breeze fan Count them: how many commands (imperatives) and how many questions?
Transcript

Tired of sleepless summer nights? Meet the new CoolNest Breeze, the quietest ceiling fan we have ever made. Its smart sensor adjusts the speed automatically, so you sleep better and save up to 50% on electricity. Imagine coming home to a cool, calm room every single night. And that's not all! Order before Sunday and get free installation, plus a five-year warranty. Thousands of families have already made the switch. Why wait? Visit your nearest store or order online today. CoolNest Breeze. Feel the difference. Terms and conditions apply. Savings compared with a standard 75-watt fan.

Spot the ad's tricks

  • Wrong: "Save up to 50%" = your bill will be cut in half.
  • Right: "up to 50%" = at most 50% — you might save only 10%.
  • Why: And the fine print says the comparison is with an old 75-watt fan. In a home that already has a new fan, the saving will be even smaller.

Ad = promise + pressure + fine print

In every ad, listen for three things: what is promised (up to?), what pressure is applied (before Sunday), and what is hidden in the last, fastest line. The slowest line sells; the fastest line tells the truth.

docs.title: 56.9 Practice — Real-world English
docs.text:
Exercise 1

What is the best strategy before listening to an announcement?

  • Predict — wait for the number, platform, time
  • Try to write every word
  • Listen only to the last line
  • Close your eyes and think of nothing

Hint: The first step of the cycle.

Answer

Predict — wait for the number, platform, time

Predict → Gist → Detail → Check. A brain that is waiting catches numbers faster.

Exercise 2

Match each signpost to its job.

A B However the same point, in simpler words For example the last point In other words the opposite point Finally an example Answer

However — the opposite point; For example — an example; In other words — the same point, in simpler words; Finally — the last point

Signposts are the map of the talk — start a new block in your notes as soon as you hear them.

Exercise 3

What has changed for the Deccan Pearl Express? (gist)

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Attention, please. Train number one two seven nine four, the Deccan Pearl Express from Pune to Hyderabad, scheduled to depart at fourteen thirty, is running late by approximately forty-five minutes. This train will now depart from platform number six, instead of platform number two.

  • It is late and the platform has changed.
  • It has been cancelled.
  • It will leave early.
  • It now goes to Mumbai.
Answer

It is late and the platform has changed.

Two changes: 'running late by approximately forty-five minutes' and 'platform number six, instead of platform number two'.

Exercise 4

Which platform should passengers go to?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

This train will now depart from platform number six, instead of platform number two. Passengers are requested to use the foot overbridge to reach platform six. Please do not cross the railway tracks.

  • platform 6
  • platform 2
  • platform 4
  • platform 12
Answer

platform 6

After 'instead of' comes the old platform (2). The new one = 6.

Exercise 5

What should Shalini Varghese do?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

This is the final boarding call for SkyIndus flight S I seven one two to Kochi. Passengers on this flight are requested to proceed immediately to gate number twenty-three, where boarding is about to close. Passenger Shalini Varghese, travelling to Kochi, please report to gate twenty-three immediately.

  • Go to gate 23 immediately.
  • Go to gate 33 after dinner.
  • Collect her bag at gate 13.
  • Wait for the next flight.
Answer

Go to gate 23 immediately.

'please report to gate twenty-three immediately' — final boarding call = the last chance.

Exercise 6

What will the temperature drop to?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Light showers are expected in the city tonight, and by tomorrow morning the rain will become heavier, especially in the northern suburbs. Temperatures will drop from thirty-four degrees to around twenty-nine.

  • around 29 degrees
  • 34 degrees
  • around 24 degrees
  • 39 degrees
Answer

around 29 degrees

'from thirty-four … to around twenty-nine' — from = now, to = the new value.

Exercise 7

Why are fishermen told not to go out to sea?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Winds from the south-west may reach fifty kilometres per hour along the coast, so fishermen are advised not to go out to sea until Thursday. However, the weekend looks brighter, with sunshine returning on Saturday.

  • because of strong winds
  • because of very hot weather
  • because it is a holiday
  • because of fog
Answer

because of strong winds

The reason comes before 'so': winds up to 50 km/h. 'are advised not to' = a warning.

Exercise 8

What is the first news story mainly about?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Good evening, and here are tonight's main stories. The city of Ambarpur will get two hundred new electric buses by the end of this year, the transport department announced today. Officials say the buses will cut fuel costs by nearly forty percent.

  • new electric buses for a city
  • higher bus ticket prices
  • a new metro line
  • a fuel shortage
Answer

new electric buses for a city

The first sentence of a news item = the whole story: 200 electric buses for Ambarpur.

Exercise 9

What are some commuter groups unhappy about?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Officials say the buses will cut fuel costs by nearly forty percent and reduce air pollution on the busiest routes. However, some commuter groups have asked why ticket prices are not coming down as well.

  • Ticket prices are not going down.
  • The buses are too noisy.
  • There are too few routes.
  • The buses are arriving late.
Answer

Ticket prices are not going down.

The criticism after 'However': the government's fuel costs fall, but tickets don't get cheaper.

Exercise 10

How much does the students' water filter cost to build?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Their project, a low-cost water filter made from clay and rice husk, costs less than three hundred rupees to build.

  • less than 300 rupees
  • about 3,000 rupees
  • exactly 30 rupees
  • more than 300 rupees
Answer

less than 300 rupees

'less than three hundred rupees' — 'less than' is part of the answer too.

Exercise 11

Why were letters often delayed before 1972?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Before that, letters were often delayed or lost. Why? Well, many towns had similar names, and letters were addressed in many different languages.

  • Towns had similar names and addresses were in many languages.
  • There were not enough postmen.
  • Trains were very slow.
  • Stamps were too expensive.
Answer

Towns had similar names and addresses were in many languages.

The lecturer asked 'Why? Well, …' herself and gave two reasons.

Exercise 12

What does the first digit of a PIN code show?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

A PIN code has six digits, and each part has a job. The first digit tells you the region. For example, one covers Delhi and much of the north, while six covers Tamil Nadu and Kerala.

  • the region
  • the post office
  • the sorting district
  • the state capital
Answer

the region

'The first digit tells you the region.' What follows 'For example' is only an example.

Exercise 13

What does the lecturer do after saying 'In other words'?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Finally, the last three digits point to the individual post office. In other words, the number moves from big to small, just like an address.

  • She repeats the idea in a simpler way.
  • She gives the opposite view.
  • She starts a new topic.
  • She asks the students a question.
Answer

She repeats the idea in a simpler way.

'In other words' = the same point in simpler words — the best line for a summary.

Exercise 14

What does Kamla mean by 'the problem wasn't interest, it was access'?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

I gave my old books to a school near my village, and within a week, the children had read all of them. They kept asking for more. That's when I realised the problem wasn't interest. It was access.

  • The children wanted to read but had no books.
  • The children were not interested in books.
  • The school did not allow books.
  • The books were too difficult.
Answer

The children wanted to read but had no books.

They read all the books in a week and asked for more — there was interest; there were no books.

Exercise 15

Why did they paint the bus bright yellow?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Yes, an old school bus. We removed the seats, added shelves, and painted it bright yellow, so children can see it coming from far away.

  • so children can see it from far away
  • because yellow paint is cheap
  • because it was a school bus
  • to protect the books from the sun
Answer

so children can see it from far away

'so children can see it coming from far away' — the purpose comes after 'so'.

Exercise 16

What does 'save up to fifty percent' really promise?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Its smart sensor adjusts the speed automatically, so you sleep better and save up to fifty percent on electricity.

  • You may save less than 50%.
  • You will always save exactly 50%.
  • You will save more than 50%.
  • The fan costs 50% less.
Answer

You may save less than 50%.

'up to' = a maximum. The real saving may be less — the oldest trick in advertising.

Exercise 17

Listen and write.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

Passengers are requested to use the foot overbridge.

'are requested to' = a formal 'please'. 'overbridge' is one word.

Exercise 18

Listen and write (you may write the numbers in digits).

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

Temperatures will drop from thirty-four degrees to around twenty-nine.

thir-ty-FOUR and twen-ty-NINE — the -ty numbers; and the 'from … to' pattern.

Exercise 19

Listen and write.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

The problem wasn't interest. It was access.

The 't' in 'wasn't' is soft — but it reverses the whole meaning.

Exercise 20

Speak slowly and clearly, like a station announcer.

Answer

Say: Please do not cross the railway tracks

In announcements 'do not' is said in full (not don't) for emphasis. Say the -s of 'tracks' clearly.

Next step

This week, listen to one real recording every day — a station announcement, a radio weather report, or a short podcast — and make five lines of notes using the template above. If you are preparing for an exam, see IELTS, TOEFL and your level.

docs.title: Chapter 22: Reported speech
docs.text:
Reporting what someone said — reported speech

We do this all day: "Mummy said to eat your food", "The boss said to come tomorrow". In English this is called reported speech, and it has one big rule — the tense steps one step back. Whatever someone said is now old news, so its tense also goes down one step of the ladder. In this chapter you will see that ladder in a picture.

In one line

If the reporting verb is in the past (said, told, asked), move the tense inside one step back. If the outer verb is in the past, the inner tense steps back — present → past, past → past perfect.

docs.title: 22.1 Five things change
docs.text: # What changes Direct Reported 1 The quotation marks and comma go; "that" comes in He said, "I am tired." He said that he was tired. 2 Pronouns change "I am tired." … he was tired. 3 The tense steps one back "I am tired." … he was tired. 4 Time words change "I will come tomorrow." … he would come the next day. 5 Place words change "Sit here." … to sit there.

docs.title: 22.2 The tense ladder — one step back
docs.text:
This is the heart of the whole chapter. On the left is the tense the speaker used, and on the right is the tense you use when reporting. Notice — everything steps down by one.

Figure 22.1. Green box = what was said. Orange box = the form used when reporting. Past Perfect is the last step of the ladder — there is no room to go back any further.

docs.title: 22.3 How pronouns change
docs.text:
The rule is easy: a pronoun changes according to the view of the person reporting. "I" belonged to the speaker — now it becomes "he" or "she".

Direct Reported Example I, me, my he/she, him/her, his/her He said, "I lost my pen." → He said he had lost his pen. we, us, our they, them, their They said, "We are busy." → They said they were busy. you, your me/him/her (depending on who it was said to) She told me, "You are late." → She told me I was late. he, she, it, they stay the same She said, "He is away." → She said he was away.

docs.title: 22.4 Time and place words
docs.text:
Direct Reported now then today that day tonight that night tomorrow the next day / the following day yesterday the previous day / the day before last night the previous night next week the following week two days ago two days before here there this / these that / those come go
  • Direct: She said, "I am going to Delhi tomorrow."
  • Reported: She said that she was going to Delhi the next day. Three changes: I → she, am → was, tomorrow → the next day.

docs.title: 22.5 When the tense does not change
docs.text:
The tense does not always step back. There are four situations where it stays as it is — and it is very important to know them, otherwise your English sounds artificial.

Situation Example The reporting verb is in the present He says that he is busy. Something that is always true The teacher said that the sun rises in the east. It is still true now She said she works in a bank. (she still does) It is already Past Perfect He said, "I had finished." → He said he had finished.

docs.title: 22.6 Reporting questions
docs.text: Two things happen here: "that" is not used, and the order goes back to normal — the helping verb moves behind the subject. The question mark disappears too.

docs.title: WH questions — the WH-word is the connector
docs.text: Direct Reported He asked, "Where do you live?" He asked where I lived. She asked, "What is your name?" She asked what my name was. They asked, "Why did he leave?" They asked why he had left.

docs.title: Yes/No questions — add "if" or "whether"
docs.text:
Direct Reported He asked, "Are you ready?" He asked if I was ready. She asked, "Did you call him?" She asked whether I had called him. Mother asked, "Have you eaten?" Mother asked if I had eaten.

Once reported, a question is no longer a question

  • Wrong: He asked me where was I going?
  • Right: He asked me where I was going.
  • Why: A reported question is now a statement. So the order is normal, and it ends with a full stop — not a question mark.

docs.title: 22.7 Orders, requests and advice
docs.text:
There is one trick for all of these: "to" + V1. For a negative, use "not to" + V1. And the reporting verb changes according to the tone of what was said.

Type Reporting verb Direct Reported Order ordered / told "Stand up!" He ordered me to stand up. Request requested / asked "Please help me." She requested me to help her. Advice advised "You should rest." He advised me to rest. Forbidding forbade / told… not to "Don't touch it." She told me not to touch it. Suggestion suggested "Let's go out." He suggested going out. Wish / blessing prayed / wished "May you succeed!" He wished that I might succeed.

docs.title: 22.8 say, tell, ask — three words, three habits
docs.text:
These three words cause the biggest reported-speech mistake in Indian English. The only difference is which one takes a person directly.

Verb How it works Correct say a person does not follow directly — "to" is needed He said to me… / He said that… tell a person follows directly — no "to" He told me that… ask a person follows directly He asked me if…

'She said me' — the most common mistake

  • Wrong: She said me that the shop was closed.
  • Right: She told me that the shop was closed.

  • Why: A person does not follow "say" directly. You have two options: She told me… or She said to me…. The easy way — whenever you want to name the person, always use tell.

  • Wrong: He told that he would come.

  • Right: He said that he would come. / He told me that he would come.
  • Why: After "tell" you must say who was told. "Told that" on its own is unfinished.

docs.title: 22.9 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
Top reported-speech mistakes

  • Wrong: She said that she is coming tomorrow.
  • Right: She said that she was coming the next day.

  • Why: "Said" is in the past, so the inner tense steps one back — is → was, and tomorrow → the next day.

  • Wrong: He asked me that where I live.

  • Right: He asked me where I lived.

  • Why: "That" is not used in questions. The WH-word does the joining itself.

  • Wrong: My father told me that study hard.

  • Right: My father told me to study hard.

  • Why: For orders and advice use "to + V1" — not "that".

  • Wrong: She asked me do I know the way.

  • Right: She asked me if I knew the way.

  • Why: For yes/no questions use "if" or "whether", with normal order. "Do/does/did" disappear.

  • Wrong: He said that he will help me.

  • Right: He said that he would help me.

  • Why: will → would. In the same way can → could, may → might, must → had to.

  • Wrong: The teacher said that water boiled at 100 degrees.

  • Right: The teacher said that water boils at 100 degrees.

  • Why: For something that is always true, the tense does not step back.

  • Wrong: He told me that don't go there.

  • Right: He told me not to go there.
  • Why: To forbid, use "not to + V1" — a short, direct form.

Four steps, every time

1. Identify the type — statement, question, or order? 2. Choose the right connector — that / if-whether / WH-word / to. 3. Change the pronouns. 4. Step the tense one back, and change the time and place words.

docs.title: 22.10 Practice — Reported speech
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Report this: She said, "I am very tired."

  • She said that she is very tired.
  • She said that she was very tired.
  • She said that I was very tired.
  • She told that she was very tired.

Hint: 'Said' is in the past, so what happens inside?

Answer

She said that she was very tired.

Two changes: the pronoun I → she, and the tense am → was. 'Said' is in the past, so the tense steps one back.

Exercise 2

Report this: He asked, "Where is the bank?"

  • He asked where is the bank.
  • He asked that where was the bank.
  • He asked where the bank was.
  • He asked where was the bank?

Hint: When a question is reported, the order goes back to normal.

Answer

He asked where the bank was.

A reported question is now a statement — so 'the bank was', with a full stop at the end. No 'that' either.

Exercise 3

Report this: Mother said, "Don't play in the sun."

  • Mother said that don't play in the sun.
  • Mother told not to play in the sun.
  • Mother told me not to play in the sun.
  • Mother said me not to play in the sun.

Hint: It is a prohibition.

Answer

Mother told me not to play in the sun.

To forbid, use 'not to + V1'. And after 'tell' you must say who was told, so 'told me'.

Exercise 4

In which sentence will the tense NOT step back?

  • He said, "I am ill."
  • She said, "The earth moves round the sun."
  • They said, "We are leaving."
  • He said, "I will call you."

Hint: Which one is always true?

Answer

She said, "The earth moves round the sun."

For something that is always true (a universal truth), the tense stays as it is — 'She said that the earth moves round the sun.'

Exercise 5

He said, "I will come tomorrow." → He said that he ___ come the next day.

Hint: What is the reported form of will?

Answer

would

will → would. In the same way can → could, may → might, shall → should.

Exercise 6

She asked, "Are you coming?" → She asked ___ I was coming.

Hint: The connector for a yes/no question.

Answer

if / whether

When reporting a yes/no question we use 'if' or 'whether'. Both are correct — 'whether' is a little more formal.

Exercise 7

Ravi ___ me that the train was late.

Hint: A person ('me') follows directly — so which verb?

Answer

told

A person follows 'tell' directly — told me. 'Said me' is wrong; 'said to me' is fine.

Exercise 8

There is one mistake in this sentence — tap the wrong word.

My sister said me that she would help.

Answer

Wrong word: said.

Corrected: My sister told me that she would help.

A person does not follow 'say' directly. Say 'told me', or 'said to me'.

Exercise 9

Find the wrong word.

He asked me that where I was going.

Answer

Wrong word: that.

Corrected: He asked me where I was going.

'That' is not used when reporting a question. The WH-word joins the two parts by itself.

Exercise 10

One word is wrong — catch it.

The doctor advised him that rest for a week.

Answer

Wrong word: that.

Corrected: The doctor advised him to rest for a week.

Advice and orders take 'to + V1' — 'to rest'. 'That' does not work here.

Exercise 11

Put the words in the correct order to make a reported sentence.

Words: she / work / finished / me / that / her / told / She / had

Answer

She told me that she had finished her work

After 'tell' comes the person (me), then 'that', then the tense steps one back — 'has finished' becomes 'had finished'.

Exercise 12

Match each direct form with its reported form.

A B I write he would write I wrote he could write I will write he had to write I can write he wrote I must write he had written Answer

I write — he wrote; I wrote — he had written; I will write — he would write; I can write — he could write; I must write — he had to write

Present → past, past → past perfect, will → would, can → could, must → had to. Every step of the ladder goes down in the same direction.

Exercise 13

Now say this line aloud — reported speech you will use every day.

Answer

Say: He told me that he would call me the next day

Three things to get right together: 'told me' (not said me), 'would' (not will), and 'the next day' (not tomorrow). Saying it aloud helps all three come together.

What to do next

Tonight, before you sleep, report three things from your day to someone — "My boss told me that…", "My friend asked me if…", "Mummy told me to…". Three sentences a day. In a week the ladder will settle in your head by itself.

docs.title: Chapter 27: Rhythm & stress
docs.text:
Rhythm and stress — which word to say strongly

All your sounds can be right, your grammar can be right, and your English can still sound robotic. There is only one reason: we say every word with the same force. English is an uneven language — some words shine, and the rest step back, almost disappearing. People who work on this one thing start sounding "fluent" at once — even if their vocabulary is exactly the same as before.

In one line

Hindi is a more even-beat language — each syllable gets almost the same time. English is a stress-beat language — the stressed parts are long and strong, and the other parts are weak and short. That is why English spoken with a Hindi beat sounds "flat".

docs.title: 27.1 Word stress — in one word, only one part shines
docs.text:
Every big English word has one syllable that is stressed: you say it longer, louder, and a little higher in pitch. The other syllables are weak and short. If you stress the wrong syllable, the word can become impossible to understand.

Figure 27.1. The tall orange bar = the stressed syllable. Notice — when the word changes its form, the stress moves to a new place . Remember: one word = one shining syllable.
  • He is a photographer, and this is his photograph. Both words in one line — you can clearly hear the difference in where the stress falls.

docs.title: When the stress changes, the meaning changes
docs.text:
Many English words are both a noun and a verb, and the only difference is the stress: in the noun the stress is on the first syllable, in the verb on the second syllable.

Word Noun (a thing) Verb (an action) Listen record RE-cord — a written account re-CORD — to save on a device present PRE-sent — a gift pre-SENT — to show or give increase IN-crease — a rise in-CREASE — to make bigger object OB-ject — a thing ob-JECT — to disagree contract CON-tract — a written agreement con-TRACT — to shrink conduct CON-duct — behaviour con-DUCT — to carry out

A small memory map

Noun = stress at the front. Verb = stress at the back. Noun comes first, verb comes later — as if the word itself kept the same order.

docs.title: Some reliable patterns
docs.text:
Ending Where the stress goes Examples Listen -tion / -sion the syllable just before it inforMAtion, deciSIon, educAtion -ity just before it aBIlity, opporTUnity, uNIversity -ic just before it ecoNOmic, fanTAStic, speCIfic -ate (verb) the third syllable from the end CElebrate, EDUcate, comMUnicate -ee the last syllable employEE, trainEE, agrEE Two-syllable nouns almost always the first syllable TAble, WINdow, DOCtor, TEAcher

The stress we get wrong most often

  • Wrong: de-VE-lop-MENT — two stresses
  • Right: de-VEL-op-ment — only one stress

  • Why: A word has only one stress. Stressing two places makes it sound like two words.

  • Wrong: hos-pi-TAL

  • Right: HOS-pi-tal

  • Why: The last syllable becomes a weak "tul". We say the full "TAL" instead.

  • Wrong: in-ter-es-TING

  • Right: IN-tres-ting — three syllables, not four

  • Why: The middle "e" almost disappears. That is the work of the schwa.

  • Wrong: com-FOR-TA-BLE (four equal syllables)

  • Right: KUMF-tuh-bul
  • Why: English speakers swallow the middle "or". Three syllables, stress on the first.

docs.title: 27.2 Sentence stress — which words shine in a sentence
docs.text:
This is the real secret. In a whole sentence, only the words that carry the meaning are said strongly. The other words — the ones that only join the sentence together — are said weakly, quickly, almost swallowed.

Content words — strong Function words — weak Which Nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs, question words a/an/the, is/am/are/was, can/will/have (helpers), of/to/in/at, and/but, I/he/she/it, that/this (when not stressed) Why These carry the real information. Cut them out and the message is lost. These are only the frame. Cut them out and the message is still clear. Test If you had to send a telegram, which words would you keep? Those are the content words. Figure 27.2. First say only the orange words — WANT · BUY · TICKet · MORNing · TRAIN . Then fill in the small words in between, without force. The whole sentence falls into the right beat by itself.
  • I want to buy a ticket for the morning train. Five beats. First say only the five big words like thumps, then the whole sentence.
  • She was waiting for me at the bus stop. Beats: WAIT-ing · BUS · STOP. "was, for, at, the" are all weak.
  • Can you send me the file before the meeting? Beats: SEND · FILE · be-FORE · MEET-ing. "Can you" sounds almost like "kuhnyuh".

docs.title: 27.3 Weak words — how they really sound
docs.text:
When a function word has no stress, its vowel becomes a schwa and the word gets very short. This is not "lazy" English — this is correct English.

Written Spoken In a sentence Listen to tuh I want tuh go. of uhv a cup uhv tea and un / n bread n butter for fuh waiting fuh you can kuhn I kuhn do it. at uht look uht this are uh What uh you doing? have (helper) uhv I uhv finished.

One important exception

When you want to put special stress on a function word, you say it in full: "I said I can do it, not I can't." So weakening is the rule, but you can always stress a word when you need to.

docs.title: 27.4 One sentence, five meanings — just by changing the stress
docs.text:
This drill will open your ears for good. It is one sentence — "I didn't say she stole my bag." The meaning changes depending on where the stress falls.

Stress on this word Meaning Listen I didn't say she stole my bag. I did not say it — someone else said it. I didn't say she stole my bag. I never said that — you misunderstood. I didn't say she stole my bag. Someone else stole it — not her. I didn't say she stole my bag. She took it, but did not steal it — maybe she borrowed it. I didn't say she stole my bag. The bag belonged to someone else, not me.

How to practise this

Say it five times, each time stressing a different word. To stress a word means: make it a little longer, a little louder, and a little higher in pitch. When you can hear all five differences yourself, your ear is ready.

docs.title: 27.5 Joined words — English "sticks together"
docs.text:
Native speakers do not pause between words. The end of one word sticks to the start of the next. That is why it sounds like they are "speaking very fast" — in fact they are not fast, the words are joined.

Written What you hear Listen What is your name? Wot-sure-naim Do you want to go? Juh-wanna-go I am going to call him. Aim-gonna-call-im Did you eat? Dijoo-eet Can I help you? Kun-ai-help-yoo Let me know. Lem-me-no

Please note

You learn this for listening, not because you must speak this way. You can say the full "What is your name?" — it is perfectly fine, clear and correct. But when someone says "Wot-sure-naim", you will not get stuck — that is the benefit.

docs.title: 27.6 The rise and fall of the voice (intonation)
docs.text:
Type of sentence Voice Example Listen A normal statement Falls at the end ↘ I live in Pune. A yes/no question Rises at the end ↗ Do you live in Pune? A WH- question Falls at the end ↘ Where do you live? Counting a list Rises in the middle ↗, falls on the last item ↘ I need pens, books and a bag. Asking politely A slight rise ↗ — a flat, direct tone sounds harsh Could you help me, please?

A habit that sounds harsh

  • Wrong: "Give me the file." — flat, with a falling voice
  • Right: "Could you give me the file?" — with a slightly rising voice
  • Why: It is not only the words — the direction of your voice also makes you polite. A question said with a falling voice sounds like an order.

docs.title: 27.7 Daily rhythm drill
docs.text:
This drill takes 2 minutes. For each sentence, first say only the big words while clapping, then fill in the whole sentence.

  • I NEED to FINish this WORK by TOmorrow. Four beats. "to, this, by" are completely weak.
  • Could you TELL me where the STAtion IS? Three beats. The voice rises slightly at the end — it is a question.
  • The MEEting has been POSTponed to NEXT WEEK. Four beats. Swallow "has been" — "uhz-bin".
  • I'm SORry, I didn't CATCH that LAST part. Three beats. You can use this line every day — the most natural way to say "I did not understand".

docs.title: 27.8 Practice — Rhythm and stress
docs.text:
Exercise 1

What is the basic difference between Hindi and English rhythm?

  • Hindi is more even-beat, English is stress-beat
  • In English every syllable is equal
  • The two are exactly the same
  • Hindi has stress, English does not

Hint: Which language gives each syllable the same time?

Answer

Hindi is more even-beat, English is stress-beat

That is why English spoken with a Hindi beat sounds flat. In English some words shine and the rest are pushed down.

Exercise 2

Which syllable is stressed in 'photographer'?

  • TOG (second syllable)
  • PHO (first syllable)
  • ra (third syllable)
  • pher (fourth syllable)
Answer

TOG (second syllable)

pho-TOG-ra-pher. Notice: in 'photograph' the stress is on PHO, but when the word changes form the stress moves.

Exercise 3

What is the noun/verb stress rule? (record, present, increase)

  • Noun on the first syllable, verb on the second
  • Noun on the second syllable, verb on the first
  • Both on the first syllable
  • There is no rule

Hint: Noun first, verb later.

Answer

Noun on the first syllable, verb on the second

RE-cord (a thing) / re-CORD (to do). PRE-sent (a gift) / pre-SENT (to show).

Exercise 4

Which words are said strongly in a sentence?

  • Content words — nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs
  • Articles and prepositions
  • Only the first and last word
  • All words equally
Answer

Content words — nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs

The words with real information shine. Words like a/the/of/to/is are only the frame — they get pushed down.

Exercise 5

Where is the stress in 'information'?

  • MA — infor-MA-tion
  • IN — IN-formation
  • for — in-FOR-mation
  • tion — informa-TION

Hint: The syllable just before -tion.

Answer

MA — infor-MA-tion

In words ending in -tion and -sion the stress is always on the syllable just before it: deci-SI-on, educ-A-tion.

Exercise 6

What does 'I didn't say SHE stole my bag' mean?

  • Someone else stole it, not her
  • I said nothing
  • The bag was not mine
  • She did not steal it, she borrowed it
Answer

Someone else stole it, not her

The stress is on 'she', so the sentence points away from her to someone else. Change the stress, change the meaning.

Exercise 7

How many stressed syllables does one word have? ___

Hint: Write the number.

Answer

ek / 1 / one

One word = one shining syllable. Stressing two places (de-VE-lop-MENT) is the most common mistake.

Exercise 8

In a sentence 'to' has no stress — when spoken it sounds like ___.

Hint: The weak schwa sound.

Answer

tuh / tu / ta

I want tuh go. In function words without stress the vowel becomes a schwa.

Exercise 9

Which word in this sentence should NOT be stressed? Tap it.

I want to buy a ticket.

Answer

Wrong word: a.

Corrected: I WANT to BUY a TICKet — 'a' is a completely weak 'uh'.

The article 'a' is a function word — the weakest word of all. Say 'uh', not 'ay'.

Exercise 10

Match the type of sentence to the direction of the voice.

A B I live in Pune. WH- question, falls Do you live in Pune? polite, a slight rise Where do you live? falls at the end Could you help me? rises at the end Answer

I live in Pune. — falls at the end; Do you live in Pune? — rises at the end; Where do you live? — WH- question, falls; Could you help me? — polite, a slight rise

Yes/no questions go up; statements and WH- questions go down. A question with a falling voice sounds like an order.

Exercise 11

Put the sentence in the right order, then say it with the beats.

Words: to / need / I / by / finish / work / tomorrow / this

Answer

I need to finish this work by tomorrow

Beats: NEED · FIN-ish · WORK · TO-morrow. The 'to, this, by' in between are weak.

Exercise 12

A five-beat sentence. First say only the big words while clapping, then the whole sentence.

Answer

Say: I want to buy a ticket for the morning train

WANT · BUY · TICK-et · MOR-ning · TRAIN. 'to, a, for, the' almost disappear.

Exercise 13

Noun-verb stress. Say both forms together.

Answer

Say: This is a record. Please record it.

RE-cord (noun) then re-CORD (verb). The difference should be clearly audible.

Exercise 14

The -tion stress. Make the right syllable shine.

Answer

Say: I need more information about the decision

infor-MA-tion, deci-SI-on. In both, the stress is just before -tion/-sion.

Exercise 15

A polite question — let your voice rise slightly at the end.

Answer

Say: Could you tell me where the station is

Beats on TELL · STA-tion · IS. If the voice falls it will sound like an order, not a question.

Exercise 16

Now change the stress — stress 'she'.

Answer

Say: I didn't say she stole my bag

Make 'she' longer, louder and a little higher. Keep the other words weak — then the difference is audible.

Exercise 17

A line you can use every day. Three beats.

Answer

Say: I'm sorry I didn't catch that last part

SOR-ry · CATCH · LAST. Swallow 'I didn't' quickly — aidunt.

What next?

For one week, do just one thing: whenever you listen to English, notice only which words come out strongly. Do not even try to understand the meaning — just listen to the beat. In seven days your ear will change. Next chapter: Fluency and filler words — the real cure for getting stuck while speaking.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Sentence structure
docs.text:
Sentence structure — how a sentence is built

With parts of speech we met the bricks — noun, verb, adjective. Now we will see how these bricks build a wall. In English the order of words is almost fixed, and the moment you understand this order, even the longest sentence starts to look easy. All the later chapters — tenses, modals, clauses — run on this same map.

In one line

A sentence is a group of words with a subject and a verb that expresses a complete thought. Subject + verb + complete meaning — you need all three to have a sentence.

  • Birds fly. Only two words, yet a full sentence — it has a subject and a verb.
  • My sister teaches maths. = My sister is a maths teacher.
  • In the morning. (not a sentence) No subject, no verb — it is only a fragment, so the meaning is unfinished.

docs.title: 4.1 Subject and Predicate — the two halves of a sentence
docs.text:
Every sentence can be cut into two halves in the middle. Once you can see this cut, choosing the right form of the verb (is or are, go or goes) becomes easy — because the verb always listens to the subject.

Figure 4.1. Subject = what the sentence is about. Predicate = everything from the verb onwards.

Subject and predicate

Subject = what the sentence is about. Predicate = the verb and everything after it. To find the subject, ask the verb "who?" or "what?". The form of the verb (is/are, go/goes) is always decided by the subject.

  • The children in the park | are playing cricket. Who is playing? "The children in the park" — the whole group is the subject, so we use "are".
  • Learning English | is not difficult. A subject can also be an activity — "learning English" is not difficult.

The hidden subject

In commands and requests the subject is not visible, but it is there — you. Sit down. = (You) sit down. Please close the door. = (You) please close the door.

docs.title: 4.2 Hindi is SOV, English is SVO — why the order is fixed
docs.text:
In Hindi we can say "Ram ne Shyam ko maara" or "Shyam ko Ram ne maara" — the meaning stays the same, because "ne" and "ko" show who did what to whom. English has no small markers like these. There, who is doing the action is shown only by position.

Figure 4.2. In Hindi ne / ko show the roles, so the order is free. In English, position tells you everything.

The fixed English order

In English the order is the meaning: Subject → Verb → Object. The verb always comes right after the subject, never at the end. If the words change places, the meaning changes.

Hindi order (S O V) English order (S V O) Main chai peeta hoon. (I tea drink) I drink tea. Wo roz akhbaar padhti hai. (She daily newspaper reads) She reads the newspaper daily. Bachchon ne khana kha liya. (The children food eaten) The children have eaten the food. Hum kal Jaipur jaayenge. (We tomorrow Jaipur will go) We will go to Jaipur tomorrow.

When you translate in your head

When you turn Hindi into English, first pick up the verb and put it next to the subject. "Main roz subah park me chalta hoon" → I walk in the park every morning. The other words (where, when) come after the verb, at the end.

docs.title: 4.3 Five building blocks — S, V, O, C, A
docs.text:
Every English sentence is built from five bricks. You need to remember their names, because dictionaries, grammar books and this book will all talk using these names.

Block Job Question Example S — Subject what the sentence is about Who? What? Ravi plays. V — Verb an action or being What does it do / what is it? Ravi plays. O — Object what the action falls on What? Whom? Ravi plays cricket. C — Complement says who or what the subject is Who is it? What is it like? Ravi is the captain. A — Adverbial place, time, manner Where? When? How? Ravi plays in the evening.

Object or complement? Try the '=' test

A sentence has five blocks: S, V, O, C, A. To tell an object from a complement, use "=": She became a doctor → she = doctor (complement). She met a doctor → she ≠ doctor (object).

  • The tea tastes sweet. tea = sweet → "sweet" is a complement. A complement can be an adjective too.
  • The boy broke the glass. boy ≠ glass → "the glass" is the object; the action fell on it.

docs.title: 4.4 Five core patterns
docs.text:
The good news is that thousands of English sentences are really built on just five patterns. The verb decides which pattern is used — some verbs work alone, some need an object, some need two.

Figure 4.3. Each colour is one job: subject, verb, object, complement, adverbial. The verb decides the pattern.

Five patterns

Almost every sentence is one of these five: SV, SVO, SVC, SVOO, SVOA. The verb decides which one applies. Extra words for when, where and how are added on top of these.

Pattern Verbs like these Example SV arrive, sleep, cry, laugh, fall The guests arrived. SVO eat, buy, love, read, make We bought a scooter. SVC be, become, seem, look, feel The room looks clean. SVOO give, send, show, tell, teach, buy She sent me a photo. SVOA put, keep, place, leave (where?) He put the milk in the fridge.

Extra words don't change the pattern
