The baby slept peacefully in the cradle after lunch. — this is still SV. The parts about how, where and when are decoration; if you remove them the sentence is still complete. But in SVOA the A is needed: "He put the milk." feels unfinished — where did he put it?

docs.title: 4.5 Sentences with two objects — to whom and what
docs.text:
With verbs like give, send, show and tell there is one person and one thing. You can arrange them in two ways, and both are correct — you only have to be careful with the small word "to".

Figure 4.4. When the person comes first, there is no to . When the thing comes first, put to (or for ) before the person.
  • He told us a story. / He told a story to us. = He told a story to us.
  • Papa bought me a cycle. / Papa bought a cycle for me. With buy, make, cook we use "for", not "to".

explain, describe, suggest — the person does not come first

  • Wrong: Please explain me the rule.
  • Right: Please explain the rule to me.
  • Why: explain, describe, suggest and say do not use the SVOO pattern. The thing comes first, then "to" + the person.

docs.title: 4.6 Phrase and Clause — the difference is one pair
docs.text:
To understand a long sentence you have to break it into pieces. The pieces are of two kinds, and there is one way to tell them apart: look inside the piece for a subject + verb pair.

Figure 4.5. Clauses inside a sentence, phrases inside a clause — like small boxes inside bigger boxes.

Phrase vs clause

A phrase = a group of words without a subject + verb pair (in the morning). A clause = a group that has its own subject and verb (when the rain stopped). A sentence has one or more clauses.

Type of phrase Built around Example Noun phrase a noun a very old temple Verb phrase a main verb + helping verbs she has been waiting Prepositional phrase starts with a preposition under the bridge Adjective phrase an adjective The film was really boring. Adverb phrase an adverb He spoke very slowly.

This vocabulary will be useful later

In the clauses chapter we will see how two clauses are joined — with and, but, because, who, which. For now, just be sure of this: a clause has a verb, a phrase does not.

docs.title: 4.7 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
Common mistakes with order and patterns

  • Wrong: Yesterday I market went.
  • Right: Yesterday I went to the market.

  • Why: This is the Hindi SOV order ("main market gaya") copied directly. In English the verb comes right after the subject, and after "go" we put "to" before a place.

  • Wrong: This movie very good.

  • Right: This movie is very good.

  • Why: In Hindi we can say "ye film bahut achhi", but in English there is no sentence without a verb. The SVC pattern needs a linking verb like "is".

  • Wrong: Myself Rahul.

  • Right: I am Rahul. / My name is Rahul.

  • Why: "Myself Rahul" has neither a correct subject nor a verb. "Myself" is never a subject — it only takes the place of an object: I hurt myself.

  • Wrong: My brother he works in Pune.

  • Right: My brother works in Pune.

  • Why: One subject per clause. "My brother" is the subject, so "he" is a repeat — remove it.

  • Wrong: Why you are late?

  • Right: Why are you late?
  • Why: In a question the helping verb comes before the subject. This is a fixed change of order in English; it does not happen in Hindi.

docs.title: 4.8 How to break down any sentence
docs.text:
When a long sentence doesn't make sense, don't panic. Ask these four questions in order — every sentence will open up.

Step What to ask What you get 1 What is the action or state of being? Verb (V) 2 Ask the verb "who? / what?" Subject (S) 3 After the verb, "what? / whom?" — and the "=" test Object (O) or Complement (C) 4 "Where? When? How?" Adverbial (A)
  • My grandmother makes pickles every summer. V = makes · S = my grandmother · O = pickles · A = every summer → SVO + extra.

docs.title: 4.9 Practice — Sentence structure
docs.text:
Exercise 1

'The baby is sleeping.' — which pattern is this?

  • SV
  • SVO
  • SVC
  • SVOA

Hint: Is anything else needed after the verb?

Answer

SV

'is sleeping' is the complete verb, and nothing is needed after it. No object, no complement — so it is SV.

Exercise 2

'My uncle became a pilot.' — what is 'a pilot' here?

  • Complement
  • Object
  • Adverbial
  • Subject

Hint: Try the '=' test.

Answer

Complement

uncle = pilot — both are the same person. When the '=' works, it is a complement, not an object.

Exercise 3

'She gave her friend a book.' — which pattern?

  • SVOO
  • SVO
  • SVOA
  • SVC
Answer

SVOO

There are two objects — 'her friend' (to whom) and 'a book' (what). So it is S V O O.

Exercise 4

Which of these is a clause, not a phrase?

  • because she was tired
  • in the morning
  • a very tall boy
  • under the old bridge

Hint: Look for a subject + verb pair.

Answer

because she was tired

'she was' — here both a subject (she) and a verb (was) are present, so this is a clause. The other three have no such pair; they are phrases.

Exercise 5

'Every morning, my grandfather walks in the park.' — what is the subject?

  • my grandfather
  • Every morning
  • the park
  • walks

Hint: Ask the verb: who walks?

Answer

my grandfather

The verb is 'walks'. Who walks? — my grandfather. 'Every morning' is at the start of the sentence, but it tells you the time, not the subject.

Exercise 6

This tea ___ very hot.

Hint: Without a verb the sentence is unfinished.

Answer

is

This is the SVC pattern — tea = hot. You need the linking verb 'is' to join the subject to the complement. In Hindi 'chai bahut garam' is fine, but not in English.

Exercise 7

There is one extra word in this sentence — tap it.

My sister she teaches English in Delhi.

Answer

Wrong word: she.

Corrected: My sister teaches English in Delhi.

'My sister' is already the subject. A second subject 'she' in one clause is a repeat — remove it.

Exercise 8

Find the wrong word.

Please explain me this sentence.

Answer

Wrong word: me.

Corrected: Please explain this sentence to me.

'explain' does not take the two-object pattern. The thing comes first, then 'to me'.

Exercise 9

Put it in the right English order.

Words: drink / every / morning / I / tea

Answer

I drink tea every morning

Subject (I) → verb (drink) → object (tea) → time (every morning). The verb does not go at the end as it does in Hindi.

Exercise 10

Make a sentence in the SVOA pattern.

Words: keys / table / She / on / the / the / put

Answer

She put the keys on the table

S (She) + V (put) + O (the keys) + A (on the table). 'put' needs a 'where', so you can't remove the A.

Exercise 11

Match each pattern to its example.

A B SV The soup is hot. SVO He told us a story. SVC The bus arrived. SVOO Ravi plays cricket. Answer

SV — The bus arrived.; SVO — Ravi plays cricket.; SVC — The soup is hot.; SVOO — He told us a story.

arrive needs nothing (SV), play takes an object (SVO), is is followed by an identity or state (SVC), and tell takes a person + a thing (SVOO).

Exercise 12

Now say this line — put the verb 'went' right after the subject.

Answer

Say: Yesterday I went to the market

Saying it aloud settles the SVO order on your tongue. The more times you say it correctly, the faster the 'I market went' habit will go.

What next?

Today take any three lines from an English newspaper and find the S, V and O in each. If you do this for five days, your brain will start to break up long sentences by itself when you read them.

docs.title: Chapter 49: Sentences & paragraphs
docs.text:
From sentence to paragraph — one idea, said clearly

Your grammar is right, your spelling is right, and yet your writing is often tiring to read. The reason is usually the same: the sentences are either very short and jerky, or one long train that keeps running on "and… and… so…". In this chapter we will learn how to join sentences, and how to arrange them into a paragraph that the reader understands the first time.

In one line

A paragraph is a group of sentences about one idea: the first sentence states it, the middle sentences support it, and the last sentence closes it. One paragraph = one idea. The first line announces it, the middle lines give proof, and the last line wraps it up.

docs.title: 49.1 From choppy bits to flowing sentences
docs.text:
Very short sentences sound like a robot; in a very long sentence the reader keeps looking for a place to breathe. Good writing sits between the two.

Figure 49.1. Yellow = jerky, green = flowing, red = never-ending.

Join or split

Two short sentences are about the same thing → join them (and, but, because, when, which). A sentence has grown longer than 25 words, or has two "and"s → split it and add a full stop.

  • ✗ I reached the station. The train was late. I waited. I had tea. Four pieces — all correct, but jerky to read.
  • ✓ When I reached the station, the train was late, so I waited and had a cup of tea. when + so joined all four pieces into one flowing sentence.
  • ✓ The new manager, who joined last week, has already cut our meeting time in half. "The manager joined last week" is tucked inside the main sentence with who.

docs.title: 49.2 The paragraph burger — topic, support, closing
docs.text:
Every good paragraph has the same shape, whether it is a college essay or an office report. Think of it as a burger: a bun on top and bottom, and plenty of filling in between.

Figure 49.2. Without the buns the burger falls apart; without the filling it is just bread.

The burger formula

1 topic sentence (the subject + your opinion) → 2–4 support sentences (reason, example, number) → 1 closing sentence (wrap up the point or give the next step). Office email or essay — this is the structure.

Model: one complete paragraph

Walking to work is the easiest way to stay fit. Topic sentence — the subject (walking) + the opinion (easiest way to stay fit).

It needs no gym fee and no extra time, because you are travelling anyway. For example, a twenty-minute walk each way adds up to more than three hours a week. That is more than the 150 minutes of activity that doctors usually suggest. Three supports — a reason (because), an example (for example), proof (150 minutes).

So if your office is close, leave the bike at home. Closing — it gives the reader something to do.

docs.title: 49.3 The topic sentence — the whole point in the first line
docs.text:
Managers, teachers and examiners all read in a hurry, and often only the first line of every paragraph. If the first line says nothing, the rest of the paragraph does not get read either.

The test for a good topic sentence

A topic sentence has two things: the subject + your opinion or point about it. "Online classes" is only a subject; "Online classes save time but make it harder to ask questions" is a complete topic sentence.

Weak opening Strong topic sentence In this paragraph I will tell about my city. Pune is a city where old wadas and new IT parks stand side by side. As we all know, technology is very important. UPI has made it possible for a street vendor to accept payment from anyone. Exercise is a thing which is good. Even ten minutes of exercise a day can lift your mood. I want to say something about our project. Our project is two weeks behind because the vendor delivered late. Since ancient times, man has used water. Most Indian cities lose a large share of their water to leaking pipes.
  • Our project is two weeks behind because the vendor delivered late. The very first line says what happened (two weeks behind) and why (vendor late) — so the manager has a reason to keep reading.

docs.title: 49.4 One paragraph, one idea
docs.text:
When two or three different points get into one paragraph, the reader forgets what it began with. Hold every line up against the topic sentence.

Figure 49.3. The point about the canteen may be true — but it does not belong in the library paragraph.

One question for every line

"Does this line support the topic sentence?" Yes → keep it. No → either delete it or start a new paragraph. Also start a new paragraph when the time, the place or the speaker changes, or when the opposite argument begins.

docs.title: 49.5 Linking words — however, therefore, for example
docs.text:
Linking words are like road signs: they tell the reader in advance which way the next line will turn — another point, the opposite point, a result, or an example.

Figure 49.4. The moment the reader sees the signboard, they know where the thought is heading.

Using linking words correctly

First identify the job (adding, contrast, result, example), then choose the word. If it comes at the start of a sentence, put a comma after it: "However, the cost is high." Don't use one in every line — two or three per paragraph are enough.

Job Words Example Add a point moreover, in addition, also The flat is cheap. Moreover, it is near the metro. Contrast however, on the other hand The flat is cheap. However, it has no lift. Result therefore, as a result The road was closed. As a result, we were late. Example for example, for instance Some apps save time. For example, UPI. Order first, then, finally First, fill the form. Then, pay the fee. Reason because, since, due to + noun We stayed in because it rained. · due to the rain Summary in short, overall Overall, the trip was worth it.
  • The flat is cheap. However, it is on the fifth floor and has no lift. Pause slightly after However — the listener understands that a drawback is coming.

docs.title: 49.6 Before and after — fixing a weak paragraph
docs.text:
Now let's put everything together. Below is a paragraph like a real college student's — the grammar mistakes are few, but there is no structure. See how the same content becomes clear.

Before — the weak paragraph

Library is important. Our library closes at 5 pm. Many students are working in day time. And they come in evening and library is closed and they go back and they cannot study. Also canteen food is very bad. So library should open late.

After — the improved paragraph

Our college library should stay open until 9 pm. At present it closes at 5 pm, which is exactly when many students finish their part-time jobs. For example, in my class of sixty, at least fifteen students work during the day and can study only in the evening. As a result, they either crowd into small rented rooms or do not study at all. Keeping the library open for four more hours would cost little, but it would give these students a fair chance.

  • A topic sentence has arrived "Library is important" is replaced by a clear demand: open until 9 pm.
  • The "and… and… and…" train is broken up One long sentence became three clear ones, with the help of which and either… or.
  • Proof and numbers added "Many students" became "fifteen out of sixty" — now the point has weight.
  • The canteen line was removed It was a different idea — it will get its own paragraph.
  • Linking words and a closing sentence For example and As a result joined the lines; the last line wrapped up the point.

docs.title: 49.7 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
These mistakes show up rarely in grammar books, but you meet them every day in emails, reports and exam answers — often because we carry the Hindi sentence pattern straight into English.

Real mistakes in paragraphs and joining sentences

  • Wrong: I reached the office at nine, my manager was not there, I waited for one hour.
  • Right: I reached the office at nine, but my manager was not there. I waited for an hour.

  • Why: Three complete sentences cannot be joined by commas alone. Bring in a joining word (but) or use a full stop.

  • Wrong: Although it was raining, but we went out.

  • Right: Although it was raining, we went out.

  • Why: In Hindi you use both "haalaanki… lekin"; in English "but" does not go with although. Keep only one.

  • Wrong: Due to I was ill, I could not submit the assignment.

  • Right: Because I was ill, I could not submit the assignment.

  • Why: "Due to" is followed by a noun (due to my illness). When a full clause (I was ill) follows, use "because".

  • Wrong: The hotel was clean. Moreover, it was very expensive.

  • Right: The hotel was clean. However, it was very expensive.

  • Why: Moreover adds one more point in the same direction. A drawback after a good point is a contrast — however.

  • Wrong: In this paragraph I am going to tell about my city. As we all know, Pune is a nice city.

  • Right: Pune is a city where old wadas and new IT parks stand side by side.
  • Why: Don't talk about the paragraph — just talk about the subject. "As we all know" adds nothing either; delete it.

Linking words are like salt

If you start every sentence with "Moreover…", "Furthermore…" or "Also…", your writing will feel heavy and artificial. Most sentences do not need a linking word at all — the right order joins them by itself.

docs.title: 49.8 Practice — Paragraphs
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Which is the best topic sentence for a paragraph on the benefits of cycling?

  • In this paragraph I will tell about cycling.
  • Cycling to work saves money, keeps you fit and cuts traffic.
  • Cycling is a thing.
  • As we all know, cycling is very very good.
Answer

Cycling to work saves money, keeps you fit and cuts traffic.

A good topic sentence gives both the subject and the opinion, and it hints at the three supporting points to come. 'In this paragraph I will tell' says nothing.

Exercise 2

It rained heavily all night. ___, the match was cancelled.

  • As a result
  • However
  • For example
  • Moreover
Answer

As a result

The rain is the cause and the cancelled match is the result — so 'As a result' (or Therefore).

Exercise 3

The flat is quite small. ___, it is only ten minutes from my office.

  • However
  • Therefore
  • For example
  • As a result
Answer

However

The first line gives a drawback and the second a benefit — for a contrast, use 'However'.

Exercise 4

In a paragraph about saving water at home, which line does NOT fit?

  • Fix leaking taps as soon as you notice them.
  • Use a bucket instead of a hose to wash the car.
  • Our society also needs a new gym.
  • Turn off the tap while brushing your teeth.
Answer

Our society also needs a new gym.

The gym is a different idea. One paragraph = one idea — the other three lines all support saving water.

Exercise 5

The ___ sentence tells the reader what the whole paragraph is about.

Answer

topic

The topic sentence is the first line of the paragraph — the whole point in a single sentence.

Exercise 6

A good paragraph talks about only one main ___.

Answer

idea / point

One paragraph, one idea. When a new idea comes, start a new paragraph — that way the reader does not lose the way.

Exercise 7

Many students work during the day. ___ example, fifteen students in my class have part-time jobs.

Answer

For

'For example' brings in an example, and at the start of a sentence it is followed by a comma.

Exercise 8

One word in this sentence is unnecessary — tap it.

Although the train was late, but we reached the meeting on time.

Answer

Wrong word: but.

Corrected: Although the train was late, we reached the meeting on time.

In Hindi you use both 'haalaanki… lekin', but not in English. 'But' never goes with 'Although' — keep only one.

Exercise 9

Find the wrong word.

Due to I was unwell, I missed the class.

Answer

Wrong word: Due.

Corrected: Because I was unwell, I missed the class.

'Due to' is followed by a noun (due to my illness). When a full clause (I was unwell) follows, use 'Because'.

Exercise 10

Match each linking word to its job.

A B however example therefore adding another point for example the last point moreover contrast finally result Answer

however — contrast; therefore — result; for example — example; moreover — adding another point; finally — the last point

however = contrast, therefore = result, for example = example, moreover = addition, finally = the end of a sequence.

Exercise 11

Put the words in the right order to make a sentence.

Words: saves / money. / time / new / plan / and / the / However, / both

Answer

However, the new plan saves both time and money.

When 'However' starts a sentence, a comma follows it. Then comes the plain subject + verb + object.

Exercise 12

Say this line — pause briefly after 'As a result'.

Answer

Say: As a result, the project was finished on time.

A comma after a linking word means a short pause when speaking. The listener can tell that a result is coming.

What to do next

Open your last long email or assignment. Read only the first line of each paragraph — do they give you the whole story? If not, rewrite those first lines. This one habit will change your writing.

docs.title: Chapter 32: Small talk & opinions
docs.text:
Small talk and giving opinions — starting, keeping going, ending

The office lift, the wedding buffet, the tea break at a conference — these two or three minutes of talk build relationships. Many of us go quiet here, because one question keeps going round in the mind: "What do I say?" The truth is that small talk needs nothing deep — it only needs a frame: how to start, how to keep it going, how to give your opinion, and how to leave gracefully. Every line has a 🔊. Listen, say it along, and try it with someone tomorrow.

docs.title: 32.1 The small-talk map — four steps
docs.text:
When the path is clear in your mind, half of the nervousness goes. Every good short conversation passes through these four steps — and the middle two steps go round again and again.

Figure 32.1. Steps 2 and 3 are a see-saw — you ask a question, they answer, you add your own thought, then a new question. When the talk cools down, go to step 4.

Four steps

Open → Follow up → Share → Close. The middle two steps (a question and your own thought) go round again and again — this is what keeps the conversation alive. The goal of small talk is not to collect information, it is to connect.

Topics to avoid at a first meeting

Safe: weather, traffic, the event you are at, food, work, travel, movies, cricket. Avoid: salary, "when are you getting married?", weight, religion, politics. Among us these questions are asked with affection, but in an English-speaking setting they feel very personal.

docs.title: 32.2 Starting a conversation — weather, work, and where you both are
docs.text:
The easiest opener is whatever is in front of both of you — the same place, the same weather, the same food. One short statement, then a question. That is all.

Where English line Listen Wedding / party So, how do you know the bride and groom? Conference Is this your first time at this conference? Weather It's so hot today, isn't it? Rain Looks like the rain's finally here. Work What kind of work do you do? Office How's your week going so far? Food Have you tried the paneer? It's really good. A new face Hi, I don't think we've met. I'm Kavya.

The opener formula

Statement + question: "Great music tonight. Do you know the band?" The statement sets the scene; the question gives the other person a chance to speak. A statement alone ("Hot day.") or a question alone ("Your name?") feels unfinished.

Mini-dialogue — the tea break at a conference

Situation: it is the tea break at a conference. You are standing alone, and another person beside you is also alone. Say your lines first, then Meera's lines too.

  • You: Hi! Is this your first time at this conference? The opening — a question about the place you are both in.
  • Meera: No, second time, actually. Last year's was in Bengaluru. "actually" = in fact. She gave an extra detail — a good sign.
  • You: Oh, nice. I'm Rohan, by the way. I work in logistics. "by the way" lets the name slip in easily, in the middle.
  • Meera: Nice to meet you, Rohan. I'm Meera. I'm a data analyst. A name and a job — now the way is open for a follow-up.
  • You: So what brings you here this year? = Why did you come this year? A very natural follow-up.
  • Meera: Mostly the AI sessions. My team wants to try some new tools. Now you can ask: "Oh, which tools?" — and the talk is rolling.

docs.title: 32.3 Keeping it going — follow-up questions
docs.text:
Conversations often die right here: a question comes, a one-word answer goes back, then silence. There are two tools to avoid this — the ping-pong answer, and good follow-up questions.

Figure 32.2. The detail gives the other person a new topic, and the question sends the ball back to their side.

The ping-pong answer

Answer + one extra detail + a question back. "Pune. I moved here for work last year. What about you?" A one-word answer drops the ball on the floor — then both people just stand there.

  • Oh, really? How did you get into that? = How did you start that work? The best question about anyone's job.
  • What's that like? = What is it like? Use it for a new city, a new job, anything.
  • That sounds interesting. What do you enjoy most about it? = What is the best part? People happily talk about what they like.
  • How long have you been doing that? = Since when have you done this?
  • And what about you? = And you? The shortest line for sending the ball back.

Turn a closed question into an open one

Closed: "Do you like Pune?" → the answer is only yes or no. Open: "What do you like about Pune?" → the answer brings a story. Questions that start with what, how or why keep the talk going longer.

docs.title: 32.4 Giving your opinion — I think, In my view, To be honest
docs.text:
An opinion brings life to a conversation. But when you translate straight from Hindi, an opinion often sounds too harsh. In English an opinion is usually kept a little soft — and how soft is something you choose with the phrase.

Figure 32.3. In everyday talk the middle step ( I think ) is the safest. Use the top step only when you have a solid reason. Line When Listen I think the new metro has really helped. An everyday, normal opinion In my view, the second half of the film was better. Thoughtful, a little formal To be honest, I didn't enjoy the food much. A truth the other person may not like Personally, I prefer working from the office. Your own taste — not forcing it on others I might be wrong, but I think it's going to rain. Very soft, you are not sure If you ask me, cricket is more fun in the stadium. Casual, among friends

Opinion + reason

An opinion on its own sounds weak — add because: "I think remote work is great because I save two hours a day." And in place of "According to me", say "I think" or "In my view".

docs.title: 32.5 Agreeing and disagreeing — without a fight
docs.text:
Disagreeing is not bad; the way you do it can be. A plain "No, you are wrong" ends the talk right there. English speakers first acknowledge what the other person said, and then give their own view.

Figure 32.4. Even as you move to the right, the voice stays soft. The strongest form of disagreement is I see it differently — not you are wrong .

The disagreeing formula

Acknowledge + but + your view. "That's a fair point, but I think traffic is the bigger problem." The first part shows respect, the second gives your opinion. You need both.

Mini-dialogue — a debate about working from home

Situation: at lunch, your colleague Aman says working from home is better. You half agree and half do not.

  • Aman: I think working from home is so much better. An opinion — with "I think".
  • You: I know what you mean. No traffic, right? Acknowledge first — "I understand you".
  • Aman: Exactly! I save almost two hours a day. Opinion + reason.
  • You: That's true. But to be honest, I find it harder to focus at home. Acknowledge + but + your view. Disagreeing without a fight.
  • Aman: Fair enough. I guess it depends on the person. "Fair enough" = OK, you have a good point.
  • You: Yeah, I suppose it does. Both are happy — the argument is over, the friendship stays.

docs.title: 32.6 Ending the conversation — gracefully
docs.text:
A good conversation should have a good ending too. Turning away without a word, or suddenly saying "OK, bye", feels rude. Three small steps — and you leave a good memory behind.

Figure 32.5. The signal gets the other person ready, the reason keeps them from taking offence, and the warm line is what they remember.
  • Well, it was really nice talking to you. "Well…" — the shortest and clearest signal.
  • I should let you get back to your friends. = I will not keep you here. The reason is about them — a very polite way.
  • I'm going to grab some food before it's all gone. A light, casual reason — useful at parties.
  • I need to catch up with a colleague, but let's talk later. "catch up with" = to meet someone and hear their news.
  • Let's stay in touch. Are you on LinkedIn? Use it if you want the relationship to continue.
  • Enjoy the rest of the evening! The last warm line.

The three-step ending

Signal ("Well…") + reason ("I should go and say hi to my boss") + warm line ("It was lovely meeting you"). Keep the reason short and true. Disappearing without a word, or a flat "OK, bye" — both feel rude.

docs.title: 32.7 A complete conversation — from start to finish
docs.text:
Now everything together — opener, follow-up, ping-pong, opinion, agreement and ending. Say both roles; saying the other person's lines also gets your ear ready.

Mini-dialogue — the wedding buffet

Situation: a long buffet queue at the reception. Priya is standing in front of you, and you do not know her.

  • You: This queue is moving so slowly! Everything looks delicious, though. The opener — a statement about what is in front of you.
  • Priya: I know! Someone told me the biryani is the best thing here. She picked up the thread and added a detail.
  • You: Good to know. So, are you from the bride's side or the groom's? The easiest follow-up at a wedding.
  • Priya: The bride's. We went to college together. And you? Ping-pong: answer + detail + a question back.
  • You: I work with the groom. I'm Vikram, by the way. The name comes in with "by the way".
  • Priya: I'm Priya. Nice to meet you. What do you two work on? An open question — "What are you working on?"
  • You: We build apps for hospitals. It's busy, but I really enjoy it. An answer + a feeling. Now Priya has something to talk about.
  • Priya: That sounds interesting. I think technology in healthcare is the future. An opinion — with "I think".
  • You: I couldn't agree more. Well, I'll let you get your food. It was lovely talking to you. Agreement, then signal + reason + warm line.
  • Priya: You too, Vikram. Enjoy the biryani! A good ending — both smile and part.

docs.title: 32.8 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
These are less grammar mistakes and more translation mistakes — they come from carrying a Hindi pattern into English. The listener understands, but it sounds odd.

Common small-talk mistakes

  • Wrong: What is your good name?
  • Right: What's your name? / Sorry, I didn't catch your name.

  • Why: "Good name" is a word-for-word copy of "shubh naam". It carries respect for us, but sounds odd in English.

  • Wrong: Myself Rahul, from Pune.

  • Right: I'm Rahul. I'm from Pune.

  • Why: An introduction does not start with "Myself". Just "I'm…" — short and natural.

  • Wrong: I am agree with you.

  • Right: I agree with you.

  • Why: "Agree" is a verb by itself — it does not need "am". The same for the negative: "I don't agree", not "I am not agree".

  • Wrong: According to me, the film was boring.

  • Right: I thought the film was boring. / In my view, it was boring.

  • Why: "According to" is for other people's words — according to the news, according to my doctor. For your own opinion use "I think".

  • Wrong: So, how much do you earn? When are you getting married?

  • Right: So, what do you enjoy most about your job?
  • Why: Salary and marriage are seen as very personal at a first meeting. Ask about the work, not the earnings.

docs.title: 32.9 Practice — Small talk
docs.text:
Exercise 1

You want to start talking to a stranger at a conference tea break. Which is the most natural opener?

  • Is this your first time at this conference?
  • What is your good name?
  • How much salary do you get?
  • Myself Rohan, tell me about you.
Answer

Is this your first time at this conference?

A question about the place you both share — the safest and the most natural. The other three are either translations or too personal.

Exercise 2

What should you add to your opinion to make it stronger?

  • a reason with 'because'
  • the word 'definitely' twice
  • 'according to me' at the start
  • a louder voice
Answer

a reason with 'because'

Opinion + reason = a strong opinion. 'I think X because Y' — the listener may disagree, but will not take you lightly.

Exercise 3

You disagree with a colleague. Which reply is the most polite?

  • You are wrong.
  • That's a fair point, but I see it differently.
  • No, no, that is not correct.
  • I am not agree.
Answer

That's a fair point, but I see it differently.

The formula: acknowledge + but + your view. The first part shows respect. 'I am not agree' is also wrong grammar.

Exercise 4

I ___ with you. The traffic is terrible these days.

Hint: You do not need 'am'.

Answer

agree / totally agree / completely agree

'Agree' is a verb by itself — 'I agree', not 'I am agree'.

Exercise 5

Well, it was really nice ___ to you.

Hint: A line for ending a talk — verb + ing.

Answer

talking / speaking

'It was nice talking to you' — the warmest line for the end of a conversation.

Exercise 6

One word in this introduction sounds odd — tap it.

Myself Anjali and I work in a bank.

Answer

Wrong word: Myself.

Corrected: I'm Anjali and I work in a bank.

An introduction starts with 'I'm…', not 'Myself…'.

Exercise 7

Put the words in the right order — make an open follow-up question.

Words: do / What / most / job / you / your / about / enjoy

Answer

What do you enjoy most about your job

Wh-word + do + you + verb — this is an open question, and its answer is not just yes or no.

Exercise 8

Match each line to its job.

A B How did you get into that? disagreeing politely To be honest, I didn't like it. ending the conversation I see your point, but… follow-up question I'll let you get back to it. an honest opinion Answer

How did you get into that? — follow-up question; To be honest, I didn't like it. — an honest opinion; I see your point, but… — disagreeing politely; I'll let you get back to it. — ending the conversation

Every line has a job — a question, an opinion, a disagreement, an ending. These steps keep small talk moving.

Exercise 9

Say the line for leaving a party — warm and clear.

Answer

Say: It was really nice talking to you

Join 'talking to you' together — 'tawking-tu-yu'. The voice falls on the last 'you'.

Exercise 10

Now show how to disagree politely.

Answer

Say: That's a fair point, but I see it differently

Pause a little after 'but' — it shows you really listened to them.

Exercise 11

Say an opener — with the voice rising at the end of the question.

Answer

Say: Is this your first time here

In a yes/no question the voice rises on the last word — 'here?'

What next?

This week, have a four-step conversation with one new person — it could be the society guard or the new intern at the office. The first time will feel odd; by the third time it will be a habit.

docs.title: Chapter 48: Spelling rules
docs.text:
Spelling rules — memorise less, understand more

One wrong spelling in an email — recieve, seperate, definately — and the reader immediately thinks the writer was careless. The good news is that English spelling is not as crazy as it looks. A handful of rules handle most words, and we will memorise the leftover exceptions in one list.

In one line

Most English spelling follows a few rules about adding endings — double the consonant, drop the e, change y to i. Learn the rules first, then memorise the exceptions. Understand the rules first, then memorise only the exceptions — not the whole dictionary.

docs.title: 48.1 When does a consonant double?
docs.text:
stopped or stoped? beginning or begining? This question comes up in office emails every day. The answer is hidden in three small questions — follow the chart below once.

Figure 48.1. Double only if all three answers are yes . If even one is no , keep the consonant single.

The 1-1-1 rule

One syllable, one vowel, one final consonant + a suffix that starts with a vowel = the consonant doubles: stop → stopped, big → bigger. In a longer word, only when the stress is on the last syllable: begin → beginning, but visit → visited.

  • We stopped the meeting at five. stop = one syllable, one vowel (o), one consonant (p) → stopped.
  • This is only the beginning. be-GIN — the stress is on the last syllable, so the n doubles: beginning.
  • She visited her parents on Sunday. VI-sit — the stress is on the first syllable, so the t stays single: visited.

British twist — travel, cancel, label

In British English, a final l always doubles, wherever the stress is: travelled, cancelled, labelled, modelling. American English keeps it single: traveled, canceled. India follows British English, so in school and at the office write travelled.

docs.title: 48.2 When does the silent e drop?
docs.text:
The last e of make is not pronounced — and that e causes the most mistakes when you add an ending. The rule is simple: look at the first letter of the suffix.

Figure 48.2. One word, two paths. The first letter of the suffix decides whether the e stays or goes.

The silent-e decision

The suffix starts with a vowel (-ing, -able, -ed) → drop the e: make → making, use → usable. The suffix starts with a consonant (-ful, -ment, -ly) → keep the e: care → careful, move → movement.

Word Vowel suffix (e dropped) Consonant suffix (e kept) make making — hope hoping hopeful care caring careful move moving movement use usable useful manage managing management achieve achieving achievement

Exceptions you must memorise

Words with c / g keep the e so the sound stays soft: noticeable, manageable, courageous. The e drops for no obvious reason: truly, argument, ninth, awful. Words ending in ee do not drop the e: seeing, agreeing, fleeing.

docs.title: 48.3 When does y become i?
docs.text:
happyness or happiness? studys or studies? Just look at the letter right before the y — that gives you the answer.

Figure 48.3. You only need to look at one letter — the y's neighbour.

The y rule

Consonant + y → i: happy → happiness, study → studied. Vowel + y → y stays: play → played. And before -ing the y never changes: studying, carrying.

  • She studies late and still looks happier than all of us. stud-y → studies (d is a consonant); happ-y → happier.
  • The children enjoyed the play. enjo-y → o is a vowel, so the y stays: enjoyed.

Four old exceptions

day → daily, pay → paid, say → said, lay → laid. These have vowel + y, yet the y still became i — just memorise them.

docs.title: 48.4 i before e — and its exceptions
docs.text:
receive or recieve, believe or beleive — mixing up ie and ei is the most common spelling mistake among Indian writers. The old rhyme still works; you just need to remember all of it.

ie or ei — a three-line trick

The "ee" sound → ie: believe, piece, achieve. Right after c → ei: receive, ceiling, receipt. The "ay" sound → ei: eight, weigh, neighbour.

When Spelling Examples The "ee" sound ie believe, achieve, piece, field, chief, niece, brief After c, with the "ee" sound ei receive, receipt, ceiling, deceive, perceive The "ay" sound ei eight, weight, neighbour, vein, reign Exceptions — learn by heart ei seize, weird, either, neither, protein, foreign, leisure, their After c but still ie (the sound is not "ee") ie science, ancient, efficient, society
  • I received the receipt from my neighbour. receive, receipt — ei after c. neighbour — the "ay" sound, so ei.

docs.title: 48.5 -able or -ible
docs.text:
acceptable or acceptible? Both sound the same, so your ear does not help. But there is a simple test that works for most words.

Figure 48.4. Use the scissors: cut off the suffix and see what is left.

The -able / -ible test

When you remove the suffix and a whole word is left → -able (acceptable, comfortable). When only a broken piece is left → -ible (possible, visible, terrible). This test works for most words.

Some words break the test

responsible, flexible, accessible, sensible — whole words are hidden inside them, yet they take -ible. And noticeable, changeable keep the e so that the c/g sound stays soft. Memorise these six separately.

docs.title: 48.6 British or American — colour or color
docs.text:
There are two spelling systems, and both are correct. But in India, schools, board exams, government work and most newspapers follow British spelling. Trouble starts when software quietly switches to American spelling.

Pattern British (India) American -our / -or colour, favour, behaviour color, favor, behavior -re / -er centre, metre, theatre center, meter, theater -ise / -ize organise, realise, apologise organize, realize, apologize -ll / -l travelled, cancelled, jewellery traveled, canceled, jewelry -ogue / -og catalogue, dialogue catalog, dialog -ce / -se licence (noun), defence license, defense -yse / -yze analyse, paralyse analyze, paralyze Different words programme, cheque, tyre, grey program, check, tire, gray

The real mistake is mixing them

Writing "color" is not a mistake — the mistake is writing both colour and color in one email. In Word or Google Docs, set the language to English (India) or English (UK). For computers, program is used in both systems, and -ize is not wrong in British English either — just pick one system and keep it throughout the document.

docs.title: 48.7 The 30 words we misspell most
docs.text: This list comes from mistakes that really show up in Indian offices, colleges and job applications. Each word has a small trick — if you remember the trick, you will remember the spelling.

docs.title: The double-letter game
docs.text: Correct Common mistake How to remember accommodation accomodation Two c's, two m's — the room is big enough to fit both doubles. occurrence occurence Two c's, two r's, and -ence at the end. recommend reccomend re + commend: one c, two m's. necessary neccessary A shirt has one Collar and two Sleeves — one c, two s's. committee commitee Everything doubles: mm, tt, ee. embarrass embarass So much shame that you need two r's and two s's. beginning begining be-GIN + n + ing — the 1-1-1 rule. tomorrow tommorow to + morrow: one m, two r's.

docs.title: Vowel trouble
docs.text: Correct Common mistake How to remember separate seperate "There is a rat in separate." definitely definately "Finite" is hiding inside: de-FINITE-ly. privilege priviledge No d, no a: pri-vi-lege. grammar grammer It ends in -ar; the word has two a's. calendar calender It ends in -ar, just like grammar. independent independant It ends in -ent: in-de-pen-dent. existence existance exist + ence — all the vowels are e. maintenance maintainance It comes from maintain, but the "ai" is lost: main-te-nance.

docs.title: ie/ei and hidden letters
docs.text: Correct Common mistake How to remember receive recieve Right after c comes e-i. achieve acheive The "ee" sound and no c — so i-e. believe beleive "Never believe a lie." foreign foriegn It is an exception — ei. Learn it by heart. government goverment govern + ment — don't leave out the n. environment enviroment environ + ment — the n is here too. Wednesday Wensday Say it in your head as you write: Wed-nes-day.

docs.title: Special ones for Indian English
docs.text:
Correct Common mistake How to remember until untill till has two l's, until has only one. across accross a + cross — only one c. truly truely The e of true drops (an exception). pronunciation pronounciation pronounce has "ou", but pronunciation has only "u". argument arguement The e of argue drops. colleague collegue col + league — the same spelling as a cricket league. guarantee gaurantee g-u-a: u first, then a.

Five words a week

Don't try to memorise the whole list in one day. Pick five words each week, write each one five times by hand while saying it aloud, and use each of them at least once in that week's emails. The list is finished in six weeks.

docs.title: 48.8 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
These sentences are like real office emails and applications. Each one has a spelling mistake — and behind each mistake is a rule we have already studied above.

Real spelling mistakes from offices and colleges

  • Wrong: I am writting to inform you about the delay.
  • Right: I am writing to inform you about the delay.

  • Why: The silent e of write drops → writing (one t). written has two t's — that is a different word.

  • Wrong: We will definately recieve the payment by Monday.

  • Right: We will definitely receive the payment by Monday.

  • Why: de-FINITE-ly. And after c it is always e-i: receive.

  • Wrong: Kindly accomodate my request for a seperate room.

  • Right: Please accommodate my request for a separate room.

  • Why: accommodate has two c's and two m's. "A rat" is hiding in separate.

  • Wrong: It was a priviledge to work with such a commited team.

  • Right: It was a privilege to work with such a committed team.

  • Why: privilege has no d. com-MIT — the stress is on the last syllable, so the t doubles: committed.

  • Wrong: I do not want to loose this oppurtunity.

  • Right: I do not want to lose this opportunity.
  • Why: lose = to no longer have, loose = not tight. op-por-tu-ni-ty — it begins with "port", with two p's.

Spell-check doesn't catch everything

loose/lose, their/there, its/it's, then/than, affect/effect — these are all real words, so no red line appears. Before sending an email, read it aloud once; the ear catches what the eye misses.

docs.title: 48.9 Practice — Spelling
docs.text:
Exercise 1

One spelling in this sentence is wrong — tap that word.

We will definately send the report today.

Answer

Wrong word: definately.

Corrected: We will definitely send the report today.

'Finite' is hiding inside: de-FINITE-ly. There is no 'a' anywhere in this word.

Exercise 2

Find the word with the wrong spelling.

I have made a seperate folder for each client.

Answer

Wrong word: seperate.

Corrected: I have made a separate folder for each client.

'There is a rat in separate' — sep-A-rate. The middle letter is a, not e.

Exercise 3

One word is spelled wrongly — find it.

The hotel could not give accomodation to all the guests.

Answer

Wrong word: accomodation.

Corrected: The hotel could not give accommodation to all the guests.

accommodation has two c's and two m's. Leaving out one m is the most common mistake.

Exercise 4

Tap the wrong word.

Did you recieve my email about the meeting?

Answer

Wrong word: recieve.

Corrected: Did you receive my email about the meeting?

Right after c comes e-i: receive, receipt, ceiling.

Exercise 5

Which word doubles its final consonant when you add -ing?

  • begin
  • visit
  • open
  • happen

Hint: Say each word aloud — where does the stress fall?

Answer

begin

In be-GIN the stress is on the last syllable, so beginning. In VI-sit, O-pen and HAP-pen the stress is on the first syllable — so visiting, opening, happening, with a single consonant.

Exercise 6

Which spelling is correct?

  • comfortible
  • visible
  • acceptible
  • dependible
Answer

visible

'vis' alone is not a word, so -ible. comfort, accept and depend are whole words — they take -able: comfortable, acceptable, dependable.

Exercise 7

Which spelling system is used in Indian schools, board exams and government work?

  • British
  • American
  • Both mixed in one document
  • There is no rule
Answer

British

India uses British spelling — colour, centre, organise, travelled. American is not wrong, but keep to one system in one document.

Exercise 8

In American English, 'centre' is written ___.

Answer

center

British -re, American -er: centre/center, metre/meter, theatre/theater.

Exercise 9

The silent e drops when the suffix starts with a ___ — as in make + ing = making.

Hint: Consonant or vowel?

Answer

vowel

If the suffix starts with a vowel (-ing, -able, -ed), the e drops: making, usable. If it starts with a consonant (-ful, -ment), the e stays: careful, movement.

Exercise 10

Match each word + suffix to its correct form.

A B happy + ness stopped make + ing careful stop + ed played care + ful happiness play + ed making Answer

happy + ness — happiness; make + ing — making; stop + ed — stopped; care + ful — careful; play + ed — played

happy: consonant + y, so y → i. make: a vowel suffix, so the e drops. stop: 1-1-1, so it doubles. care: a consonant suffix, so the e stays. play: vowel + y, so the y stays.

Exercise 11

Put the words in the right order to make a sentence.

Words: this / colleagues / to / definitely / recommend / my / would / I / hotel

Answer

I would definitely recommend this hotel to my colleagues

Subject (I) + would + adverb (definitely) + verb (recommend) + object. Watch the spelling too: definitely, recommend (one c, two m's), colleagues.

Exercise 12

Now say this line — pronounce each hard word clearly, in parts.

Answer

Say: It is necessary to separate the old receipts

Remember the parts: NE-ces-sa-ry, SEP-a-rate, re-CEIPT (the p is silent). Saying words in parts also fixes the spelling in your mind.

What to do next

Make a list called "my spellings" in your phone's notes. Whenever you misspell a word and spell-check catches it, add it to the list. By the end of the month, that list will be your most useful dictionary.

docs.title: Chapter 17: Subject-verb agreement
docs.text:
Subject-verb agreement — "He go" or "He goes"?

Agreement means a match — the subject and the verb must match. Hindi has this match too, but in a different way (ladka jaata hai / ladke jaate hain), so you already know the idea. There are only two trouble spots. First, in English the -s goes with the singular (it feels backwards!). Second, sometimes the real subject hides behind the words in between. This chapter clears up both for good.

In one line

A singular subject takes a singular verb; a plural subject takes a plural verb. One subject → a singular verb. Many subjects → a plural verb. And remember: an -s on a verb means singular.

docs.title: 17.1 The basic chart
docs.text:
Subject Present Simple be (present) be (past) have I go am was have You go are were have He / She / It goes is was has We go are were have They go are were have

The double trick of -s

An -s on a noun makes it plural: boy → boys. An -s on a verb makes it singular: go → goes. So in one sentence the -s goes either on the noun or on the verb — not on both. The boy runs ✓ The boys run ✓ The boys runs ✗

docs.title: 17.2 Find the real subject — words in between don't count
docs.text:
This is where most mistakes happen. A long phrase comes between the subject and the verb, and your brain takes the last word of that phrase as the subject. The trick: put an imaginary glass over the middle part and forget it.

Figure 17.1. Blue word = the real subject. Pink dotted box = the part that has no effect on the verb. Green arrow = what matches what.

None of these in-between words change the verb

of, with, along with, together with, as well as, including, besides, in addition to, accompanied by The minister, along with his officers, has arrived. The subject is "the minister" — one person. The "officers" make no difference.

docs.title: 17.3 Always singular — remember these
docs.text:
Subject Correct Wrong each Each boy has a book. Each boy have… every Every student was present. Every student were… everyone / everybody Everyone knows it. Everyone know it. someone / somebody Somebody is at the door. Somebody are… nobody / no one Nobody came. — anyone / anybody Does anybody know him? Do anybody know… either / neither (on their own) Neither is correct. Neither are correct. one of + plural One of my friends is a doctor. One of my friend is… the number of The number of cases is rising. The number of cases are… each of / every one of Each of the girls sings well. Each of the girls sing…

'one of my friend' — two mistakes at once

  • Wrong: One of my friend are coming today.
  • Right: One of my friends is coming today.
  • Why: Think: "one of my friends". "Friends" is plural, but the sentence is about one person — so the verb is singular (is). The same rule works for "one of the best players", "one of my sisters" and so on.

docs.title: 17.4 "A number of" vs "The number of"
docs.text: Phrase Meaning Verb Example a number of several, many plural A number of students are absent. the number of the count, the total singular The number of students is falling. a lot of / plenty of depends on the noun look at the noun A lot of water is wasted. · A lot of people are waiting. 50% of / half of depends on the noun look at the noun Half of the cake is gone. · Half of the boys are here.

docs.title: 17.5 Two subjects joined together — what then?
docs.text:
Joining word Rule Example and plural Ravi and Sita are friends. and (one single thing) singular Bread and butter is my breakfast. or / nor matches the nearer subject Ravi or his brothers are coming. either… or matches the nearer subject Either the boys or the teacher is wrong. neither… nor matches the nearer subject Neither the teacher nor the boys are wrong. not only… but also matches the nearer subject Not only the players but also the coach was blamed.

A smart tip

In either/or and neither/nor sentences, if you can, put the plural subject last. Then the verb is plural and the sentence sounds more natural. Neither the manager nor the workers were happy.

docs.title: 17.6 Collective nouns — one or many?
docs.text:
Team, family, class, committee, government, jury, staff — these are groups. When the group acts as one unit, use a singular verb; when the people in the group act separately, use a plural verb.

  • The team is playing well today. The whole team as one unit — singular.
  • The team are arguing among themselves. The members are arguing with each other — separate people, so plural.

Three words that are always plural

police, people, cattle — the verb is always plural with these. The police have arrested him. ✓ The police has arrested him. ✗ Many people were waiting. ✓

docs.title: 17.7 Looks plural, but is singular
docs.text:
Type Words Example Names of subjects mathematics, physics, economics, politics, statistics Mathematics is my favourite subject. Diseases measles, mumps, diabetes Measles is contagious. Reports news The news is good. Uncountable information, advice, furniture, luggage, work, money This information is useful. Distance, money, time — seen as one unit — Ten kilometres is a long walk. · Five hundred rupees is too much. Name of a book / film — "Three Idiots" is a great film.

And the opposite — looks singular, but is plural

scissors, trousers, jeans, spectacles, pliers, scales — things with two parts are plural: My spectacles are broken. But with "a pair of" the verb becomes singular: A pair of scissors is missing.

docs.title: 17.8 There is / There are
docs.text:
"There" is not the subject — the subject comes after it. So the verb matches the noun that comes after it.

  • There is a problem with the laptop. One problem — singular.
  • There are three problems in this file. Three problems — plural.

docs.title: 17.9 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
Top agreement mistakes

  • Wrong: He don't know my name.
  • Right: He doesn't know my name.

  • Why: With he/she/it we use "does". "Don't" is only for I, you, we, they.

  • Wrong: My parents is very supportive.

  • Right: My parents are very supportive.

  • Why: "Parents" is plural — are. For one person, say "My father is".

  • Wrong: Everyone have their own problems.

  • Right: Everyone has their own problems.

  • Why: "Everyone" looks like it means many people, but grammatically it is singular — has. (Using "their" afterwards is fine; it is normal English today.)

  • Wrong: The police is looking for him.

  • Right: The police are looking for him.

  • Why: "Police" is always plural. For one officer, say "a policeman is".

  • Wrong: Mathematics are difficult for me.

  • Right: Mathematics is difficult for me.

  • Why: Subjects that end in -s (mathematics, physics, economics) are singular.

  • Wrong: One of my cousin works in Dubai.

  • Right: One of my cousins works in Dubai.

  • Why: After "one of" the noun is plural, but the verb is singular. Remember both together.

  • Wrong: The list of items are on the table.

  • Right: The list of items is on the table.

  • Why: The subject is "the list" — one list. "Of items" is a phrase in between; remove it.

  • Wrong: My brother and I is going to Goa.

  • Right: My brother and I are going to Goa.
  • Why: Two subjects joined by "and" = plural. Also mind the order — "My brother and I", not "I and my brother".

Four steps, every time

1. Find the verb. 2. Ask "who or what?" — the answer is the subject. 3. Remove everything between the subject and the verb. 4. Now see whether the subject is one or many — and choose the verb to match.

docs.title: 17.10 Practice — Subject-verb agreement
docs.text:
Exercise 1

One of my cousins ___ in Canada.

  • live
  • lives
  • are living
  • have lived

Hint: How many people is the sentence about?

Answer

lives

'One of my cousins' means 'ONE of my cousins'. The sentence is about one person, so the verb is singular — lives.

Exercise 2

The box of chocolates ___ on the fridge.

  • are
  • is
  • were
  • have

Hint: What is the real subject — the box or the chocolates?

Answer

is

The subject is 'the box' — one box. 'Of chocolates' is a phrase in between; remove it and 'The box is' is left.

Exercise 3

Neither the principal nor the teachers ___ present.

  • was
  • were
  • is
  • has

Hint: Which subject is nearest to the verb?

Answer

were

With neither…nor, the verb matches the nearest subject. The nearest is 'the teachers' — plural, so 'were'.

Exercise 4

The police ___ already caught the thief.

  • has
  • have
  • is
  • was

Hint: Is 'police' singular or plural?

Answer

have

'Police' is always plural in English — have. For one officer we say 'a policeman has'.

Exercise 5

Every student ___ (have) a separate roll number.

Hint: Which form comes after 'every'?

Answer

has

'Every' and 'each' are always singular, however many people come after — so 'has'.

Exercise 6

There ___ two pens and a pencil in my bag.

Hint: What comes after 'There'?

Answer

are

'There' is not the subject — the noun after it is. 'Two pens' is plural, so 'are'.

Exercise 7

Mathematics ___ my favourite subject.

Hint: Ending in -s does not make a word plural.

Answer

is

Mathematics, physics, economics, politics end in -s but are singular, so 'is'.

Exercise 8

There is one mistake in this sentence — tap the wrong word.

My younger brother don't like sweets.

Answer

Wrong word: don't.

Corrected: My younger brother doesn't like sweets.

The subject 'my younger brother' = he. With he/she/it we use 'doesn't', not 'don't'.

Exercise 9

Find the wrong word.

One of my friend works in a bank.

Answer

Wrong word: friend.

Corrected: One of my friends works in a bank.

After 'one of' the noun is always plural — friends. The verb is still singular — works.

Exercise 10

One word is wrong — catch it.

The quality of these mangoes are very poor.

Answer

Wrong word: are.

Corrected: The quality of these mangoes is very poor.

The subject is 'the quality', one thing. Remove 'of these mangoes' and 'The quality is' is left.

Exercise 11

Match each subject with the correct verb.

A B Everyone is My parents are The news were My spectacles knows A number of boys know Answer

Everyone — knows; My parents — know; The news — is; My spectacles — are; A number of boys — were

Everyone is singular → knows. Parents is plural → know. News is singular → is. Spectacles is plural → are. 'A number of' is plural → were.

Exercise 12

Put the words in the correct order.

Words: this / thirty / number / class / is / of / in / The / students

Answer

The number of students in this class is thirty

'The number of' always takes a singular verb — is. 'A number of students' would take 'are'.

Exercise 13

Now say this line aloud — there are three agreements to handle.

Answer

Say: One of my friends has a shop and his brothers work there

'One of my friends' is singular → has. 'His brothers' is plural → work. Two kinds of agreement in one sentence — saying it aloud builds the habit.

What to do next

When you write, read your text once with your finger on the verbs only — stop at each verb and ask "who is its subject?". This one-minute check will catch 90% of your agreement mistakes by itself.

docs.title: Chapter 3: The eight parts of speech
docs.text:
The 8 parts of speech — the full map

English has hundreds of thousands of words, but only eight jobs. Every word goes into one of these eight boxes. The day these eight boxes make sense, you stop memorising grammar and start seeing it. This chapter is the map of the whole book; every other chapter opens one of these eight boxes.

In one line

A part of speech is the job a word does in a sentence. Not what the word is, but what it is doing in the sentence.

docs.title: 3.1 First, one sentence with all the jobs
docs.text:
Below is a short sentence that shows seven of the eight jobs together. Look at the colours — the same colours are used for the same jobs all through the book, so your eye will get used to them.

Noun

Pronoun

Verb

Adjective

Adverb

Preposition

Conjunction

Interjection

  • Wow! She quickly opened the old box under the bed, and we laughed. = What a surprise! She opened the old box under the bed in a hurry, and we laughed.
Figure 3.1. The map of the whole book. The sentence in the middle, eight jobs around it — and each job has its own colour.

docs.title: 3.2 The eight boxes, one line each
docs.text:
Type What it does Question to ask Example Noun The name of a thing, person, place or idea Who? What? My sister lives in Pune. Pronoun A word that takes the place of a noun Who is being talked about? She called me. Verb An action, a state of being, or a condition What is happening? Ravi reads every night. Adjective Tells you something about a noun What kind? How many? Which one? A heavy bag. Adverb Tells you about a verb, an adjective or another adverb How? When? Where? How much? He walks slowly. Preposition Shows how a noun is related to another word Where? When? How? The pen is on the desk. Conjunction Joins two words or two sentences What is it joined to? Tea or coffee? Interjection A sudden feeling What is the feeling? Oh! I forgot.

Split the eight into two groups

First, the four big players — noun, pronoun, verb, adjective — without them a sentence cannot be built. Then the four joiners and decorators — adverb, preposition, conjunction, interjection — they make a sentence better. The first four are the walls; the other four are the paint and the curtains.

docs.title: 3.3 One word, two jobs — this is the real game
docs.text:
The biggest misunderstanding is that a word is always one type. It is not. The sentence decides the job, not the word. Look — the same word "water" is sometimes a noun and sometimes a verb:

  • The water is cold. Here "water" is the name of a thing — a noun.
  • Please water the plants. Here "water" is an action — giving water — so it is a verb.
Word In one job In another job book noun — I lost my book. verb — Let's book the tickets. fast adjective — a fast car adverb — He runs fast. light noun — Switch on the light. adjective — This bag is light. before preposition — before lunch conjunction — Call me before you leave. that pronoun — That is mine. conjunction — I know that he came.

A three-step way to identify a word

1. Take the word out — does the sentence fall apart? If yes, the word is essential (noun / verb). 2. Ask what it is telling you about — a noun? Then it is an adjective. A verb? Then it is an adverb. 3. Is a noun coming right after it, and does it show place or time? Then it is a preposition.

docs.title: 3.4 Noun and Pronoun — the name and the name's shortcut
docs.text:
The noun is the foundation of every sentence. The pronoun is its shortcut, so that you don't have to say the same name again and again.

  • Repeated: Meera said Meera would bring Meera's books. It hurts the ear, doesn't it? That is why pronouns exist.
  • Clear: Meera said she would bring her books. The name once, then a pronoun — this is natural English.

docs.title: 3.5 Verb — the heart of the sentence
docs.text:
If you have to pick just one thing, pick the verb. No complete sentence can be made without a verb. A verb does three kinds of work:

What the verb is telling you Example Action — something is happening She writes poems. Being — existence He is a teacher. Condition — a state The soup tastes salty.

docs.title: 3.6 Adjective and Adverb — a confusing pair
docs.text:
People mix these two up a lot, but the difference is one line: an adjective touches a noun, an adverb touches a verb.

  • She is a careful driver. "careful" tells you what kind of driver she is — it is about a noun, so it is an adjective.
  • She drives carefully. "carefully" tells you how she drives — it is about a verb, so it is an adverb.

Careful — -ly is not always an adverb

friendly, lovely, costly, silly — these are all adjectives, even though they end in -ly. And fast, hard, late, early are adverbs without any -ly. So don't identify a word by its look — identify it by its job.

docs.title: 3.7 Preposition, Conjunction, Interjection — three small helpers
docs.text:
Preposition — the relationship

It comes before a noun and tells you place, time or manner. The keys are inside the drawer.

Conjunction — the glue

It joins two parts. I wanted tea, but there was no milk.

Interjection — a sudden feeling

It stands apart from the rest of the sentence, and often takes a !. Oh no! The bus has left.

What about articles? (a, an, the)

Some books treat a / an / the as a ninth type — the "determiner". In this book we keep them in the adjective family, because they too tell you something about a noun. They have a whole chapter of their own.

docs.title: 3.8 Break a sentence apart yourself
docs.text:
In the sentence below, the job of every word is written under it. First think for yourself, then match the colours.

Figure 3.2. Taking a normal sentence apart — this is how you start to see grammar.

docs.title: 3.9 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
Mistakes that come from choosing the wrong part of speech

  • Wrong: Myself Ravi.
  • Right: I am Ravi. / My name is Ravi.

  • Why: "Myself" is a reflexive pronoun — it can never take the place of the subject. When you introduce yourself you need a subject: I. This mistake comes from translating the Hindi "main Ravi" word for word.

  • Wrong: She drives very careful.

  • Right: She drives very carefully.

  • Why: "drives" is a verb, and a verb needs an adverb. An adjective (careful) only goes with a noun — a careful driver.

  • Wrong: He don't know the answer.

  • Right: He doesn't know the answer.

  • Why: "He" is third person singular, so the helping verb must be singular too — does. The verb has to agree with the subject; in Hindi this agreement is not so strict, so it gets missed.

  • Wrong: I need some informations.

  • Right: I need some information.

  • Why: "Information" is an uncountable noun — it has no plural. If you need to count, say two pieces of information.

  • Wrong: Let us discuss about this topic.

  • Right: Let us discuss this topic.

  • Why: "Discuss" does not need a preposition — the object comes straight after it. In Hindi we say "iske baare me baat karein" (talk about this), which is why "about" sneaks in.

  • Wrong: She is my cousin brother.

  • Right: He is my cousin.
  • Why: "Cousin" is a complete noun by itself — there is no need to add brother or sister. In English a cousin can be a boy or a girl.

docs.title: 3.10 A two-minute exercise
docs.text: Do this today: take any English sentence — from a newspaper, a YouTube caption, anywhere — and point at each word and say "noun… verb… adjective…". At first it will be slow. After a week it will start to happen by itself, and you will begin to spot your own mistakes while writing.

docs.title: 3.11 Practice — Parts of speech
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Which part of speech is 'quickly' in this sentence? — 'He quickly finished his homework.'

  • adverb
  • adjective
  • verb
  • noun

Hint: Ask: what is it telling you about?

Answer

adverb

'quickly' tells you the manner of finishing — so it is about the verb. A word that tells you about a verb is an adverb.

Exercise 2

'Please book two tickets.' — what is 'book' here?

  • verb
  • noun
  • adjective
  • preposition

Hint: Forget the word, look at the job.

Answer

verb

Here 'book' is an action — to reserve. The same word becomes a noun in 'I lost my book', because the sentence decides the part of speech, not the word.

Exercise 3

Which word takes the place of a noun?

  • pronoun
  • adverb
  • conjunction
  • interjection
Answer

pronoun

Pro + noun means 'in place of a noun'. That is why we say 'she' instead of repeating Meera.

Exercise 4

'I waited, but she never came.' — what is 'but'?

  • conjunction
  • preposition
  • adverb
  • pronoun
Answer

conjunction

'but' is joining two whole sentences, and joining is the job of a conjunction. If it were a preposition, a noun would come right after it.

Exercise 5

She is a ___ singer. (adjective form of 'beauty')

Hint: It tells you about the noun 'singer', so you need an adjective.

Answer

beautiful

A noun takes an adjective — beautiful singer. 'beautifully' is an adverb, and goes with a verb: she sings beautifully.

Exercise 6

He sings ___. (adverb form of 'beauty')

Hint: Now it is about the verb 'sings'.

Answer

beautifully

To tell you about a verb you need an adverb. That is why it is beautifully here, and beautiful with singer.

Exercise 7

One word in this sentence is the wrong part of speech — tap it.

She speaks English very fluent.

Answer

Wrong word: fluent.

Corrected: She speaks English very fluently.

'speaks' is a verb, so to tell you about it you need an adverb — fluently. 'fluent' is an adjective, and goes with a noun: fluent English.

Exercise 8

Find the wrong word.

Myself Ravi from Jaipur.

Answer

Wrong word: Myself.

Corrected: I am Ravi from Jaipur.

The reflexive pronoun 'myself' cannot be a subject — you need 'I'. This mistake comes from translating the Hindi 'main Ravi' word for word.

Exercise 9

Match each part of speech to its job.

A B Noun tells you about a noun Verb shows a noun's relationship Adjective a sudden feeling Preposition the name of a thing or person Interjection an action or being Answer

Noun — the name of a thing or person; Verb — an action or being; Adjective — tells you about a noun; Preposition — shows a noun's relationship; Interjection — a sudden feeling

Every word does one job, and that job is its part of speech. Once you get used to the colours, you will start to see it by yourself.

Exercise 10

Make the sentence in the right order — the normal order of article, adjective, noun, verb, adverb.

Words: The / old / walked / slowly / man

Answer

The old man walked slowly

The basic English order is: article + adjective + noun (the subject), then the verb, then the adverb. With the adverb after the verb, the sentence sounds natural.

Exercise 11

Which word is an adjective even though it ends in -ly?

  • friendly
  • quickly
  • slowly
  • loudly

Hint: Ask: does it go with a noun?

Answer

friendly

'friendly' tells you about a noun — a friendly dog — so it is an adjective. This is why you should identify words by their job, not by -ly.

Exercise 12

Now say this sentence aloud. Careful — say both l's in 'carefully' clearly.

Answer

Say: She drives carefully every day

When speaking, the adverb comes after the verb, so 'drives carefully' flows together. Saying 'careful' makes the English sound odd.

What next?

Keep this map in mind — in the next eight chapters we will open the boxes one by one. The next chapter is Noun, because every sentence starts there.

docs.title: Chapter 2: The sounds of English
docs.text:
English sounds — the ones Hindi doesn't have

English has 26 letters, but about 44 sounds. This is where all the trouble starts: we read the letters, and we assume that what is written is what we should say. In Hindi, that assumption works — you say what is written in Devanagari. In English, it doesn't. In this chapter we will work on the sounds that your tongue has never made until now — because Hindi never needed them.

In one line

Your pronunciation is not wrong because something is "missing" in you — it is wrong because your mouth has only learnt Hindi positions so far. Learn the new position, and the sound will come by itself. This is a skill, not luck. A muscle just needs to be taught.

docs.title: 2.1 Written ≠ spoken
docs.text:
First, listen to these three sets. The words look alike, but they sound completely different:

Words Listen What people wrongly say What it really is put / but both "ut" put = "puut", but = "bat" come / home both "ome" come = "kum", home = "hoam" though / through / tough all three "ough" the same tho, throo, taf — three different sounds

So, one rule

When you see a new word, first listen, then speak. Don't guess from the spelling. That is why every line in this book has a 🔊.

docs.title: 2.2 Eight sounds that Hindi doesn't have
docs.text:
These are the eight that make or break your pronunciation. For each one, the mouth position is written down — read it and try it right away. It is better if you have a mirror in front of you.

Sound Words Where to put your mouth Listen /θ/ TH without voice think, three, mouth Put the tip of your tongue just out between your upper and lower front teeth. Blow air out; no sound from the throat. It is not the Hindi "थ" — in that one the tongue stays behind the teeth. /ð/ TH with voice this, they, mother Same tongue position — between the teeth. But now add a buzz in the throat. Put a finger on your throat; you should feel it vibrate. /v/ very, van, love Put your upper teeth on your lower lip, and make a sound from the throat. The lips are not rounded. The teeth must touch. /f/ fan, phone, laugh Exactly the same position as /v/ — upper teeth on the lower lip — but no sound from the throat, only air. It is not the Hindi "फ"; that one uses both lips. /z/ zoo, buzz, is, was Make an /s/ — tongue behind the upper teeth, thin air — and add a buzz in the throat. Like the buzzing of a bee. /æ/ cat, man, bad Open your mouth wide, jaw down, as if showing your throat to a doctor. A sound between "अ" and "ऐ". It is not "कैट". /ə/ schwa about, doctor, sofa Leave your mouth completely relaxed and let out a light "uh". No effort at all. This is the most common sound in English — and the most ignored. /ʒ/ vision, measure, usual Make a "sh", then add a voice from the throat in the same position. "zh" — not like "झ", but a long, buzzing "sh".

docs.title: 2.3 Where is the tongue — a map of three positions
docs.text:
In Hindi, "त" puts the tongue behind the teeth, and "ट" touches the palate (the roof of the mouth). The English T is in between the two — on the raised ridge just behind the teeth. And TH goes out between the teeth. Look at this map:

Figure 2.1. The English T falls between the Hindi त and ट . That is why a T said like ट sounds heavy to a foreign ear, and a T said like त sounds a bit soft.

Try it now — 10 seconds

Say "टाइम". Then move your tongue slightly back and say "time". You will hear the difference clearly.

docs.title: 2.4 Short and long vowels — one mistake, a hundred words
docs.text:
In Hindi we know the difference between "इ" and "ई". English has the same difference, but the spelling doesn't show it — so we ignore it. The result: "ship" and "sheep" sound the same. A long vowel is not just longer; the mouth shape is also a little different.

Figure 2.2. Blue bar = short sound (ends quickly). Orange bar = long sound (stretched). The letters are the same, but the length changes the meaning.
  • The ship is big. / The sheep is big. = A boat is big / an animal is big. One small slip, and the meaning changes.
  • My glass is full. / He is a fool. = My glass is not empty / he is a silly person. Stretching "full" can be dangerous!

docs.title: 2.5 Schwa — the biggest secret of English
docs.text:
The most common sound in English is not a, e, i, o or u — it is /ə/ schwa: a completely relaxed, effortless "uh". A syllable that is not stressed almost disappears in English and turns into a schwa. We Indian speakers say every syllable in full — that is why our English sounds flat and a bit robotic.

Word What we say What it really is Listen doctor dok-TOR DOK-tuh (relaxed ending) about E-BAUT uh-BOWT (relaxed beginning) computer KOM-PYU-TAR kuhm-PYOO-tuh banana BA-NA-NA buh-NAA-nuh support SUP-PORT suh-PORT

The schwa rule

Don't say the unstressed part fully — swallow it. In a word only one part shines; the other parts stay in the background. There is a whole "Rhythm and stress" chapter on this — but start here.

docs.title: 2.6 Hindi habits that English catches immediately
docs.text:
Five habits, five cures

  • Wrong: "iskool", "istation", "ispeak"
  • Right: school, station, speak — straight from "s"

  • Why: Hindi words don't begin with two consonants, so we add an "i" in front. Cure: first say only "sssss", then add "kool" in the same breath — "sss-kool".

  • Wrong: "filim" (film), an extra sound inside "homewark"

  • Right: film — "l" and "m" together, nothing in between

  • Why: Between two consonants we slip in a small "i" without noticing. Say it slowly: "fi—lm".

  • Wrong: "wery" or "vindow" — mixing up V and W

  • Right: very (teeth on lip) / window (rounded lips)

  • Why: Hindi has one "व"; English has two different sounds. The full cure is in the next chapter.

  • Wrong: "is" with an "s" sound — buzz as "bus"

  • Right: is, was, buzz — with a buzz in the throat

  • Why: /z/ is not in Hindi, so we slip back to /s/. Put a finger on your throat and say "zzzz" — you should feel it vibrate.

  • Wrong: Giving every word equal stress — "I AM GO-ING TO MAR-KET"

  • Right: I'm GOing to the MARket — two words shine, the rest are relaxed
  • Why: English rhythm is uneven. Speaking in a flat, even way is the biggest "accent" that people notice.

docs.title: 2.7 Silent letters — written but not spoken
docs.text:
Silent letter Words Say Listen K (kn-) know, knife, knee no, naif, nee W (wr-) write, wrong, wrist rait, rong, rist B (-mb) comb, climb, thumb koam, klaim, tham L talk, walk, half, could tok, wok, haaf, kud T listen, castle, often lisun, kaasul, ofun H hour, honest, honour aawar, onist, onar

A small, sure gain

Just remembering these six lines will make an immediate difference to your speaking — because these words come up every day. In "I don't know" you don't say the K at all.

docs.title: 2.8 The daily 5-minute drill
docs.text:
Say these five lines once every day. All the new sounds come together in them:

  • I think these three things are true. The TH drill — "think/these/three/things" has two kinds of TH.
  • Very few of my friends have a van. V and F — in both, the upper teeth touch the lower lip.
  • The zoo was closed because of the rain. The /z/ drill — zoo, was, closed, because: all four have a buzz in the throat.
  • The school bus stops at the station. The "s" start drill — never "iskool", "istop", "istation".
  • The doctor asked about my computer. The schwa drill — DOK-tuh, uh-BOWT, kuhm-PYOO-tuh. Keep the unstressed parts relaxed.

docs.title: 2.9 Practice — English Sounds
docs.text:
Exercise 1
