How many sounds are there in English?

  • About 44
  • Exactly 26
  • About 33
  • Exactly 52

Hint: There are 26 letters — the sounds are more than that.

Answer

About 44

26 letters, but about 44 sounds. That is why guessing pronunciation from spelling is wrong.

Exercise 2

What happens in your mouth when you say /v/?

  • Upper teeth on the lower lip, buzz in the throat
  • Both lips rounded together
  • Tongue between the teeth
  • Tongue pressed to the palate

Hint: Where are the teeth?

Answer

Upper teeth on the lower lip, buzz in the throat

For /v/ the teeth must touch the lip. If you round your lips, it becomes /w/.

Exercise 3

What is the difference between the TH in 'think' and in 'this'?

  • 'this' has a buzz in the throat, 'think' does not
  • In 'this' the tongue stays behind
  • 'think' uses both lips
  • No difference, they are the same sound
Answer

'this' has a buzz in the throat, 'think' does not

The tongue position is the same in both — between the teeth. The only difference is voice: think = only air, this = buzz.

Exercise 4

Which is the most common sound in English?

  • Schwa /ə/ — a relaxed 'uh'
  • The long /iː/ as in 'sheep'
  • /t/
  • /æ/ as in 'cat'

Hint: The one that needs no effort from the mouth.

Answer

Schwa /ə/ — a relaxed 'uh'

Unstressed parts turn into a schwa: DOK-tuh, kuhm-PYOO-tuh. Saying every letter in full is what creates a 'flat' accent.

Exercise 5

Why do we say 'iskool' for 'school'?

  • Hindi words don't begin with two consonants
  • 'sch' means 'isk'
  • English speakers say it that way too
  • 's' is a silent letter
Answer

Hindi words don't begin with two consonants

The tongue adds a vowel in front for comfort. Cure: first stretch 'sss', then say 'kool' in the same breath.

Exercise 6

Remove the silent letter — which letter in 'know' is never spoken? ___

Hint: The first letter.

Answer

k / K

The K in kn- is always silent: know = no, knife = naif, knee = nee.

Exercise 7

Which letter is silent in 'listen'? ___

Answer

t / T

listen = li-sun. In the same way, castle = kaa-sul, and the T in 'often' is almost silent too.

Exercise 8

Match each sound to its mouth position.

A B /θ/ think both lips rounded, teeth don't touch /v/ very the /s/ position + a buzz in the throat /w/ wet tongue between the teeth, only air /z/ zoo upper teeth on the lower lip Answer

/θ/ think — tongue between the teeth, only air; /v/ very — upper teeth on the lower lip; /w/ wet — both lips rounded, teeth don't touch; /z/ zoo — the /s/ position + a buzz in the throat

Every sound is a position. Get the position right, and the sound comes right by itself.

Exercise 9

One word in this sentence is spelled wrongly — tap it.

I go to iskool every morning.

Answer

Wrong word: iskool.

Corrected: I go to school every morning.

'school' — straight from s. The extra 'i' sound in front is a Hindi habit, not English.

Exercise 10

The TH drill — slowly, with the tongue between the teeth.

Answer

Say: I think these three things are true

think and three have only air; these has a buzz. Both kinds of TH in one sentence.

Exercise 11

The V and F drill. Your teeth should be on the lower lip.

Answer

Say: Very few of my friends have a van

very, few, friends, have, van — the same teeth-and-lip position five times.

Exercise 12

Start with 's' — don't add 'i'.

Answer

Say: The school bus stops at the station

school, stops, station — all straight from s. Practise by stretching 'sss' first.

Exercise 13

The /z/ drill — a buzz in the throat.

Answer

Say: The zoo was closed because of the rain

zoo, was, closed, because — /z/ in all four. Keep a finger on your throat; it should vibrate.

Exercise 14

The schwa drill — leave the unstressed parts relaxed.

Answer

Say: The doctor asked about my computer

DOK-tuh, uh-BOWT, kuhm-PYOO-tuh. Don't try to say every letter in full.

What next?

This chapter is a foundation — don't try to "finish" it in one go. Come back twice a week and repeat the sounds in the tables. The next step: the Fix your pronunciation chapter, where you'll find separate drills and minimal pairs for each sound.

docs.title: Chapter 15: The twelve tenses
docs.text:
All 12 tenses — one map

People say "English has 12 tenses", and it sounds like twelve separate things to memorise. The truth is that the 12 tenses are not 12 things — they are just 3 × 4. Three times (past, present, future) and four aspects (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous). That's all. The day this 3 × 4 table settles in your head, the tension about tenses is over.

In one line

A tense tells you when the action happens and in what state it is — finished, going on, or completed before some point. A tense tells you two things: when the action happened, and what its state was at that time.

docs.title: 15.1 First understand this: 3 times × 4 aspects
docs.text:
Every action happens at some time — already gone (past), now (present), or still to come (future). That gives us three columns.

And in each time, the action can be in one of four states. These are the four rows, and this is the real magic:

State (aspect) Meaning Hindi feel Simple It just happened / happens / will happen. A single point, or a habit. "main gaya" (I went), "main jaata hoon" (I go) Continuous It was going on / is going on / will be going on at that time. "main jaa raha tha" (I was going) Perfect It was / is / will be complete before some point. "main jaa chuka tha" (I had already gone) Perfect Continuous It has been going on for a while, and it also tells you for how long. "main do ghante se jaa raha hoon" (I have been going for two hours)

How to read the name

The name of a tense is its formula. Read "Past Perfect Continuous" backwards: Continuous means -ing, Perfect means had/have, and Past means the helping verb is in the past form → had been + -ing. Once you can get the formula from the name, there is nothing to memorise.

docs.title: 15.2 The whole map — 12 tenses on a timeline
docs.text:
The picture below is the summary of this whole chapter. Look at it carefully once: time runs from left to right, and the orange line in the middle is NOW. In each box, look at the small timeline to see where the action sits — on a point, stretched like a line, or finished before a point.

Figure 15.1. Filled circle = the point of the action. Thick line = the action is going on. Empty circle = the other point before which the action finished. Orange dotted line = NOW.

Past

Present

Future

docs.title: 15.3 The four forms of a verb — the fuel for the whole machine
docs.text:
To make tenses you need only four things. They are called V1, V2, V3 and V-ing. If you know these four forms, the 12 tenses build themselves.

Form Name write go eat play V1 base form write go eat play V1-s he/she/it form writes goes eats plays V2 past form wrote went ate played V3 past participle written gone eaten played V-ing present participle writing going eating playing Figure 15.2. BE, HAVE and WILL — three helping verbs. The order you join them in makes the tense. The order is always: will → have → been → V-ing .

docs.title: 15.4 All twelve formulas in one table
docs.text:
Everything is in one place here. Write it out once and stick it on the wall — in two weeks you will know it.

Tense Formula Example Use Present Simple V1 / V1-s She writes letters. habits and facts Present Continuous am/is/are + V-ing She is writing a letter. happening right now Present Perfect have/has + V3 She has written the letter. done, with a result now Present Perfect Cont. have/has been + V-ing She has been writing for an hour. still going on, for how long Past Simple V2 She wrote a letter. finished at a known past time Past Continuous was/were + V-ing She was writing a letter. in progress at a past time Past Perfect had + V3 She had written it before I came. done before another past event Past Perfect Cont. had been + V-ing She had been writing since morning. going on for a while before a past point Future Simple will + V1 She will write a letter. decisions and promises Future Continuous will be + V-ing She will be writing at 5 pm. in progress at a future time Future Perfect will have + V3 She will have written it by Monday. done before a future deadline Future Perfect Cont. will have been + V-ing She will have been writing for two hours. going on for a while up to a future point

docs.title: 15.5 The four present tenses — up close
Present Simple — habits and facts
docs.text:
This tense is not for "right now". It is for habits, routines, and things that are always true. This is the biggest source of confusion.

  • I catch the 8 o'clock bus every day. = Every day, I take the 8 o'clock bus. — a daily habit.
  • Water boils at 100 degrees. = It is always true that water boils at 100 degrees. — a fact.
  • He does not like coffee. = Coffee is not something he enjoys. — in the negative it is "does not + V1", not "likes".

The -s is only for he / she / it

I write · you write · he writes · we write · they write. And as soon as do/does or a modal appears, the -s goes away: He does not write**, not "does not writes".

docs.title: Present Continuous — right now, at this moment
docs.text:
• I am reading this chapter right now. = At this moment, I am reading this chapter.
  • We are moving to Pune next month. = The move to Pune next month is already arranged. — for a firm plan, it can be used for the future too.

Some verbs don't go into -ing

  • Wrong: I am having a car.
  • Right: I have a car.

  • Why: When have means "own", it doesn't take -ing. But when it means "eat/do", it does: I am having lunch — that is perfectly fine. Other verbs like this: know, understand, like, want, need, believe, belong, see (meaning "look").

  • Wrong: I am knowing him since childhood.

  • Right: I have known him since childhood.
  • Why: "Know" is a state, not an action — so no -ing.

docs.title: Present Perfect — done, but no time is given
docs.text:
The biggest rule of Present Perfect: it never goes with a past time. If you are saying "yesterday", "last week" or "in 2019", you need Past Simple.

  • I have finished my homework. = My homework is done now. — when I did it is not part of the meaning.
  • She has just left. = She left a moment ago. — it just happened, and the effect is fresh.
  • I have never seen snow. = In my whole life, I have not seen snow. — life experience.

docs.title: Present Perfect Continuous — "for how long"
docs.text:
Use this tense when you want to say for how long something has been going on. And this is the tense where Indian speakers make their biggest mistake.

'since three years' — the most common mistake

  • Wrong: I am working here since three years.
  • Right: I have been working here for three years.
  • Why: There are two mistakes here. (1) When an action started in the past and is still going on, you need have been + -ing, not am working. (2) for = how long (three years), since = starting from when (2022, Monday, morning).

docs.title: 15.6 The four past tenses
docs.text:
When to use it Tense Example A finished action, with a known time Past Simple I met him yesterday. A long background action in the past, interrupted by something Past Continuous I was cooking when he called. Two past actions — the one that happened first Past Perfect The train had left before we reached. How long something had been going on up to a past point Past Perfect Cont. She had been waiting for an hour.

The Past Continuous + Past Simple pair

When telling a story, this pair comes up again and again: the long action in Continuous, the sudden one in Simple. I was crossing the road when the bike hit me. = I was in the middle of crossing the road, and then a bike hit me.

docs.title: 15.7 The four future tenses
docs.text:
English has several ways to talk about the future, and not all of them use "will". This difference shows up clearly in fluency.

Form When Example will + V1 A decision made now, a promise, a prediction OK, I will help you. be going to A plan made earlier, or a result you can already see coming I am going to start a shop. am/is/are + V-ing A firm, scheduled arrangement I am meeting her at six. will be + V-ing In progress at a later time At nine I will be travelling. will have + V3 Complete before a deadline By May I will have finished it.

No future in a time clause

After when, if, after, before, until, as soon as, "will" doesn't come — even if you are talking about the future. I will call you when I reach home. "when I will reach" is wrong. Use will only once in a sentence.

docs.title: 15.8 Signal words — words that reveal the tense
docs.text:
Some words almost always go with one tense. In exams and in speaking, this shortcut is very useful.

If you see these words Tense every day, usually, often, always, never, generally Present Simple now, right now, at the moment, look!, listen! Present Continuous just, already, yet, ever, never, so far, recently Present Perfect for + duration, since + point, how long, all day Perfect Continuous yesterday, last night, ago, in 2019, then Past Simple while, at that time, all evening Past Continuous before, after, by the time, already (in the past) Past Perfect tomorrow, next week, soon, in future Future Simple by Monday, by then, by the end of… Future Perfect

docs.title: 15.9 The tense mistakes we really make
docs.text:
Top tense mistakes — and the right forms

  • Wrong: Yesterday I have gone to the market.
  • Right: Yesterday I went to the market.

  • Why: "Yesterday" is a definite past time. Present Perfect never goes with a past time — there you need Past Simple (V2).

  • Wrong: He don't know the answer.

  • Right: He doesn't know the answer.

  • Why: With he/she/it use does. And after does the verb has no -s: "doesn't know", not "doesn't knows".

  • Wrong: I am working here since 2019.

  • Right: I have been working here since 2019.

  • Why: Started in the past + still going on = have/has been + V-ing.

  • Wrong: If I will get the job, I will shift to Mumbai.

  • Right: If I get the job, I will shift to Mumbai.

  • Why: After "if" use the present; "will" goes in the main clause. Never in both.

  • Wrong: I am having two brothers.

  • Right: I have two brothers.

  • Why: Relationships and possessions are expressed with "have", not "am having".

  • Wrong: She did not came to class.

  • Right: She did not come to class.

  • Why: did has already done the work of the past — so the verb stays in V1.

  • Wrong: I will tell you when he will come.

  • Right: I will tell you when he comes.

  • Why: In a time clause (when/after/before/until) there is no future — the present is used.

  • Wrong: He has came home.

  • Right: He has come home.
  • Why: After have/has/had you always need V3, not V2. come-came-come, go-went-gone, see-saw-seen.

Three rules that save 80% of mistakes

1. If you see a past time (yesterday, ago, last…) → V2, not have/has. 2. After have/has/had → V3. After do/does/did → V1. 3. Only one "will" per sentence — never in the if/when part.

docs.title: 15.10 Practice — All 12 tenses
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Yesterday she ___ a new phone.

  • has bought
  • bought
  • have bought
  • is buying

Hint: A definite past time is given.

Answer

bought

'Yesterday' is a past time, and Present Perfect doesn't go with a past time — so use plain V2, 'bought'.

Exercise 2

Look! The baby ___ .

  • cries
  • cried
  • is crying
  • has cried

Hint: 'Look!' means right now, at this moment.

Answer

is crying

Words like Look! / Listen! / right now mean the action is going on at this moment — so Present Continuous.

Exercise 3

By next March, I ___ in this company for five years.

  • will work
  • will be working
  • will have been working
  • am working

Hint: How long, up to a deadline in the future.

Answer

will have been working

To say how long something has gone on up to a future point, use Future Perfect Continuous — will have been + V-ing.

Exercise 4

The film ___ before we reached the hall.

  • started
  • has started
  • had started
  • was starting

Hint: Two past actions — which one happened first?

Answer

had started

With two past actions, the one that happened first takes Past Perfect (had + V3). The film started first; we arrived later.

Exercise 5

She ___ (go) to the gym every morning.

Hint: 'every morning' = a habit.

Answer

goes

A habit takes Present Simple, and with 'she' the verb gets -s — goes.

Exercise 6

I ___ been waiting here since four o'clock.

Hint: Which helping verb goes with I?

Answer

have

Use 'have' with I/you/we/they and 'has' with he/she/it. The action started earlier and is still going on, so it is have been + -ing.

Exercise 7

He didn't ___ (come) to the office yesterday.

Hint: didn't has already shown the past.

Answer

come

After 'did / didn't' the verb stays in V1 — not 'didn't came' but 'didn't come'.

Exercise 8

There is one mistake in this sentence — tap the wrong word.

Yesterday I have gone to the market with my mother.

Answer

Wrong word: have.

Corrected: Yesterday I went to the market with my mother.

There is a past time (yesterday), so the Present Perfect 'have' is wrong — plain 'went' is needed.

Exercise 9

Find the wrong word.

My father is having an old scooter.

Answer

Wrong word: having.

Corrected: My father has an old scooter.

When 'have' means 'own', it doesn't take -ing. 'Having lunch' is fine; 'having a scooter' is not.

Exercise 10

One word is wrong — spot it.

Please call me when you reached the station.

Answer

Wrong word: reached.

Corrected: Please call me when you reach the station.

The time is in the future, so the past 'reached' is wrong. After 'when' we use the simple present — 'when you reach'.

Exercise 11

Put the words in the right order — a Past Continuous and Past Simple pair.

Words: off / the / went / a / when / lights / book / reading / was / I

Answer

I was reading a book when the lights went off

The long, ongoing action goes in Past Continuous (was reading), and the sudden one in Past Simple (went off). This is the usual order for telling a story.

Exercise 12

Match each tense to its use.

A B I write done, with a result now I am writing finished before another past action I have written going on for a while, still now I had written a habit or a permanent fact I have been writing going on right now Answer

I write — a habit or a permanent fact; I am writing — going on right now; I have written — done, with a result now; I had written — finished before another past action; I have been writing — going on for a while, still now

Simple = a point or a habit. Continuous = going on. Perfect = complete. Perfect Continuous = how long it has been going on.

Exercise 13

Now say this line aloud — join 'have been' without a pause.

Answer

Say: I have been learning English for two years

In speech, 'have been' sounds almost like 'hav-bin'. And remember — it is 'for two years', not 'since two years'.

What to do next

Start a small habit today: write three sentences about yourself each day — one past, one present, one future. Then change them into continuous and perfect. In a week the 12 tenses won't be something to memorise; they'll be something you feel.

docs.title: Chapter 38: Topic words: daily life
docs.text:
Everyday topics — health, money, shopping, travel, home

You know the grammar, but your mind goes blank when you have to say "my throat is sore" in English at the chemist? This chapter gives you the words and full sentences for five everyday topics — health, money and banks, shopping and returns, travel, and home repairs. Each topic has a table, some ready-made lines, a mini-dialogue, and the Indian English mistakes we really make. Every line has a 🔊 — listen and say it along.

docs.title: 38.1 Remember chunks, not single words
docs.text:
Learning the single word "fever" is not enough — you need the whole chunk: I've got a fever. That is why every word in this chapter comes with a chunk (a short sentence). When the time comes to speak, your brain doesn't have to join anything together; the chunk simply comes out.

Figure 38.1. Five topics, with five to ten chunks each. Together they cover about 80% of everyday conversation.

The chunk rule

Always learn a word together with its partner words: a sore throat, make a payment, a connecting flight, the tap is leaking. There is a whole chapter on fixed pairs: Which word goes with which.

This chapter is about words. For full conversations with a doctor, a shopkeeper and an auto driver, see Everyday conversations, and for saying numbers like ₹1,25,000, see Number, date, time, paise.

docs.title: 38.2 Health and doctors — describing a problem in English
docs.text:
The first thing to tell a doctor or chemist is what the problem is. English has two easy patterns: I've got a … (British, spoken) or I have a … (correct everywhere). And for a feeling in the whole body: I feel …

In Hindi In English Note Gala kharab / gale me dard I've got a sore throat. sore = painful Bukhaar hai I've got a fever / a temperature. "temperature" is common in the UK Sar dard I've got a headache. don't forget "a" Zukaam, naak beh rahi I've got a cold / a runny nose. a blocked nose = naak band Khaansi I've got a cough. dry cough = a cough without phlegm Chakkar aa rahe I feel dizzy. feel + adjective Ulti jaisa lag raha I feel sick. US: nauseous Pet kharab I've got an upset stomach. loose motions = diarrhoea Kamzori I feel weak and tired. — Pair mud gaya (moch) I've sprained my ankle. sprain = a twisted joint Khujli, daane I've got an itchy rash. rash = red spots on the skin
  • I've got a sore throat and a slight fever. = My throat hurts and I have a mild fever.
  • I've had a temperature since Monday. = I have had a fever since Monday. (Use I've had with "since".)
  • I feel dizzy every time I stand up. = Whenever I stand up, my head spins.
  • My back hurts when I bend down. = Bending down gives me back pain. The verb for pain is hurt.

docs.title: At the chemist — getting medicine
docs.text:
In India we say "medical store", and everyone here understands it. In British English it is a chemist or a pharmacy; in American English a drugstore. A note written by a doctor = a prescription; medicine you can get without one is over the counter.

  • Can you suggest something for a sore throat? = Asking the chemist to recommend something for your throat.
  • Do I need a prescription for this? = Can I buy this without a doctor's note?
  • What's the dose for a ten-year-old? = How much medicine should a ten-year-old child take?
  • Does it have any side effects? Will it make me sleepy? = Are there any unwanted effects? Will I feel drowsy?

Mini-dialogue — at the chemist's

Situation: you have had a cough for two days. You are at the chemist's.

  • You: Hi. Can you give me something for a cough? = State the problem directly — "something for a …".
  • Chemist: Is it a dry cough, or is there phlegm? = phlegm (flem) is the thick mucus from your chest.
  • You: It's dry. And my throat's a bit sore. = "a bit" means "a little" — very common in speech.
  • Chemist: Try this syrup. Two spoons, three times a day, after meals. = Take it three times each day, after eating.
  • You: Great, thanks. How much is it? = Asking the price.

✗

I am having fever since two days.

✓

I've had a fever for two days.

have / have got

a fever

for

I've had

✗

My stomach is paining.

✓

My stomach hurts. / I've got a stomach ache.

hurt

…ache

docs.title: 38.3 Money and banks — from an account to UPI
docs.text:
Banking English doesn't need many words, just the right partner for each: you withdraw money, deposit it, transfer it, and make a payment — not "do" a payment.

Word Meaning Partner / example account your record of money at a bank open a savings account balance how much money is in the account check your balance deposit to put money in deposit cash withdraw to take money out withdraw ₹2,000 from an ATM transfer to move money from one account to another transfer money to a friend loan money you borrow and pay back take out / repay a loan interest the extra money charged (or earned) on money an interest rate of 9% EMI a fixed instalment paid every month pay an EMI of ₹8,500 credited / debited money came in / went out ₹500 was debited statement a list of all transactions download a bank statement
  • I need to withdraw some cash. Is there an ATM nearby? = I want to take out some cash. Is there a cash machine close by?
  • My salary is credited on the first of every month. = My salary reaches my account on the 1st of each month.
  • The interest rate on this loan is nine per cent a year. = The loan charges 9% interest every year. (UK: per cent; US: percent.)
  • Money was debited from my account, but the payment failed. = The money left my account, but the payment didn't go through. (The first line of a bank complaint.)

docs.title: EMI and UPI — explaining them to a foreigner
docs.text:
We say both of these words every day in India, but people abroad don't know them. If you ever have to explain, keep these lines ready:

  • An EMI is a fixed amount you pay every month to repay a loan, including the interest. = EMI stands for Equated Monthly Instalment — the same amount each month, interest included.
  • UPI is a system that lets you send money instantly from your phone, straight from one bank account to another. = UPI stands for Unified Payments Interface — instant bank-to-bank payment from a phone.
  • You just scan the QR code, enter the amount and your PIN, and it's done. = Three simple steps: scan, enter the amount and PIN, finished.
  • Can I pay by UPI, or is it cash only? = Do you accept UPI, or only cash? (pay by card / UPI / cheque, pay in cash.)

pay by, pay in

To name the method, use pay by card / UPI / cheque, and for cash pay in cash (or just pay cash). Don't say "I'll pay from card" — say "I'll pay by card."

✗

Please do the payment by Friday.

✓

Please make the payment by Friday.

make

Please pay by Friday.

✗

Do you have change of 500?

✓

Do you have change for a 500-rupee note?

change for

docs.title: 38.4 Shopping and returns — fit, exchange, refund
docs.text:
Trying on clothes in a shop, changing a size, sending an online order back — ten or twelve words cover all of these. The most important verb is fit: whether clothes are the right size.

Word Meaning Example try on to wear something to see how it looks Can I try this on? fitting room the room for trying on clothes (trial room) Where's the fitting room? fit to be the right size It doesn't fit. suit to look good on you (colour, style) Blue really suits you. receipt the paper that proves you paid Keep the receipt. exchange to swap for something else Can I exchange it? refund money given back I'd like a refund. out of stock none left in the shop It's out of stock. on sale sold at a lower price These are on sale.
  • Do you have this in a bigger size? = Is there a larger size of this?
  • Do you have it in any other colour? = Does it come in a different colour? (UK: colour, US: color.)
  • The jacket fits well, but the colour doesn't really suit me. = The size is right, but the colour doesn't look good on me.
  • What's your return policy? = What are your rules for returning things?
  • The parcel arrived damaged, so I'd like to return it. = The parcel came broken, so I want to send it back. (A line for online returns.)
  • When will I get my refund? = When will my money come back?

Mini-dialogue — the return counter

Situation: you bought a shirt yesterday and found it too small at home.

  • You: Hi, I bought this shirt yesterday, but it's too tight. = When you bought it + what the problem is.
  • Staff: No problem. Would you like to exchange it or get a refund? = Do you want a swap or your money back?
  • You: I'd like to exchange it for a large, please. = exchange X for Y.
  • Staff: Sure. Do you have the receipt? = receipt — the "p" is silent: ri-SEET.
  • You: Yes, here you go. = Said when you hand something over — "here it is".

✗

This shirt is not fitting me. Give one size big.

✓

This shirt doesn't fit. Could I try a size bigger?

fit

it fits / it doesn't fit

Could I try…?

✗

I want to return back this phone.

✓

I'd like to return this phone.

return

docs.title: 38.5 Travel — from booking to the platform
docs.text:
Whether by train or flight, a journey follows a straight line: book, check in, board, arrive. Each step has its own words — and so do the problems: delayed, cancelled, missed.

Figure 38.2. The words on top = the steps (verb or noun). The words below = the short phrase you will hear or say at that step. Word Meaning Example book (verb) to reserve a ticket I booked a seat. one-way / return one direction / there and back a return ticket boarding pass the paper (or phone pass) to get on the plane Show your boarding pass. board to get on a plane, train or ship Boarding starts at 6:40. delayed late The flight is delayed. connecting flight a second flight that continues your journey I have a connecting flight. layover a stop between two flights a three-hour layover platform the place where you board a train It leaves from platform 5. waitlisted WL — your seat is not yet confirmed My ticket is waitlisted.
  • Which platform does the Shatabdi leave from? = Asking which platform the Shatabdi train departs from.
  • The train is running forty minutes late. = The train is 40 minutes behind schedule.
  • My flight was delayed, and I missed my connecting flight. = My first flight was late, so I couldn't catch the next one.
  • Could I have a window seat, please? = A polite request for a seat by the window. (aisle seat = next to the walkway)
  • Is this flight on time? = Is the flight running as scheduled?

Mini-dialogue — the airport check-in counter

Situation: Pune to Delhi, then Delhi to Guwahati.

  • Staff: Good morning. May I see your ID and booking, please? = Please show your identity proof and your booking.
  • You: Here you are. I have a connecting flight to Guwahati. = Mention the onward flight early.
  • Staff: Your bag will be checked through to Guwahati. Boarding is at gate 9. = Your bag will go straight to Guwahati.
  • You: The layover is only fifty minutes. Is that enough? = The gap between flights is only 50 minutes — is that enough time?

✗

I will get down at Pune.

✓

I'll get off at Pune.

get off

get on

get in / get out of

✗

My flight got preponed to 6 am.

✓

My flight has been moved earlier / brought forward to 6 am.

Indian English habits

docs.title: 38.6 Home and repairs — something has broken
docs.text:
A tap is dripping, the lights have gone out, the AC isn't cooling — when you tell your landlord, plumber or society office, the pattern is simple: the thing + what is happening. The tap is leaking. The fan isn't working.

Problem (in Hindi) In English Who to call Nal tapak raha The tap is leaking. plumber Naali band The drain is blocked. plumber Bijli chali gayi The power's gone. / There's a power cut. — Fuse ud gaya A fuse has blown. electrician Plug point kharab The socket isn't working. electrician AC thanda nahi The AC isn't cooling. AC technician Deewar me seelan There's damp on the wall. landlord Darwaza atak raha The door is stuck. carpenter
  • The kitchen tap has been leaking since last night. = The kitchen tap started dripping last night and still is. (US: faucet)
  • The power's gone again. Is it just our building? = The electricity has failed again. Is it only in our building?
  • Could you turn on the fan, please? = A polite request to switch the fan on. (turn on / switch on — both are fine)
  • We need to get the geyser fixed before winter. = We must have the geyser repaired (by someone) before winter. ("get something fixed" — see Powerful sentences.)
  • The rent includes maintenance, but not electricity. = Maintenance is covered by the rent; the electricity bill is separate.

Mini-dialogue — phoning the landlord

Situation: the bathroom tap has been leaking for a day.

  • You: Hi Mr Sharma, it's Neha from flat 302. The bathroom tap is leaking quite badly. = Who you are + what the problem is. "quite badly" = fairly seriously.
  • Landlord: Oh, sorry about that. I'll send a plumber tomorrow morning. = A plumber will come tomorrow morning.
  • You: Thanks. Could he come before ten? I leave for work at half past ten. = Fix the time — with a polite question.

✗

Please on the fan and off the light.

✓

Please turn on the fan and turn off the light.

on / off

turn on / switch on

turn off / switch off

✗

Light has gone.

✓

The power's gone. / There's a power cut.

power

electricity

docs.title: 38.7 Small but common mistakes — and what next
docs.text:
Some words don't belong to one topic but come up in everyday talk — family, taking leave from work, being out of the house. These are the three you will hear most.

✗

He is my cousin brother.

✓

He's my cousin.

cousin

my cousin, Rahul

my male cousin

my brother

✗

The doctor gave me a medicine for three days.

✓

The doctor gave me some medicine / some tablets for three days.

medicine

some medicine

tablets, capsules

✗

I have less balance in my account.

✓

My balance is low. / I don't have enough money in my account.

low / high

not enough

low balance

Your topic, your list

For each topic, make a note on your phone: 5 chunks you will say this week. Going to the chemist? Say the first 3 lines aloud, then go. A word you don't use is forgotten in two weeks. A word you have spoken stays.

docs.title: 38.8 Practice — Everyday topics
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Doctor: What seems to be the problem? You: I've got a sore ___.

  • throat
  • neck
  • voice
  • mouth

Hint: Your throat hurts.

Answer

throat

Pain in the throat = a sore throat. Neck is the outside of the body.

Exercise 2

I've ___ a fever since last night.

Hint: since + present perfect; the third form of have.

Answer

had

It is still going on and there is 'since' → I've had a fever since last night.

Exercise 3

Tap the wrong word.

My head is paining since morning.

Answer

Wrong word: paining.

Corrected: I've had a headache since morning.

For pain use 'hurt' or '...ache': My head hurts / I've got a headache.

Exercise 4

Match each banking word to its meaning.

A B withdraw a fixed monthly instalment deposit extra money charged on a loan EMI take money out interest put money in Answer

withdraw — take money out; deposit — put money in; EMI — a fixed monthly instalment; interest — extra money charged on a loan

withdraw = take out, deposit = put in, EMI = monthly instalment, interest = the extra charge on money.

Exercise 5

Do you have change ___ a 500-rupee note?

  • for
  • of
  • to
  • in
Answer

for

To break a note we say 'change for': change for a 500-rupee note.

Exercise 6

One word is wrong — find it.

Please do the payment by Friday.

Answer

Wrong word: do.

Corrected: Please make the payment by Friday.

The partner of payment is 'make': make a payment.

Exercise 7

This shirt doesn't ___. Do you have it in a bigger size?

Hint: Being the right size.

Answer

fit

Use 'fit' for size; use 'suit' when colour or style looks good on you.

Exercise 8

Why do the passengers have to wait?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Attention please. Flight 452 to Kolkata is delayed by forty minutes. The new departure time is seven fifteen pm. Passengers are requested to wait near gate twelve.

  • The flight is delayed
  • The flight is cancelled
  • The gate has changed
  • Boarding has started
Answer

The flight is delayed

'is delayed by forty minutes' = forty minutes late.

Exercise 9

What is the new departure time?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Attention please. Flight 452 to Kolkata is delayed by forty minutes. The new departure time is seven fifteen pm. Passengers are requested to wait near gate twelve.

  • 7:15 pm
  • 6:35 pm
  • 7:50 pm
  • 6:15 pm
Answer

7:15 pm

'seven fifteen pm' = 7:15 pm.

Exercise 10

Leaving a train: 'I'll get ___ at Pune.'

  • off
  • down
  • out
  • away
Answer

off

Train, bus, plane: get on / get off. Car, auto: get in / get out of.

Exercise 11

Where is the mistake?

Please on the fan, it is very hot.

Answer

Wrong word: on.

Corrected: Please turn on the fan, it's very hot.

'on' is not a verb on its own — turn on / switch on.

Exercise 12

The electricity has failed — which is natural English?

  • There's a power cut.
  • Light has gone.
  • Current is not there.
  • Electric went off.
Answer

There's a power cut.

Electricity for the whole house = power: There's a power cut / The power's gone.

Exercise 13

How many times a day should the syrup be taken?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Can you suggest something for a cough? Is it a dry cough? Yes, and my throat is a bit sore. Try this syrup. Two spoons, three times a day. If it doesn't get better in three days, please see a doctor.

  • Three times a day
  • Twice a day
  • Once at night
  • Every three hours
Answer

Three times a day

'Two spoons, three times a day' — two spoonfuls, three times each day.

Exercise 14

What should you do if it doesn't get better in three days?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Can you suggest something for a cough? Is it a dry cough? Yes, and my throat is a bit sore. Try this syrup. Two spoons, three times a day. If it doesn't get better in three days, please see a doctor.

  • See a doctor
  • Buy a new syrup
  • Take four spoons
  • Come back to the shop
Answer

See a doctor

'please see a doctor' — go and consult a doctor.

Exercise 15

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

The kitchen tap is leaking. Could you send a plumber today?

tap = the water outlet, leaking = dripping; 'Could you…?' is a polite request.

Exercise 16

Put the words in order.

Words: a / I / to / would / like / it / exchange / large / for

Answer

I would like to exchange it for a large

exchange X for Y — 'I would like to' is a polite opening.

Exercise 17

What is the natural way to say 'He is my cousin brother'?

  • He's my cousin.
  • He's my cousin-brother.
  • He's my brother cousin.
  • He's my real cousin brother.
Answer

He's my cousin.

In English 'cousin' covers both — don't add brother/sister.

Exercise 18

Now try saying it to the chemist.

Answer

Say: I've had a sore throat since yesterday

I've had + since — a problem that is still going on.

What to read next

Now the words of the office and the wider world: Work and the world. And to use these words in full conversations, go back to Everyday conversations.

docs.title: Chapter 39: Topic words: work & world
docs.text:
Work and the world — office, technology, environment, news

You hear "stakeholder" and "deliverable" in meetings, "inflation" and "emissions" in the news, and you need the same words in an IELTS essay. This chapter gives you the words for four big topics — but not on their own. With each word you get its family (economy, economic, economical) and its partner (meet a deadline, reduce emissions). These two things are what turn B1 into B2–C1.

docs.title: 39.1 One word, a whole family, fixed partners
docs.text:
At B2–C1 level you are not only asked what a word means — you are expected to know whether it is a noun or an adjective, and which verb goes with it. When you learn one word, learn its four or five forms along with it.

Figure 39.1. One root, six forms. Each form has its own partner — economic growth, but an economical car. (US spelling: economize.)

Three questions for every new word

(1) What is its family? (2) Which verb or adjective goes with it? (3) What would be my own sentence? For prefixes and suffixes see One word, ten words, and for partners see Which word goes with which.

docs.title: 39.2 Office and meetings
docs.text:
Before a meeting there is an agenda, during it a discussion, afterwards minutes and action items, and then everyone's follow-up — until the deadline arrives. It is a cycle.

Figure 39.2. The whole journey of a meeting — each word with its verb: circulate the agenda, take the minutes, meet the deadline. Word Meaning Fixed partner agenda the list of topics for a meeting set / circulate the agenda minutes the written record of a meeting take / share the minutes deadline the last date or time meet / miss / extend a deadline follow up (v) / follow-up (n) to check or act again later follow up on the order stakeholder a person with an interest in the work key stakeholders deliverable something you must hand over agree on the deliverables priority what comes first a top priority · prioritise escalate to take a problem to a higher level escalate an issue delegate to give a task to someone else delegate a task to someone bandwidth (spoken) time and energy to take on work I don't have the bandwidth.
  • I'll circulate the agenda by Monday evening. = I'll send the agenda to everyone by Monday evening.
  • We're on track to meet the deadline. = We will finish in time. (on track = going as planned)
  • Could we extend the deadline to Friday? = Can we move the deadline later, to Friday?
  • I'll follow up with the vendor and update everyone. = I'll check with the supplier and tell everyone the result.
  • We need sign-off from all the key stakeholders. = All the important people must approve it. (sign-off = final approval)
  • If the client doesn't reply by Wednesday, let's escalate it. = If there's no answer by Wednesday, we'll raise it with senior people.

follow up or follow-up?

Verb = two words: I'll follow up tomorrow. Noun / adjective = with a hyphen: a follow-up email, a quick follow-up. The same rule applies to log in / login, set up / setup, back up / backup. An action = two words; the name of a thing = one word.

✗

I will do the follow up and revert back.

✓

I'll follow up and get back to you.

follow up

Indian English habits

✗

We must finish before deadline.

✓

We must meet the deadline. / We must finish before the deadline.

deadline

meet the deadline

The lines to say in a meeting (interrupting, agreeing, taking on work) are in Interview and office — here we only cover words.

docs.title: 39.3 Technology
docs.text:
We say most tech words in English already, so the mistakes are not in the word but in the verb and preposition: log in to the app, download **from, upload to**.

Word Meaning Partner download / upload copy to your device / copy to the internet upload a file to the drive log in / log out enter / leave an account log in to your account sign up to create a new account sign up for a free trial update a newer version install the latest update crash to stop working suddenly The app keeps crashing. freeze to get stuck and stop responding (hang) My laptop froze. back up to save an extra copy back up your photos bandwidth how much data the internet can carry low bandwidth outage a period when a service is down a network outage encrypted turned into a secret code, so it is safe end-to-end encrypted
  • I can't log in to the portal. It says my password has expired. = I'm unable to enter the portal because my password has expired.
  • The app has been crashing since the last update. = The app has kept stopping suddenly since the last update. (With "since" use has been + -ing; without "since": "It keeps crashing.")
  • Please back up your files before you install the update. = Save a copy of your files before updating.
  • The video call keeps breaking up. I think my bandwidth is low. = The call keeps cutting out — probably because my internet is slow.
  • There was a nationwide outage, so payments failed for two hours. = The service was down across the country, and payments didn't work for two hours.

✗

My laptop got hanged.

✓

My laptop froze. / My laptop hung.

hang

hung

froze

stopped responding

✗

I will login and check.

✓

I'll log in and check.

log in

login

your login details

the login page

✗

Please send me the soft copy.

✓

Please send me the file / a PDF.

the file, a digital copy, a printed copy / a printout

docs.title: 39.4 Environment — from pollution to renewables
docs.text:
Environment words appear in essays, the news and interviews. The word-family rule helps most here: pollute (verb), pollution (noun), polluted (adj), pollutant (a substance that causes pollution).

Word Meaning Partner pollution harmful dirt in air, water or soil air / water / noise pollution emissions smoke and gases released into the air cut / reduce emissions carbon footprint the carbon your activities release reduce your carbon footprint renewable never runs out (like sun or wind) renewable energy fossil fuels coal, petrol, gas depend on fossil fuels sustainable able to continue for a long time sustainable development deforestation cutting down forests tackle deforestation biodiversity the variety of living things loss of biodiversity climate change long-term change in the weather tackle / address climate change
  • Every winter, air pollution in Delhi reaches dangerous levels. = Each winter the air in Delhi becomes dangerously polluted.
  • The AQI is over 400 today, so schools are closed. = AQI stands for Air Quality Index. "over" means "more than".
  • India wants to get half its electricity from renewable sources. = Half of the power should come from sun, wind and similar sources.
  • Electric buses could cut the city's emissions significantly. = Electric buses could greatly reduce the city's pollution from vehicles.
  • Growth has to be sustainable, not just fast. = Growth must be able to last, not only be quick.

The sustain family

sustain (v) → sustainable (adj) → sustainability (n) → sustainably (adv) → unsustainable (the opposite). "The current pace of growth is unsustainable" — a strong line for an essay.

✗

The pollution is very much in Delhi.

✓

Pollution is very high in Delhi. / Delhi's air is badly polluted.

high / low

docs.title: 39.5 News and society — economy, elections, policy
docs.text:
Whether you read a newspaper, listen to the news or write an essay, you will meet these words again and again. Learn the verbs of rising and falling with them: rise, fall, grow, drop, remain stable.

Word Meaning Partner economy a country's system of money and trade the economy grew by 7% inflation the rate at which prices rise inflation rose / fell to 5% unemployment the state of having no job high youth unemployment budget the government's plan for income and spending present the budget election voting to choose leaders hold / win an election turnout how many people voted a record turnout policy an official plan or rule announce / introduce a policy survey a set of questions asked to many people conduct a survey · the survey found… subsidy government help that lowers a price a fuel subsidy
  • Inflation fell to four per cent last month. = The rate of price rise dropped to 4% last month. (fell to = reached that level; fell by = dropped by that amount)
  • The government has announced a new policy on electric vehicles. = The government has made a new EV policy public.
  • Voter turnout was the highest in thirty years. = More people voted than in any election in the last thirty years.
  • A recent survey found that 60 per cent of young people want to work abroad. = Survey found that — a fixed opening for essays and reports.
  • The new tax is controversial; small traders strongly oppose it. = People disagree about the new tax — small traders are strongly against it.

✗

Unemployment is an economical problem.

✓

Unemployment is an economic problem.

economic

economical

✗

The survey says 60% people use UPI daily.

✓

The survey found that 60% of people use UPI daily.

of

of

of

found / showed

docs.title: 39.6 Headline English — small words, big meaning
docs.text:
Newspaper headlines have their own grammar: articles are missing, the present simple = something that already happened, to + verb = something in the future, and short, punchy words. Once you understand these, the news becomes much easier.

Headline Full meaning Trick RBI holds rates steady The RBI has kept interest rates unchanged. present = it has happened Govt to launch EV policy The government is going to launch a policy. to = about to happen Floods hit Assam Floods have affected Assam. hit = affected Minister quits A minister has resigned. quit = resign Prices soar Prices have risen sharply. soar = rise very fast Talks fail Negotiations have failed. talks = negotiations
  • RBI holds rates steady as inflation eases. = Prices are rising more slowly, so the RBI did not change interest rates. (ease = become less severe)
  • Govt to boost spending on rural roads. = The government will spend more on village roads. (boost = increase)
  • Heatwave grips north India; schools shut. = Extreme heat has taken hold of north India, and schools are closed. (grip = take a strong hold)

Small headline words

bid = an attempt · curb = limit or control · slam = criticise harshly · probe = investigation · row = a public argument · back = support · axe = cancel or cut. To practise understanding the news, see Real-World English.

docs.title: 39.7 B2–C1 words — one word, three partners
docs.text:
These ten words are useful in meetings, news and essays alike. Learn each one together with its partner and its family; only then will it become part of your own English. (For bigger verbs, also see Verb upgrades and Advanced words.)

Word (level) Meaning Partner · family significant (B2) large enough to matter a significant increase · significantly implement (B2) to put a plan into action implement a plan · implementation allocate (B2) to set aside (money, time) for a purpose allocate funds · allocation mitigate (C1) to make something less harmful mitigate the risk · mitigation unprecedented (C1) never having happened before an unprecedented rise substantial (C1) large and solid a substantial amount · substantially transparent (B2) open and clear, nothing hidden a transparent process · transparency accountable (C1) responsible for your actions hold someone accountable · accountability viable (C1) able to work in practice a viable option · viability scalable (C1) able to be made bigger a scalable solution · scale up
  • We need a backup supplier to mitigate the risk of delays. = A second supplier will reduce the danger of late deliveries.
  • The city has allocated ₹200 crore to clean the river. = The city has set aside ₹200 crore for cleaning the river.
  • Leaders must be held accountable for their promises. = Leaders should be made answerable for what they promised.
  • Solar power is now a viable option for most homes. = Solar power can now realistically work for most homes.
  • The pandemic caused an unprecedented shift to online work. = The pandemic brought a move to online work that had never happened before.

One paragraph — all four topics together

  • At this week's meeting, the key stakeholders agreed to implement the new travel policy. Most meetings will now be online, which should cut emissions and save a substantial amount of money. A staff survey found that 70 per cent of employees support the change. = Office (stakeholders, implement), environment (cut emissions), news (survey found) — and one C1 word (substantial).

docs.title: 39.8 Practice — Work and the world
docs.text:
Exercise 1

We're on track to ___ the deadline.

  • meet
  • do
  • reach
  • make

Hint: The strongest partner of deadline.

Answer

meet

meet / miss / extend a deadline.

Exercise 2

I'll ___ up with the client tomorrow and let you know.

Hint: To check again later — a two-word verb.

Answer

follow

follow up (verb) — follow-up (noun): a follow-up email.

Exercise 3

Tap the wrong word.

My laptop got hanged during the meeting.

Answer

Wrong word: hanged.

Corrected: My laptop froze during the meeting.

For computers use hung / froze. 'Hanged' is only for execution.

Exercise 4

Which one is correct?

  • I'll log in and check.
  • I'll login and check.
  • I'll do login and check.
  • I'll log-in and check.
Answer

I'll log in and check.

The verb is log in (two words). login is the noun: login details.

Exercise 5

Match each word to its meaning.

A B emissions how many people voted renewable government help that lowers a price turnout smoke and gases released into the air subsidy never runs out Answer

emissions — smoke and gases released into the air; renewable — never runs out; turnout — how many people voted; subsidy — government help that lowers a price

emissions, renewable — environment; turnout, subsidy — words from the news.

Exercise 6

One word is wrong.

Unemployment is a serious economical problem.

Answer

Wrong word: economical.

Corrected: Unemployment is a serious economic problem.

economic = of the economy; economical = cheap to run.

Exercise 7

A recent survey found that 60 per cent ___ young people want to work abroad.

Hint: The small word after a percentage.

Answer

of

60 per cent of people, half of the class.

Exercise 8

Headline: 'Govt to launch EV policy'. What does it mean?

  • The government is going to launch it.
  • The government has launched it.
  • The government launched it last year.
  • The government refused to launch it.
Answer

The government is going to launch it.

In a headline, 'to + verb' = the future.

Exercise 9

Electric buses could ___ the city's emissions.

  • cut
  • do
  • make
  • low
Answer

cut

cut / reduce emissions — a fixed partner.

Exercise 10

What happened to inflation?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Here is the business news. Inflation fell to four point two per cent in September, the lowest level this year. Economists say lower food prices were the main reason. The central bank is expected to keep interest rates unchanged next week.

  • It fell
  • It rose
  • It stayed the same
  • It doubled
Answer

It fell

'Inflation fell to four point two per cent' — it dropped to 4.2%.

Exercise 11

According to economists, what was the main reason?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Here is the business news. Inflation fell to four point two per cent in September, the lowest level this year. Economists say lower food prices were the main reason. The central bank is expected to keep interest rates unchanged next week.

  • Lower food prices
  • Higher interest rates
  • Cheaper petrol
  • A new tax
Answer

Lower food prices

'lower food prices were the main reason' — food became cheaper.

Exercise 12

Who will send the minutes?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Okay, let's wrap up. Priya will send the minutes by this evening. Arjun, can you follow up with the client about the budget? And just a reminder, the deadline for the first draft is Thursday.

  • Priya
  • Arjun
  • The client
  • Nobody
Answer

Priya

'Priya will send the minutes by this evening.'

Exercise 13

When is the deadline for the first draft?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Okay, let's wrap up. Priya will send the minutes by this evening. Arjun, can you follow up with the client about the budget? And just a reminder, the deadline for the first draft is Thursday.

  • Thursday
  • This evening
  • Tuesday
  • Next week
Answer

Thursday

'the deadline for the first draft is Thursday.'

Exercise 14

Listen and write.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

The server crashed last night, so please back up your files.

crash = to stop working suddenly; back up (verb) is two words.

Exercise 15

What does 'mitigate the risk' mean?

  • make the danger less harmful
  • make the danger bigger
  • ignore the danger
  • measure the danger
Answer

make the danger less harmful

mitigate (C1) = to make less harmful; noun: mitigation.

Exercise 16

Put the words in order.

Words: very / Pollution / Delhi / winter / in / high / is / this

Answer

Pollution is very high in Delhi this winter

Pollution is 'high', not 'very much'.

Exercise 17

Say this line in a meeting.

Answer

Say: Could we extend the deadline to Friday

extend a deadline — with a polite 'Could we…?'.

What to read next

Use these words in your writing: Essays and Reports has the full structure, and CV and LinkedIn has action verbs for the office. For everyday words, see Everyday topics.

docs.title: Chapter 10: Verbs
docs.text:
Verb — the heart of the sentence

A verb is a word that shows an action, an occurrence or a state. If you could fix only one thing in all of English grammar, fix the verb — because tense, voice, agreement and making questions all depend on it. This chapter is a little long, but after it many other chapters will start to feel easy.

In one line

A verb shows an action, a state, an occurrence or possession. A verb can show something being done (action), a condition (state), something that happens (occurrence), or having something (possession). Without a verb, a sentence is not complete.

  • She writes a letter. Action — something is being done: she writes a letter.
  • He is happy. State — no action, just a condition: he feels happy.
  • It rained yesterday. Occurrence — something happened, nobody did it: there was rain yesterday.
  • They have a car. Possession — someone owns something: the car belongs to them.

docs.title: 10.1 Types of verb — the whole tree
docs.text:
Verbs can be divided in several ways, and these divisions overlap. One verb can be a "main verb", "transitive" and "irregular" all at once — like write. So don't think of the tree as a competition; think of it as four separate questions.

Figure 10.1. Look at a verb through four questions, not one split. Each question gives you different information.

docs.title: 10.2 Main verb and helping verb
docs.text:
In a sentence, the real meaning comes from the main verb. The small verbs that come with it — is, am, are, has, have, will, do — help to make tenses, questions and negatives. These are called auxiliary or helping verbs.

  • She is writing a letter. "writing" is the real action; "is" only shows that it is happening right now.
  • Do you know him? "Do" comes first to make the question; the meaning is in "know".
Helping verb Forms Job be is, am, are, was, were, been, being making continuous and passive have have, has, had making perfect tenses do do, does, did questions, negatives and emphasis

All three can also be main verbs

I have a bike. — here "have" is the main verb itself. I have finished my work. — here "have" is the helper and "finished" is the main verb. Check whether another verb follows — that decides which one it is.

docs.title: 10.3 Modal verbs — the ones that never change
docs.text:
Modals are helping verbs that show possibility, ability, permission or obligation. They have two fixed rules, and remembering both is enough.

The two fixed rules for modals

1. After a modal, the verb is always in its base form — no -s, no -ing, no to. 2. A modal never changes itself — no -s, no -ed. ✓ She can swim. ✗ She cans swim. ✗ She can swims.

Modal What it shows Example can ability, general permission I can drive. could past ability, politeness Could you help me? may formal permission, possibility May I come in? might weaker possibility It might rain today. will future, promise I will call you. would politeness, imagination I would like tea. shall suggestion (formal) Shall we start? should advice You should rest. must strong obligation You must wear a helmet. ought to moral duty We ought to help them.

can and could — the difference when asking permission

Can I borrow your pen? — fine among friends. Could I borrow your pen? — more polite, good with someone senior. May I borrow your pen? — the most formal, for an office or an interview.

docs.title: 10.4 Transitive and intransitive — does it take an object?
docs.text:
After the verb, ask "what?" or "whom?". If you get an answer, the verb is transitive. If the question makes no sense, the verb is intransitive.

Verb Question Answer Type She wrote a poem. Wrote what? a poem ✓ Transitive He slept early. Slept what? no answer ✗ Intransitive They helped us. Helped whom? us ✓ Transitive The baby laughed. Laughed what? no answer ✗ Intransitive

Many verbs can be both

The bell rang. (intransitive) / She rang the bell. (transitive) The window broke. / He broke the window. So look at the verb inside the sentence, not in a list.

An intransitive verb needs a preposition

  • Wrong: We will reach at Delhi at 9.
  • Right: We will reach Delhi at 9.

  • Why: "Reach" is transitive — it takes its object directly. But "arrive" is intransitive, so it needs a preposition: arrive in Delhi, arrive at the airport.

  • Wrong: Let us discuss about the plan.

  • Right: Let us discuss the plan.
  • Why: "Discuss" is transitive, so the object follows directly. Hindi has "ke baare me" (about), which is why "about" sneaks in. In the same way: enter the room (not enter into), marry her (not marry with her).

docs.title: 10.5 Linking verbs — verbs that build a bridge
docs.text:
A linking verb shows no action. It connects the subject to its identity or condition — like a bridge.

Figure 10.2. With a linking verb, both ends are the same thing; with an action verb, the action leaves the subject and lands on the object. Linking verb Example Note be (is, am, are, was, were) He is busy. the most common seem, appear She seems tired. it looks that way become, get, turn, grow The sky turned dark. change feel, look, smell, sound, taste This tastes sweet. the senses remain, stay He remained calm. staying the same

After a linking verb, use an adjective, not an adverb

✓ The food tastes good. ✗ The food tastes well. ✓ She looks beautiful. ✗ She looks beautifully. These verbs describe the subject, not an action. The subject is a noun, and a noun needs an adjective.

docs.title: 10.6 The five forms of a verb
docs.text:
Every English verb has five forms. Dictionaries usually list three — V1, V2, V3 — and these three are what you use to build tenses.

Form Name walk (regular) write (irregular) Where it is used V1 base walk write present, after a modal, with to V1-s third person walks writes with he / she / it V2 past simple walked wrote simple past V3 past participle walked written after have/has/had, in the passive V-ing present participle walking writing continuous tenses

The difference between regular and irregular

Regular: V2 and V3 both just add -ed — play → played → played. Irregular: the word changes inside — go → went → gone. English has about 200 irregular verbs, but 60-70 are enough for everyday use.

docs.title: Irregular verbs you use every day
docs.text:
V1 V2 V3 V1 V2 V3 go went gone eat ate eaten see saw seen take took taken do did done give gave given come came come run ran run buy bought bought bring brought brought think thought thought teach taught taught speak spoke spoken break broke broken write wrote written drive drove driven begin began begun drink drank drunk put put put cut cut cut

Mixing up V2 and V3

  • Wrong: I have saw that movie.
  • Right: I have seen that movie.

  • Why: After "have / has / had" you always need V3 — seen, gone, done, written. V2 (saw) is only for the past on its own: I saw that movie.

  • Wrong: He did not went to school.

  • Right: He did not go to school.
  • Why: "did" has already shown the past — so the main verb stays in its base form. We don't show the past twice in one sentence.

docs.title: 10.7 Finite and non-finite verbs
docs.text:
A finite verb changes with the subject and the tense — it is the real verb of the sentence. A non-finite verb doesn't change; it works like a noun or an adjective.

Type Form Example Job Finite changes with subject + tense She plays. / They played. the real verb Infinitive to + V1 I want to sleep. works like a noun Gerund V-ing, used as a noun Swimming is good exercise. works like a noun Participle V-ing or V3, used as an adjective a broken glass / a running train works like an adjective

Only one finite verb per clause

I want to go home. — "want" is finite, "to go" is non-finite. So the tense goes only on "want": I wanted to go home. You never say "to goed" — now you can see why.

After a preposition, use a gerund, not an infinitive

✓ She is good at singing. ✗ good at to sing ✓ I look forward to meeting you. ✗ to meet you Here "to" is a preposition, not part of an infinitive — so use -ing.

docs.title: 10.8 Stative verbs — the ones that don't go in the continuous
docs.text:
Some verbs show a state, not an action. A state doesn't "go on" — it just is — so we don't put these verbs into -ing.

Category Verbs Thinking know, think (meaning "believe"), believe, understand, remember, forget, mean Feelings like, love, hate, want, need, prefer Senses see, hear, smell, taste (meaning "have a flavour") Ownership have (meaning "own"), own, belong, possess Being be, seem, appear, cost, weigh, contain

docs.title: 10.9 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
The most common Indian-English mistakes with verbs

  • Wrong: I am having a car.
  • Right: I have a car.

  • Why: When "have" means ownership, it is a stative verb — it doesn't go in the continuous. "I am having" is fine only when an action is happening: I am having lunch, I am having a bath.

  • Wrong: He don't know the answer.

  • Right: He doesn't know the answer.

  • Why: He / she / it are third person singular, and their helping verb is "does". And notice — after "does" the main verb stays in the base form: doesn't know, not doesn't knows.

  • Wrong: I am agree with you.

  • Right: I agree with you.

  • Why: "Agree" is a complete verb on its own — it doesn't need "am" before it. The Hindi "main sehmat hoon" has "hoon" (am) in it, which is why "am" sneaks in.

  • Wrong: She is knowing the answer.

  • Right: She knows the answer.

  • Why: "Know" is stative — knowing is a state, not an action. That is why "I am knowing", "I am understanding" and "I am liking" are all wrong.

  • Wrong: We discussed about the project yesterday.

  • Right: We discussed the project yesterday.

  • Why: "Discuss" is transitive — it takes its object directly, with no preposition. Same list: enter the hall, attend the meeting, answer the question, reach home.

  • Wrong: One of my friend don't like coffee.

  • Right: One of my friends doesn't like coffee.

  • Why: Two mistakes at once: after "one of" you need a plural noun (friends), but the real subject is "one" — singular — so the verb is singular too: doesn't.

  • Wrong: Please revert back to me soon.

  • Right: Please reply to me soon.

  • Why: "Revert" means to go back to an earlier state, not to reply. And "back" repeats the idea. In an office email, write "please reply" or "please get back to me".

  • Wrong: He can plays the guitar very well.

  • Right: He can play the guitar very well.
  • Why: After a modal the verb is always in the base form. The modal has already taken care of the job, so the verb needs no -s.

docs.title: 10.10 A short memory map
docs.text: After this Verb form Example he / she / it (present) V1 + s She goes. do / does / did V1 She didn't go. modal (can, will, must…) V1 She can go. have / has / had V3 She has gone. is / am / are / was / were V-ing (or V3 in the passive) She is going. to V1 She wants to go. preposition (at, of, in, for…) V-ing She is tired of waiting.

docs.title: 10.11 Practice — Verbs
docs.text:
Exercise 1

She ___ the answer to this question.

  • knows
  • is knowing
  • knowing
  • are knowing

Hint: Is this verb stative or an action?

Answer

knows

'Know' is a stative verb — knowing is a state, not an ongoing action. So we don't use it in the continuous, even when we mean right now.

Exercise 2

He ___ live in Mumbai anymore.

  • doesn't
  • don't
  • isn't
  • didn't

Hint: The negative for third person singular.

Answer

doesn't

'He' is third person singular, so the helping verb is 'does'. 'don't' goes only with I, you, we, they.

Exercise 3

I have ___ that film twice already.

  • seen
  • saw
  • see
  • seeing

Hint: Which form comes after 'have'?

Answer

seen

After have / has / had you always use V3 (the past participle) — seen. 'saw' is V2, which is for the plain past on its own: I saw that film.

Exercise 4

Which sentence is correct?

  • She can play the sitar.
  • She can plays the sitar.
  • She cans play the sitar.
  • She can to play the sitar.
Answer

She can play the sitar.

After a modal the verb is in its base form, and the modal itself never changes. So not 'cans', not 'plays', not 'to play'.

Exercise 5

'The soup tastes ___.' — what fills the gap?

  • delicious
  • deliciously
  • deliciousness
  • tastily

Hint: 'taste' is a linking verb here.

Answer

delicious

After a linking verb you use an adjective, because it describes the subject — what the soup is like. An adverb would be used only to describe how an action is done.

Exercise 6

I am looking forward to ___ you next week. (meet)

Hint: 'to' here is a preposition, not an infinitive.

Answer

meeting

In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, and after a preposition we use a gerund (-ing). That is why 'to meet' is wrong here.

Exercise 7

He did not ___ to the office yesterday. (go)

Hint: 'did' has already shown the past.

Answer

go

After 'did' the verb stays in the base form, because the past is already in 'did'. We don't show the past twice in one sentence.

Exercise 8

Tap the wrong word in this sentence.

I am having two brothers and one sister.

Answer

Wrong word: having.

Corrected: I have two brothers and one sister.

When 'have' means a relationship or ownership, it is stative — it doesn't go in the continuous. 'I am having' works only for actions like eating or drinking.

Exercise 9

Find the wrong word.

We discussed about the new policy in the meeting.

Answer

Wrong word: about.

Corrected: We discussed the new policy in the meeting.

'Discuss' is a transitive verb — it takes its object directly. 'about' comes in from the Hindi 'ke baare me', but in English it is extra.

Exercise 10

'It rained heavily last night.' — what is the verb showing here?

  • occurrence
  • possession
  • state
  • action

Hint: Nobody did anything; it just happened.

Answer

occurrence

Rain isn't something anyone does; it is an event — so it is an occurrence. 'She writes' would be an action, 'He is happy' a state, and 'They have a car' possession.

Exercise 11

Match each sentence with what its verb shows.

A B She writes a letter. occurrence He is happy. possession It rained yesterday. action They have a car. state Answer

She writes a letter. — action; He is happy. — state; It rained yesterday. — occurrence; They have a car. — possession

A verb shows one of four things — an action, a state, an occurrence, or possession.

Exercise 12

We ___ a big house in the village. (possession, present)

Hint: Someone owns something.

Answer

have

For possession use 'have / has' — We have, She has. 'have' meaning possession is stative, so we don't say 'We are having a house'.

Exercise 13

Match each verb form with where it is used.

A B after have / has V-ing — going, writing after a modal V1 + s — goes, writes after is / am / are V3 — gone, written with he / she in the present V1 — go, write Answer

after have / has — V3 — gone, written; after a modal — V1 — go, write; after is / am / are — V-ing — going, writing; with he / she in the present — V1 + s — goes, writes

The form of a verb is decided by the word before it. Once you remember these four pairs, half the work of tenses is done.

Exercise 14

Put the words in the right order — it uses a modal.

Words: wear / must / helmet / riding / while / You / a

Answer

You must wear a helmet while riding

The order is subject + modal + V1 + the rest. After 'must', 'wear' stays in the base form — never 'wears'.

Exercise 15

Say this line aloud — say 'doesn't' in one breath.

Answer

Say: He doesn't know the answer

If we say 'does not' as two separate words, the habit of 'he don't' doesn't go away. Saying 'doesn't' as a single word brings out the right form automatically.

What to do next

Take five irregular verbs every day and say all three forms out loud — go went gone, see saw seen. In two weeks the whole list will be on your tongue, and you will already know half of the tenses chapter.

docs.title: Chapter 36: Word formation
docs.text:
One word, ten words — the magic of prefixes and suffixes

The cheapest way to grow your vocabulary is not memorising new words — it is spotting the relatives of the words you already know. Do you know happy? Then you also know unhappy, happiness, happily, unhappiness — you just did not realise it. Pieces added at the start (prefixes) change the meaning, and pieces added at the end (suffixes) change the job of the word. After this chapter, every long new word will look like a set of small pieces.

docs.title: 36.1 One root, a whole family — word family
docs.text:
Learning a word together with its family has two benefits: you get four words for the effort of one, and it becomes easy to pick the right form in a sentence. Mistakes like "He spoke happy" or "Her happy was clear" stop right here.

Figure 36.1. Going up (un-) = the opposite meaning. Going left or right (-ness, -ly) = the same meaning, a new job. The colour shows whether the word is a noun, an adjective or an adverb.
  • She looks happy. She smiled happily. Her happiness was clear. One root, three jobs: how she looks (adjective), how she smiled (adverb), what we could see (noun).

Two kinds of pieces

A prefix (at the start) changes the meaning of a word: happy → unhappy. A suffix (at the end) changes the job of a word: happy (adj) → happiness (noun) → happily (adverb).

docs.title: 36.2 Prefixes — add at the start, change the meaning
docs.text:
Seven prefixes are so common that hundreds of everyday English words are built from them. Once you remember what they mean, you can guess unknown words too — misread = to read wrongly.

Prefix Meaning Examples un- not / opposite unhappy · unfair · unlock dis- not / opposite dislike · disagree · disconnect im- / in- not impossible · incorrect · invisible re- again / back redo · rewrite · return mis- wrongly misunderstand · misspell · mislead pre- before preview · prepaid · preheat over- too much overeat · overload · overconfident
  • I think you misunderstood me. Let me rephrase that. = You understood me wrongly. I will say it again in different words.
  • Don't overcook the rice, and please preheat the oven. = Do not cook the rice too long, and heat the oven first.

A prefix never changes the spelling

A prefix is simply stuck on the front — the spelling of the root stays the same. That is why two identical letters sometimes meet: un + necessary = unnecessary, mis + spell = misspell, dis + satisfied = dissatisfied.

docs.title: 36.3 Which "not" — un, dis, in, im, il, ir
docs.text:
There are six prefixes that mean "not", and they cause the most confusion — "unpossible", "unregular". The good news: half of them follow a firm rule, and that rule only looks at the first letter of the root.

Figure 36.2. The top three rules exist to make speaking easier — say in-possible and your tongue will turn it into im-possible by itself.

The first-letter rule

p, m, b → im- (impossible) · l → il- (illegal) · r → ir- (irregular). There is no rule for un- / dis- / in- — learn them as pairs with each word. If in doubt, check a dictionary — a word like "unpossible" does not exist.

docs.title: 36.4 Suffixes that make nouns — -tion, -ment, -ness
docs.text:
Formal English, emails and reports are full of nouns — "We made a decision" instead of "We decided". Three suffixes make most nouns: the name of an action (-tion, -ment) and the name of a quality (-ness).

Word → noun Suffix Example inform → information -tion Thanks for the information. educate → education -tion Education changes lives. decide → decision -sion It was a hard decision. develop → development -ment The city needs development. agree → agreement -ment We signed an agreement. pay → payment -ment The payment is due today. kind → kindness -ness Thank you for your kindness. happy → happiness -ness Money can't buy happiness.

Name of an action, name of a quality

Verb + -tion / -ment = noun (inform → information, agree → agreement). Adjective + -ness = noun (kind → kindness). A final y becomes i before -ness: happy → happiness. Also, a silent final "e" often drops: educate → education, decide → decision.

docs.title: 36.5 Adjectives and adverbs — -ful, -less, -able, -ly
docs.text:
These four suffixes are the heart of description. One noun can give two opposite adjectives (-ful and -less), and if you add -ly to them, they can describe a verb.

Figure 36.3. One root, four words. The top path means with attention , the bottom path means without attention . Suffix Meaning Examples -ful full of careful · useful · hopeful -less without careless · useless · hopeless -able can be done readable · washable · comfortable -ly adjective → adverb quickly · carefully · happily

One l, two l's

-ful always has only one l: careful, useful, beautiful — never "carefull". But when you add -ly, two l's appear: careful + ly = carefully. Watch out: friendly, lovely, lonely end in -ly but they are adjectives — "a friendly person".

docs.title: 36.6 -ize and some old roots
docs.text:
-ize turns a noun or an adjective into an action (a verb) — you see it everywhere in office English. Many long words are also built from old Latin roots; once you recognise one root, a whole bunch of words makes sense.

Word + -ize = verb Example modern modernize We need to modernize the office. real realize I didn't realize it was so late. summary summarize Can you summarize the report? priority prioritize Let's prioritize the urgent tasks. apology apologize I apologize for the delay.

The British spelling -ise (realise, apologise) is also perfectly correct, and both are used in India. Just keep to one style in a document.

Figure 36.4. One root, six words. The prefix gave the direction (im = in, ex = out, re = back), the root gave the action (carry). Root Meaning Words port carry transport · export · portable dict say predict · dictionary · contradict spect look carefully inspect · respect · spectator vis / vid see visible · vision · video scrib / script write describe · script · subscribe

Long word? Break it up

Prefix + root + suffix: in-spect-ion = the act of looking inside (a check); pre-dict-able = can be said in advance. Break an unknown word into pieces — half of the meaning will appear by itself.

docs.title: 36.7 Six families — in one table
docs.text:
These are the families whose forms are most often used wrongly. Read each line aloud from left to right — you will learn four words in one go.

Verb Noun Adjective Adverb decide decision decisive decisively succeed success successful successfully create creation creative creatively care care careful carefully differ difference different differently attract attraction attractive attractively
  • She succeeded because she worked carefully. Her success was no accident. Three family members, three jobs — the adverb goes with the verb, the noun stands alone.

The notebook habit

When you write down a new word, write its whole family next to it — verb, noun, adjective, adverb. A box that stays empty (like a common adverb for "differ") is useful information too.

docs.title: 36.8 The mistakes we really make
docs.text:
These mistakes happen because we choose the right root but the wrong form — a verb instead of a noun, an adjective instead of an adverb, or the wrong "not" prefix.

Common word-formation mistakes

  • Wrong: This is unpossible.
  • Right: This is impossible.

  • Why: "possible" starts with p → im-. In the same way unregular → irregular, unlegal → illegal.

  • Wrong: Her behave in the meeting was rude.

  • Right: Her behaviour in the meeting was rude.

  • Why: A noun is needed after "Her ___ was". behave = verb, behaviour (US: behavior) = noun.
